Two standard fixes:

Bonferroni (after Carlo Bonferroni): divide \(\alpha\) by the number of tests, so for \(20\) tests call a result significant only if \(p<0.05/20=0.0025\). Why it works: each test now fires by luck with chance at most \(0.0025\), so the chance that any of the \(20\) fires is at most \(20\times0.0025=5\%\) (\(1-0.9975^{20}=4.9\%\) for independent tests), back from \(64\%\).
An omnibus test (for reference: this chapter does not work one) is one test across all the models and datasets at once (one test at \(\alpha\) for all the models, so luck gets one chance rather than one per pair), such as the Friedman test (a rank-based test across several models), followed by pairwise comparisons run only after it finds some difference. These are called post-hoc tests, but they are planned before any result is seen, unlike the after-the-fact choice of test that §8.2 warns against; Demšar (2006) recommends this design.

Report the protocol. State the number of seeds or folds, the test (paired \(t\) or Wilcoxon) and \(\alpha\); mark wins with, for example, \(^{*}p<0.05\), \(^{**}p<0.01\). This is what a careful reader will ask for: a few seeds plus a paired test that comes out significant turns “our number is bigger” into “our number is reliably bigger across seeds.”

In practice. When comparing two recommender models:

Pair runs on the same seeds (or folds, remembering the caution above that a \(t\)-test over folds is optimistic) whenever both models can be scored on the same units: pairing cancels each unit’s shared difficulty, though it spends degrees of freedom (§8.2).
Use a paired \(t\)-test when the per-pair differences look roughly normal; switch to the Wilcoxon signed-rank test when they are heavy-tailed or have an outlier (the pair-count floor is in §8.6, Step 2).
Default to two-sided unless you pre-registered (wrote down before running anything) a directional (one-sided) hypothesis: on §8.4’s seeds that halves \(p\) from \(0.00086\) to \(0.00043\) (§8.6, Step 1).
When you test many variants or datasets at once, correct for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni: divide \(\alpha\) by the number of tests; or Holm’s stepwise refinement, §8.6, Step 3).
Always report an effect size and a 95% confidence interval alongside \(p\) — a tiny gain can be “significant” with enough seeds yet matter nothing in deployment.

The Evaluation Metrics chapter’s “evaluate honestly” section builds directly on this protocol.



8.6 The recipe — a runnable significance-test checklist
The prose above scatters the moving parts; here they are as one ordered procedure you can run top to bottom on a real A-vs-B comparison. Each step is a decision; the answer routes the next one.
Step 0 — fix the pairing unit, and pair on it. Decide what each pair is — one seed, one cross-validation fold, or one test user (per-user scores) — and evaluate both models on the same units, so \(d_i=A_i-B_i\) cancels that unit’s shared difficulty (§8.2). Score both models on every one of the \(n\) units: a unit missing for either model cannot be paired, so it drops out. (Seeds are the usual unit in recommender-system ablation studies, experiments that remove one component of a model at a time to measure what it contributes: model A the full model, model B the same model without that component, so on §8.4’s seeds \(\bar d=8\) would be what the component adds. The worked example below uses \(n=5\) seeds.)
Step 1 — choose sidedness, before looking at the data. Two-sided (“A differs from B”) is the default and the safe choice. Use one-sided (“A is better than B”) only if you pre-registered that direction — it halves the \(p\)-value when the result goes the pre-registered way (our example: two-sided \(p=0.00086\) vs one-sided \(0.00043\)) and gives a \(p\) near \(1\) when it goes the other way, so claiming it post hoc, after seeing A win, is a classic way to manufacture significance.
Step 2 — pick the test from the shape of the differences \(d_i\). Look at the \(n\) values \(d_i\) (not the raw scores):

roughly symmetric / bell-ish \(\to\) paired \(t\)-test (§8.3). With only a handful of pairs you cannot really check normality, so the \(t\)-test is used by convention for a few roughly symmetric \(d_i\) with no outlier (a working rule from practice, not a guarantee, not tested here).
visibly heavy-tailed, or with a wild outlier \(\to\) Wilcoxon signed-rank (it ranks the \(d_i\), so one freak seed can’t dominate). But mind the floor: with all \(d_i\) the same sign the smallest two-sided \(p\) Wilcoxon can return is \(2/2^{n}\), so it needs \(n\ge 6\) to even reach \(p<0.05\) (\(2/2^{5}=0.0625\) at \(n{=}5\); \(2/2^{6}=0.03125\) at \(n{=}6\) — verified below). Why \(2/2^{n}\)? If A and B were equally good, each difference would be \(+\) or \(-\) with probability \(\tfrac12\), independently — like \(n\) fair coin flips — so “all positive” has probability \((\tfrac12)^{n}\) (§1: independent chances multiply); a two-sided test also counts “all negative”, so the most extreme result possible has \(p=2\times(\tfrac12)^{n}=2/2^{n}\). Below that floor, collect more pairs (the \(t\)-test is all that is left; report that an outlier makes it unreliable).

The choice, as three questions in order:

Do the \(d_i\) show heavy tails or an outlier? If not (symmetric, bell-ish), use the paired \(t\)-test (§8.3) and go on to the \(p\)-value.
If they do, are there enough pairs for Wilcoxon to reach \(p<0.05\), the floor above (\(2/2^{n}\))? If so, use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
If there are not enough, it cannot reach \(p<0.05\): get more pairs, as said above.

Either way the \(p\)-value comes from whichever test you ran, and Step 3 (multiplicity) and Step 4 (effect size and CI) follow.
Step 3 — correct for multiplicity if you ran more than one test. Comparing A against \(m\) baselines, or across \(m\) datasets, runs \(m\) tests, and each carries its own \(\alpha\) chance of a false positive — so the chance that at least one fires by luck balloons. With \(m=3\) independent tests at \(\alpha=0.05\) and no real differences, the chance that none fires is \(0.95^{3}\) (§1: independent chances multiply), so the chance that at least one does is \(1-0.95^{3}\approx0.14\); with \(m=20\) it is \(1-0.95^{20}\approx0.64\).
Divide the bar: Bonferroni uses \(\alpha/m\) (compare each \(p\) to \(0.05/m\)). Holm is a stepwise version: sort the \(m\) \(p\)-values from smallest to largest; compare the smallest with \(\alpha/m\), the next with \(\alpha/(m-1)\), and so on up to the largest with \(\alpha/1\); stop at the first one that fails — it and every larger \(p\) are not significant. For \(p=0.012,\,0.020,\,0.024\) and \(m=3\), Bonferroni’s bar \(0.0167\) keeps only \(0.012\), while Holm’s bars \(0.0167,\,0.025,\,0.05\) keep all three (§8.7, Case 3, runs one where the two agree).
Holm is never more conservative, because its first bar is Bonferroni’s \(\alpha/m\) and every later bar is larger; and it keeps the same guarantee: with no real differences, the chance that any test fires stays at most \(\alpha\). A single pre-planned A-vs-B comparison needs no correction.
Step 4 — report the effect size with its CI, never \(p\) alone. Quote \(\bar d\) (the mean gain) and its 95% CI \(\bar d \pm t^{*}s_d/\sqrt n\) beside \(p\). The CI says both how big and how sure; it is significant at \(\alpha=0.05\) exactly when it excludes \(0\) (a \(99\%\) interval goes with \(\alpha=0.01\)) — the same verdict as the \(t\)-test (a rank test can differ: in §8.7’s Case 2 the \(t\)-interval is \([-4.2,\,19.2]\), which includes \(0\), while Wilcoxon gives \(p=0.031\)), but its width also shows how small the true gain could be: an interval like \([0.1,\,0.3]\) milli-NDCG@10 excludes \(0\) yet allows a gain of only \(0.1\), whereas §8.5’s \([5.5,\,10.5]\) keeps even its smallest plausible gain at \(5.5\).
The recipe on the worked example, end to end (the same five seeds, \(d=[7,9,7,11,6]\)):

Unit = seed, \(n=5\) (Step 0). Two-sided, pre-chosen (Step 1). The \(d_i\) show no outlier or heavy tail, so paired \(t\)-test (Step 2): \(t=8.94\), \(df=4\), \(p\approx 0.00086<0.05\) \(\to\) reject \(H_0\). A single comparison, so no multiplicity correction (Step 3). Report (Step 4): \(\bar d=+8\) milli-NDCG@10, 95% CI \([5.5,\,10.5]\) (excludes \(0\) ✓), \(p<0.001\). Cross-check: Wilcoxon on these five gives \(p=0.0625\) — it cannot beat its \(n{=}5\) floor (Step 2).

The same recipe as one runnable listing:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
A = np.array([409,410,412,410,410])      # model A, milli-NDCG@10
B = np.array([402,401,405,399,404])      # model B, same 5 seeds
d = A - B                                # paired differences (Step 0)
n = len(d); dbar = d.mean(); sd = d.std(ddof=1)
t = dbar / (sd/np.sqrt(n)); df = n - 1
p_two = 2*stats.t.sf(abs(t), df)         # two-sided p   (Step 1)
tstar = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df)           # 95% CI multiplier, df=4
ci = (dbar - tstar*sd/np.sqrt(n), dbar + tstar*sd/np.sqrt(n))
print(round(t,2), df, round(p_two,5))    # -> 8.94 4 0.00086   (Step 2)
print(round(dbar,1), [float(round(c,1)) for c in ci])   # -> 8.0 [5.5, 10.5]  (Step 4)
print(round(stats.wilcoxon(d,method="exact").pvalue,4))  # -> 0.0625  (floor at n=5)
print([2/2**k for k in (5,6)])           # -> [0.0625, 0.03125]  (why n>=6)


8.7 Three worked cases that flip the verdict
A significance test earns its place when it can change a decision. Here are three short cases, each in the milli-NDCG@10 units of §8.4; \(d_i\) is again A’s per-seed score minus B’s, so a positive \(d_i\) means A won that seed.
Case 1 — a positive headline the data cannot back. Five seeds give \(d=[7,-2,9,-5,1]\). The mean gain is \(\bar d=+2.0\) — positive, so the headline says A wins. But the seeds disagree in sign (A won three, lost two), so the spread is large: \(s_d=5.916\), \(\text{SE}=5.916/\sqrt5=2.646\), hence \(t=2.0/2.646=0.76\) on \(4\) df, \(p=0.49\), and the \(95\%\) CI is \(2.0\pm2.776(2.646)=[-5.3,\,+9.3]\) — it straddles \(0\). Verdict: do not claim A is better. The lesson §8.4’s clean win could not teach: what decides is the mean relative to its wobble, the standard error (\(0.89\) there, \(2.65\) here), never the headline mean alone (\(+8\) there, \(+2\) here).
Case 2 — when the \(t\)-test is fooled, rank instead (Wilcoxon by hand). Six seeds: \(d=[2,3,1,4,5,30]\) — five small consistent wins and one outlier.

The \(t\)-test chokes. The \(30\) inflates \(s_d\) to \(11.11\), so \(\mathrm{SE}=11.11/\sqrt6=4.54\) and \(t=7.5/4.54=1.65\) on \(5\) df, \(p=0.16\) — “not significant,” even though every seed favored A (with \(6\) seeds, df \(=5\) and \(t^{*}=2.571\), so the \(95\%\) CI is \(7.5\pm2.571(4.54)=[-4.2,\,19.2]\), which includes \(0\)).
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test throws away magnitudes and keeps only signs and ranks. Rank the \(|d_i|\): \(\{1,2,3,4,5,30\}\to\) ranks \(1,2,3,4,5,6\). Sum the ranks of the negative differences — there are none — so \(W^{-}=0\) (and \(W^{+}=21\)); the statistic is \(W=\min(W^{+},W^{-})=0\).
Its \(p\)-value. With all \(n=6\) signs agreeing, the two-sided \(p\) hits its floor \(2/2^{6}=0.031<0.05\) — significant. Why \(2/64\): if A and B were equal, each of the \(2^{6}=64\) patterns of signs is equally likely (the coin-flip argument of Step 2), and only two of them, all \(+\) and all \(-\), give \(W=0\). One step less extreme — \(W=1\), only the smallest difference having the minority sign — adds two more patterns (that sign negative, or positive), so \(4\) of the \(64\) are at least that extreme and \(p=4/64=0.0625\), above \(0.05\). Counting wins (§8.1’s game) would give the same \(2/64\) for six wins of six; ranks pay off when there is a loss: with one small loss (\(W=1\)) Wilcoxon gives \(4/64=0.0625\), while five wins of six by counting gives \(14/64=0.22\).
Verdict. Same data, opposite verdict: the rank test shrugged off the outlier that wrecked the \(t\)-test (the “outlier” branch of the §8.6 recipe).

Case 3 — test enough models and one wins by luck (multiplicity). You compare \(m=3\) candidates against the baseline and get \(p=\{0.012,\,0.030,\,0.045\}\). Uncorrected, all three clear \(0.05\) — three “wins.” But three tests give three shots at a false positive. Bonferroni divides the bar: compare each \(p\) to \(\alpha/m=0.05/3=0.0167\). Now only \(0.012\) survives. (Holm — the sorted \(p\)-values against \(\alpha/3=0.0167\), \(\alpha/2=0.025\) and \(\alpha/1=0.05\) — agrees: \(0.012<0.0167\) passes, then \(0.030>0.025\) fails, and Holm stops there.) After correction, the evidence for models 2 and 3 is no longer strong enough to claim a win. They may still be real improvements — but three tests gave luck three chances, so these data cannot tell them apart from luck. The figure Multiple comparisons can manufacture false wins below draws the three \(p\)-values against both bars.






Figure 3.23: Multiple comparisons can manufacture false wins. Three models tested against one baseline give raw \(p\)-values \(0.012,0.030,0.045\) — all under the uncorrected \(0.05\) line (dashed), so all three look like wins. Dividing the bar by the number of tests (Bonferroni: solid line at \(0.05/3=0.0167\)) leaves only model 1 significant; models 2 and 3 fall in the gap between the lines — the zone where luck alone could have produced the “win”. The more models you try, the likelier luck alone supplies a “win” (at least one: \(5\%\), \(14\%\), \(64\%\) at \(m=1,3,20\), §8.5).




The through-line. In all three cases the headline number, the wrong test, or an uncorrected \(p\) gave a verdict the evidence did not support: a positive mean we could not tell apart from noise, a “non-significant” \(t\) the rank test overturned, three “wins” of which only one survives correction. That is why significance testing, not the headline number, is what turns a result into a finding. For per-user scores far from a bell, the bootstrap CI needs no bell-shape assumption: it re-draws the test users at random with replacement (one user may be drawn twice), recomputes the score each time, and reads the interval off those scores. A redraw of four users scoring \(0.2,\,0.4,\,0.6,\,0.8\) might be \(0.4,\,0.4,\,0.8,\,0.2\) (mean \(0.45\) against \(0.5\)); thousands of redraws give a spread of means, and the middle \(95\%\) is the interval. Evaluation Metrics §11d works it.

text:
9. Exercises
Twelve by-hand problems spanning §1–§8. Each is (compute) — a number to crank, (concept) — a why-question to reason out, (extend) — push an idea one step past the text, or (apply) — use it as the book will. They follow the sections in order, §1 first and §8 last. Each problem is self-contained except E7(c), which builds on E5, and E10, which builds on E9; they reuse this chapter’s own setups (the coin, softmax scores, paired seeds), most with fresh numbers; nothing needs a calculator beyond arithmetic, a square root, \(\ln\), \(\log_2\) (on a calculator, \(\log_2 x=\ln x/\ln 2\)) and \(e^{x}\). Full worked solutions are in the Solutions appendix at the back of the book — try each first, then check.
E1 (compute) — expectation and variance of a tiny random variable. A fair four-sided die shows \(x\in\{1,2,3,4\}\), each with probability \(\tfrac14\). Using \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_x x\,p(x)\) and the shortcut \(\operatorname{Var}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2\) (§1), compute \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}[X]\). (The six-sided die in §1 gave \(3.5\) and \(35/12\); redo the arithmetic for four faces.)
E2 (concept) — name that distribution. For each description, name which of §2’s five distributions (Bernoulli, Categorical, Gaussian, Laplace, Beta) it is, and give its parameter(s): (a) “did this user finish the episode they started?”; (b) “which one of \(5\) shelves did they open first?”; (c) the error of a rating predictor whose log has a few typos far off the scale; (d) a belief about a coin’s unknown bias, written as the pseudo-count form “I’ve effectively seen \(6\) heads and \(2\) tails.” For (d), state the \((\alpha,\beta)\) and, using \(\mathbb{E}[\theta]=\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)\), its mean. Finally: for the Bernoulli in (a) with \(p=0.8\) (the §3 coin), give \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}[X]\) from \(\mathbb{E}[X]=p,\ \operatorname{Var}[X]=p(1-p)\).
E3 (compute) — odds → logit → sigmoid. A second coin lands heads with \(p=0.7\). (a) Compute its odds \(p/(1-p)\). (b) Compute the logit \(\ln\!\big(p/(1-p)\big)\). (c) Now treat that logit as a model score \(z\) and run it through the sigmoid \(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\); compare the result with \(p\). (d) As a separate check, evaluate \(\sigma(3)\).
E4 (compute) — softmax of three scores. A classifier emits scores \(\mathbf z=[1,0,0]\) for classes \(A,B,C\). Using \(\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf z)_c=e^{z_c}/\sum_k e^{z_k}\) (§3) with \(e^{1}\approx2.718\), compute the three probabilities (round to three decimals) and confirm they sum to \(1\). Which class wins, and do \(B\) and \(C\) come out equal? Say why in one line, using §3.
E5 (compute) — MLE for a coin. You flip a coin 8 times and see 6 heads, 2 tails. Write its unknown heads-probability as \(\theta\), as in §4; the likelihood is \(L(\theta)=\theta^{6}(1-\theta)^{2}\). Set the derivative of \(\log L(\theta)=6\ln\theta+2\ln(1-\theta)\) to zero (§4’s method, with the two slopes from the toolkit box at the end of §1) and solve for \(\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}\). Hand-check by plugging your answer back into \(\tfrac{6}{\theta}=\tfrac{2}{1-\theta}\).
E6 (apply) — Bayes’ rule, a bot detector. §5’s medical test in a recommender’s setting: \(2\%\) of accounts are bots, \(\Pr(S)=0.02\) (here \(S\) is “a bot”); a bot detector flags \(95\%\) of bots, \(\Pr(+\mid S)=0.95\), and \(10\%\) of human accounts, \(\Pr(+\mid\neg S)=0.10\). An account is flagged. (a) Compute the evidence \(\Pr(+)\) via the law of total probability, then the posterior \(\Pr(S\mid+)\) with Bayes’ rule. (b) Redo it by the counting picture over \(10{,}000\) accounts (how many true vs false positives?) and confirm you get the same number. Why is it so far below \(95\%\)? (One line, using §5.)
E7 (extend) — MLE vs MAP: the prior as a regularizer. Take the same coin as E5 (6 heads, 2 tails) and add a moderate Beta\((4,4)\) prior (§6; it acts like three heads and three tails already seen). (a) Using Beta–Bernoulli conjugacy (“add the counts to the prior exponents”), write the posterior as a Beta\((\alpha_{\text{post}},\beta_{\text{post}})\). (b) Its MAP estimate is the mode \(\dfrac{\alpha_{\text{post}}-1}{\alpha_{\text{post}}+\beta_{\text{post}}-2}\) — compute it. (c) Compare the three numbers — MLE (E5), the prior mean \(0.5\), and your MAP — and say in one sentence which way the prior pulled the estimate, and what the analogous L2 effect on a weight would be. (d) With §6’s firm Beta\((10,10)\) prior instead, how many heads in \(8\) flips does the MAP need to exceed \(0.6\)?
E8 (compute) — entropy, cross-entropy, KL. Truth is a fair coin \(p=[0.5,0.5]\); a model predicts \(q=[0.7,0.3]\) (a new \(q\): the §7 text works \([0.9,0.1]\) and \([0.8,0.2]\)). Compute (a) the entropy \(H(p)\) in bits (\(\log_2\)); (b) the cross-entropy \(H(p,q)=-\sum_x p(x)\ln q(x)\) in nats; (c) the KL divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)=\sum_x p(x)\ln\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\) in nats; and (d) verify the identity \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)=H(p,q)-H(p)\) (use \(H(p)\) from (a), converted to nats). Useful logs: \(\ln 0.5=-0.693,\ \ln 0.7=-0.357,\ \ln 0.3=-1.204\).
E9 (apply) — a paired \(t\)-test over seeds. Model A and model B are evaluated on the same 5 seeds; the per-seed differences \(d_i=A_i-B_i\) (fresh numbers, in the milli-NDCG@10 units of §8.4) are \(d=[3,5,4,6,2]\). Compute (a) the mean \(\bar d\); (b) the sample standard deviation \(s_d=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_i(d_i-\bar d)^2}\); (c) the standard error \(s_d/\sqrt{n}\) and the statistic \(t=\bar d/(s_d/\sqrt n)\) with its degrees of freedom. The two-sided critical value at \(\alpha=0.05\) is \(2.776\) for df \(=4\) and \(2.571\) for df \(=5\); use the one for your df. Do you reject \(H_0\)? (d) Give the 95% CI \(\bar d\pm t^{*}\,(s_d/\sqrt n)\) with that critical value \(t^{*}\). Does it include \(0\), and does that agree with (c)?
E10 (concept) — more seeds and the standard error. In E9 the standard error was \(s_d/\sqrt n\). (a) If you re-ran the experiment with \(n=10\) seeds and the spread \(s_d\) and the mean gain \(\bar d\) stayed at their E9 values, what would happen to the standard error, and hence to \(t\) and the chance of detecting a real gain (the test’s power)? Give the factor by which the standard error shrinks and \(t\) grows, and say in words what happens to power. (b) Now suppose the per-seed differences are independent and each has variance \(4\) (standard deviation \(2\)). What are the variance and the standard deviation of the average of \(n=10\) of them? Which of the two shrinks by the factor \(n\), and which by \(\sqrt n\)?
E11 (compute) — Wilcoxon signed-rank by hand. Six paired seed-differences are
\[d=[+3,+1,+5,-2,+4,+6]\quad(\text{A minus B, as in §8}).\] (a) Rank the absolute values \(|d_i|\) smallest to largest. (b) Sum the ranks of the negative differences to get \(W^{-}\), and of the positive ones to get \(W^{+}\) (the two add up to \(1+2+\dots+6=21\)). (c) The statistic is \(W=\min(W^{+},W^{-})\); recall (§8.7) that at \(n=6\) the smallest two-sided \(p\) is the floor \(2/2^{6}=0.031\), reached only when all signs agree (\(W=0\)). Is this result significant at \(\alpha=0.05\)? (Count how many of the \(2^{6}=64\) equally likely sign patterns give a \(W\) at most as small as yours; that count over \(64\) is the two-sided \(p\).)
E12 (apply) — ship, or not? You test four new models against a baseline. The best improves NDCG@10 by \(+0.004\) (that is \(+4\) milli-NDCG@10, the units of §8.4) over 5 seeds, with a \(95\%\) CI of \([+0.0003,\,+0.0077]\) and a raw \(p=0.04\). (a) From that CI alone, would you conclude the model is better? (b) You ran four tests, not one — apply Bonferroni at \(\alpha=0.05\): does \(p=0.04\) survive? (c) Ship or not, and why, in two lines? (The §8.7 lesson, as a decision.)

The main downstream uses of this chapter’s ideas (a list of the main uses, not of every one: a concept with no row, such as the Law of Large Numbers, mostly serves this chapter’s own arguments):








Foundation (here)
Used in
As…

scores → probabilities; BPR’s \(\sigma\); InfoNCE

Significance test: paired \(t\) (§8)

The main line through the book (the table above lists other chapters that use these pieces too, such as Evaluation Metrics for §8 and Bandits & Online Recommendation for §2 and §6):
      THIS CHAPTER (probability → likelihood → Bayes → MAP)
        │
        ▼
   LOSS FUNCTIONS & REGULARIZERS
        loss = −log p(data|θ);  regularizer = −log p(θ)
        MAP  = argmin (loss + reg)
        │
        ▼

title: 3  Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning
text:
11. Glossary







Term
Plain meaning




Random variable
A quantity whose value is uncertain (coin, die, temperature).


Sample space / event
The set of possible outcomes / a subset of them.


PMF / PDF
Probability mass (discrete) / density (continuous) function; sums/integrates to 1.


CDF \(F(x)\)
Cumulative distribution function \(F(x)=\Pr(X\le x)\) — the running total of probability; a different function describing the same distribution.


Expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) / mean \(\mu\)
Probability-weighted average value.


Variance \(\sigma^2\)
Expected squared distance from the mean; spread.


Standard deviation \(\sigma\)
\(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[X]}\); the spread in the same units as \(X\) (§1).


Law of Large Numbers
The sample average converges to the expectation as samples accumulate.


Conditional probability \(\Pr(A\mid B)\)
Probability of \(A\) given \(B\) occurred \(=\Pr(A\cap B)/\Pr(B)\).


Independence
\(\Pr(A\cap B)=\Pr(A)\Pr(B)\); one event tells you nothing about the other.


Complement \(\neg B\)
“Not \(B\)”; \(\Pr(\neg B)=1-\Pr(B)\) (§1).


Joint / marginal
Joint \(p(x,y)=\Pr(X{=}x\text{ and }Y{=}y)\), the chance of each pair of values; marginal \(p(x)=\sum_y p(x,y)\) (sum the joint over the other variable — the row totals in the margin of the grid).


Law of total probability
\(\Pr(A)=\sum_j\Pr(A\mid B_j)\Pr(B_j)\) over cases \(B_j\) that do not overlap and together cover every outcome (e.g. \(B\) and \(\neg B\)); the engine of Bayes’ evidence term.


Loss
A single number scoring how badly a model’s predictions fit the data; training adjusts the model to make it small (§2).


Bernoulli
One yes/no with parameter \(p\); \(-\log\) → BCE.


Categorical
One of \(K\) classes; \(-\log\) → cross-entropy; paired with softmax.


Gaussian (Normal)
Bell curve \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\); \(-\log\) → squared error (MSE) when \(\sigma\) is the same fixed number for every point (§4).


Laplace
Peaked/heavy-tailed \((\mu,b)\); \(-\log\) → absolute error (MAE) when \(b\) is the same fixed number for every point.


Beta
Distribution over a probability; conjugate prior for Bernoulli.


Mode
The most plausible value — where a distribution peaks (for a continuous variable the height of the curve at the mode is a density, not a probability: §1); for Beta\((\alpha,\beta)\) with \(\alpha,\beta>1\) it is \((\alpha-1)/(\alpha+\beta-2)\) (§2, §6).


Noise
A random error added on top of a true value (a bathroom scale’s reading is your true weight plus a small random wobble) (§2).


Regression
Predicting a real number, such as a price (§2).


Robustness
Resistance to a few wildly-off values: the Laplace / MAE / median are robust, the Gaussian / MSE / mean are not (§2).


Normalizing constant
The factor that makes a density’s area (or a list of probabilities) equal \(1\); Beta\((2,2)\) has \(6\) (§2).


Pseudo-count
The heads and tails a Beta prior behaves as if already seen: \(\alpha-1\) and \(\beta-1\) (§2).


Median
The middle value once the data are sorted; the single value that minimizes the total absolute error (§2).


Odds
\(p/(1-p)\).


Logit (log-odds)
\(\ln\!\big(p/(1-p)\big)\); maps \((0,1)\to(-\infty,\infty)\).


Sigmoid \(\sigma(z)\)
\(1/(1+e^{-z})\); inverse of the logit; score → probability.


Softmax
Multi-class sigmoid; scores → a probability distribution.


One-hot
A list with a single \(1\) and \(0\)s elsewhere, like \([1,0,0]\) (§3).


Temperature \(\tau\)
Divides the scores before a softmax: a small \(\tau\) gives a nearly one-hot output, a large \(\tau\) a nearly uniform one (§3).


Gradient
The slope (or slopes) a model follows downhill when it trains (§3; Calculus primer).


Multi-label
Several independent yes/no labels at once, such as a film that is both a comedy and a drama; each gets a sigmoid (§3).


Monotonic
Here, increasing (a bigger input always gives a bigger output), like \(\log\) and \(e^{x}\), so it keeps the ranking of any list (§3).


InfoNCE
A contrastive training loss: a softmax that must pick a matching pair out of mismatched ones (§3; §7 for its link to mutual information).


BPR
Bayesian Personalized Ranking: a loss that teaches a recommender to rank an item a user chose above one they did not; it applies a sigmoid to the score gap (§3).


Likelihood \(L(\theta)\)
\(p(\text{data}\mid\theta)\) read as a function of \(\theta\) (data fixed).


Log-likelihood
\(\log L(\theta)\); products become sums.


NLL
Negative log-likelihood \(=-\log L\); minimizing it = MLE; this is a loss.


Surprise / self-information
\(-\log p(x)\); how surprising an outcome is (\(0\) if certain, \(\to\infty\) if rare).


Entropy \(H(p)\)
\(-\sum p\log p\): average surprise / uncertainty (maximal at uniform). In bits with \(\log_2\) (the average yes/no questions, or bits to store one sample, as in §7’s examples), in nats with \(\ln\).


Bits / nats
Units of entropy: \(\log_2\) gives bits, \(\ln\) gives nats; \(1\) bit \(=\ln 2\approx0.693\) nats (§7).


Binary entropy
The entropy of a two-outcome variable with probabilities \(\theta\) and \(1-\theta\): \(-\theta\log_2\theta-(1-\theta)\log_2(1-\theta)\), which peaks at \(1\) bit for \(\theta=\tfrac12\) (§7).


Cross-entropy \(H(p,q)\)
\(-\sum p\log q\); surprise of \(p\)’s outcomes scored by model \(q\) — the standard classification loss.


KL divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)\)
\(H(p,q)-H(p)\ge0\); extra surprise from using \(q\) not \(p\); asymmetric (a divergence, not a distance).


Mutual information
How much knowing one variable tells you about another: the KL divergence between their joint distribution and the product of their separate ones; zero exactly when they are independent (§7).


Variational autoencoder (VAE) / ELBO
A network that learns to generate new data / its training objective, the evidence lower bound, which can never exceed the log of the evidence (§5); it contains a KL term that keeps each example’s code near a prior (§7).


Knowledge distillation
Training a small model to match a large model’s output probabilities; the KL divergence measures the mismatch (§7).


RLHF / policy
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: tuning a language model toward the answers people prefer / the rule a model uses to choose its outputs; a KL penalty keeps the tuned policy near the original (§7).


t-SNE / variational inference
Drawing high-dimensional data as a 2-D map by making a KL divergence small / replacing a hard-to-compute posterior (§5) by the closest member of a simpler family, closest measured by KL (§7).


Decision tree / information gain
A flowchart of yes/no questions that sorts examples into groups / how much a question reduces the entropy of the labels; the tree asks the question with the largest gain first (§7).


Maximum-entropy model
Among all distributions that match what you know, the most uncertain one: knowing nothing about a die, \(\tfrac16\) for each face (§7).


Entropy bonus / exploring
In reinforcement learning (RL, learning by trial and reward), a reward proportional to the entropy of a model’s choices / what the bonus buys: trying actions other than the one that looks best so far (§7).


MLE
Maximum Likelihood Estimate; \(\theta\) that best explains the data.


Bayes’ rule
posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior.


Prior \(p(\theta)\)
Belief about \(\theta\) before data.


Evidence \(p(D)\)
Normalizer; data probability averaged over \(\theta\), each \(\theta\) weighted by its prior (a.k.a. marginal likelihood).


Posterior \(p(\theta\mid D)\)
Updated belief after data.


MAP
Maximum A Posteriori; the \(\theta\) at the peak of the posterior — it maximizes likelihood \(\times\) prior, i.e. minimizes loss \(+\) regularizer.


Weights
A model’s learned parameters, collected in one list \(\theta\) (§6), the numbers a regularizer keeps small.


Regularizer
A penalty added to the loss that keeps the parameters well-behaved; under MAP it is \(-\log p(\boldsymbol\theta)\) — a Gaussian prior gives L2 (weight decay), a Laplace prior gives L1 (lasso) (§6).


Regularization strength \(\lambda\)
The weight on the penalty in “loss \(+\,\lambda\times\) penalty”; a narrower prior is a larger \(\lambda\) (\(1/(2s^2)\) for L2, \(1/b\) for L1, against a summed negative log-likelihood; rescaled for an average loss) (§6).


L2 norm / L1 norm \(\lVert\boldsymbol\theta\rVert_2,\lVert\boldsymbol\theta\rVert_1\)
The length of the weight list as the root of the sum of squares / as the sum of absolute values; their penalties come from the Gaussian and Laplace priors (§6).


Conjugate prior
A prior whose posterior is the same family (Beta↔︎Bernoulli).


Base-rate effect
A rare condition (low prior) makes even an accurate test’s positives mostly false.


Sensitivity / false-positive rate
\(\Pr(+\mid S)\), the chance a test flags a true case / \(\Pr(+\mid\neg S)\), the chance it wrongly flags a healthy one (§5).


Random seed
The number that fixes a training run’s random choices; another seed gives a slightly different, equally valid result (§8).


Test set / fold
Data held back to measure a trained model / one of the \(k\) slices of cross-validation, each taking a turn as the test set (§8).


Null hypothesis \(H_0\)
The skeptical default “no real difference”; a test asks whether the data are strong enough to reject it.


\(p\)-value
Probability, if \(H_0\) were true, of a result at least this extreme (for the \(t\)-test: a ratio \(\lvert t\rvert\) at least this large; either direction for a two-sided test); small = significant. NOT \(\Pr(H_0\text{ true})\).


Significance level \(\alpha\)
The pre-set bar (usually \(0.05\)); reject \(H_0\) if \(p<\alpha\).


Type I / II error
False positive (reject true \(H_0\)) / false negative (miss a real effect).


Power
The probability that a test detects a real difference when there is one; having more pairs gives more power, and pairing the models on the same seeds helps when their scores rise and fall together (§8.1; §8.2, §8.3).


NDCG@10
Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain at \(10\): a ranking score that rewards putting the items a user wanted near the top of a list of \(10\); bigger is better (§8.4).


Paired \(t\)-test
Tests whether the true mean of the per-pair differences is \(0\), using their sample mean \(\bar d\): \(t=\bar d/(s_d/\sqrt n)\).


Standard error (SE)
\(s_d/\sqrt n\) — how much an estimate wobbles across repeats; shrinks with more data.


Central Limit Theorem
The average of many independent noisy pieces is approximately bell-shaped around the truth; with enough pairs it keeps the \(t\)-test a fair approximation when the differences are not exactly normal, but not with a handful (§8.3, Fact 2).


Confidence interval (CI)
\(\bar d \pm t^{*}s_d/\sqrt n\); the effect size with its uncertainty. A \(95\%\) CI excludes \(0\) exactly when the two-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\) is significant (a \(99\%\) CI goes with \(\alpha=0.01\); §8.5, §8.6 Step 4).


Degrees of freedom (df)
\(n-1\) for the paired test; sets which Student-\(t\) curve gives the \(p\)-value.


Student-\(t\) distribution
The spread of \(t\)-values pure luck produces — a bell with fatter tails than the Gaussian when there are few pairs, shaped by the df (§8.3).


Critical value
The cutoff that pure luck exceeds only \(\alpha\) of the time (\(2.776\) for df \(=4\), \(\alpha=0.05\), two-sided) (§8.3).


Wilcoxon signed-rank
Non-parametric paired test (ranks, not values); use when differences aren’t normal and there are at least \(6\) pairs (below that it cannot reach \(p<0.05\); §8.6).


Effect size
The magnitude of the difference (\(\bar d\)); report it alongside \(p\) (significance \(\ne\) size).


One- vs two-sided test
Two-sided asks “A \(\ne\) B” (the default); one-sided asks “A \(>\) B”: it halves \(p\) when the result goes the pre-registered way and gives \(1-p/2\) (near \(1\) for a clear result) when it goes the other way; valid only if the direction was pre-registered (§8.6, Step 1).


Pre-registered
Written down before running anything (a directional hypothesis, the tests to be run), so it cannot be chosen after seeing the data (§8.5).


Ablation study
An experiment that removes one component of a model at a time to see what each contributes (§8.6, Step 0).


Bonferroni / Holm
Multiple-comparison fixes for \(m\) tests: Bonferroni compares each \(p\) to \(\alpha/m\); Holm is a stepwise version that is never more conservative: it keeps every result Bonferroni keeps, and sometimes more (for \(p=0.012,\,0.020,\,0.024\) Bonferroni keeps one, Holm all three; §8.6 Step 3).


Multiple comparisons
Running several tests at once: each carries its own \(\alpha\) chance of a false positive, so the chance that at least one fires by luck grows (\(1-0.95^{3}\approx0.14\) for three tests; §8.5, §8.6 Step 3).


Omnibus / post-hoc test
An omnibus test (such as the Friedman test) asks one question across all the models and datasets at once; post-hoc pairwise tests, planned in advance, run only after it finds some difference (§8.5). This planned use is not the after-the-fact choice that §8.2 warns against.


Bootstrap
Estimating how much a score wobbles by re-drawing the test cases at random with replacement (a case may be drawn more than once) many times and recomputing the score each time; it needs no bell-shape assumption (Evaluation Metrics §11d; named in §8.7).

title: 4  Loss Functions & Regularizers
text:
Part A — The general machine-learning picture
From Graphs to LightGCN and Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning keep saying “trained with a loss plus a regularizer.” From Graphs to LightGCN §15 states the objective of LightGCN (a graph-based recommender model; He et al., 2020): the Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) loss of §9 plus an L2 penalty on the size of the model’s parameters (§5.1) — and points here for the rest. This chapter builds those two words from absolute zero — first for all of machine learning (ML), then narrowing to recommendation. After this chapter, the loss/regularizer lines in every other chapter should read like plain English.
What this chapter assumes: school algebra and a calculator, plus three earlier chapters if their ideas are not yet second nature. Read the Linear-Algebra primer (chapter 1, Linear Algebra for Machine Learning) for the length of a vector (its §1) and cosine similarity (its §4) that §2 and §5 use, and for the transpose, identity matrix and determinant (its §2) that §5.1 and §11 use, and the singular value decomposition (its §6) that §11 touches.
Read the Calculus primer (chapter 2, Calculus for Machine Learning) for the chain rule and the sigmoid’s slope (its §3) that §2.3 and §9 use, the gradient and its contour lines (its §4), the gradient descent that §3 uses (its §5) and convexity (its §6); and the Probability primer (chapter 3, Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning) for the distributions and the sigmoid that §2 uses, the entropy and Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of its §7 that §2.3 recaps, and for the likelihood / prior / posterior / maximum a posteriori (MAP) ideas that §6 uses. (Other chapters cite this one by its title, Loss Functions & Regularizers.)

title: 4  Loss Functions & Regularizers
section: 1. What is a loss function? (and why “loss”?)
text:
1. What is a loss function? (and why “loss”?)
Suppose you are learning to guess how long a bus ride takes, and after every guess someone tells you how far off you were. To improve, you need one number for “how bad were my guesses so far?”, and a way to make it smaller. A machine-learning model works the same way: it is a function with adjustable numbers (parameters, written \(\theta\)) that training learns from the data, and training means choosing \(\theta\). The single number that says “how bad is the current \(\theta\)?”, which we then make as small as possible, is the loss.

A loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) maps the current parameters to a single real number measuring how badly the model’s predictions disagree with the data. Training = minimizing it.

Worked example. Take one training point: the input is \(x=2\) and the true value is \(y=6\). The model has one parameter, \(\theta=w\), and predicts \(\hat y=w\cdot x\) (§3 trains exactly this model). Score three values of the parameter by the squared miss \((\hat y-y)^2\):



Table 4.1: The loss turns “how bad is this value?” into one number per value; training is the search for the value with the smallest number.











the parameter \(w\)
prediction \(\hat y=2w\)
loss \((\hat y-6)^2\)
what it means




bad: \(1\)
\(2\)
\(16\)
far from \(6\): a large loss, so \(w\) needs to move


better: \(2.6\)
\(5.2\)
\(0.64\)
close: a small loss, so little left to fix


perfect: \(3\)
\(6\)
\(0\)
on target: nothing left to fix







Why is it called loss?
The word comes from statistical decision theory (Abraham Wald, 1930s–40s; Wald, 1939). There, a loss function quantifies the penalty you incur for a wrong decision — exactly as in everyday English: a bad estimate makes you “lose” something (money, accuracy). Machine learning (ML) borrowed the term wholesale: predict 4 stars when the truth is 1, and you have “lost” 3 stars’ worth of accuracy.


The pile of near-synonyms (and their shades of meaning)
You will see several words for almost-the-same thing. They differ only in emphasis:








Word
Where it came from
Shade of meaning




Loss
decision theory (Wald)
penalty for one wrong prediction


Cost
optimization / control
often the total loss summed/averaged over the whole dataset


Error
everyday English: the gap between a guess and the truth
stresses “distance from the right answer”


Objective
optimization
the most neutral word — the function you optimize (could be min or max)


Risk
decision theory (Wald); made central to ML by Vapnik’s empirical risk minimization (Vapnik, 1991; defined just below)
the expected loss over the true data distribution


Criterion
code: the usual variable name for the loss object in PyTorch, a popular machine-learning software library
just the chosen loss object in code



One of these deserves a real definition because it appears constantly:

Empirical Risk. We cannot average the loss over the true distribution (we don’t have it), so we average over the training sample. That sample-average is the empirical risk, and minimizing it is Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) — the formal name for “fit the training data.” (Three ratings missed by \(0.5\), \(-1\) and \(0\) have an empirical risk of \(0.42\) under squared loss, worked below.) Empirical = “from observed data”; risk = “expected loss.” Most supervised training — learning from examples that each come with their correct answer, the \(y_n\) below (a film paired with its true rating, \(4\)) — is ERM plus a regularizer (§4). (Self-supervised learning, met in §11, instead invents its training task from unlabeled data, with no human-supplied answers.)

\[
\underbrace{\hat{R}(\theta)}_{\text{empirical risk}} \;=\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} \ell\big(\hat{y}_n(\theta),\, y_n\big),
\]
where \(\ell\) is the per-example loss (lowercase \(\ell\)), \(\hat{y}_n\) the prediction, \(y_n\) the truth. The capital \(\mathcal{L}\) or \(\hat{R}\) is the average over all \(N\) examples. The book says loss for both; the letter tells which: \(\ell\) for one example, \(\mathcal{L}\) for the average over the data (the table’s cost). For example, three ratings whose predictions miss by \(0.5\), \(-1\) and \(0\) have per-example squared losses \(0.25\), \(1\) and \(0\), so the empirical risk is \((0.25+1+0)/3=0.4167\approx0.42\) — a single number for the whole sample, which is the number training lowers. (In the recommendation sections \(\mathcal{L}\) is written as a sum over the sampled terms; dividing by their number rescales \(\lambda\), not the minimizer.)

Takeaway. A loss turns “how wrong are these parameter values?” into one number; the empirical risk averages it over the training data; training searches for the parameter values that make it small. Later sections change which number is measured (§2) and what is added to it (§4).

title: 4  Loss Functions & Regularizers
section: 2. The taxonomy of losses (and the name of each)
text:
2. The taxonomy of losses (and the name of each)
A recommender is asked three different kinds of question about the same user. How many stars will Ann give this film? — a number. Will she click it? — yes or no. Which of these films will she pick? — a choice among many. One formula cannot score all three fairly: a miss of \(0.5\) stars, a wrong click prediction and a wrong pick are different kinds of mistake, so each kind gets its own loss. Which loss you pick is decided by what kind of thing you are predicting.









What is predicted
Example question
Loss family
Section




a number
stars Ann will give
regression
§2.1


a label
click or no click
classification
§2.2–§2.3


a distribution or a similarity
which film she picks from many; which items fit together
distribution and contrastive (learning by comparing a match against mismatches)
§2.4



Which log? Here and throughout this chapter, \(\log\) means the natural logarithm \(\ln\) (base \(e\approx2.718\)), so a loss built from a log (cross-entropy and its relatives, from §2.2 on) is measured in nats. Information theory often uses \(\log_2\) instead, measured in bits; the two differ only by a constant factor (a value in bits is \(1/\ln 2\approx1.443\) times the same value in nats), and this chapter says bits only when it means base 2. On a calculator, use the ln key — the log key is base 10.

2.1 Regression losses — predicting a number
Used when the target \(y\) is continuous (a temperature, a price, a 1–5 rating). Write the residual \(r=\hat y-y\) (prediction minus truth); as a running example, suppose you predict \(\hat y=4.5\) for a true rating \(y=4\), so \(r=0.5\).
Mean Squared Error (MSE) / “squared loss” / “L2 loss”.
\[
\ell_{\text{MSE}} = (\hat{y}-y)^2, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_n (\hat{y}_n-y_n)^2.
\]

Per component: \(\hat y-y\) is the residual \(r\); squaring makes the penalty grow with the square of the miss and discards the sign; \(\tfrac1N\sum_n\) averages over the \(N\) examples. (Running example: \(r^2=0.5^2=0.25\).)
Name: literally the mean of the squared errors. Why “L2 loss”? The L2 norm of a vector is its ordinary length, \(\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+\cdots}\) (Linear-Algebra primer §1). Summed over the examples, \(\sum_n(\hat y_n-y_n)^2\) is the squared L2 norm of the vector of residuals — its length with the square root dropped. (§5.1 meets the same norm again, as a regularizer.)
The squaring punishes a big miss far more than a small one (being off by 4 costs 16, not 4) — so MSE is sensitive to outliers. The figure The shapes of the losses (§2.2) draws the whole parabola.
Why squared and not, say, to the 4th power? Because of a deep fact we prove in §6: squared error is what you get if you assume the noise in your data is Gaussian (bell-curve), with the same spread for every point. Least squares (Legendre, 1805; Gauss’s probabilistic justification, 1809) is the classic fitting rule of statistics; fitting by the least sum of absolute errors (the mean absolute error below) is older still (Boscovich, 1757).

Mean Absolute Error (MAE) / “L1 loss”.
\[
\ell_{\text{MAE}} = |\hat{y}-y|, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{MAE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_n |\hat{y}_n-y_n|.
\]

Per component: the bars \(|\cdot|\) (absolute value) drop the sign, so the penalty grows only linearly with the miss (the V in §2.2’s figure The shapes of the losses); \(\tfrac1N\sum_n\) averages over the \(N\) examples. (Running example: \(|r|=|0.5|=0.5\).)
Name: mean of the absolute errors. Why “L1 loss”? The L1 norm of a vector is the sum of its entries’ absolute values (Linear-Algebra primer §1), so \(\sum_n|\hat y_n-y_n|\) is the L1 norm of the vector of residuals. On §1’s three residuals \(0.5,-1,0\): L1 norm \(0.5+1+0=1.5\), L2 norm \(\sqrt{1.25}=1.118\), whose square \(1.25\) is the sum of squared errors.
Being off by 4 costs 4, not 16 → robust to outliers, but the kink at 0 makes it non-differentiable there: the slope jumps from \(-1\) to \(+1\), so at exactly \(0\) you use a subgradient — any stand-in slope between \(-1\) and \(+1\) (Calculus primer §3). It corresponds to Laplace noise and targets the median rather than the mean.

Why MAE “targets the median”. Those last two claims are the whole reason to reach for MAE, so both are worth unpacking. Ask each loss the simplest possible question: if you had to predict one number \(c\) for a whole set of values \(y_1,\dots,y_N\), which would it pick? Take the derivative of each total with respect to \(c\). For the absolute value, each term \(\lvert c-y_n\rvert\) has slope \(+1\) when \(c>y_n\) (raising \(c\) moves it further from \(y_n\)) and \(-1\) when \(c<y_n\); adding those up gives (the number of points below \(c\)) minus (the number above \(c\)), written with \(\#\) for “how many”: \[
\frac{d}{dc}\sum_n (c-y_n)^2 \;=\; 2\sum_n (c-y_n),
\qquad
\frac{d}{dc}\sum_n \lvert c-y_n\rvert \;=\; \#\{y_n<c\} \;-\; \#\{y_n>c\}.
\]
Setting the first to zero gives \(\sum_n(c-y_n)=0\), i.e. \(c=\bar y\) — the mean. The second does not measure anything; it counts. It is negative while more points lie above \(c\) than below (so pushing \(c\) up lowers the total), positive once more lie below, and it changes sign exactly where the two counts balance — the median. (For even \(N\) any value between the two middle points is a minimizer: there, as many points lie below \(c\) as above, the counting slope is \(0\), and the total is flat — for \(1,2,3,4\) it is \(4\) at every \(c\) from \(2\) to \(3\). The flat stretch comes from the same straight-line pieces that give MAE its kink; squared error, curved everywhere, always has exactly one minimizer.)
The contrast lives in what each derivative is made of. The squared version carries every residual \(c-y_n\) at its full size, so a point far away pulls hard and drags \(c\) toward itself. The absolute version keeps only its sign: every point casts exactly one vote, and a point \(100\) away votes no louder than a point \(1\) away. That is outlier-robustness in one line.

Each loss does prefer its own summary (the lowest total in its column: \(18\) for MAE at the median, \(206.8\) for MSE at the mean), exactly as the derivatives predict. (The counting slope shows it for MAE: at \(c=3.5\) one rating lies below and four above, slope \(1-4=-3\), still downhill; at \(c=4.5\) it is \(3-2=+1\), already uphill; so the bottom is in between, at the median \(4\).) The total of absolute misses is a single valley with corners only at the ratings, so its values at \(3\), \(4\) and \(5\) (\(21\), \(18\), \(19\)) already show the bottom at the median.
But look at what MSE chose: \(7.2\) is higher than every clean rating in the set, and off the \(1\)–\(5\) scale altogether. One bad row moved the squared-loss prediction into nonsense; the absolute-loss prediction did not move at all, because the \(20\) only ever cast one vote. (With the \(2.0\) logged correctly the mean is \(3.6\) and the median \(4\): the slip moved the mean from \(3.6\) to \(7.2\) and left the median at \(4\).)
Why “Laplace noise”. §6 shows that assuming Gaussian noise and minimizing the negative log-likelihood is squared error. Run that same recipe with the Laplace density \(p(r)\propto e^{-\lvert r\rvert/b}\) (Probability primer §2, where it is drawn against the Gaussian), with spread \(b\), and the \(-\log\) leaves \(\ln(2b)+\lvert r\rvert/b\) — MAE, scaled by \(1/b\) and shifted by a constant that training cannot change. Same machinery, different assumption about the errors: MSE says “errors are bell-shaped, a big one is shocking”; MAE says “errors have heavier tails than a bell curve, a big one is expected” (beyond three standard deviations, \(1.4\%\) against \(0.27\%\); Probability primer §2). Choosing between them is choosing which of those two sentences describes your data.
Huber loss — the compromise.
\[
\ell_\delta = \begin{cases} \tfrac12(\hat{y}-y)^2 & |\hat{y}-y|\le\delta \\[4pt] \delta\,|\hat{y}-y|-\tfrac12\delta^2 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]

Name: after statistician Peter Huber (1964), a founder of robust statistics.
Per component: below the threshold \(|r|\le\delta\) it is the smooth quadratic \(\tfrac12 r^2\) (MSE-like); above it, the linear \(\delta|r|-\tfrac12\delta^2\) (MAE-like). The \(-\tfrac12\delta^2\) is exactly what makes the two pieces meet without a jump at \(|r|=\delta\) (both equal \(\tfrac12\delta^2\) there). Their slopes match there too: the parabola \(\tfrac12r^2\) has slope \(r\), which equals \(\delta\) at \(r=\delta\), and the line has slope \(\delta\). So Huber is differentiable everywhere — the switch-over is a smooth seam, not a corner like MAE’s. The knob \(\delta\) (a value you choose by hand rather than learn from the data, called a hyperparameter) sets the switch-over: quadratic and differentiable near \(0\), linear and outlier-robust far out. (Running example, \(\delta=1\): \(\tfrac12 r^2=0.125\).)
How to pick \(\delta\): it is the residual size at which you stop trusting a point as “clean” and start treating it as an outlier, so set it on the scale of a typical residual. The robust-statistics default is \(\delta\approx1.345\,\hat s\) (often quoted rounded, as \(1.35\)), where \(\hat s\) is a robust estimate of the residuals’ spread (their standard deviation). This \(1.345\) is the value that keeps \(\approx95\%\) of least-squares’ efficiency when the noise really is Gaussian (Fox & Weisberg, 2018): it needs only about \(5\%\) more data than MSE to estimate as precisely (\(1/0.95\approx1.05\)).
Estimating \(\hat s\): typically \(\hat s=\text{MAD}/0.6745\), where the median absolute deviation (MAD) is the median of \(|r-\text{median}(r)|\) (not to be confused with MAE).
Why \(0.6745\): it is the point below which \(75\%\) of a standard bell curve (mean \(0\), standard deviation \(1\)) lies, so exactly half of that curve sits within \(\pm0.6745\) of \(0\), which makes \(0.6745\) that curve’s own MAD; dividing by it rescales the MAD to match a Gaussian standard deviation.
Worked number: take the five ratings \(3,4,4,5,20\) of §2.1, treat each rating’s distance from the median as a residual. The median is \(4\), the absolute deviations are \(1,0,0,1,16\), so \(\text{MAD}=1\), \(\hat s=1/0.6745=1.483\) and \(\delta\approx1.345\times1.483=1.99\approx2\) — a rating-scale number that treats the \(20\) as an outlier.
Reading the knob: smaller \(\delta\Rightarrow\) more MAE-like (more robust; the bend sits closer to \(0\), still with no corner); larger \(\Rightarrow\) more MSE-like.

2.2 Classification losses — predicting a category
Used when \(y\) is a label (spam / not-spam; which of 10 digits).
Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) / “log loss”.
\[
\ell_{\text{BCE}} = -\big[\, y\log\hat{p} + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{p})\,\big], \qquad y\in\{0,1\},
\]
where \(\hat{p}\in(0,1)\) is the model’s predicted probability of class 1. It usually comes from a sigmoid \(\sigma(z)=\tfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\) applied to the model’s raw score \(z\), called the logit (Probability primer §3); the sigmoid squashes any real number into \((0,1)\) (\(\sigma(0)=0.5\), \(\sigma(2)=0.88\), \(\sigma(-2)=0.12\)).

Per component (a switch, like the Bernoulli in Probability primer §2): the label \(y\in\{0,1\}\) selects which term lives — for a positive (\(y{=}1\)) only \(-\log\hat p\) survives, for a negative (\(y{=}0\)) only \(-\log(1-\hat p)\). Each is the surprise at the right answer: \(-\log\) of the probability the model gave it (a probability of \(0.9\) costs \(0.105\) nats, one of \(0.1\) costs \(2.303\); §2.3 defines it). (Running example: the model gives Ann’s click \(\hat p{=}0.7\); she clicks, \(y{=}1\): \(-\ln 0.7 = 0.357\) nats.)
Why “cross-entropy”? From information theory (Shannon). The entropy of a distribution is the average number of bits (binary digits, counted with \(\log_2\)) needed to encode samples from it. The cross-entropy \(H(p,q)\) is the average length needed if you encode samples from the true \(p\) using a code built for a different distribution \(q\) (here \(p\) is the true distribution — for BCE, the label \(y\) — and \(q\) is the model’s, the \(\hat p\) above). Minimizing it drives your predicted \(q\) toward the truth \(p\) — “cross” because it is between two distributions. (§2.3 gives the three facts the loss argument needs; the full build is in the Probability primer §7.)
Why “log loss”? It is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli (coin-flip) model — see §6. The log means a confident wrong answer (\(\hat{p}\to0\) when \(y=1\)) is punished enormously (\(-\log 0 = +\infty\)). No single paper introduced the loss: fitting a logistic model to binary outcomes by this likelihood is classical in statistics (Cox, 1958).

Worked, end to end (both labels). A logit \(z=0.847\) (it is \(\ln\frac{7}{3}\), chosen so that the probability is round) gives \(\hat p=\sigma(0.847)=0.70\). If she clicks, the truth is positive (\(y{=}1\)): \(\ell=-\ln 0.70=0.357\). If she does not click, the truth is negative (\(y{=}0\)); at the same confidence \(\hat p=0.70\): \(\ell=-\ln(1-0.70)=-\ln 0.30=1.204\) — over \(3\times\) larger, because the model placed \(0.70\) on the wrong class. BCE rewards confidence only when it is correct; confident-and-wrong is exactly what the \(-\log\) punishes.
Categorical Cross-Entropy (CE) — the \(K\)-class generalization, paired with softmax: \[
\ell_{\text{CE}} = -\sum_{c=1}^{K} y_c \log \hat{p}_c, \qquad \hat{p}_c = \frac{e^{z_c}}{\sum_{k} e^{z_k}}\ \text{(softmax)}.
\]

Per component (the one-hot collapse, Probability primer §7): the label \(y_c\) is \(1\) for the true class and \(0\) elsewhere, so the sum keeps a single term, \(\ell_{\text{CE}}=-\log\hat
p_{\text{true}}\) — the surprise at the correct class; the \(\hat p_c\) come from the softmax.
Why “softmax”? It is a soft (smooth, differentiable) version of argmax — the operation that returns which position holds the largest score (Probability primer §3). Instead of hard-picking the single largest score, it returns a probability distribution that leans toward the largest — a “soft maximum.” The name softmax, and its pairing with a cross-entropy score, come from Bridle (1989). This name returns in §10, in recommender systems (recsys for short).

Worked, three classes. Raw scores \(z=[2,\,1,\,0]\) for (cat, dog, bird). The exponentials are \(e^{2}=7.389,\ e^{1}=2.718,\ e^{0}=1\), summing to \(11.107\), so the softmax gives \(\hat p=[0.665,\ 0.245,\ 0.090]\) — three non-negative numbers that add to \(1\), a probability distribution, not a single probability. If the truth is cat, only that entry survives: \(\ell=-\ln0.665=0.408\). If the truth is dog, the same scores cost \(-\ln0.245\approx1.41\), more than \(3\times\) as much — the model put its largest score on the wrong class. (Argmax would answer cat and nothing else; softmax gives \([0.665,0.245,0.090]\).)
Hinge loss — the loss of the support vector machine (SVM), a classic classifier that separates two classes with the widest possible gap between them (on two clouds of points it draws the line equally far from the closest points of the two classes, the support vectors). (The soft-margin SVM it comes from is Cortes & Vapnik, 1995; the name came later, from Gentile & Warmuth, 1998, who call it the “linear hinge loss”.)
\[
\ell_{\text{hinge}} = \max(0,\; 1 - y\cdot \hat{y}), \qquad y\in\{-1,+1\}.
\]

Per component: \(y\cdot\hat y\) is the margin (positive when the score \(\hat y\) has the same sign as the label \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\)); \(1-y\hat y\) is how far short of a safe margin of \(1\) you are; \(\max(0,\cdot)\) zeroes the loss once you clear it — so only not-yet-safe examples contribute. (Running example: for a positive, \(y=+1\), a score \(\hat y=0.4\) is on the right side but not yet safe — loss \(\max(0,\,1-0.4)=0.6\); a score \(\hat y=1.3\) clears the margin — loss \(\max(0,\,1-1.3)=\max(0,-0.3)=0\), and no gradient; a score \(\hat y=-0.5\) is on the wrong side: loss \(\max(0,\,1+0.5)=1.5\), the largest of the three.)
Why “hinge”? Plot it. It is flat at zero once you are correct-with-margin, and to the left of the kink it rises as a straight ramp — the graph looks exactly like a door hinge. The kink is the hinge point. The flat region is the key idea: once an example is comfortably correct, it contributes no loss and no gradient.

Why a margin of \(1\). The \(1\) only fixes the unit of the score: doubling every score doubles every margin. The width of the gap between the classes is \(2/\lVert\mathbf w\rVert\) (between the lines \(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x=+1\) and \(-1\)) for a linear score \(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x\) (the entries of \(\mathbf w\) are its weights, the numbers that multiply the inputs), so small weights give a wide gap: \(1.41\) for \(\mathbf w=[1,1]\), \(0.71\) for \([2,2]\) — the L2 penalty of §5.1 keeps them small.
The logistic loss — BCE written on the margin. The figure below sets the regression losses of §2.1 side by side against the residual (left) and plots the classification losses against the margin \(m=y\hat y\) (right), so BCE needs rewriting in those terms. Write the label as \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\) and take \(\hat p=\sigma(\hat y)\), for the score \(\hat y\) (the raw score, the logit \(z\) of BCE above). For \(y=+1\), BCE is \(-\ln\sigma(\hat
y)=\ln(1+e^{-\hat y})\); for \(y=-1\) it is \(-\ln\big(1-\sigma(\hat y)\big)=\ln(1+e^{\hat y})\). Both are \(\ln(1+e^{-y\hat y})=\ln(1+e^{-m})\) — the logistic loss, which is BCE itself, expressed through the margin. Check it on the worked case above: a positive with score \(0.847\) has margin \(m=0.847\) and \(\ln(1+e^{-0.847})=0.357=-\ln0.70\), its BCE.

Focal loss — cross-entropy for severe class imbalance (Lin et al., 2017), introduced for detecting objects in images; recommendation, with a few positives among a sea of negatives, is a natural candidate (a claim from practice, not tested here). It down-weights the easy examples the model already gets right: \[
\ell_{\text{focal}} = -(1-p_t)^{\gamma}\,\log p_t,
\qquad p_t=\begin{cases}\hat p & \text{if } y=1,\\ 1-\hat p & \text{if } y=0.\end{cases}
\]
Read \(p_t\) as “the probability the model gives the true class”, and \(\gamma\ge0\) as a knob. The bare \(-\log p_t\) is exactly BCE (for \(y=1\) it is \(-\log\hat p\), for \(y=0\) it is \(-\log(1-\hat p)\)); focal only multiplies it by the new factor.
The added factor \((1-p_t)^{\gamma}\) is the whole idea: for an easy, already-confident example (\(p_t\to1\)) it \(\to0\), muting that example so training focuses on the hard, still-wrong ones; \(\gamma=0\) recovers plain cross-entropy. With \(\gamma=2\), for instance: an easy example with \(p_t=0.9\) has cross-entropy \(-\ln0.9=0.105\) but focal loss \((1-0.9)^2\times0.105=0.01\times0.105=0.00105\) — \(100\times\) quieter — while a hard one with \(p_t=0.1\) keeps \((1-0.1)^2\times2.303=0.81\times2.303=1.865\) of its \(2.303\). An even example, \(p_t=0.5\), keeps a quarter of its loss: \(0.25\times0.693=0.173\). The factor \((1-p_t)^{\gamma}\) only falls as \(p_t\) rises, so three examples, hard, even and easy, show it heading to \(0\). (Why “focal”: it focuses the loss on the hard cases.)

2.3 Why cross-entropy is the classification loss
§2.2 defined cross-entropy; here is why it is the natural loss for classification — the three facts information theory supplies (Shannon, 1948). (The Probability primer §7 builds entropy, cross-entropy, and the Kullback–Leibler divergence, abbreviated KL, from zero; here we recap just what the loss needs.)
Surprise (information content). How surprised should you be to observe an outcome of probability \(p\)? Define its information (or “surprise”) as
\[ I = -\log p. \]
Three facts about \(I\) are all the loss argument needs:

\(I\) is a cost. A certain event (\(p=1\)) costs \(I=-\log 1 = 0\); a rare one costs a lot. With \(\log_2\) the unit is bits — a fair coin’s heads costs exactly \(1\) bit, and the rare tails of a 99/1 coin costs \(-\log_2 0.01 \approx 6.64\).
Entropy \(H(p)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}[-\log p(x)]=-\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)\) is fixed by the data. (Here \(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}[\cdot]\) is the expectation — the average over outcomes \(x\) drawn from \(p\), Probability primer §1.) It is the irreducible average cost of encoding samples from \(p\); nothing your model does can lower it.
Cross-entropy \(H(p,q)=-\sum_x p(x)\log q(x)\) is what you pay instead when the data really comes from \(p\) but you built your code for \(q\) — and the two are linked by one identity:

\[ H(p,q) = \underbrace{H(p)}_{\text{unavoidable}} + \underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}(p\,\|\,q)}_{\ge\,0,\ \text{extra cost because } q\ne p}. \]
For example, with the truth \(p=[0.5,0.5]\) and a model \(q=[0.9,0.1]\) (call it the coin pair; §2.4 uses it again): \(H(p)=0.693\) nats (the \(1\) bit of fact 1, in natural-log units) and \(D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)=0.511\) (the KL divergence, defined just below), so \(H(p,q)=1.204\); directly, \(-0.5\ln0.9-0.5\ln0.1=0.053+1.151=1.204\) ✓.
Here \(D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\) is the KL divergence (§2.4 uses it as a loss in its own right); on the coin pair, \(0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.9}+0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.1}=-0.294+0.805=0.511\). Why the identity holds: split the log of the ratio, \(\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}=\log p(x)-\log q(x)\), and the sum separates into the two quantities above,
\[ D_{\text{KL}}(p\,\|\,q)=\underbrace{-\sum_x p(x)\log q(x)}_{H(p,q)}\;-\;\underbrace{\Big(-\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)\Big)}_{H(p)}, \]
so moving \(H(p)\) to the other side gives the identity. And \(D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)\ge 0\), with equality if and only if (mathematicians write iff) \(q=p\) — a fact called Gibbs’ inequality. Since the data fixes \(p\) — so \(H(p)\) is a constant you cannot change — minimizing cross-entropy over your model \(q\) is exactly minimizing \(D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)\), i.e. making your predicted distribution match the truth. That one sentence is why cross-entropy is the loss.
Specializing to classification. In a \(K\)-class problem the true label is a one-hot distribution \(p\) — all mass on the correct class \(c^\star\) (e.g. \(p=[1,0,0]\) for “cat”, in the order cat, dog, bird of §2.2). The sum then collapses:
\[ H(p,q) = -\sum_c p_c \log q_c = -\log q_{c^\star}. \]
So cross-entropy for one labeled example is just the negative log of the probability the model assigned to the correct class. And since \(H(p)=0\) for a one-hot \(p\), here cross-entropy \(=\) KL \(=\) the negative log-likelihood of §6 — three names, one number.

The \(-\log\) shape is the whole point: confident-correct is nearly free, confident-wrong is punished brutally (the figure below plots the curve with the table’s three rows). And on average it rewards honesty: if \(70\) of \(100\) look-alike photos are cats, the average loss \(-(0.7\ln q+0.3\ln(1-q))\) is \(0.693\) at \(q=0.5\), \(0.632\) at \(q=0.6\), \(0.611\) at \(q=0.7\), \(0.639\) at \(q=0.8\) and \(0.765\) at \(q=0.9\), lowest exactly at the true \(70\%\) (the slope \(-p/q+(1-p)/(1-q)\) is \(0\) only at \(q=p\)). That is what pushes the model toward calibrated probabilities: ones that mean what they say, so that of all the times the model says \(0.70\), about \(70\%\) really are that class. (This holds for the best model on the data it is trained on; a large trained network can still come out over-confident on new data, a finding from practice not tested here.)

Why not just use accuracy, or MSE?

Accuracy has no usable gradient — it is flat, then jumps; you cannot descend on it (two classes, true class cat: as \(q_{\text{cat}}\) rises from \(0.3\) to \(0.45\), accuracy stays \(0\) while the loss falls from \(1.204\) to \(0.799\); only crossing \(0.5\) changes accuracy, and at \(0.55\) it is \(1\) while the loss, \(0.598\), keeps falling smoothly). Accuracy here can only be \(0\) or \(1\), so one value on each side of \(0.5\) shows its whole step. Cross-entropy is its smooth, differentiable surrogate (a stand-in that falls when accuracy would rise, and can be descended).
Minimizing it gives the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE). Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the data under a Bernoulli/categorical model (§6), so minimizing it = maximizing that likelihood — the probabilistically correct objective, not an arbitrary one. (The MLE itself is the parameter value \(\theta\) you land on, not the loss.)
Clean gradient with softmax. The gradient of softmax-cross-entropy with respect to the scores \(z\) is beautifully simple: \(\partial\ell/\partial z = q - p\) (“prediction minus truth”). MSE placed on top of a sigmoid/softmax instead saturates (goes flat, as shown below) — its gradient vanishes just when the model is confidently wrong, so learning stalls. Cross-entropy does not.

Point 3, shown here for \(K=2\) classes (the \(K\)-class case follows from the same chain rule). (In §2.2’s letters, \(p\) here is the label \(y\) and \(q\) is the prediction \(\hat p\).) Take one positive example (\(p=1\)) with \(q=\sigma(z)\), and use \(\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\big(1-\sigma(z)\big)\) (Calculus primer §3). Cross-entropy gives \(\frac{d}{dz}\big[-\ln\sigma(z)\big]=-\frac{\sigma(1-\sigma)}{\sigma}=\sigma(z)-1=q-p\). MSE on the probability gives \(\frac{d}{dz}\big(\sigma(z)-1\big)^2=2\big(\sigma(z)-1\big)\,\sigma(z)\big(1-\sigma(z)\big)\).
Now let the model be confidently wrong, \(z=-5\), so \(\sigma(-5)=0.0067\): cross-entropy’s gradient is \(0.0067-1=-0.993\), a strong push, while MSE’s is \(2(-0.9933)(0.0067)(0.9933)=-0.013\) — about \(75\times\) weaker (at \(z=0\): \(-0.5\) against \(-0.25\), \(2\times\); at \(z=-0.7\): \(-0.668\) against \(-0.296\), \(2.3\times\); at \(z=-2\): \(-0.881\) against \(-0.185\), \(4.8\times\)). MSE’s gradient carries the factor \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\), the sigmoid’s slope, which is nearly \(0\) where the S-curve has gone flat; that flattening-out is what saturates means. For \(z\) below about \(-0.7\) (where MSE’s gradient peaks at \(0.30\)), cross-entropy’s push keeps growing toward \(1\) while MSE’s dies toward \(0\).
Binary case ties back to the sigmoid. With \(K=2\) classes, softmax over scores \((z_0,z_1)\) gives \(q_1 = \tfrac{e^{z_1}}{e^{z_0}+e^{z_1}} = \sigma(z_1-z_0)\) (divide top and bottom by \(e^{z_1}\)) — a sigmoid. Substituting into categorical cross-entropy recovers the BCE formula of §2.2 exactly: with scores \((0,\,0.847)\), \(q_1=\sigma(0.847)=0.70\) and the loss for class 1 is \(0.357\), §2.2’s BCE. So BCE is cross-entropy with two classes, and the sigmoid is softmax with two classes.

One-line takeaway. Classification asks the model for a probability distribution \(q\) over classes; cross-entropy measures the total coding cost of using \(q\) when the truth is \(p\) — the unavoidable \(H(p)\) plus the KL divergence (\(1.204=0.693+0.511\) on the coin pair) — and equals the negative log-likelihood — so minimizing it simultaneously matches the truth, maximizes likelihood, and trains with a clean non-saturating gradient. That triple coincidence is why it is the default classification loss.



2.4 Distribution & contrastive losses (the modern additions)
Two questions remain that are not about one label: how far is a model’s whole probability distribution from the truth, and does this item belong with that one? Each gets a loss of its own.
KL divergence — distance-ish between two distributions (the extra cost of §2.3, now as a standalone object).
\[
D_{\text{KL}}(p\,\|\,q) = \sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
\]

Why “divergence” and not “distance”? Because it is not symmetric: \(D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)\ne D_{\text{KL}}(q\|p)\); a true distance gives the same value from either end. For example, with \(p=[0.5,\,0.5]\) and \(q=[0.9,\,0.1]\): \(D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)=0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.9}+0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.1}=-0.294+0.805=0.511\), but \(D_{\text{KL}}(q\|p)=0.9\ln\frac{0.9}{0.5}+0.1\ln\frac{0.1}{0.5}=0.529-0.161=0.368\) — swap the two distributions and the “distance” changes. Kullback–Leibler, after the two authors (1951). Core to variational autoencoders (VAEs) — §11’s models, which squeeze each input into a short random code and rebuild the input from it — and to knowledge distillation (training a small model to copy a big model’s predicted probabilities, with KL measuring the mismatch; Probability primer §7 works one: KL \(0.085\) nats).

InfoNCE (information noise-contrastive estimation, decoded below) — the contrastive-learning workhorse. Contrastive learning trains embeddings (Linear-Algebra primer §1) — the lists of numbers (vectors) a model learns to represent each user, item or image, for example the two-number vector \([0.8,\,0.6]\), the positive in the figure below — by comparison: make two views of the same thing (for example, two slightly different crops of the same photo, or the same user’s history with a few interactions randomly hidden), and teach the model that the two views belong together while other things do not.
\[
\ell_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log\frac{\exp(\text{sim}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}^+)/\tau)}{\exp(\text{sim}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}^+)/\tau)+\sum_{k}\exp(\text{sim}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}_k)/\tau)}.
\]

Symbols: \(\mathbf{z}\) is the anchor (the embedding of one view), \(\mathbf{z}^+\) its positive (the other view of the same thing, or a matching item), the \(\mathbf{z}_k\) are negatives (embeddings of other things), \(\text{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)\) is a similarity (usually the cosine of the angle between the two vectors, Linear-Algebra primer §4), and \(\tau>0\) is the temperature. The denominator runs over the positive and all the negatives, so the fraction is the positive’s share of the total — a number between \(0\) and \(1\), which makes the loss \(\ge0\). The expression is exactly a softmax cross-entropy (softmax from Probability primer §3, cross-entropy from its §7) that pulls the anchor toward \(\mathbf{z}^+\) and away from the crowd.

Worked number. Take an anchor \(\mathbf{z}\) with cosine similarity \(0.8\) to its positive \(\mathbf{z}^+\) and \(0.4\) and \(0.0\) to two negatives, with temperature \(\tau=0.2\). Divide each similarity by \(\tau\) (giving \(4.0,\,2.0,\,0.0\)), exponentiate (\(e^{4}=54.6,\ e^{2}=7.39,\ e^{0}=1\)), and the positive’s softmax share — hence the loss — is
\[
\frac{54.6}{54.6+7.39+1}=\frac{54.6}{62.99}=0.867,\qquad
\ell_{\text{InfoNCE}}=-\ln 0.867=0.143.
\]
The positive is the most similar, so it already owns most of the softmax mass and the loss is small. If its similarity collapsed to \(0.0\) (level with the weaker negative, behind the stronger one), its share would fall to \(1/(1+7.389+1)=1/9.389=0.1065\) and the loss would jump to \(-\ln 0.1065=2.24\) — the gradient then pulls \(\mathbf{z}\) hard back toward \(\mathbf{z}^+\) and away from the crowd (the gradient on the positive’s similarity, \((q-1)/\tau\) with \(q\) the positive’s softmax share, grows from \(-0.67\) to \(-4.47\), almost \(7\times\) stronger). (Smaller \(\tau\) sharpens this: it magnifies the gap between the positive and the near-miss negatives.)
The temperature is a knob worth seeing at three settings. Keep the same similarities (\(0.8,\,0.4,\,0.0\)) and compare the loss when the positive is clearly ahead with the loss when it falls to \(0.0\), behind one negative:



Table 4.4: The temperature sets how sharply the loss separates a clear win from falling behind; \(\tau\) near \(0.1\) to \(0.2\) is a common starting range (a rule of thumb from practice, not tested here).
