Full softmax or sampled? The sampled-softmax row of the table above is the sampled variant, and its typical user is large-catalog retrieval with two-tower models (which embed user and item separately, score by dot product and use in-batch negatives) — which samples precisely because scoring every item is what it cannot afford. BERT4Rec belongs to the softmax family but to the full side of it: its cloze objective (hide some of the user’s items and predict them) scores the whole catalog (the sequential-recommender bullet above). Same loss shape, different denominator — and the denominator is the whole distinction.

Takeaway. Pointwise losses fit exact \(0/1\) targets, pairwise losses ask for the right order of one pair, and listwise losses score the whole list at once: softmax asks the positive to top it, LambdaRank weighs each pair by how much the list’s metric moves. A softmax step sees the whole list at once: at temperature \(1\) on Ann’s three scores it pushes the positive by \(0.371\) and both negatives (by \(0.140\) and \(0.231\)), where one BPR step touches a single pair (\(0.269\) against the \(1.0\) negative, \(0.182\) against the \(0.5\) one); at \(\tau=0.1\) the positive’s push (one minus its softmax share) shrinks to about \(0.000046\), so the gradient on its score (that push divided by \(\tau\)) is \(0.00046\). What needs repair is a sample drawn unevenly (the log-\(Q\) correction), and a full softmax over every item needs none.

title: 4  Loss Functions & Regularizers
text:
11. Recent losses — self-supervised, contrastive & LLM-aligned
A first reading may skip section 11 and return after the recommender chapters (Part III onward); it is here because the losses belong together.
Ann has clicked a few dozen of ten thousand films, so BPR learns from a thin slice of the data. Most modern losses keep BPR and add terms that squeeze more out of the data’s own structure.
Self-supervised learning (SSL) means training on a task the data sets for itself — for example, make two perturbed copies of the same user’s data and ask the model to recognize them as the same — with no extra human labels. Much of modern recsys (the subject of Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning) does not replace BPR; it adds auxiliary losses on top to fix sparsity (each user has interacted with only a tiny fraction of the items, so the data are mostly empty cells: Ann’s \(36\) clicked films among ten thousand fill about \(0.4\%\) of her row) and popularity bias (§2.4).
The total objective becomes a sum of a main ranking loss and one or more auxiliary terms. Two notable exceptions below replace BPR outright: DirectAU (alignment + uniformity) and the VAE family (reconstruction + KL). (The Spectral / Graph-Filter View goes further still: the training-free filters it is built around minimize no loss at all.)
Contrastive auxiliary loss — InfoNCE on two views (self-supervised graph learning, SGL; SimGCL; LightGCL). First, the graph words. Treat users and items as dots (nodes) and draw a line (edge) for every interaction: that is the user–item graph. Ann and three of the films she clicked are four nodes joined by three edges. Graph recommenders such as LightGCN compute each node’s embedding by passing information along the edges, a step called propagation (on the four-node graph above, Ann’s new embedding is built from her three films’ embeddings, roughly their average; From Graphs to LightGCN §7 gives the exact weights).
SGL (Self-supervised Graph Learning, Wu et al., 2021) makes two perturbed “views” of the user–item graph (e.g. by edge dropout: deleting random edges for a training step, §12), embeds the same node twice, and pulls its two views together while pushing different nodes apart — the InfoNCE of §2.4. Its later, simpler relatives, SimGCL and LightGCL, change only how the second view is made; their names end in GCL, for graph contrastive learning. SimGCL (Simple Graph Contrastive Learning, Yu et al., 2022) adds small random noise to the embeddings instead of editing the graph, and LightGCL (Cai et al., 2023) builds the view from a compressed summary of the graph made with the singular value decomposition (SVD), Linear-Algebra primer §6.
All three are graph recommenders trained with: \[
\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{BPR}}}_{\text{main ranking}} \;+\; \lambda_{\text{cl}}\,\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}}_{\text{self-supervised}} \;+\; \lambda\,\underbrace{\|\Theta\|^2}_{\text{L2}},
\]
where \(\lambda_{\text{cl}}\) (“cl” for contrastive) sets how much the contrastive term counts. Here is where “loss” and “regularizer” blur on purpose: the contrastive term is a loss by form, but it is added for its regularizing effect — it shapes the embedding geometry, spreading embeddings out. Wang and Isola (2020) showed that, as the number of negatives grows, InfoNCE’s negatives act as a uniformity term, the term DirectAU uses below, whose case shows the spreading in numbers; that this helps the long tail is a reported effect, not tested here. Full treatment in Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning.
Worked example, one total. Take two losses already computed (they come from separate toy cases, and we only add their numbers): Ann’s BPR triple from §9 (\(0.2014\)) and the InfoNCE example of §2.4 (\(0.143\)), with \(\lambda_{\text{cl}}=0.2\) and \(\lambda=0.01\). The embeddings of that triple have \(\|\Theta\|^2=2+2.5+0.125=4.625\) (the squared lengths of \(\mathbf p_u,\mathbf q_i,\mathbf q_j\)). The three terms, using the two losses exactly as printed, are \(0.2014\), \(0.2\times0.143=0.0286\) and \(0.01\times4.625=0.04625\), so \(\mathcal L=0.2014+0.0286+0.04625=0.27625\) — the ranking term dominates and the contrastive and L2 terms are small corrections that shape the geometry.
The contrastive weight \(\lambda_{\text{cl}}\) at three settings (the ranking term \(0.2014\) and the L2 term \(0.04625\) stay the same):

The second column is the contrastive term and the fourth its share of the total. Each total is the exact sum of the three terms, using the two losses as printed in §9 and §2.4.

Alignment + Uniformity (DirectAU, Wang et al., 2022) — a negative-free objective. DirectAU is a recommender trained with two geometric terms instead of sampled negatives. It first scales every user and item embedding to length \(1\), so all of them lie on a sphere (in two dimensions, the unit circle of the figure Contrastive learning, drawn on the unit circle in §2.4): \[
\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{p}_u - \mathbf{q}_i\|^2}_{\text{alignment: pull interacting pairs together}} \;+\; \gamma\underbrace{\log\,\mathbb{E}\,e^{-2\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{v}'\|^2}}_{\text{uniformity: spread everything on the sphere}}.
\]

Symbols: the first average runs over interacting user–item pairs \((u,i)\), with \(\mathbf p_u,\mathbf q_i\) the user and item embeddings of §8, here scaled to length \(1\); in the second, \(\mathbf v,\mathbf v'\) are two different embeddings of the same kind — two users, or two items (DirectAU averages the user and item versions); \(\gamma\) is the balance weight between the two terms: at \(\gamma=0.25\) the uniformity term counts a quarter as much as alignment, and the table below tries \(0.1\), \(0.25\) and \(1\) (a separate use of the letter from focal loss’s exponent \(\gamma\) in §2.2).
Names (Wang & Isola, 2020): alignment = positives land close; uniformity = embeddings spread evenly over the unit hypersphere (the sphere of all length-\(1\) vectors, in however many dimensions the embeddings have). In the DirectAU paper the uniformity term is weighted by popularity, so it concentrates on the distances between popular users and items, and the paper says this helps reduce exposure bias (items the system showed more got more clicks; both statements are the paper’s, not tested here; From Graphs to LightGCN §13 measures popularity bias itself). Note this objective has no BPR-style ranking term: alignment is its loss (the only part that uses the clicks) and uniformity is its regularizer.
Decoding the uniformity term \(\log\,\mathbb{E}\,e^{-2\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{v}'\|^2}\): for two randomly chosen embeddings \(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{v}'\), the bell-shaped similarity \(e^{-2\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{v}'\|^2}\) (a Gaussian kernel) is \(\approx1\) when they sit on top of each other and \(\to0\) when far apart; the average \(\mathbb{E}\) over random pairs measures how clumped the cloud is, and the outer \(\log\) just tames the scale. Minimizing it forces random pairs apart — spreading embeddings over the sphere, which is uniformity.
Worked: three length-\(1\) embeddings in two dimensions. One rule does all the arithmetic: for length-\(1\) vectors the squared distance is \(2-2\cos\) of the angle between them (expand: \(\|\mathbf a-\mathbf b\|^2=\|\mathbf a\|^2+\|\mathbf b\|^2-2\,\mathbf a^\top\mathbf b=1+1-2\cos\)). Bunched within \(10^\circ\) of each other (at \(85^\circ\), \(90^\circ\), \(95^\circ\)), their squared distances are \(2-2\cos5^\circ=0.0076\), \(2-2\cos10^\circ=0.0304\) and \(0.0076\) again, so the three values \(e^{-2\|\mathbf v-\mathbf v'\|^2}\) are \(0.985\), \(0.941\), \(0.985\), and the uniformity is the log of their average, \(\ln 0.970=-0.03\). Spread evenly (\(120^\circ\) apart), every squared distance is \(2-2\cos120^\circ=3\), so the uniformity is \(\ln e^{-6}=-6\). Minimizing moves the first picture toward the second (the same figure, right). The alignment term for a user at \(0^\circ\) and her item at \(30^\circ\) is \(\|\mathbf p_u-\mathbf q_i\|^2=2-2\cos30^\circ=0.268\); it would be \(0\) if the two coincided.

The balance weight \(\gamma\) in numbers. The two terms pull against each other. Take one user at \(0^\circ\) who liked two films, placed at \(+\varphi\) and \(-\varphi\). Alignment (the user’s average squared distance to her films) is \(2-2\cos\varphi\), smallest when both films sit on her; uniformity (the item version only: the one item pair, \(2\varphi\) apart) is \(-2(2-2\cos2\varphi)\), smallest when the films are opposite. The total is \(\mathcal L(\varphi)=(2-2\cos\varphi)-2\gamma(2-2\cos2\varphi)\), and its slope (from \(\frac{d}{d\varphi}\cos\varphi=-\sin\varphi\) and \(\sin2\varphi=2\sin\varphi\cos\varphi\)) is \(\mathcal L'(\varphi)=2\sin\varphi\,(1-8\gamma\cos\varphi)\): negative below the angle where \(\cos\varphi=1/(8\gamma)\) and positive above it, so that angle is the minimum. It lies between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) only when \(\gamma>1/8\); otherwise the slope is never negative and \(\varphi=0^\circ\) wins:



Table 4.18: The total is alignment \(+\ \gamma\times\) uniformity. Up to \(\gamma=1/8\) alignment wins outright and the embeddings collapse; a large \(\gamma\) spreads the films at the cost of the user’s own fit.

Generative SSL — the variational autoencoder (VAE) objective (Mult-VAE). A different SSL family, generative because it learns by rebuilding its input. An autoencoder takes each user’s click history, a vector \(\mathbf x_u\) with a \(1\) for every item the user clicked and a \(0\) elsewhere (with four items, a user who clicked items 1 and 2 has \(\mathbf x_u=[1,1,0,0]\), the toy below). It squeezes \(\mathbf x_u\) into a short code \(\mathbf z\), here a single number such as \(0.5\) (the latent code: latent = hidden, never observed directly); this step is encoding. It then tries to rebuild \(\mathbf x_u\) from \(\mathbf z\) (decoding), for instance as the item probabilities \([0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1]\) of the toy. (This \(\mathbf z\) is not §2.4’s contrastive anchor; it is the standard letter for a VAE’s code.)
A variational autoencoder (Kingma & Welling, 2014) makes the code random: for each user the encoder outputs a small bell curve of plausible codes, \(q(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x_u)\), rather than a single point. Mult-VAE (Liang et al., 2018) is a VAE for recommendation whose decoder gives a probability to every item, with a multinomial likelihood — the user’s clicks treated like repeated rolls of a many-sided die whose faces are the items. It trains by minimizing the negative evidence lower bound (ELBO; worked below: the ELBO is \(-2.288\) on a four-item toy, so the loss is \(2.288\)): \[
\mathcal{L}=-\text{ELBO}_{\beta}= \underbrace{-\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\ln p(\mathbf x_u\mid \mathbf{z})\big]}_{\text{reconstruction loss}} \;+\; \beta\underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}\big(q(\mathbf{z}\mid \mathbf x_u)\,\|\,p(\mathbf{z})\big)}_{\text{KL regularizer}}.
\]

Symbols: \(q(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x_u)\) is the encoder’s bell curve of codes for this user; \(p(\mathbf x_u\mid\mathbf z)\) is the probability the decoder gives the user’s actual clicks when started from code \(\mathbf z\); \(\mathbb E_q[\cdot]\) averages over codes drawn from \(q\) (in practice, estimated from random draws); \(p(\mathbf z)\) is the prior on codes, a standard bell curve (mean \(0\), spread \(1\), written \(\mathcal N(0,1)\)); and \(\beta\ge0\) weighs the KL term.
Why “ELBO”: it is a lower bound (a result we take as given) on the log-likelihood \(\ln p(\mathbf x_u)\) of the data, which statisticians call the evidence — hence evidence lower bound. The true likelihood would need an average over every possible code \(\mathbf z\), which cannot be computed in practice, but this bound can, so training maximizes the bound instead. With \(\beta=1\) the displayed \(\mathcal L\) is exactly minus the ELBO, so minimizing \(\mathcal L\) maximizes the ELBO; a \(\beta<1\) weakens the KL pull.
Worked (a toy): four items; the user clicked items 1 and 2, so \(\mathbf x_u=[1,1,0,0]\). Suppose that for the drawn code the decoder gives the four items probabilities \([0.4,\,0.3,\,0.2,\,0.1]\): the reconstruction loss is \(-(\ln0.4+\ln0.3)=2.120\) — the surprise at the two clicked items. And suppose the encoder’s code for this user is a one-dimensional bell curve with mean \(\mu=0.5\) and spread \(s=0.8\): its KL divergence from the prior \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) has a closed form (a standard result we take as given), \(\tfrac12(s^2+\mu^2-1-\ln s^2)=\tfrac12(0.64+0.25-1+0.446)=0.168\). So \(\mathcal L=2.120+0.168\,\beta\) — that is, \(2.288\) with \(\beta=1\), so the ELBO is \(-2.288\): treating the one drawn code as the average, \(\ln p(\mathbf x_u)\ge-2.288\), so the model gives this user’s clicks a probability of at least \(0.101\).

The weight \(\beta\) at three settings, on that toy:



Table 4.19: A larger \(\beta\) gives the KL term a larger share; in training it pulls the code toward the prior at the cost of reconstruction (§13 names the extreme, posterior collapse).











\(\beta\)
\(\mathcal L=2.120+0.168\beta\)
share from the KL term
what it means




off: \(0\)
\(2.120\)
\(0\%\)
pure reconstruction: nothing pulls the code toward the prior


middle: \(1\)
\(2.288\)
\(7\%\)
the standard VAE


high: \(4\)
\(2.792\)
\(24\%\)
the KL term is now a quarter of the objective; in training the encoder would give up some reconstruction to shrink it (this toy holds reconstruction fixed)






This has the shape of §6’s split: a reconstruction loss (the negative log-likelihood of recovering the clicks) plus a KL regularizer (§2.4) pulling the code toward the standard bell-curve prior, with one difference: the KL here constrains each user’s code, not the model’s weights. The weight \(\beta\) is annealed (a heuristic from Bowman et al., 2016, that Mult-VAE adopts) — grown slowly from \(0\) during training — so that reconstruction is learned first (for example \(\beta=0\), then \(0.5\), then \(1\) as training proceeds: on the toy \(\mathcal L\) goes \(2.120\to2.204\to2.288\), so the KL pull arrives after the reconstruction term has had the objective to itself). Liang et al. stop at a cap picked on held-out data, often below \(1\) (their figure compares caps of \(1\) and \(0.2\)), so the \(1\) here only shows the shape. Contrastive-vs-generative is Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning’s central dichotomy.
LLM-aligned loss (RLMRec). A large language model (LLM) is a very large model trained on text to predict the next word — the technology behind today’s chatbots (given “Ann likes thrillers and”, it ranks “crime” above “cooking” as the next word).
RLMRec (Ren et al., 2024; the name comes from the paper’s title, Representation Learning with Large Language Models for Recommendation) uses one to write a short text profile of each user and item — what the user likes, who would enjoy the item — turns each profile into a vector with a text-embedding model (the semantic vector, which captures what the profile means), and adds an alignment loss (a different “alignment” from DirectAU’s: here each vector is pulled toward its own LLM profile; worked below: \(0.143\) when a user’s embedding sits close to its own profile vector, \(2.24\) when it is no closer than a stranger’s) that ties those semantic vectors to the collaborative embeddings of a base recommender such as LightGCN.
It comes in two variants. In RLMRec-Con (contrastive), the alignment is an InfoNCE (§2.4) whose positive pair is a user’s (or item’s) collaborative embedding and its own profile vector, with the other users and items in the batch as negatives: a user whose collaborative embedding has cosine \(0.8\) with its own profile vector and \(0.4\) and \(0.0\) with two other users’ profiles, at \(\tau=0.2\), pays the same \(0.143\) as the worked example there; if its own profile were no closer than a stranger’s (\(0.0\)), the cost would jump to \(2.24\).
In RLMRec-Gen (generative), some users’ and items’ embeddings are hidden (masked), and the model must rebuild their profile vectors from what remains: for instance, Ann’s embedding is hidden, the graph model builds a stand-in for it from the embeddings of films she clicked, and the model pays for how far that stand-in, mapped into the profile space, lands from her real profile vector. Either way: \[
\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{BPR}} \;+\; \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}(\text{LLM} \leftrightarrow \text{CF}) \;+\; \lambda\,\|\Theta\|^2.
\]
(The paper writes the sum unweighted; an implementation can multiply the alignment term by a tuned weight, the same kind of knob as \(\lambda_{\text{cl}}\).)
The point From Graphs to LightGCN §17 will make: LightGCN embeddings are featureless IDs — vectors attached to bare identifier (ID) numbers, with no description of the user or item behind them (to the model, Ann is only a row number in a table) — which is why there is room for an LLM’s semantic signal to be aligned in. Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning §7 develops this in full.
The table to remember — what each modern loss adds to BPR.



Table 4.20: Each family of §11 with the term it adds or the loss it replaces, and the number its worked example produced (the numbers measure different things and are not comparable across rows).










Family
What it adds or replaces
Worked value (this section)




SGL, SimGCL, LightGCL
an InfoNCE term between two views
\(\mathcal L=0.27625\) in the worked total


DirectAU
replaces BPR with alignment and uniformity
uniformity \(-0.03\) bunched, \(-6\) spread; alignment \(0.268\)


Mult-VAE
replaces BPR with reconstruction plus a KL term
\(\mathcal L=2.120+0.168\beta\)


RLMRec

title: 4  Loss Functions & Regularizers
section: 12. Regularizers as actually used in recommendation
text:
12. Regularizers as actually used in recommendation
A recommender with ten thousand films and a few dozen clicks per user (Ann’s numbers) overfits easily, and it drifts toward the items everyone already likes. Which of Part A’s regularizers does it reach for? Collecting the recsys-specific regularizers (most are Part-A regularizers in disguise):

L2 / weight decay on embeddings (weight decay in the plain-SGD sense of §5.1) — the usual default, \(\lambda(\|\mathbf{p}_u\|^2+\|\mathbf{q}_i\|^2)\) in MF, \(\lambda\|E^{(0)}\|^2\) in LightGCN, where \(E^{(0)}\) is LightGCN’s table of base embeddings — one row per user and per item, before any propagation (layer \(0\)); with \(1{,}000\) users, \(10{,}000\) items and \(64\) numbers per row, it has \(11{,}000\) rows. LightGCN regularizes only the base embeddings \(E^{(0)}\) (its sole parameters) — the propagated layers have no parameters of their own. Tuning \(\lambda\) is often one of the two or three highest-impact knobs (a practitioners’ rule of thumb, not tested here); it is chosen by trying a few values and keeping the one with the best score on the validation set (§5.2).
Embedding (L2) normalization — rescale each embedding to unit length before the dot product, turning it into cosine similarity. Removes raw-magnitude effects (a partial popularity-bias control) and stabilizes softmax/InfoNCE losses: a cosine lies in \([-1,1]\), so \(e^{\text{score}/\tau}\) is at most \(e^{1/\tau}\) (\(148\) at §2.4’s \(\tau=0.2\)), however long the raw vectors were. (A vector \([3,4]\) has length \(5\) and becomes \([0.6,0.8]\). If training gives popular items longer vectors, a reported effect not tested here, normalization stops them winning a dot product by length alone.)
Edge / message / node dropout — Part-A dropout (§5.2) applied to the graph, in three flavors: edge dropout deletes random interactions (edges) for a training step (at rate \(0.2\), a graph of \(1{,}000\) interactions trains on about \(800\)); node dropout deletes whole users or items, with all their edges (at rate \(0.1\), about \(100\) of \(1{,}000\) users sit out a step); message dropout sets random numbers of the embeddings passed along the edges during propagation to \(0\) (at rate \(0.1\), about one number in ten). In NGCF (Neural Graph Collaborative Filtering, Wang et al., 2019 — the earlier graph recommender whose design LightGCN simplified), message and node dropout are plain regularization (from van den Berg et al., 2017); in SGL, node and edge dropout are literally the augmentations that create the two contrastive views (Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning). One mechanism, two readings.
The contrastive / uniformity term itself — as noted in §11, an auxiliary SSL loss added for its regularizing effect on embedding geometry. One example of the loss/regularizer line dissolving. (In §11’s worked total it contributes \(0.0286\) of \(0.27625\).)
The KL term of a variational model — in §11’s Mult-VAE, the KL part of reconstruction + KL keeps each user’s code near its prior, a regularizer whose weight \(\beta\) is grown from \(0\) during training.
Early stopping on validation NDCG@\(K\) (NDCG, §10, computed on the top \(K\) of the list) — halt when ranking quality stops improving; the same implicit regularizer as §5.2, just measured with a ranking metric.

The weight \(\lambda\) at three settings on Ann’s triple of §9 (ranking loss \(0.2014\), \(\|\Theta\|^2=4.625\)):



Table 4.21: The weight decides whether the penalty is a brake or the whole objective.











\(\lambda\)
penalty \(\lambda\|\Theta\|^2\)
penalty as a multiple of the ranking loss
what it means




off: \(0\)
\(0\)
\(0\times\)
no brake: the embeddings may grow to fit the clicks


middle: \(0.01\)
\(0.046\)
\(0.23\times\)

\(23\times\)

Mental model (carry this into From Graphs to LightGCN and Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning). Task loss = “rank the right items first.” Regularizer = “…but don’t overfit, don’t let magnitudes or popularity run away.” In practice you tune a small handful of knobs — the learning rate, the L2 weight \(\lambda\), and (if using SSL) the contrastive weight \(\lambda_{\text{cl}}\) and temperature \(\tau\) — and those dominate the results (a rule of thumb from practice, not tested here).

title: 4  Loss Functions & Regularizers
text:
13. Decision guide
You have a recommender to train. Which loss, and which regularizer? Find the row below that matches your data and your goal; the second table then says how that choice can go wrong and the fix.



Table 4.22: Loss-and-regularizer selection by scenario: BPR + L2 (row 3) is the canonical starting point for implicit-feedback ranking; the two rows above are the older pointwise eras; the rows below keep it under a graph model, add a term to it (self-supervised, LLM alignment) or replace it (alignment + uniformity, VAE, sequential cross-entropy).










Scenario
Primary loss
Regularizer




Explicit star ratings (Netflix-era)
(regularized) MSE
L2 on embeddings


Implicit feedback, pointwise
Weighted MSE (WRMF) or BCE (NCF)
L2


Implicit feedback, ranking (the default)
BPR
L2 on embeddings


Graph-based CF (LightGCN family)
BPR
L2 on base embeddings (LightGCN: no dropout)


Self-supervised graph (SGL/SimGCL/LightGCL)
BPR + InfoNCE
L2; edge dropout (SGL) or embedding noise (SimGCL); the InfoNCE term itself


Negative-free geometric
Alignment + Uniformity
(uniformity is the regularizer)


Generative / VAE (Mult-VAE)
Reconstruction (negative log-likelihood)
KL (β-annealed)


LLM-augmented (RLMRec)
BPR + alignment(LLM↔︎CF)
L2


Sequential (SASRec, BERT4Rec)

dropout, layer-norm






What goes wrong with each loss — and the fix. The table above says what to pick; this one says how each choice bites back in practice, and the standard remedy (most failure modes here were met above; the one that was not, posterior collapse, is explained in its row, and collapse and the alignment–uniformity tug of war appear in §11’s \(\gamma\) table):



Table 4.23: Each loss’s characteristic failure mode and the standard fix — most failures trace back to a mismatch between what the loss assumes and what the data actually is; the rest are settings outside their safe range.










Loss
Failure mode
Fix




MSE / WRMF
MSE put on top of a sigmoid saturates — gradient vanishes exactly when confidently wrong (§2.3); WRMF’s hard \(0\) target for un-clicked items is a lie (§7)
use cross-entropy/BPR for the order; keep MSE only for genuinely numeric targets


BCE (pointwise)
trains an absolute \(0/1\) score that a top-\(K\) ranking does not need, and the rare positives drown in negatives
switch to BPR for ranking, or focal (\(\gamma{>}0\)) under heavy imbalance


Huber
\(\delta\) mis-scaled: too large \(\to\) pure MSE (outlier-sensitive), too small \(\to\) MAE-like (outliers matter little, but nearly every residual sits on the linear piece, §2.1’s table)
set \(\delta\approx1.35\,\hat s\) (§2.1); re-estimate the spread \(\hat s\) if the residual scale drifts


BPR
uniform negatives are mostly easy, obscure items, and popular items are rarely pushed down (§2.4); one negative per step is low-signal
sample harder or more negatives (hard negatives may tilt toward popular items, a claim from practice), or move to sampled softmax for more negatives per step


Sampled softmax
when negatives are drawn in proportion to popularity (in-batch negatives, §10), popular items appear in the sampled set too often and get over-penalized
subtract the log-\(Q\) correction (§10) to debias the sampled gradient


InfoNCE / NT-Xent
\(\tau\) too small \(\to\) unstable: the pull on a collapsed positive grows as \(1/\tau\) (§2.4: \(-4.47\) at \(\tau=0.2\), larger as \(\tau\) shrinks); \(\tau\) too large \(\to\) no contrast; too few or too easy negatives \(\to\) a weak signal
tune \(\tau\) (a typical start is \(\approx0.1\)–\(0.2\)); draw more or harder negatives


Alignment + Uniformity
the two terms fight: \(\gamma\) too high spreads everything (alignment lost), too low lets the embeddings collapse to a point (every input gets nearly the same vector, so nothing is told apart; §11’s \(\gamma=0.1\) row: the user and both films all end at \(0^\circ\), alignment and uniformity both \(0\))
tune the balance weight \(\gamma\); watch alignment and uniformity move together


VAE / ELBO
a too-strong KL causes posterior collapse (the failure Bowman et al., 2016, describe, with the KL term settling at zero) — the encoder’s \(q(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x_u)\) is pushed all the way to the prior, so the code \(\mathbf z\) carries no information about the user and reconstruction degenerates (on §11’s toy, \(\mu\to0\) and \(s\to1\) drive the KL from \(0.168\) to \(0\))
anneal \(\beta\) from \(0\) (§11) so reconstruction establishes first






Bottom line. The whole field is two moves: pick a loss that matches your target (number → MSE; label → cross-entropy; order → BPR / softmax) and add a regularizer that keeps the fit honest (usually L2 on the embeddings, as in \(6\) of the decision table’s \(9\) rows, plus dropout / SSL terms as you climb toward the state of the art). BPR + L2 is the canonical recsys starting point; most of what follows in From Graphs to LightGCN and Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning is built on top of it — and The Spectral / Graph-Filter View shows when you can skip the training loss altogether.

title: 4  Loss Functions & Regularizers
text:
14. Exercises
Work these by hand — the numbers are kept tiny on purpose. Several repeat a worked example of the chapter (§2.2, §2.4, §3, §9, §10) with new numbers, so you can check your method against the text without finding the answer printed there. They run from easy to hard: seven computations first, then three questions on ideas, one small application and two extensions. Exercises 8 and 10 open with a recall question (the answer is in the section they cite, to be said in your own words) and then ask for a computation with new numbers. Full worked solutions are in the Solutions appendix at the back of the book.

(compute) A model leaves three residuals \(r=\hat y-y\) of \(\{0.5,\,-2,\,1\}\). Compute the MAE \(\tfrac1N\sum|r|\), the MSE \(\tfrac1N\sum r^2\), and the mean Huber loss with \(\delta=1\) (§2.1). Which point alone makes MSE so much larger than MAE, and is that point treated by Huber as quadratic or linear?
(compute) The model predicts probability \(\hat p=0.65\) for a positive example (\(y=1\)). Compute the BCE \(-[\,y\ln\hat p+(1-y)\ln(1-\hat p)\,]\) (§2.2). Then recompute it for the same \(\hat p=0.65\) but a negative example (\(y=0\)). Which of the two costs more, and why does that match “the surprise (\(-\log\)) at the right answer”?
(compute) A classifier outputs logit \(z\); recall \(\hat p=\sigma(z)\) and \(\ell_{\text{BCE}}=-[y\log\hat p+(1-y)\log(1-\hat p)]\). (a) At \(z=1\) (\(\hat p=\sigma(1)=0.7311\)), compute the loss for \(y=1\) and for \(y=0\). (b) At \(z=-1\) (\(\hat p=\sigma(-1)=0.2689\)), compute it for \(y=1\) and for \(y=0\). (c) Raise the logit to \(z=2.5\) (\(\hat p=\sigma(2.5)=0.9241\)) and recompute the loss for \(y=1\) and for \(y=0\): which of the two losses changed by more compared with part (a), and by how many nats?
(compute) Repeat the chapter’s §3 gradient step on a new point — model \(\hat y=w x\), point \((x{=}1,\,y{=}4)\), start \(w=1\), learning rate \(\eta=0.1\), squared-error loss — and find the new \(w\). Then add an L2 term \(\lambda w^2\) with \(\lambda=0.25\) (§5.1), recompute the gradient and the update, and state how far the new \(w\) lands from the unregularized one.
(compute) L2 with learning rate \(\eta=0.05\), \(\lambda=2\), and no data gradient. (a) What is the per-step shrink factor \((1-2\eta\lambda)\)? (b) Starting from \(w=2\), list \(w\) after \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\) steps. (c) After how many steps is \(w\) first below \(0.001\)?
(compute) Take a BPR triple like the chapter’s §9 one, with new scores: positive \(\hat r_{ui}=1.0\), negative \(\hat r_{uj}=0.2\). (a) Compute the gap \(d\), then \(\sigma(d)\), the per-triple loss \(-\ln\sigma(d)\), and the gradient \(-(1-\sigma(d))\) (§9). Now swap the two scores (a wrong triple) and recompute all four. By what factor does the loss grow, and by what factor does the gradient grow? (b) Repeat the two factors for a pair of scores \(1.5\) and \(-1.0\) (a gap of \(2.5\)): which of the two factors grows faster from the gap of part (a) to this one, and what is each factor now?
(compute) Use §2.4’s setup with new numbers: an anchor with cosine similarity \(0.6\) to its positive and \(0.3,\,-0.1\) to two negatives, temperature \(\tau=0.5\). Compute the InfoNCE loss \(-\ln\dfrac{e^{\,0.6/\tau}}{e^{\,0.6/\tau}+e^{\,0.3/\tau}+e^{\,-0.1/\tau}}\) (§2.4). Then redo it with the positive’s similarity collapsed to \(-0.1\) (a tie with the last negative), and say by what factor the loss grows.
(concept) Both L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) shrink weights, but only one drives some weights to exactly zero (§5.1). Which one, and — using the geometry of the figure Why L1 is sparse and L2 is not (§5.1) — explain in two sentences why the shape of that penalty produces exact zeros (sparsity) while the other, smooth one only shrinks toward zero. Then, with §5.1’s one-weight formulas and \(\lambda=0.6\), find what each penalty makes of three weights whose data pulls are \(a=0.2\), \(-0.5\) and \(2\), and count the exact zeros.
(concept) Both penalize weight size (§5.1). (a) Ask what each does to the weights that survive: differentiate both penalties and say how much each subtracts per gradient step from a weight of \(10\) and from a weight of \(0.01\), with learning rate \(\eta=0.1\) and \(\lambda=0.1\). (b) You have \(10{,}000\) candidate features and want a model that uses only a handful — which penalty, and what does each penalty make of a feature whose data pull is \(a=0.04\) at \(\lambda=0.1\) (§5.1’s one-weight formulas)? (c) With no data gradient and the same \(\eta\) and \(\lambda\), start a weight at \(w=0.03\) and take three steps of each penalty alone (L1 with soft-thresholding: your part (a) step, but stopped at \(0\); L2 with its shrink factor, §5.1). Where does each weight end?
(concept) §6 shows that the five losses and regularizers of its table are each the \(-\log\) of a probability. State which noise distribution on \(y\) gives the MSE loss, and which prior on \(\theta\) gives the L2 regularizer, and explain in one or two sentences why “\(-\log\) of a product” turns the MAP objective (posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior) into the sum “loss \(+\) regularizer.” Then, with spread \(s_y=1\), compute \(-\ln p(y\mid\hat y)\) for two predictions that miss by \(1\) and by \(3\), and their difference: which part of each number depends on the prediction, and which part could never change which prediction is best?
(apply) A matrix-factorization recommender (§8) stores user \(\mathbf{p}=[2,1]\) and item \(\mathbf{q}=[1,2]\), scores by the dot product \(\hat r=\mathbf{p}^{\top}\mathbf{q}\), and trains with regularized MSE \(\mathcal{L}=(r-\hat r)^2+\lambda(\|\mathbf{p}\|^2+\|\mathbf{q}\|^2)\). For an observed rating \(r=5\) and \(\lambda=0.1\), compute \(\hat r\), the squared-error term, the L2 term, and the total objective. Then treat the same user as having clicked the item \(\mathbf q\) and skipped a second item \(\mathbf q'=[1.5,0.5]\), and compute the BPR gap \(d\) and the per-triple loss \(-\ln\sigma(d)\) (§9), leaving the penalty out.
(extend) A computer using 64-bit floats stores numbers only up to about \(e^{709}\) and down to about \(e^{-745}\). (a) At score \(x=-800\), why does -log(sigmoid(x)) fail to give \(-\ln\sigma(-800)\)? Then find that value to three decimals by a route that never forms a number above that range (an overflow). (b) A softmax has logits \([800,\,802]\), so both \(e^{800}\) and \(e^{802}\) overflow. Compute \(\ln(e^{800}+e^{802})\) without forming it, and say what you did.
(extend) §10’s sampled softmax needs the log-\(Q\) correction to undo the popularity skew of its sample. Two negatives share the same raw score \(\hat r_{uj}=1\): a popular one drawn with probability \(Q=0.4\) and a rare one with \(Q=0.05\). Compute each item’s corrected contribution to the softmax denominator, \(e^{\hat r_{uj}}/Q\) (equivalently \(e^{\,\hat r_{uj}-\ln Q}\)), and state the ratio by which the rare item is up-weighted. Then, with a positive of raw score \(3\) (left uncorrected) and a third negative of raw score \(1.5\) drawn with \(Q=0.5\), compute the positive’s share of the corrected denominator (the positive plus the three negatives).

title: 4  Loss Functions & Regularizers
text:
15. Glossary







Term
Plain meaning




Activations
The numbers a layer outputs; each unit’s is computed from the previous layer’s (§5.2).


Alignment & uniformity
Pull positives together / spread embeddings on the sphere (DirectAU); its popularity-weighted uniformity is said to help reduce exposure bias (items the system showed more got more clicks; a claim of the DirectAU paper, not tested here).


Alignment loss (RLMRec)
Ties the vectors of LLM-written user/item profiles to the collaborative (CF) embeddings — contrastively (RLMRec-Con) or by rebuilding masked profiles (RLMRec-Gen).


AUC
Area under the ROC curve: the fraction of (positive, negative) pairs ordered correctly; BPR is its smooth stand-in (§9).


Batch normalization / layer normalization
Re-center and re-scale activations across a batch / within one example: \([2,4,6]\to[-1.22,0,1.22]\) (§5.2).


Bias–variance trade-off
Error splits into systematic mis-fit (bias) and sensitivity to the sample (variance); model complexity trades one against the other (§4).


BPR
Bayesian Personalized Ranking — pairwise ranking loss; “Bayesian” = its MAP derivation; default for LightGCN.


Cloze objective
Hide some of a user’s items and predict them from the rest (BERT4Rec; §10).


Contrastive learning / views
Learning embeddings by comparison: two views of the same thing are pulled together, other things pushed apart (§2.4).


Cost / objective / criterion
Near-synonyms for loss (cost = total; objective = neutral; criterion = the code object).


Cross-entropy / BCE / log loss
Classification loss; average code length (nats with \(\ln\), bits with \(\log_2\)) to encode the truth \(p\) with a code built for the prediction \(q\); BCE = −log-likelihood of a Bernoulli (categorical cross-entropy: of a categorical).


Data augmentation
Train on randomly perturbed copies of inputs; one history \([A,B,C,D]\) gives four views (§5.2).


Dropout
Randomly zero units during training; an ensemble-like regularizer; “edge dropout” on graphs.


Early stopping
Stop when validation stops improving; implicit regularizer.


Elastic net
L1 + L2 combined; “stretchable net” keeping correlated features.


ELBO
Evidence lower bound: a computable lower bound on the data’s log-likelihood that a VAE (variational autoencoder) maximizes; Mult-VAE minimizes reconstruction loss + β·KL, which is exactly −ELBO when β = 1 (§11).


Embedding
The vector of numbers a model learns to represent a user, item or other object (§2.4).


Epoch / batch
One full pass over the training data / the small group of examples used for one update (§5.2).


ERM
Empirical Risk Minimization — “fit the training data” (usually + a regularizer).


Explicit vs. implicit feedback
Star ratings vs. clicks/plays (positive-only, unlabeled negatives).


Focal loss
Cross-entropy times \((1-p_t)^\gamma\), with \(p_t\) the probability of the true class, to down-weight easy examples; for class imbalance.


Gradient descent
Update \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial\theta\); step the parameters downhill.


Hinge loss
The loss of the support vector machine (SVM), a classic classifier that separates two classes with the widest possible gap between them; flat once correct-with-margin (\(m=y\hat y\ge1\)), then a linear ramp — shaped like a hinge.


Huber loss
Quadratic near 0, linear far out; robust compromise (after P. Huber).


InfoNCE / NT-Xent
Contrastive loss: \(-\log\) of the positive’s softmax share, the denominator running over the positive and the negatives; Info = mutual-info bound, NCE = Noise-Contrastive Estimation; temperature \(\tau\).


KL divergence
Asymmetric “distance” between distributions (Kullback–Leibler); a divergence, not a metric.


Knob (hyperparameter)
A value set by hand before training (\(\delta\), \(\gamma\), \(\tau\), \(\eta\), \(\lambda\)), not learned from the data like the parameters \(\theta\) (§2.1).


L1 / lasso
\(\sum|\theta_k|\) penalty; shrinks and selects (exact zeros → sparse); = Laplace prior centered at \(0\).


L2 / ridge / Tikhonov / weight decay
\(\sum\theta_k^2\) penalty; shrinks weights smoothly toward 0; = Gaussian prior centered at \(0\). Weight decay is the same thing under plain (stochastic) gradient descent, not under Adam (hence AdamW, §5.1).


Lambda \(\lambda\) (regularization strength)
How much we weight the regularizer vs. the loss.


LambdaRank / LambdaMART
Listwise methods that write no loss, only a gradient weighted by each pair’s effect on NDCG (the per-pair gradients are Burges’s \(\lambda_{ij}\)).


Learning rate \(\eta\)
The step size in gradient descent.


Likelihood / prior / posterior
\(p(\text{data}\mid\theta)\) / \(p(\theta)\) / \(p(\theta\mid\text{data})\).


log-\(Q\) correction
Subtract \(\log\) of an item’s sampling probability from its score, so negatives drawn in proportion to popularity (e.g. in-batch negatives) do not over-penalize popular items; under uniform sampling it removes no popularity skew and only rescales the negatives’ total (§10).


log-sum-exp / softplus
\(\log\sum_i e^{z_i}\), a smooth stand-in for the largest \(z_i\) that normalizes a softmax (\(1.313\) for logits \(1\) and \(0\), against a largest logit of \(1\)); \(\text{softplus}(z)=\log(e^0+e^{z})\) is its two-term case with one logit at \(0\) (§2.4).


Logistic loss
BCE written on the margin \(m=y\hat y\) with labels \(\pm1\): \(\ln(1+e^{-m})\) (§2.2).


Loss function
A single number measuring how wrong the model is; training minimizes it.


MAE / absolute loss
Mean of absolute errors; from Laplace noise; outlier-robust; targets the median.


MAP (maximum a posteriori) estimate
Maximize posterior ∝ likelihood × prior; ⟹ minimize (−log-lik) + (−log-prior) = loss + regularizer.


Matrix Factorization (MF)
\(\hat r_{ui}=\mathbf{p}_u^\top \mathbf{q}_i\); trained with regularized MSE.


MSE / squared loss
Mean of squared errors; from Gaussian noise of the same spread for every point; outlier-sensitive.


Mult-VAE
A variational autoencoder for recommendation with a multinomial likelihood; loss = reconstruction + \(\beta\cdot\)KL (§11).


NCF / NeuMF
Neural collaborative filtering: feed user and item embeddings through a small network instead of a dot product; trained with BCE (§10).


NDCG
Normalized discounted cumulative gain: each relevant item earns \(1/\log_2(\text{rank}+1)\), divided by the best possible total; \(1\) = perfect list (§10; Evaluation Metrics §7).


Negative sampling
Drawing un-interacted items to act as negatives — uniformly by default (mostly easy, obscure items; each candidate equally likely, so a popular item, being a positive for many users and never their negative, is drawn less often overall, §2.4), or in proportion to popularity / by hardness, which over-samples popular items (§2.4, §10).


Overfitting
Memorizing training noise; great on train, poor on new data.


Pointwise / pairwise / listwise
Score each (user, item) pair alone / the order of two items / the whole list at once (softmax: does the positive top it; LambdaRank: pairs weighted by the metric).


Popularity bias / long tail
A recommender over-suggesting already-popular items at the expense of the long tail of rarely seen ones (§2.4).


Posterior collapse
A VAE’s code pushed all the way to the prior, so it carries nothing about the user (§13).


Regularization
Making an ill-posed solution “regular” (well-behaved); from Hadamard/Tikhonov.


Regularizer
A term/procedure that discourages complex solutions to improve generalization.


Residual
\(r=\hat y-y\), the miss on one point (§2.1).


Risk / empirical risk
Expected loss over the true distribution / its average on the training sample.


Sampled softmax (SSM)
Listwise cross-entropy over a positive + many sampled negatives; structurally = InfoNCE.


Shrink factor
\(1-2\eta\lambda\), what one L2 step multiplies a weight by (§5.1).


Sigmoid / logit
\(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\) squashes a raw score \(z\) (the logit) into \((0,1)\) (§2.2).


Soft-thresholding
Move a weight a fixed amount toward zero and stop at \(0\) if it would cross: \(\lambda/2\) in §5.1’s one-weight solution.


Softmax
Smooth (“soft”) version of argmax; turns scores into a probability distribution.


Supervised / self-supervised learning (SSL)
Learning from examples that come with their correct answers / from a task the data sets for itself, with no human labels (§1, §11).


Surprise
\(-\log p\) of what happened (§2.3).


Temperature \(\tau\)
Divides the scores inside a softmax: small \(\tau\) makes the winner take nearly everything (§2.4, §10).


Two-tower model
Embeds user and item with two separate networks and scores by dot product; trained with sampled softmax (§10).


Validation set
A slice of the data held out from training and used only to measure progress (§5.2).


WRMF / ALS
Weighted Regularized MF / Alternating Least Squares (implicit-feedback, squared error).



This chapter’s framework in one breath: training minimizes a loss (the −log-likelihood: how surprised the model is by the data) plus a regularizer (the −log-prior: how surprised we are by the parameters). Pick the loss to match your target — a number (MSE), a label (cross-entropy), or an order (BPR / softmax) — and add a regularizer (usually L2 on the embeddings) to keep it honest. Nearly everything in From Graphs to LightGCN and Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning is a specific instance of that one sentence — and the training-free filters of The Spectral / Graph-Filter View are the instructive exception.

title: 5  Neural Networks & Back-propagation
text:
1. A single neuron (from the linear model)
A neural network is, stripped of mystique, a stack of linear maps with a nonlinearity between them, trained by gradient descent (Calculus primer §5) using gradients computed by the chain rule (Calculus primer §3). That one sentence is the entire idea; this chapter unpacks it from zero, and the centrepiece is a single neuron, then a small two-layer network, whose forward pass (the numbers flowing from the input to the output) and one back-propagation step (back-prop for short; §5) we compute entirely by hand. It matters because this is how most of the learned models in this book are trained (§10), and it is the base on which the next chapter, Representation Learning & the Transformer, builds.
What this chapter assumes: from the three math primers, the dot product / matrix–vector product (Linear-Algebra primer; used from §1), the chain rule, partial derivatives, the Jacobian and gradient descent (Calculus primer §3, §4, §8, §5; used in §5), and the sigmoid, softmax and the normal distribution with its variance (Probability primer §1–§3; used in §2, §4 and §6); from Loss Functions & Regularizers, what a loss is (§1; used in §4), the bias–variance trade-off (§4; used in §7) and the regularizers (§5; used in §7). Not assumed: any earlier knowledge of neural networks; the neuron, the layer and back-propagation are built here from zero. This chapter is where the chain rule earns its keep.
Whether Ann will like a film depends on several clues at once: how much action it has, how funny it is, how long it runs. You want one score out of all of them, with each clue allowed to count for more or for less. How do you build that score? This section builds it, and a whole network turns out to be many such scores wired together.
A neural network is a stack of linear maps (each one turns inputs into scores by weighted sums, as a matrix–vector product, Linear-Algebra primer §3) with a nonlinearity between them: §2 explains the nonlinearity, §3 the stacking, and §5–§6 the training. Its one repeated part is the neuron (also called a unit). Start with the simplest model: a weighted sum of inputs plus a constant, exactly the score from the Linear-Algebra primer’s dot product.
\[
z \;=\; w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_n x_n + b \;=\; \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b.
\]
A neuron then applies a function \(\phi\) (the activation function, §2) to that score: \(a = \phi(z)\). The result \(a\) (\(a\) for activation) is the neuron’s output, its post-activation value — the partner of the pre-activation \(z\). When §3 puts many neurons side by side, their outputs \(a\) are collected into one vector, written \(\mathbf{h}\).
Worked example. Inputs \(\mathbf{x}=[1,2]\), weights \(\mathbf{w}=[0.5,-0.5]\), bias \(b=0\): \[
z = (0.5)(1)+(-0.5)(2)+0 = 0.5 - 1.0 = -0.5.
\]
That single number is the neuron’s score; §2 squashes it into an output.
In one line: a neuron is a weighted sum plus a bias, \(z=\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x+b\). Back to Ann: with ratings of \(1\) for action and \(2\) for funniness (invented for the example) and weights \(0.5\) and \(-0.5\), her score for the film is \(-0.5\), because funniness counts against it.

title: 5  Neural Networks & Back-propagation
text:
\(\mathbf{x}\) — the inputs (features).
\(\mathbf{w}\) — the weights (how much each input matters; learned).
\(b\) — the bias (a constant offset, shifting the threshold; learned).
\(z\) — the pre-activation (the raw score; for a classifier’s last layer it is called the logit, Probability primer §3).



Why “neuron,” “weights,” “bias.” The model is loosely inspired by a biological neuron that fires when its inputs exceed a threshold. The weights weight each incoming signal; the bias is the firing threshold moved to the other side of the equation. The single unit with a step activation (output \(1\) if \(z\ge 0\), else \(0\) — an on/off switch) is the historic perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958) — perceive + -tron.

title: 5  Neural Networks & Back-propagation
section: 2. Activation functions — and why a nonlinearity is essential
text:
2. Activation functions — and why a nonlinearity is essential
Bob likes a film when it is a comedy or a thriller, but not when it mixes both. A score made only by adding up clues cannot say “one or the other, not both”. What has to be put between two sums so that a stack of them is more than one sum? This section answers that.
The activation function \(\phi\) takes the score \(z\) and produces the neuron’s output. The three you meet first:



Table 5.1: The three canonical activation functions — sigmoid for probability outputs, tanh for zero-centered hidden layers, and ReLU as the usual default, which avoids the vanishing-gradient problem for \(z>0\) (the box below explains); Nair & Hinton (2010) used rectified linear units as the hidden units of restricted Boltzmann machines.











Name
Formula
Range
Note




Sigmoid
\(\sigma(z)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\)
\((0,1)\)
“probability-like”; from the Probability primer §3


Tanh (hyperbolic tangent)
\(\tanh(z)=\dfrac{e^{z}-e^{-z}}{e^{z}+e^{-z}}\)
\((-1,1)\)
a sigmoid stretched to \((-1,1)\) and centered on \(0\): \(\tanh(z)=2\sigma(2z)-1\)


ReLU (rectified linear unit)
\(\max(0,z)\)
\([0,\infty)\)
the usual default hidden-layer activation since the early 2010s (a claim from practice, not tested here) — cheap, no vanishing slope for \(z>0\)







Why “activation,” “tanh” and “ReLU.” Activation = how strongly the neuron “fires.” Tanh is short for hyperbolic tangent: it plays for the hyperbola the role the ordinary tangent function plays for the circle — hence the name (most calculators have a tanh key). ReLU = Rectified Linear Unit: “rectified” (as in a rectifier that clips negatives to zero) + “linear” (it is the identity for \(z>0\)).

Worked example. \(\text{ReLU}(-2)=0\) and \(\text{ReLU}(3)=3\). Applying sigmoid to §1’s score: \(\sigma(-0.5)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{0.5}}=0.3775\). Applying tanh to the same score: \[
\tanh(-0.5)=\frac{e^{-0.5}-e^{0.5}}{e^{-0.5}+e^{0.5}}=\frac{0.6065-1.6487}{0.6065+1.6487}=\frac{-1.0422}{2.2552}=-0.4621
\]
— negative, because tanh keeps the sign of its input, where the sigmoid’s output is always positive. The table’s “stretched sigmoid” claim is one line of algebra: \(2\sigma(2z)-1=\dfrac{2}{1+e^{-2z}}-1=\dfrac{1-e^{-2z}}{1+e^{-2z}}\), and multiplying top and bottom by \(e^{z}\) gives exactly the tanh formula.






Figure 5.1: The three activations: sigmoid squashes to \((0,1)\), tanh to \((-1,1)\) (zero-centered), ReLU passes positives and zeros negatives (note its kink, the corner at \(0\), and flat slope for \(z<0\)). The bend each one adds is the nonlinearity — without it, stacked layers collapse to a single line (below).




Why ReLU is the usual default. Sigmoid and tanh saturate — far from \(0\) their curves go flat, so the slope \(\to 0\) and gradients (§5: the loss’s slope per nudge of a weight) vanish, stalling the early layers of a deep net (many layers, §3): the sigmoid’s slope is \(0.25\) at \(z=0\), \(0.105\) at \(z=2\) and only \(0.018\) at \(z=4\).
With weights of size about \(1\) or less, ten layers each passing back at most \(0.25\) leave at most \(0.25^{10}\approx10^{-6}\) of the gradient. (With weights near \(4\) the factor per layer is \(0.25\times4=1\); §6 sets the starting weights with care.) ReLU’s slope is exactly \(1\) for \(z>0\), so the gradient flows back undiminished (the usual reason it largely replaced squashing activations: a claim from practice, not tested here). The flip side: a unit stuck at \(z<0\) gets zero gradient and can stay “dead”.

Two variants soften the dead unit by giving negatives a small non-zero output and slope. Leaky-ReLU (Maas et al., 2013) is \(\max(0.01z,\,z)\) (a slope of \(0.01\) is a common choice), so \(\text{Leaky-ReLU}(-2)=-0.02\) instead of \(0\). GELU (Gaussian error linear unit; Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016) multiplies \(z\) by the probability that a standard bell-curve (Gaussian) variable — mean \(0\), variance \(1\) — lands below \(z\) (Probability primer §1–§2): a smooth ReLU look-alike. For \(z=-2\) that probability is \(0.02275\) (the bell’s thin left tail, read from a table of the standard bell curve or computed by software rather than worked out by hand), so \(\text{GELU}(-2)=-2\times0.02275=-0.0455\).
Why the nonlinearity matters — the crucial point. Put several neurons side by side and their weight vectors stack, one per row, into a matrix \(W\): that is a layer (§3 builds it properly). Now stack two linear layers — no activation — with weight matrices \(W^{(1)}\) and \(W^{(2)}\) (the \((1)\) and \((2)\) in parentheses are layer numbers, labels and not powers). You get \(W^{(2)}(W^{(1)}\mathbf{x}) = (W^{(2)} W^{(1)})\mathbf{x}\) — still just one linear map, because a product of matrices may be regrouped (Linear-Algebra primer §3: grouping does not matter, only order does). No amount of stacking adds power. A two-line check, with \(W^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(W^{(2)}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf x=[1,1]\): \[
\underbrace{W^{(1)}\mathbf x=[3,\,1],\quad W^{(2)}[3,\,1]=[3,\,4]}_{\text{layer by layer}}
\qquad\qquad
\underbrace{W^{(2)}W^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix},\quad \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}\mathbf x=[3,\,4]}_{\text{one matrix}}
\]
— the single matrix \(W^{(2)}W^{(1)}\) does both layers’ work. The nonlinearity \(\phi\) between layers is what lets a deep network bend space and represent functions a single line cannot — the classic example being XOR (exclusive-or: output \(1\) if and only if exactly one input is \(1\), i.e. the two inputs differ), which no single straight line can separate (panel (a) of the figure after the next example) but a 2-layer net can (two weight matrices, with one hidden layer of neurons between input and output; §3 builds one).
Worked example — a 2-layer net that computes XOR. Two hidden neurons (neither input nor output, §3; each is §1’s neuron with ReLU) and one output neuron with no activation; the hat in \(\hat y\) (“y-hat”) marks the network’s prediction: \[
h_1=\text{ReLU}(x_1+x_2),\qquad h_2=\text{ReLU}(x_1+x_2-1),\qquad \hat y=h_1-2h_2 .
\]
