Pairing helps only when the two models’ scores rise and fall together across seeds, as they do here (the correlation between the two columns is \(0.71\)); if they moved independently, pairing would gain nothing. The test also covers only the randomness of training. Which users happen to be in the test set is a separate source of luck, and the bootstrap below handles it.
A confidence interval, and what to do when the metric isn’t Gaussian (bell-shaped: most values near the middle, few far out). For model A alone: mean \(0.420\), sample standard deviation \(0.016\), \(\text{SE}=0.016/\sqrt5\approx0.0072\), so the \(95\%\) confidence interval (CI) is a Student-\(t\) interval with the same \(n{-}1{=}4\) degrees of freedom and \(t^{*}=2.776\) (Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning §8): \(0.420\pm2.776(0.0072)=0.420\pm0.020=[0.400,\,0.440]\).
But per-user scores are usually not Gaussian (most users score \(0\), a few score \(1\)), so the cleaner tool is the bootstrap (Efron, 1979): resample the test users with replacement a few thousand times, recompute the metric each time, and read the \(2.5\)th and \(97.5\)th percentiles (the value below which \(2.5\%\), respectively \(97.5\%\), of the resampled scores fall) as the interval. It assumes no distribution at all. Report the interval, not just the point estimate.
Bootstrap, with numbers. For the non-Gaussian per-user case above: say \(20\) test users give HR@10 \(=1\) for \(6\) of them (mean \(0.30\)). One resample-with-replacement repeats some users and drops others for \(7/20=0.35\); another gives \(5/20=0.25\). Over a few thousand resamples, the \(2.5\)/\(97.5\) percentiles land at \([0.10,\,0.50]\) — wide for just \(20\) users, and assuming no distribution at all.
The verdict, made concrete — and it is the gain’s interval that decides. Take the paired example above: B beats A by a headline \(+0.002\) NDCG@10, with the \(5\) per-seed gains \(d=[+0.01,-0.01,+0.02,-0.01,0.00]\): \(\bar d=+0.002\), but they swing in sign, so \(\text{SE}=0.0058\), the paired \(t=0.34\) (\(p=0.75\)), and the \(95\%\) CI of the gain is \([-0.014,\,+0.018]\) — it includes \(0\). So the \(+0.002\) is within run-to-run noise and you do not ship B on this evidence. The headline mean never told you that; its interval did. (Test mechanics and three more cases: Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning §8.7, where the per-seed gap is A’s score minus B’s, so the roles of A and B are swapped.)
In one line: a gain counts only if its interval clears \(0\); Bob’s \(+0.002\) had \(p=0.75\) and a \(95\%\) interval of \([-0.014,+0.018]\), so it is not shown to be better.






Figure 8.6: Significance is whether the gain’s interval clears \(0\). Top: the observed B-vs-A gain, \(\bar d=+0.002\) with \(95\%\) CI \([-0.014,+0.018]\), crosses \(0\) — the win is within noise, so do not ship. Bottom: a hypothetical gain whose CI \([+0.010,+0.015]\) sits entirely above \(0\) — ship. Two results can share a positive headline mean yet differ here; the interval, not the mean, is the verdict.





11e. Are the scores themselves meaningful? Calibration
Bob’s film site prints a percentage beside every film it shows Ann: “80% match”. Bob asks whether Ann really likes four of every five films marked 80%. Ranking metrics cannot answer, because they only look at the order of the films. This part checks the numbers themselves.
Many uses need the score to be a trustworthy probability: a “watch-probability” shown to the user, a threshold for whether to recommend at all, or blending scores across models. A model is calibrated if, among items it scores \(0.8\), about \(80\%\) are actually clicked.
Check it with a reliability diagram: group the predictions into bins of similar predicted value (say, all predictions near \(0.8\)) and plot each bin’s predicted vs observed click rate; points on the diagonal mean calibrated. The one-number summary is the Expected Calibration Error (ECE): the average absolute gap (its size, ignoring sign) between predicted and observed rates, each bin weighted by its share of the predictions.
Worked, two bins of \(5\) items. A high-confidence bin predicts \(0.80\) but only \(3/5=0.60\) click (gap \(0.20\)); a low bin predicts \(0.20\) and \(1/5=0.20\) click (gap \(0\)). So \[\text{ECE}=\tfrac12(0.20)+\tfrac12(0)=\boxed{0.10},\] and the model is over-confident (its scores promise more clicks than happen), as the figure below shows. With five items in a bin the arithmetic stays small; a real bin holds hundreds, so a gap of \(0.20\) on five items proves nothing by itself.






Figure 8.7: Reliability (calibration) diagram for the §11e worked example. Each dot is one prediction bin: the x-coordinate is the bin’s mean predicted probability; the y-coordinate is the fraction of items in that bin that were actually clicked. The dashed diagonal is perfect calibration (\(\hat{p}=\) observed rate). The blue dot (low bin: \(\hat{p}=0.20\), observed \(=0.20\)) lies on the diagonal. The red dot (high bin: \(\hat{p}=0.80\), observed \(=0.60\)) sits below the diagonal by \(0.20\) — the model is over-confident. The hollow circle marks where that bin would sit if it were calibrated, \((0.80, 0.80)\). ECE is the weighted average of these gaps: \(\tfrac{1}{2}(0.20)+\tfrac{1}{2}(0)=0.10\).




Why the names. Each bin is weighted by its share of the predictions, so ECE is the gap you would expect for a prediction picked at random; to calibrate is to adjust an instrument until its readings match reality; a reliability diagram shows whether the scores can be relied on as probabilities.

The plain idea. Think of a weather forecaster. On the days she says “80% chance of rain”, it should rain on about four days in five. If it rains on only three of five such days, her “80%” is not a probability: still fine for sorting days from wet to dry, but wrong for deciding whether to carry an umbrella. Our toy model is that forecaster. On its five films marked \(0.80\) the user liked only \(3\), so the correct label is \(0.60\). Calibration is relabelling: print \(0.60\) where the model said \(0.80\) and leave \(0.20\) alone. No film changes place, only the numbers beside them. The ECE of \(0.10\) says how far off the labels are on average.
The fixes are cheap post-hoc rescalings, applied afterwards to an already-trained model’s scores: Platt scaling (Platt, 2000: fit an S-shaped curve to the raw scores) or isotonic regression (fit a staircase that never goes down). Both recalibrate the numbers without ever reversing the ranking: Platt keeps the order exactly when the fitted slope \(a\) is positive (the normal case), and isotonic regression’s flat steps can merge neighboring scores into ties. The two boxes below show how each is fitted; skip them on a first reading.

Side issue: how Platt scaling is fitted. Platt scaling and isotonic regression both learn a map from a model’s raw score \(s\) to a calibrated probability. Here \(s\) is the number the model computes before any squashing into \([0,1]\), and it can be any real number; for a model whose last step is a sigmoid it is the logit of its probability, \(s=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}\) (Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning §3). So the model’s \(0.80\) comes from \(s=\ln\frac{0.8}{0.2}=\ln 4=1.386\), and its \(0.20\) from \(s=-1.386\). The map is fitted on the validation set of §11a, never on the test set.
Platt scaling fits a two-parameter S-curve: find two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) that minimize the cross-entropy (the log loss of §1) between the binary click labels and \[p_{\text{cal}} = \sigma(a\,s + b), \qquad \sigma(z)=\tfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}},\] where \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid, the S-shaped function that squashes any real number into \((0,1)\) (Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning §3). The curve always has this S shape; only its position (\(b\)) and slope (\(a\)) are fitted, which is cheap even on large validation sets.
Worked. Fitting the ten validation items of the ECE example (a computer does the minimizing) gives \(a\approx0.65\) and \(b\approx-0.49\). Check it by hand: the high bin’s \(s=1.386\) becomes \(\sigma(0.65\times1.386-0.49)=\sigma(0.41)=0.60\), exactly its observed rate, and the low bin’s \(s=-1.386\) becomes \(\sigma(-1.39)=0.20\), which was already right. With two bins and two numbers to fit, the best fit reproduces both observed rates. It is the pair \((a,b)\) acting together, not \(a\) alone, that moves \(0.80\) down to \(0.60\) while leaving \(0.20\) in place.

The second fix, isotonic regression, is fitted differently.

Side issue: how isotonic regression is fitted. It fits a free monotone (non-decreasing) step function, a staircase that never goes down as the score goes up (“isotonic” means order-preserving), with no fixed shape such as the sigmoid assumed. Its fitting rule, the pool-adjacent-violators (PAV) algorithm, is simple enough to run by hand. It is more flexible than Platt scaling, but needs more validation data to avoid over-fitting (copying the noise of a small sample into the steps).
Worked. Five validation items, sorted by raw score:



raw score \(s\) (sorted)
\(-1.2\)
\(-0.4\)
\(0.3\)
\(0.9\)
\(1.6\)




clicked? (\(1\) = yes)
\(0\)

\(1\)
\(1\)


calibrated \(g(s)\) after PAV
\(0\)
\(0.5\)
\(0.5\)
\(1\)
\(1\)



A calibrated map must never go down as the score rises, but the click row has a \(1\) followed by a \(0\), a violation. PAV pools such a pair of neighbors into their average, \(\tfrac{1+0}{2}=0.5\), giving the last row. No value now drops below the one before it, so this staircase is the calibrated map: among all non-decreasing rows it is the one closest to the clicks in squared error (the sum of squared differences, here \(0.5\)).
Had the pooled value still sat below its left neighbor, PAV would pool again; it needs only about one pass along the sorted list, so its work grows in step with the number of items \(n\), written \(O(n)\), “order \(n\)”. Note the tie it created: items 2 and 3 now share \(0.5\) although their raw scores differ, so break such ties with the raw score.
Both fixes are post-hoc: they are applied to a frozen model’s output scores without any retraining, and a non-decreasing map never swaps two items (only isotonic regression’s ties can merge neighbors). The key reference is Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (2005, at the International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML), who benchmarked both methods across classifiers (models that sort inputs into classes). As they report it, Platt scaling works best when a model’s distortion is sigmoid-shaped, as for support vector machines (SVMs) and boosted trees, two classic families of classifiers, while isotonic regression can correct any monotone distortion but over-fits more easily and does worse than Platt scaling when data are scarce (reported there, not tested here).

In one line (calibration): a score of \(0.80\) should mean \(80\%\); in the toy the \(0.80\) bin was right \(60\%\) of the time, an ECE of \(0.10\), and a post-hoc rescaling repairs the numbers without changing the order.


11f. The five lenses as one checklist
You have now met five separate ways a number can mislead: a leaky split, a sampled ranking, an offline score that real users do not share, a gap that is only luck, and scores that do not mean what they say. Nobody keeps five sections in mind while reading a paper, so this subsection folds them into one list to run down before trusting any result.

The one-paragraph protocol checklist. Before trusting any Recall@K / NDCG@K: (1) split by time if you can, and never leak; (2) rank against the full catalog, or disclose the sampling; (3) treat offline as a proxy and confirm with an A/B test; (4) report mean \(\pm\) std over seeds with a significance test, and always state \(K\) and binary-vs-graded relevance; (5) if the raw scores are read as probabilities, check calibration and rescale them if needed (§11e). The fanciest metric on a leaky, sampled, single-seed protocol is worth less than Recall@20 measured correctly.


In practice. Start with the cheap, standard pair: Recall@\(K\) (or NDCG@\(K\)) plus one beyond-accuracy number — coverage or Gini is enough. Serendipity is aspirational: it needs a baseline and user labels, so it is rarely computed in published work (a claim from practice, not tested here). Rank against the full item catalog, not a sampled handful of negatives — Krichene & Rendle (2020) showed that sampled top-\(K\) metrics can reverse which model wins versus full ranking.
The three graph collaborative-filtering (CF) recommenders behind this book’s graph chapters — NGCF (neural graph collaborative filtering), LightGCN and SGL (self-supervised graph learning) — are evaluated that way in their papers, with full ranking; Datasets & Benchmarks §4 records the protocol, while the graph chapters quote the Recall@20 results and do not restate it. Finally, guard against leakage: if interactions are timestamped, use a global temporal split so nothing from the test period (or its future) leaks into training. On this point those same three models are not the ones to copy: they are evaluated on a random per-user split, which does not guard against it (Datasets & Benchmarks §4).


→ Which frameworks enforce this? The Implementation Choices appendix §5 lists the toolkits that bake in these protocols (RecBole, Cornac, Elliot — open-source software toolkits for running recommender experiments) and the papers behind each pitfall here — Krichene & Rendle on sampled metrics, Ferrari Dacrema et al. on under-tuned baselines, Ji et al. (2023) on data leakage.

In one line: a trustworthy number needs a leak-free split, full-catalog ranking, an online check, a gain whose interval clears zero and, when scores are read as probabilities, calibration (ECE \(0.10\) in the §11e toy): in the example above, a \(+0.002\) gain had a \(95\%\) interval of \([-0.014,+0.018]\) and was not worth shipping.

title: 8  Evaluation Metrics
section: 12. Bias, fairness, and the feedback loop
text:
12. Bias, fairness, and the feedback loop
Cara never clicked on Vendetta. Did she dislike it, or did the site simply never show it to her? The log cannot tell. This section names the biases that this blindness creates, shows how they grow over time, and ends with the fix and with a second question: good for whom?
Every metric so far quietly assumed the test set was a fair sample of what the user would have liked. It is not. A recommender’s logged data is not a random sample: it is what the system itself chose to show and what the user then chose to click. The parts of this section: the biases that creates (§12.1–§12.2), the loop that makes them worse (§12.3), the standard tool to correct them, inverse propensity scoring (IPS) (§12.4), and the second question metrics usually skip: not just is the list good? but good for whom? (§12.5), and the practitioner takeaways (§12.6).

12.1 The core problem — the data is missing-not-at-random (MNAR)
Why not simply count the clicks? Because the clicks we have come only from the films the system chose to show.
Statisticians call data MNAR — Missing-Not-At-Random when whether a value is observed depends on the value itself (and on choices that correlate with it). Recommendation logs are the textbook case: you mostly observe interactions for items the system promoted, so the missing entries are missing for a reason, not by coin-flip. Computing a metric naively over this log therefore measures the old system’s habits as much as the new model’s quality — the estimate is biased.

Why “MNAR.” Read literally: the data that is Missing is missing Not At Random. The comfortable opposite is missing completely at random (MCAR): the gaps are pure coin-flips, unrelated to anything — the assumption that lets you ignore the problem, and one that recommender logs almost never satisfy (a claim from practice, not tested here). Statisticians also name a middle case, missing at random (MAR): whether a value is missing may depend on other things that were recorded — say, the list position an item was shown in — but not on the missing value itself.

In one line: a film shown to \(20\) of \(100\) users can only collect clicks from those \(20\); the other \(80\) are missing, not negative.


12.2 The bias taxonomy
A film is liked by \(80\%\) of users and still earns few clicks. Why? Three biases, defined once each. They are distinct but feed one another (§12.3).

Selection / exposure bias — users can only interact with items they were shown. Un-shown items have no feedback, so their absence from the clicks says nothing about whether the user would have liked them. (“Selection” = the system selected what to expose; “exposure” = only exposed items can be judged.) Toy, the film of §12.1 shown to \(20\) of \(100\) users: its clicks can come only from those \(20\); the other \(80\) users have given no feedback at all, and their silence means “not shown”, not “disliked”.
Position bias — within a shown list, items higher up get more clicks regardless of true relevance, simply because they are seen first (a claim from practice, not tested here; the toy assumes its rates). A rank-1 slot can out-click a more relevant rank-8 item — so a click is partly a vote for position, not only for quality. Toy, with assumed looking rates: users look at rank \(1\) with probability \(0.9\) and at rank \(8\) with probability \(0.2\), and click what they look at if they like it. A film \(V\) liked by \(50\%\) of users, shown at rank \(1\), earns \(0.9\times0.5=0.45\) clicks per page shown; a film \(Z\) liked by \(80\%\), shown at rank \(8\), earns \(0.2\times0.8=0.16\). \(V\) out-clicks \(Z\) about \(2.8\) times although \(Z\) is the better film.
Popularity bias — already-popular items (the head of the popularity curve, as opposed to the long tail of §10) dominate exposure and feedback, crowding out the long tail (a claim from practice, not tested here). Toy, with assumed counts: in a catalog of \(10\) films the \(3\) most popular take \(70\) of every \(100\) clicks, about \(23\) clicks each, while each of the other \(7\) films gets about \(4\). The toy of §12.3 shows how that gap grows. This is the Gini / long-tail effect of §10, made dynamic — see From Graphs to LightGCN §13 for the numerical version.




Table 8.6: The three logging biases. Each makes the recorded clicks an unfair sample of true preference, so a metric computed naively on the log rewards the old system’s exposure policy, not only the new model’s quality.










Bias

In one line: three biases tilt the log; in the toy a film liked by \(50\%\) at rank \(1\) earns \(0.45\) clicks against \(0.16\) for one liked by \(80\%\) at rank \(8\).


12.3 The feedback loop — why bias compounds
The three biases are tied together by a dynamic that makes them grow over time:

the model recommends popular / high-position items → users interact with those (because those are what they saw) → the new interactions are logged as training data → that data is even more skewed toward the popular / high-position items → the next model trained on it is more biased → it recommends those items even harder …

This is the “rich get richer” spiral: a small head-start in exposure becomes a self-reinforcing advantage. Bias is not a one-off measurement error you correct once; in practice it is reported to amplify with every retraining cycle if left alone (a claim from practice, not tested here; the toy below shows the mechanism under an assumed rule). It must be designed against continuously (§12.6), and audited over time, not just at a single snapshot. The figure draws the cycle; the toy after it puts numbers on it.






Figure 8.8: The recommendation feedback loop. What the model recommends shapes what users can click; those biased clicks become the next model’s training data; the next model is more skewed still. Because the skew compounds every cycle (the red center), bias must be designed against continuously — measuring it once is not enough.



The loop, with numbers. Two films, \(X\) and \(Y\), are equally good: each is clicked by \(30\%\) of the users it is shown to. The first model gives \(X\) \(60\) of every \(100\) slots and \(Y\) \(40\). Clicks follow exposure, \(60\times0.3=18\) on \(X\) and \(40\times0.3=12\) on \(Y\), so \(X\) holds \(60\%\) of the clicks.
The next model is trained on those clicks and sharpens: its exposure share for each film is proportional to the square of that film’s share of the clicks. With \(s\) the share of slots \(X\) holds, \[s_{\text{next}}=\frac{s^2}{s^2+(1-s)^2},\qquad\text{round 1: }\ \frac{0.6^2}{0.6^2+0.4^2}=\frac{0.36}{0.52}=0.692 .\] Each round applies the rule to the previous round’s output, with its clicks again proportional to its exposure, so each row is the next. Four rows are enough to see it: by round 3 the tail film holds \(4\) slots in \(100\), and further rounds push it only closer to \(0\). Carrying the fractions exactly (round 2 is \(81/97=0.8351\); starting from the rounded \(0.69\) instead would print \(0.83\)):



Table 8.7: Two equally good films under the sharpening rule \(s_{\text{next}}=s^2/(s^2+(1-s)^2)\), starting from a \(60/40\) split. The tail film \(Y\) loses its slots in three retrainings although its quality never changed.

The films are equally good, yet \(Y\) falls from \(40\) slots to \(4\) in three rounds: the whole drift is made by the loop and none by quality. At \(50/50\) the rule changes nothing, but that balance is unstable: any tilt grows. The squaring is our assumption, a stand-in for a model that puts the apparent winner in the better positions (§12.2), so that it gains more than its share of the clicks; with the exponent \(1\) there would be no drift at all, and the exponent of a real system is unknown.
In one line: two equally good films, a \(60/40\) start and a rule that gives the leader slightly more than its share: the tail film falls from \(40\) slots to \(4\) in three retrainings.


12.4 IPS — inverse propensity scoring (the standard fix)
If the problem is that some items were shown far more than others, the fix is to re-weight each observed interaction by how unlikely it was to be observed in the first place. That is IPS — Inverse Propensity Scoring (for evaluating recommenders: Schnabel et al., 2016).

Propensity = the probability that an item was shown / observed (its propensity to be seen). Call it \(p\) (not the \(p\)-value of §11d). In practice \(p\) is estimated from the logs — for instance as the fraction of sessions in which the item was displayed (an item shown in \(20\) of \(100\) sessions has \(p=0.2\)). It is measured most reliably on a small slice of traffic where items are shown in random order, so that exposure is known exactly (a claim from practice, not tested here).
Weight each observed interaction by \(\boxed{1/p}\) — the inverse of its propensity (\(p=0.2\) gives weight \(5\)). An over-exposed item (high \(p\)) gets down-weighted; a rarely-shown item (low \(p\)) gets up-weighted, so its one hard-won click counts for more. When \(p\) is the true exposure probability and is never \(0\) for an item that matters, the re-weighted count is an unbiased estimate — right on average — of the metric you would have measured under uniform exposure (the worked example below shows exactly what that means); an estimated \(p\) is only approximately unbiased, and clipping or self-normalizing (below) trade the rest for less noise.

Worked example (check by hand). Take two new items, unrelated to §3’s list and to the films of §12.3: item \(X\) was shown with propensity \(p_X=0.8\), item \(Y\) with \(p_Y=0.2\). A click on each contributes its inverse propensity: \[
\text{click on }X \;\to\; \frac{1}{p_X}=\frac{1}{0.8}=\boxed{1.25},
\qquad
\text{click on }Y \;\to\; \frac{1}{p_Y}=\frac{1}{0.2}=\boxed{5}.
\] So a click on the rarely-shown \(Y\) is worth \(5/1.25=\boxed{4\times}\) a click on the heavily-shown \(X\) in the unbiased estimate. Intuition: \(Y\) “had to overcome” being shown only a quarter as often as \(X\) (\(0.2\) vs \(0.8\)), so each \(Y\)-click is far stronger evidence of genuine preference.
Now the whole estimate — why dividing by \(p\) removes the bias. Suppose \(X\) and \(Y\) are in truth equally good: each is clicked \(30\%\) of the times it is shown. Over \(100\) sessions the old system shows \(X\) in \(80\) of them (\(24\) clicks) and \(Y\) in \(20\) (\(6\) clicks), so the raw click counts make \(X\) look \(4\times\) better. IPS re-weights every click by \(1/p\): \(X\) gets \(24\times1.25=30\) and \(Y\) gets \(6\times5=30\) — equal, and exactly the \(30\) clicks each item would have earned had it been shown in all \(100\) sessions (uniform exposure). That is what unbiased means here: on average, the re-weighted count lands on the number you would have seen if every item had been shown equally, whatever the old system’s habits.
Applied to a metric: IPS-weighted recall. Back on §3’s list (relevant items \(\{B,C,E,G\}\), top-5 \([A,B,C,D,E]\), hits \(B,C,E\)), suppose the logs say that \(B\) and \(C\) were shown with propensity \(0.8\) and \(E\) and \(G\) with \(0.2\) (assumed values for the toy). The weights \(1/p\) are \(1.25\), \(1.25\), \(5\) and \(5\). Raw Recall@5 gives every relevant item one vote: \(3/4=0.75\). The IPS-weighted Recall@5 gives each relevant item its weight and divides the weight of the hits by the weight of all the relevant items: \[\text{Recall@5}_{\text{IPS}}=\frac{1.25+1.25+5}{1.25+1.25+5+5}=\frac{7.5}{12.5}=0.60 .\]
The score falls from \(0.75\) to \(0.60\) because the item the list missed, \(G\), was a rarely shown one: it is \(1\) of \(4\) items in the raw count (\(25\%\)) but \(5\) of the \(12.5\) weight (\(40\%\)). Dividing by the total weight (the self-normalized form) keeps the score between \(0\) and \(1\) at the price of a little bias. The same re-weighting works for other metrics. For a Hit Rate over users, a user whose hit came from an item with \(p=0.2\) counts \(5\) instead of \(1\) in the sum (before any normalizing). This weighted recall is this book’s self-normalized adaptation of the estimators in Schnabel et al. (2016), not their exact formula.

Why “inverse propensity.” You weight by the inverse (\(1/p\)) of the propensity (\(p\), the chance of being shown). This is exactly the \(1/Q\) importance-weighting behind the sampled-softmax log-\(Q\) correction in Loss Functions & Regularizers §10 — there you divide by an item’s sampling probability to undo a biased negative sampler; here you divide by its exposure probability to undo a biased logging policy (the rule by which the old system decided what to show). Same idea — un-bias an estimate by dividing out the probability that produced the sample — in a different place. (Caveat: tiny propensities give huge weights and noisy estimates, so in practice they are clipped.)

In one line: weight each click by \(1/p\): \(X\) and \(Y\) both come out at \(30\), and on the running list the IPS-weighted Recall@5 is \(0.60\) against the raw \(0.75\).


12.5 Fairness — “good for whom?”
Accuracy metrics ask is the list good? Fairness asks the sharper question: good for whom? (The survey of Ekstrand et al., 2022, is the standard reference.) Recommendation is inherently multi-stakeholder — at least users, providers (item creators / sellers), and the platform — and a list that is great on average can be systematically worse for some group. Two sides:

Consumer / user-side fairness — is recommendation quality (Recall, NDCG, …) comparable across user groups (e.g. by age, gender, region)? Unfair if one group reliably gets worse lists.
Provider / item-side fairness — is exposure comparable across item creators / groups? The long tail being starved of exposure (§10) is partly a provider-fairness problem: a few providers can capture most of the recommendation slots, as in the toy below.

Two standard group-fairness definitions, borrowed from classification, one line each:

Demographic parity — equal selection / exposure rate across groups (each group is recommended / shown at the same rate, whatever share of each group would like the item).
Equal opportunity — equal true-positive rate (TPR) across groups: the share of the truly relevant cases that get surfaced, the idea of §8 counted over users instead of items (among users who would like an item, each group is equally likely to actually have it surfaced).

Both, on tiny numbers. Demographic parity (provider exposure): a feed has \(100\) recommendation slots and two provider groups that each own half the catalog: the popular studios fill \(85\) slots, the long-tail creators \(15\). The exposure rates are \(0.85\) vs \(0.15\) — a parity gap of \(0.70\), where parity would require \(0.50/0.50\).
Equal opportunity (consumer TPR): among the users who genuinely would like a given item, what fraction get it in their top-\(K\)? Group 1: \(120\) of \(200\) → TPR \(0.60\); group 2: \(80\) of \(200\) → TPR \(0.40\) — an equal-opportunity gap of \(0.20\). The two ask different questions: parity wants equal exposure regardless of preference; equal opportunity wants an equal hit-rate among those who would actually like the item — a model can satisfy one and fail the other.
These can trade off against accuracy. Toy, with assumed click rates: a popular-studio slot is clicked \(10\%\) of the time and a long-tail slot \(6\%\). The unconstrained \(85/15\) split of \(100\) slots earns \(85\times0.10+15\times0.06=9.4\) clicks; forcing \(50/50\) earns \(50\times0.10+50\times0.06=8.0\), about \(15\%\) fewer. Whether real systems pay this price, and how much, varies (a claim from practice, not tested here). There is no free lunch: fairness is a deliberate choice about which good you are optimizing, the same lesson as §1’s “different metrics measure different goods.”
In one line: the parity gap (\(0.85\) against \(0.15\) is \(0.70\)) and the equal-opportunity gap (\(0.60\) against \(0.40\) is \(0.20\)) are different checks, and forcing parity in the toy costs about \(15\%\) of the clicks.


12.6 Practitioner takeaways


Report by group, not just on average. Break out exposure / coverage (§10) per user and per provider group — an aggregate number hides who is being underserved.
Prefer IPS-corrected offline metrics for click data (the worked recall of §12.4), since raw clicks carry position and exposure bias. Estimate the propensity \(p\) (the chance an item was shown, §12.4) from exposure logs — an item’s display-count share, a fitted position-bias curve (the chance of a click at each list position, estimated from the logs), or, most reliably in practice (a claim from practice, not tested here), a small randomized-exposure slice (traffic where items are shown in random order, so exposure is known exactly) — and clip extreme propensities (put a floor under \(p\), which caps the weight \(1/p\)) so one rarely-shown item can’t dominate the estimate.
Stratify by popularity, not just the average. Report NDCG/Recall on head vs. tail items (head: the few most popular; tail: the many rarely seen, §10) separately: a model can lift top-line NDCG purely by serving the popular head better while the tail rots, and only a per-bucket split reveals it (the same lesson as the Gini coefficient, §10). Toy, with assumed scores: model M1 scores NDCG \(0.30\) on head items and \(0.05\) on tail items, model M2 \(0.34\) and \(0.02\). With \(80\%\) of the test cases on head items, the top-line NDCG rises from \(0.250\) to \(0.276\) while the tail score falls to \(0.4\) of its old value.
Audit the feedback loop over time, not once. The “rich get richer” skew (§12.3) is a trajectory: track concentration (Gini, §10) and group exposure across successive retrainings, and confirm real gains with an A/B test (§11c), the only judge the loop cannot fool.


In one line: the log shows only what was shown; the loop turns a \(60/40\) tilt into \(96/4\) in three rounds, IPS re-weights by \(1/p\), and fairness asks for whom the list is good.

title: 8  Evaluation Metrics
text:
13. Which metric, when?
Bob has a dozen scores on his screen and one slot in the report. Which number should he put there? The answer depends on what Bob’s site is for, so this section maps each goal to a metric and ends with one rule that covers them all.



Table 8.8: Which evaluation metric to reach for, by goal — there is no single “best” metric; the right one encodes what you mean by a good recommendation.









Your goal
Reach for




Predict a rating accurately (★1–5)
RMSE (punish big misses) or MAE (robust)


Top-\(K\) list, “find all the good items”
Recall@K


Top-\(K\) list, “don’t waste slots”
Precision@K (or F1@K for balance)


Just need one good item, fast
MRR (or HR@K)


Position + graded relevance (the default)
NDCG@K


Binary relevance, every relevant item should rank high
MAP


Overall ranking quality (pairwise)
AUC (ties to BPR, Loss Functions & Regularizers §9)


Is the catalog used / list varied / fresh?
coverage, diversity, novelty, serendipity, Gini


Is the score a trustworthy probability?
ECE (§11e) and LogLoss (§1)


Is the list fair to each group?
per-group metrics: demographic parity, equal opportunity (§12.5)






Golden rule: report at least one accuracy metric and at least one beyond-accuracy metric — a single number hides the popularity trap. Always state the \(K\) (Recall@10 \(\ne\) Recall@50) and whether relevance is binary or graded.
In one line: pick the metric that matches the goal in the table, report one accuracy number and one beyond-accuracy number, and always say \(K\): on the running list Recall@3 is \(0.50\) but Recall@5 is \(0.75\).

title: 8  Evaluation Metrics
text:
14. Exercises
Work these by hand — the numbers are kept tiny on purpose. Several use a second user, introduced in exercise 2, so that you compute fresh numbers instead of re-reading the chapter’s; the chapter’s running example (relevant set \(\mathcal{R}=\{B,C,E,G\}\), top-5 list \([A,B,C,D,E]\) with hits at ranks 2, 3, 5) returns as a comparison in exercise 5. Full worked solutions are in the Solutions appendix at the back of the book.

(compute) A rating model predicts \([3,5,2,4]\) for four movies whose true ratings are \([4,5,4,3]\). Compute the MAE and the RMSE (§2). Which of the two is larger here, and which single prediction is most responsible for that gap?
(compute) A second user has relevant set \(\{C,F,G\}\) and receives the top-5 list \([C,A,F,B,D]\). Compute this user’s Precision@5, Recall@5, and F1@5 (§4). State in one phrase what each of the three numbers is telling you.
(compute) Reciprocal rank and MRR (§5), for three users. The first is the second user of exercise 2. For the other two users the first relevant item sits at rank 5 and at rank 3 of their top-5 lists. Compute the three reciprocal ranks and the MRR averaged over the three users.
(compute) For the second user of exercise 2, compute the Average Precision (§6): find the ranks of the hits, the precision at each hit position, and divide their sum by the number of relevant items. Show the Precision@\(k\) values you used.
(compute) Compute the NDCG@5 (§7) of the second user’s list (exercise 2): its DCG@5, the ideal IDCG@5 (all three of their relevant items at the top), then the ratio. Is it higher or lower than the running list’s \(0.593\), and why, in one line? (Useful: \(\log_2 3\approx1.585\), \(\log_2 4=2\).)
(apply) AUC as a pairwise probability (§8). A model scores two relevant items \(\{0.8,\,0.5\}\) and two irrelevant items \(\{0.6,\,0.3\}\). List the \(2\times2=4\) (relevant, irrelevant) pairs, count how many the model orders correctly (relevant scored higher), and report the AUC. Is it above the \(0.5\) of random guessing?
(apply) IPS-weighted recall (§12.4). For the second user of exercise 2 (relevant films \(\{C,F,G\}\), top-5 list \([C,A,F,B,D]\)) the logs say the three relevant films were shown with propensities \(p_C=0.5\), \(p_F=0.25\) and \(p_G=0.1\). (a) Give the weight \(1/p\) of each film. (b) Compute the IPS-weighted Recall@5 (the weight of the hits divided by the weight of all the relevant films) and, for comparison, the raw Recall@5. (c) Which film accounts for most of the difference between the two numbers, and why?
(extend) Gini and serendipity (§10). (a) A 5-item catalog is recommended with counts \([6,3,1,0,0]\) (10 recommendations, mean \(\mu=2\)); compute the Gini coefficient \[G=\frac{\sum_i\sum_j|x_i-x_j|}{2n^2\mu}\] and say whether this catalog is more or less concentrated than the chapter’s \([8,2,0,0,0]\) (\(G=0.72\)). (b) Of the second user’s 2 relevant hits (exercise 2), suppose one — item \(C\) — is a blockbuster that a popularity baseline would have shown anyway; compute serendipity@5 and say how it compares with the Precision@5 you found in exercise 2, and why.
(apply) Two lists, four metrics (§4, §5, §7). A user has \(4\) relevant films. List P puts two of them at ranks \(1\) and \(2\) of its top \(5\); list Q puts two at ranks \(3\) and \(5\). (a) Compute Precision@5 and Recall@5 of each list. (b) Compute the reciprocal rank and the NDCG@5 of each (the ideal DCG@5 for four relevant films is \(2.562\), §7). (c) If only the first suggestion is ever used, which of the four metrics would you trust, and how many times larger is list P’s value than list Q’s on it? Answer in one sentence.
(apply) Full against sampled (§11b). A catalog has \(8\) items. For model P the held-out item has full rank \(5\) (four items score higher, three lower); for model Q it has full rank \(6\) (five higher, two lower). Each is re-ranked against \(3\) negatives drawn at random from the other \(7\) items and scored by HR@2. (a) Under full ranking, does either model score a hit? (b) There are \(35\) ways to choose \(3\) negatives from \(7\) (ordered picks divided by orderings, as in §11b). For P, in how many does the held-out item land in the top \(2\) of its four candidates? Answer the same for Q. (c) In one line, what do your two fractions say about comparing a sampled HR@2 with a full-ranking HR@2?
(apply) Looks better, but should you ship? Model B beats A by a headline \(+0.003\) NDCG@10. Over \(5\) shared seeds the per-seed gains are \[d=[+0.012,\,-0.006,\,+0.011,\,-0.004,\,+0.002].\] (a) Compute the mean gain \(\bar d\) and say whether it is positive. (b) Compute its \(95\%\) confidence interval (CI) from the five gains, using the \(t\) multiplier \(2.776\) for \(5\) runs (§11d): does it clear \(0\)? (c) Ship B or not, and give the one-sentence reason (§11d).
(apply) Calibration (§11e). A model’s predictions fall in three bins. Bin 1: predicted \(0.9\), \(10\) predictions, \(7\) clicked. Bin 2: predicted \(0.6\), \(20\) predictions, \(9\) clicked. Bin 3: predicted \(0.2\), \(10\) predictions, \(2\) clicked. (a) Compute the observed click rate and the gap (predicted minus observed) in each bin. (b) Compute the ECE from the absolute gaps, weighting each bin by its share of the \(40\) predictions. (c) Is the model over-confident or under-confident? Say in one line how the signs of the gaps show it.
(extend) Fairness (§12.5). A feed has \(60\) slots and two provider groups that each own half the catalog; the popular studios get \(45\) slots and the long-tail creators \(15\). (a) Compute the two exposure rates and the demographic-parity gap. (b) Among users who would like a given film, group 1 gets it in their top-\(K\) for \(38\) of \(50\) users and group 2 for \(21\) of \(60\). Compute the two true-positive rates and the equal-opportunity gap. (c) Suppose a slot given to a studio earns \(0.10\) clicks and one given to a creator \(0.06\) (assumed values). Compare the clicks earned by the \(45/15\) split with those of an equal \(30/30\) split.

section: 15. Where this fits in the book
text:
15. Where this fits in the book







Metric (here)
Where it shows up




Recall@K, NDCG@K
Recall@20 is the number quoted in From Graphs to LightGCN §12 and The Spectral / Graph-Filter View §4 (which also prints one NDCG@20 pair); Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning §7 also reports Recall@10, Recall@20 and NDCG@20, for LightGCN and for RLMRec (a method that adds knowledge from a large language model to such a graph recommender)


RMSE/MAE
Traditional Recommender Systems §6 (rating prediction; the Netflix Prize, a famous rating-prediction competition)


AUC ↔︎ BPR
Loss Functions & Regularizers §9 — BPR trains on correctly ordered (relevant, irrelevant) pairs through a smooth stand-in for the 0/1 pair count, so it pushes AUC up without maximizing it exactly


Coverage / Gini / long-tail
From Graphs to LightGCN §13 (popularity bias, worked numerically) and the self-supervised fixes in Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning


Evaluation protocol (§11)
full ranking, the split choice (random per-user in the graph chapters; leave-one-out or a temporal split where leakage matters) and per-seed significance: how the literature behind those chapters is measured and where it leaks (protocol recorded in Datasets & Benchmarks §4)



Carry this forward: rating error (RMSE/MAE) grades numbers; ranking metrics (Precision / Recall / F1 / HR / MRR / MAP / NDCG / AUC) grade the ordered list — NDCG is the default; beyond-accuracy metrics (coverage/diversity/novelty/serendipity/Gini) grade the list’s health. Pick the metric that matches what you actually want, and never report accuracy alone.

title: 8  Evaluation Metrics
text:
16. Glossary







Term
Plain meaning




Relevant item
A ground-truth item the user actually likes.


@K
Evaluated over the top \(K\) recommended positions only.


MAE / MSE / RMSE
Mean Absolute / Mean Squared / Root-Mean-Squared rating error.


Hit Rate (HR@K)
Fraction of users with \(\ge 1\) relevant item in the top-\(K\).


Precision@K
Of the \(K\) shown, the fraction relevant.


Recall@K
Of all relevant items, the fraction in the top-\(K\).


F1@K
Harmonic mean of precision and recall.


Harmonic mean
The reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals; for two numbers \(P,R\) it is \(2PR/(P+R)\), dragged down by the smaller one (\(0.6\) and \(0.75\) give \(0.667\)).


MRR
Mean Reciprocal Rank — each user’s reciprocal rank (RR), \(1/\)rank of the first relevant item (\(0\) if none in the top-\(K\)), averaged over users.


AP / MAP
Average Precision (Precision@\(k\) summed over hit positions, divided by \(|\mathcal{R}|\)) / its mean over users.


DCG / IDCG / NDCG
Discounted Cumulative Gain (gains \(2^{\text{rel}}-1\), each divided by \(\log_2(i+1)\) at rank \(i\)) / its ideal / the normalized ratio in \([0,1]\).


AUC / ROC
Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve = P(score of a random relevant > random irrelevant) = the fraction of correctly ordered (relevant, irrelevant) pairs.


LogLoss
Log loss, or binary cross-entropy: the average of \(-\ln\)(the probability given to what happened); \(0.9\) on a click and \(0.2\) on a non-click give \(0.164\).


TPR / FPR
True- / false-positive rate: the share of the relevant / irrelevant items scoring at or above a threshold (a cut-off score); lowering the threshold step by step traces the ROC curve.


Coverage
Fraction of the catalog ever recommended.


Diversity
Average dissimilarity within a recommended list.


Novelty
Non-obviousness, often \(-\log_2(\text{popularity})\).


Serendipity
Relevant and surprising: hits a popularity baseline would not have shown, divided by \(K\).


Popularity baseline
A simple recommender that shows everyone the same most-popular items.


Gini coefficient
Concentration of recommendations on few items: \(0\) = perfectly even; the maximum, all on one of \(n\) items, is \((n-1)/n\) — near \(1\) only for a large catalog.


Lorenz curve
The share of recommendations held by the least-recommended fraction of the catalog; Gini \(=A/(A+B)\), the gap below the diagonal over the whole triangle.


Train/test split
How held-out test data is chosen: a random split, leave-one-out (LOO: each user’s chronologically last interaction), or a global temporal split (one cut-off date for everyone).


Validation set
A third slice, carved from the training data, used to choose settings (hyper-parameters, when to stop, calibration maps); the test set is touched once, at the very end.


Data leakage
Test-period information seeping into training; silently inflates every metric.


Full vs. sampled ranking
Rank the true item against the whole catalog vs. a few sampled negatives; the latter is inconsistent across papers and optimistic (with one held-out item per user, as in leave-one-out, fewer competitors mean the item can only rank higher).


A/B test (online eval)
Serve two models to live user halves and compare a business metric — the real verdict.


CTR / impression
Click-through rate \(=\) clicks \(/\) impressions, where an impression is one showing of an item to a user.


Significance (paired \(t\)-test)
Is a gain bigger than run-to-run seed noise? Report mean \(\pm\) standard deviation over seeds and a \(p\)-value.


Standard error (SE)
The standard deviation of a mean: the sample standard deviation of the values (divided by \(n-1\), not \(n\)) divided by \(\sqrt n\); pairing the runs shrinks it when the runs share luck (\(0.0107\) unpaired against \(0.0058\) paired in §11d).


Degrees of freedom
The number of values still free to vary once their mean is fixed: \(n-1\) for \(n\) runs (\(4\) for \(5\) seeds).


Percentile
The \(q\)th percentile is the value below which \(q\%\) of the values fall; the bootstrap reads its interval from the \(2.5\)th and \(97.5\)th.


Cosine similarity
How alike two vectors point: \(1\) for the same direction, \(0\) for nothing in common when the features are never negative.


Bit
The information in one fair coin flip; an event of probability \(\tfrac12\) carries \(1\) bit, and \(-\log_2 p\) bits in general.


IPS-weighted recall
Recall with each relevant item weighted by \(1/p\) and divided by the total weight: \(0.60\) against the raw \(0.75\) on the running list (§12.4).


Random seed
The starting number of the random-number generator; each seed gives one independent training run.


Bootstrap
Resample the test users with replacement thousands of times and read the metric’s \(2.5\)th / \(97.5\)th percentiles as its interval — no distribution assumed.


Calibration / ECE
A model is calibrated if items it scores \(0.8\) are clicked about \(80\%\) of the time; the Expected Calibration Error averages the per-bin absolute gap between predicted and observed rates, weighting each bin by its share of predictions.


Reliability diagram
Predicted vs. observed rate, one point per bin; calibrated points lie on the diagonal.


Platt scaling
Calibrates a raw score \(s\) with a fitted S-curve \(\sigma(as+b)\); keeps the ranking exactly when the slope \(a>0\).


Isotonic regression (PAV)
Calibrates with a fitted non-decreasing staircase; the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm averages neighbors that break the order, which can create ties.


MNAR data
Missing-Not-At-Random: whether an interaction is observed depends on what the system chose to show — recommender logs are the textbook case (the opposite, missing completely at random, is pure coin-flip missingness).


Selection / exposure bias
Only items the system showed can get feedback; un-shown items look “disliked” by silence.


Position bias
Higher-ranked slots draw more clicks regardless of true relevance.


Feedback loop
Recommend → click → log → retrain on skewed data → more skew; the “rich get richer” spiral that compounds bias.


Propensity / IPS
Propensity = probability an item was shown; inverse propensity scoring (IPS) re-weights each interaction by \(1/\)propensity to undo exposure bias.


Demographic parity
Equal selection / exposure rate across groups.


Equal opportunity
Equal true-positive rate across groups (the truly-relevant are surfaced equally).


Provider vs. consumer fairness
Comparable exposure across item creators (provider) vs. comparable quality across user groups (consumer).

title: 9  Sequential & Session-Based Recommendation
text:
1. From a matrix to a sequence: what order adds
Traditional Recommender Systems modeled recommendation as filling in a user–item matrix. That view quietly threw away something every real log carries: order. Bob did not just watch Titanic and Vendetta — he watched Titanic then Vendetta, and what he reaches for next can depend more on what he reached for last (a claim from practice, not tested here). This chapter builds the order-aware recommenders from zero: the data is now a sequence, the task is predict the next item, and the models climb from a one-step Markov chain (guess the next film from the last one alone) to self-attention (each film in the session looking at the other films), in two models called SASRec and BERT4Rec — the same machinery the Transformer chapter built, now reading a session instead of a sentence.
What this chapter assumes. Four things from earlier chapters, each explained again where it is used; nothing else is assumed.
This chapter is the on-ramp to the era of large language models (LLMs): SASRec and BERT4Rec are the Transformer applied to item sequences, and an LLM is itself a sequence model.
Bob rated Titanic 4 and Vendetta 5, and the site must pick his next film. A table of ratings cannot say which film he watched first, yet the order may matter more than the stars. This section turns the table into a time-ordered list and names the task the rest of the chapter solves.
Collaborative filtering (CF) — the central approach of Traditional Recommender Systems, which fills a user’s blanks from other users’ ratings — asks “what rating goes in this empty cell?” — a question about a static matrix in which the rows could be shuffled and nothing would change. But a recommendation log is a stream of events in time. Take Bob from that chapter’s running example: his row of the user–item matrix holds Titanic 4, Vendetta 5 and a blank for Matrix (three films this chapter abbreviates T, V and M). In a log, those two ratings arrive as two events, one after the other: \[
\text{Bob's history} = (\ \text{Titanic},\ \text{Vendetta},\ \underbrace{?}_{\text{next}}\ ).
\]
Two facts the matrix cannot see: the events have an order (Titanic came before Vendetta), and the most recent ones usually matter most (what you watched an hour ago says more about your next click than what you watched a year ago: a claim from practice, not tested here).
The order is real information. Bob’s two films can arrive in \(2\times1=2\) orders, (Titanic, Vendetta) or (Vendetta, Titanic), and the matrix stores both the same way; a session of three films can arrive in \(3\times2\times1=6\) orders, and the matrix keeps none of them. (The models in this chapter see only the order of events — 1st, 2nd, 3rd — not the clock time between them, so time is not modelled here; time-aware variants add the gaps as an extra input, beyond our scope. Time returns in §6, where the test split must respect it.) Sequential recommendation is the problem of using that order.
A note on the cast. The viewing logs in this chapter are sessions with their own histories: what each person watched, in order, over a longer time than the ratings snapshot of Traditional Recommender Systems. They are not that matrix. So Ann’s and Cara’s logs in later sections need not match their rows there (in that matrix Ann has not rated Vendetta, and Cara has not rated Titanic); only Bob’s two ratings above are taken from it. Likewise the exercise logs, and the sessions of §5 and §6 (where Bob watches Matrix although his matrix cell is “?”), are their own logs, not the ratings table.
Two settings, one task. The literature splits on how much you know about the user:
(The literature uses “sequential recommendation” both for the umbrella problem and, narrowly, for the long-history setting of the first bullet; this chapter means the umbrella unless it says “long-history”.)
Both reduce to the same core question — next-item prediction:
The shape of the answer is unchanged from Traditional Recommender Systems: a score per item, ranked. What changes is the input — an ordered prefix instead of a user id — and so what the model must capture: which earlier items, in which order, predict what comes next.
Next-item prediction on Bob. The catalog here is the three films Titanic, Vendetta and Matrix. Bob’s prefix is (Titanic, Vendetta), so the model must score all \(3\) films for the next slot, and with \(K=2\) the site shows the \(2\) highest of the \(3\). Whether the true next film (suppose it is Matrix, as §5 will) lands in that short list is what §6 grades (at \(K=1\); one aside there uses \(K=2\)).
In one line: a matrix keeps Bob’s two ratings but not their order, which has \(2\times1=2\) possibilities; a sequence model keeps the order and scores all \(3\) films of the catalog for the next slot.

title: 9  Sequential & Session-Based Recommendation
text:
Sequential recommendation — you have a long, identified history for each user (their whole watch list), and predict the next item in it.
Session-based recommendation — you have only the current, short, often anonymous session (the handful of clicks since the page loaded), with no user id at all — nothing that ties this visit to an earlier one. This is the harder case, said to be very common in e-commerce (a claim from practice, not tested here): a logged-out visitor with three clicks (Wang et al., 2021, survey the methods built for it). §6 shows how a raw log is cut into such sessions.




Given the items seen so far, \((i_1, i_2, \dots, i_{t-1})\) — \(i_1\) is the first item, \(i_2\) the second, and so on; such a beginning of a list is called a prefix — score every item of the catalog (all the items the site offers) for being the next one, \(i_t\), and recommend the top-\(K\) (the \(K\) highest-scoring items).








Figure 9.1: Three views of the same interactions. Traditional Recommender Systems reads them as a static matrix (rows can be shuffled — no order). This chapter reads one user’s history as an ordered sequence and predicts the next item. The next chapter reads them as a graph of who-touched-what. Bob’s data appear in all three (T \(=\) Titanic, V \(=\) Vendetta, M \(=\) Matrix): his matrix row (outlined: T 4, V 5, M blank), his history Titanic then Vendetta then the unknown next item, and his two graph edges. Ann’s and Cara’s logs in later sections are separate sessions, not these rows.




Why “sequential” and “session.” Sequential = the model consumes an ordered sequence of past items. Session = one unbroken visit (the clicks between arriving and leaving); session-based models work from that short window alone, with no long-term profile.

title: 9  Sequential & Session-Based Recommendation
section: 2. The simplest sequence model: Markov chains
text:
2. The simplest sequence model: Markov chains
Ann has just finished Titanic. Which film will she press play on next? The cheapest guess is to look at what other viewers pressed after Titanic, and count. This section turns that counting into a table of odds, and then shows what the table cannot do.
Start with the crudest possible use of order: the next item depends only on the last one. A (first-order) Markov chain models the sequence by a table of transition probabilities \(P(\text{next}=i \mid \text{last}=l)\) — “after \(l\), how often does \(i\) follow?” (read the bar \(\mid\) as “given”; \(l\) is the last item, \(i\) a candidate next item) — estimated by counting in the log.

Why “Markov.” After Andrey Markov, who studied processes with the memoryless property: the next state depends only on the current state, not the full history. A first-order chain remembers exactly one step back.

Worked example — transitions by counting. Take four tiny sessions over our three movies — Titanic (T), Vendetta (V), Matrix (M); the second one is Bob’s session so far: \[
\text{T}\!\to\!\text{V}\!\to\!\text{M},\qquad \text{T}\!\to\!\text{V},\qquad \text{V}\!\to\!\text{M},\qquad \text{T}\!\to\!\text{M}.
\]
Count every adjacent (from \(\to\) to) pair, and file each count in a table whose rows are the last item and whose columns are the next item:



Table 9.1: Counts of each adjacent (from, to) pair in the four sessions; rows are the last item, columns the next item.

From T we see \(\text{T}\!\to\!\text{V}\) twice and \(\text{T}\!\to\!\text{M}\) once (\(3\) transitions out of T); from V we see \(\text{V}\!\to\!\text{M}\) twice (\(2\) out of V); from M we see nothing, because Matrix ended every session it appeared in. Dividing each count by its row total gives the transition probabilities: \[
P(\text{V}\mid\text{T})=\tfrac{2}{3}\approx0.667,\quad
P(\text{M}\mid\text{T})=\tfrac{1}{3}\approx0.333,\quad
P(\text{M}\mid\text{V})=\tfrac{2}{2}=1.0.
\]
Per component: the numerator is how often that specific pair occurred; the denominator is how often the from-item appeared as a “from” at all — so every row that has any outgoing transitions becomes a normalized vote that sums to \(1\) (the T row: \(0+0.667+0.333=1\)).
Two gaps show in the table. Matrix’s row is empty — nobody moved on from Matrix in our log — so the chain has no prediction after it at all (\(\tfrac00\) is undefined); and in any row that does have transitions, it gives every pair it never saw probability \(0\) (Titanic after Vendetta, for instance). The factorized model below is built to fix both gaps.
Reading the table: a user whose last movie was Titanic is predicted to watch Vendetta next (probability \(0.667\), the bigger count); a user whose last was Vendetta is sent to Matrix (\(1.0\)) — so Bob, whose session so far ends in Vendetta, is sent to Matrix, the very blank in his rating-matrix row. (Bob’s own session T\(\to\)V is one of the four we counted, which is harmless in a toy and would not be allowed in a real test, §6.) The whole “model” is a counted table.






Figure 9.2: A first-order Markov chain counted from four sessions. Each arrow is \(P(\text{next}\mid\text{last})\), estimated by dividing the transition count by the row total. After Titanic, Vendetta is the likely next watch (\(0.667\), thick) over Matrix (\(0.333\), thin); after Vendetta, Matrix is certain in this toy (\(1.0\)) — so Bob, whose session ends in Vendetta, is sent to Matrix. Matrix has no outgoing arrow: nobody moved on from it in the four sessions. The model is just these counted, row-normalized arrows.



The two limits — and the fix. A plain Markov chain has no memory beyond the last item (it cannot learn “users who saw both Titanic and Vendetta like Inception”), and it is not personalized (everyone shares one transition table).
The classic remedy for the second limit is Factorizing Personalized Markov Chains (FPMC) (Rendle et al., 2010), which scores the next item as a sum of two dot products (a dot product multiplies two vectors entry by entry and adds: \([a,b]\cdot[c,d]=ac+bd\) — Linear-Algebra primer §4): one from matrix factorization (MF), the user-meets-item score of Traditional Recommender Systems §5, and one from a learned Markov step. (The first limit — memory of more than one step — is what the recurrent network of §3 and the attention model of §4 remove.)
\[
\hat s(u,\,\text{last}=l,\,\text{next}=i)\;=\;\underbrace{\mathbf p_u\cdot\mathbf q_i}_{\text{matrix factorization: does }u\text{ like }i?}\;+\;\underbrace{\mathbf q'_l\cdot\mathbf q''_i}_{\text{Markov: does }i\text{ follow }l?}.
\]
Every symbol, in words:

\(\hat s\) — the predicted score (the hat marks an estimate, as in the \(\hat r\) of Traditional Recommender Systems); FPMC ranks the candidates by it. It is a score, not a probability.
\(u\) — the user; \(l\) — the last item they interacted with; \(i\) — a candidate next item.
\(\mathbf p_u\) — user \(u\)’s taste vector, and \(\mathbf q_i\) — item \(i\)’s trait vector: vectors of the kind Traditional Recommender Systems §5 builds (this chapter’s own toy numbers are below), whose dot product is a “does \(u\) like \(i\)?” score.
\(\mathbf q'_l\) — a second vector of item \(l\), used when it is the item just watched (the “from” side of a transition); \(\mathbf q''_i\) — a third vector of item \(i\), used when it is the candidate next item (the “to” side). The primes are only labels (read “q-prime” and “q-double-prime”), not derivatives.

So every item carries three vectors: \(\mathbf q\) for its traits, \(\mathbf q'\) for when it is the item just watched, and \(\mathbf q''\) for when it is a candidate next item. Why two transition vectors instead of reusing \(\mathbf q\)? A dot product is symmetric — \(\mathbf q_{\text{T}}\cdot\mathbf q_{\text{V}}=\mathbf q_{\text{V}}\cdot\mathbf q_{\text{T}}\) — so one vector per item would force “Vendetta after Titanic” and “Titanic after Vendetta” to score the same, yet in our log T→V happened twice and V→T never. Transitions have a direction; separate “from” and “to” vectors give them one.
What the two terms do: the first is exactly the MF score of Traditional Recommender Systems §5 (user taste meets item traits); the second replaces the counted transition table with a learned one — “\(i\) tends to follow \(l\)” becomes the dot product \(\mathbf q'_l\cdot\mathbf q''_i\), which can score pairs never seen together (the same low-rank trick that let MF fill blank cells). FPMC is, in one line, MF plus a factorized Markov step — the hinge between the static matrix and the deep sequence models below. (Rendle et al. average the second term over a whole basket of last items; with a single last item it is exactly the formula above.)
Worked example — FPMC scores Bob’s next film. FPMC needs learned vectors, so suppose training on a larger log (our four sessions are a sample of it) produced the \(d=2\) vectors below — two numbers each. For the trait vectors \(\mathbf q\) we use this chapter’s own toy item embeddings (learned item vectors of the kind Traditional Recommender Systems §5 builds, but a fresh set: there Titanic is \([2,0]\)), which every later section reuses so that only the mechanism changes: Titanic \(=[1,0]\), Vendetta \(=[0,1]\), Matrix \(=[1,1]\). Bob’s taste vector is \(\mathbf p_{\text{Bob}}=[0.4,\,0.5]\) (he leans a little more to Vendetta’s feature, as his 5 for Vendetta against 4 for Titanic suggests).



Table 9.2: The toy vectors of each item: traits \(\mathbf q\) (matrix factorization), \(\mathbf q'\) when just watched, \(\mathbf q''\) as the candidate next item.

from \(\mathbf q'\) (just watched)
to \(\mathbf q''\) (candidate next)
