title: Appendix C — Generating Features with Large Language Models
section: 5. The harness — turning prompts into a pipeline
text:
5. The harness — turning prompts into a pipeline
A single prompt in a notebook is a demo. Generating profiles for millions of users and items, reliably and affordably, is an orchestration problem — the “harness” around the LLM call. The pieces that matter:

Versioned prompt templates. Keep the prompt in code as a parameterized, versioned template (not pasted strings). When you change the prompt, the profiles change — so the version is part of the cache key.
Structured output + validation. Request JSON, then validate against a schema and retry on a parse/validation failure (with a stricter reminder). Never let an unparseable generation enter the feature store (the table described in the last bullet below).
Batching & concurrency. Profiles are independent, so process them in batches (many items per request where the API allows) and with bounded concurrency (a worker pool), not one blocking call at a time. This is where the wall-clock lives.
Caching & idempotency. Hash each input (the item text + the prompt version) and record the hash in a cache that indexes the stored profile; regenerate only when the input or prompt changes. A catalog is mostly static, so item profiles are generated once; a user’s history keeps growing, so user profiles need a refresh policy (say, regenerate after \(N\) new interactions or weekly, whichever comes first — a design choice).
Cost & rate limits. Budget up front: (number of users + items) × (tokens per profile, prompt plus reply) × (price per token). At an illustrative blended $0.50 per million tokens for prompt and reply together, 2 million users and items at an assumed 330 tokens each is \(660\) million tokens, about $330 once; refreshing \(1\) million active users weekly is \(330\) million tokens, about $165 a week. The same 330 tokens spent at query time, for \(10\) million requests a day, would be \(3.3\) billion tokens, about $1,650 a day. So the 330 is an assumption and the budget a model, not a measurement.
What the budget leaves out. Three things would raise a real bill: a user’s history prompt is longer than \(330\) tokens, replies are billed above prompts (a blended price hides the split), and the embedding step is billed on top. Because generation is offline and scheduled, it is a batch cost you can run on cheap/off-peak capacity — not a per-request tax (the enhancer advantage, Large Language Models and Recommendation §2.3).
An offline feature store. The output is a table: id → (profile, vector, prompt_version, input_hash, generated_at). The serving path reads vectors from this store and never calls the LLM; a scheduled job refreshes profiles for new or changed items and users.

The loop below caches by hash, validates every reply, and stores only valid profiles, writing the store before the cache so that a crash leaves nothing cached that was not stored.
generate_profiles(items, prompt_v):     # B = items per LLM request
  key(x) = hash(x.text, prompt_v)       # cache key: text + prompt version
  for batch in chunks(items, size=B):   # batching
    todo = [x for x in batch
            if cache.miss(key(x))]      # idempotency
    if not todo: continue               # all cached: no LLM call
    outs = llm.batch(render(prompt_v, todo),
                     json_schema=PROFILE)      # JSON shape of section 2
    for x, out in zip(todo, outs):
      if not valid(out):
        out = retry(x, prompt_v, max=2) # validate + bounded retry
      if not valid(out):
        log_and_skip(x); continue       # never store a failed profile
      store.put(x.id, out.profile, embed(out.profile),
                prompt_v, key(x), now)  # upsert: safe to repeat
      cache.put(key(x))                 # key index over the store
# skipped items stay uncached: the next run retries them
That loop — batch, skip-cached, structured-call, validate, embed, store — is the difference between “I tried a prompt” and “I have a feature pipeline.”
crumbs: C  Generating Features with Large Language Models

title: Appendix C — Generating Features with Large Language Models
text:
6. Does the feature actually help?
Generating a profile is easy; proving it helps is the discipline. Two checks, both from Evaluation Metrics:

Ablate. Train the backbone with and without the LLM feature on the same protocol (full-ranking NDCG@K (normalized discounted cumulative gain) / Recall@K, mean ± std over seeds, a significance test — Evaluation Metrics §11). The question is the delta, not the headline.
Stratify by popularity. Report the gain on head vs. tail items (the few most-interacted items against the many rarely-interacted ones) separately (Evaluation Metrics §12.6). The semantic feature should help most on the cold tail (expected, not tested here); if the only lift is on the head, the profiles are adding little the collaborative signal didn’t already have.

A worked ablation. Train two identical backbones — same LightGCN, same dimension, same five seeds — differing only in whether the semantic feature is fused. Say NDCG@10 comes out:

no feature: \(0.28,\,0.30,\,0.29,\,0.31,\,0.32\) \(\to\) mean \(\mathbf{0.300}\)
+ LLM feature: \(0.30,\,0.31,\,0.32,\,0.33,\,0.34\) \(\to\) mean \(\mathbf{0.320}\)

The headline gap is \(+0.020\), but the right test is paired, because the two runs share seeds: the per-seed deltas are \([+0.02,+0.01,+0.03,+0.02,+0.02]\), mean \(\bar d=0.020\), sample std \(0.00707\), so the standard error (SE) is \(0.00707/\sqrt5=0.00316\) and the paired-\(t\) (Evaluation Metrics §11d) is \[t=\frac{0.020}{0.00316}=6.3\] on \(4\) degrees of freedom (d.f.), giving a two-sided \(p=0.003\) (the five seeds treated as independent runs) — comfortably under \(0.05\). The gain is larger than the seed-to-seed noise on this protocol (an unpaired, pooled-variance two-sided \(t\)-test on the same ten numbers gives \(t=2.0\) on \(8\) d.f., \(p=0.08\), because it ignores that each seed moved both runs together). Had the per-seed deltas been \([+0.04,+0.03,+0.02,+0.02,-0.01]\) — the same mean, one seed worse — the same test gives \(t=2.4\), \(p=0.075\), and the correct report would be no significant gain: on these five seeds the feature cannot be told apart from noise.
And the caveat from Large Language Models and Recommendation §2.3: a misaligned profile can hurt. RLMRec’s authors report that shuffling the profile vectors between nodes lowers performance (Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning §7), and KAR’s \(-2.5\%\) (\(0.1473\to0.1436\)) on the SGL backbone (§4) shows a semantic input ending below the base model; the paper’s only comment on KAR’s weaker results is a hedged guess that input features “may not effectively align” the text with behaviour and are “more susceptible to irrelevant noise”, which it does not test. That a merely poor profile hurts is plausible but not tested here. The pipeline is only as good as the profiles and the alignment — measure, don’t assume.

title: Appendix C — Generating Features with Large Language Models
text:
7. Where this leads: profile density
This appendix used one short profile per node. Here density means how many profiles each user or item gets, counted here simply as profiles per node: this appendix has density 1, and a variant with 3 profiles per user triples the user-side generation, from \(330\) million to \(990\) million tokens per weekly refresh of §5’s 1 million users.
The open research question, as this appendix reads it, is how rich and how faithful that generated signal should be: longer multi-aspect profiles, several profiles per node, profiles distilled from reviews or knowledge, how densely to generate them against cost, and, just as much, how to align that signal so it helps rather than drowns the collaborative structure. Large Language Models and Recommendation §5 asks two nearby questions for the enhancer line, whether the semantic view aligns with real collaborative structure and whether thin-data items gain most, and lists both as open. Profile coverage and profile accuracy are this appendix’s own reading, not questions §5 names. The pipeline here is the on-ramp; how far to push density and quality is live research.

title: Appendix C — Generating Features with Large Language Models
text:
8. Glossary







Term
Plain meaning




Backbone
The collaborative model that scores at serving time (LightGCN here; From Graphs to LightGCN), the one the LLM feature is fused into.


Adaptor
A small trained network that maps the LLM’s vector into the recommender’s space and shrinks it, as in KAR (§4).


Profile
A short LLM-written description of a user’s taste or an item’s character, used as input to an embedder.


Semantic embedding
A fixed-length vector encoding the meaning of the profile text (from a frozen sentence encoder), distinct from the CF latent space.


Enhancer pipeline
Using an LLM offline to manufacture features for a fast collaborative backbone that serves.


Structured output / JSON mode
Forcing the LLM to emit schema-valid JSON, so the result is very likely parseable (§5 still validates).


Harness / orchestration
The engineering around the LLM call — templates, validation, batching, retries, caching, cost control.


Idempotency
Re-running the pipeline on unchanged input does no new work (hash → cache hit), so a profile is regenerated only when its input or the prompt version changes.


Feature store
The table of generated id → (profile, vector) the serving path reads; the LLM is never on the serving path.


Alignment
Pulling a node’s semantic vector and collaborative vector together (contrastive, Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning §7) so the two spaces agree.


Contrastive (InfoNCE) term
Added to the recommender’s loss: it pulls a node’s collaborative and projected semantic vectors together (the numerator) and pushes its collaborative vector away from other nodes’ semantic vectors (the denominator).


Projection \(g\)
The small network that maps the semantic vector into the collaborative space so the two can be compared (§4).


Concat (early fusion)
Append the LLM feature vector to the ID embedding — the quick first try, at the cost of a fatter serving vector. A frozen vector adds a fixed content score; only an adaptor or an FM or MLP scorer lets the model re-weigh it (§4).

title: Appendix D — Reinforcement Learning for Recommendation
text:
1. From bandits to reinforcement learning
The bandit chapter let the recommender choose what to show and learn from the feedback, but under one quiet assumption: each action is one-shot, so what you show now does not change what situation you face next. Reality often breaks that. Recommend episode 1 and episode 2 becomes relevant that wasn’t before; fill a feed with clickbait and you win today’s clicks but lose tomorrow’s session. The moment actions move the world forward, you are no longer maximizing the next click; you are maximizing long-term reward, and that is reinforcement learning (RL).
What this appendix assumes. It assumes the bandit setting of Bandits & Online Recommendation (the bandit is the one-step special case of what follows) and the idea of a click reward. Sections 1-4 also lean on the expected value and standard deviation of Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning and on gradient ascent (gradient descent of Calculus for Machine Learning with the sign flipped, to climb instead of descend); section 4 adds normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG; Evaluation Metrics), cross-entropy (Loss Functions & Regularizers §2.2) and Large Language Models and Recommendation §2.2. It is a thin frontier appendix: a map, not a full course, with hand-checkable micro-examples, four of them the main ones (a discounted return and a choice that long-term reward changes, both in §1; a slate’s value, in §2; a group-relative advantage, in §4); for the full theory, Sutton & Barto is the text.
Suppose a streaming service picks what to show Ann tonight. If the pick changes what she will want tomorrow, judging each pick by its own click is not enough, and we need a way to write the whole situation down. RL writes it as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) (Markov: the state carries everything about the past that matters for what comes next), which has four pieces and a discount:
For example, Ann’s state is “watched 3 comedies this week”, the action is to show a comedy slate, the reward is \(1\) (she clicks), and the transition takes her to “watched 4 comedies” with probability \(0.8\) or to “left the app” with probability \(0.2\).
A policy \(\pi(a\mid s)\) is not one of the pieces: it is the solution, the rule mapping states to actions, which is what we learn. Here \(\pi\) names the policy, not \(3.14159\), and \(\pi(a\mid s)\) is the probability that it picks action \(a\) in state \(s\) (in the choice example below, always showing quality is \(\pi(\text{quality}\mid s)=1\)).
The goal is not the next reward but the return \(G\). We maximize its expected value, averaged over the random transitions, rewards and the policy’s own choices. The return is the cumulative discounted long-term reward, \(G = r_0 + \gamma\,r_1 + \gamma^2\,r_2 + \cdots = \sum_{t\ge 0}\gamma^{t}\,r_t\), where \(\gamma\in[0,1)\) is the discount factor — how much less a reward one step later is worth than one now (it both encodes “sooner is better” and, for bounded rewards, keeps an infinite sum finite: a reward of \(1\) at every step sums to \(1/(1-\gamma)=10\) at \(\gamma=0.9\)).
The value \(V(s)\) is the expected return from state \(s\) under a policy, and the action-value \(Q(s,a)\) the expected return from taking \(a\) in \(s\) and then following that policy (the box below prints both: \(Q(\text{quality})=1.4\) and the value \(V(s)=1.4\) of the greedy policy). RL methods learn one of these and act greedily (take the action with the highest \(Q\)) or explore, as a bandit does; policy-gradient methods (§3) instead learn the policy directly.
Q-learning (Watkins & Dayan, 1992) learns \(Q(s,a)\) by moving each estimate toward the reward now plus \(\gamma\) times the best \(Q\) at the next state (the idea behind temporal-difference (TD) learning, Sutton, 1988). For example, with a current estimate \(Q=1.0\), reward \(0.5\), best next-state \(Q=1.4\) and \(\gamma=0.9\), the target is \(0.5+0.9\cdot1.4=1.76\), and a step size (the learning rate) of one half moves the estimate to \(1.0+0.5(1.76-1.0)=1.38\).
A bandit is an MDP in which actions never change the next state: one state (the plain bandit) or a fresh context each round (the contextual bandit). That is why the explore / exploit machinery of Bandits & Online Recommendation reappears here, now wrapped around long-term value. The figure below draws the loop.
In short: RL is a bandit whose actions also move the state, judged by the discounted return instead of the next reward alone.

title: Appendix D — Reinforcement Learning for Recommendation
Appendix D — Reinforcement Learning for Recommendation
section: 2. Why RL is genuinely hard in recommendation
text:
2. Why RL is genuinely hard in recommendation
RL is alluring for recommendation — “optimize long-term engagement, not next-click clickbait” — but four obstacles make it hard in practice, and a from-zero reader should know them before reaching for it. The four obstacles are claims from practice, not tested here (the decomposition in the first is the cited exception):

A combinatorial action space. The action is often a whole slate of items, so the number of actions is astronomically large. Q-learning (§1) must score every action: a page of 10 items from 1,000 candidates is about \(10^{30}\) ordered slates, so plain Q-learning cannot be used. SlateQ (slate Q-learning; Ie et al., 2019) is one fix: if the user consumes one item per slate (or none) and reward and transition depend only on it, a slate’s value decomposes into per-item \(Q\)-values weighted by the chance each item is chosen. For per-item values \(2,1,0.5\) chosen with probabilities \(0.4,0.3,0.2\) (from an assumed choice model, the user’s rule for picking among the shown items; the other \(0.1\) is no choice, taken as worth \(0\)) the slate is worth \(0.4\cdot2+0.3\cdot1+0.2\cdot0.5=1.2\). Choosing the best slate is still a separate optimization (an exact linear program, or a greedy rule).
It is off-policy in practice. You cannot let a half-trained agent experiment on real users for months, so you must learn from logged data collected by a different (old) policy — the hard, bias-prone off-policy setting (the same logged-data problem behind the bandit offline replay of Bandits & Online Recommendation). For example, a log of 1,000 sessions in which the old policy showed comedy \(90\%\) of the time gives only about 100 sessions of anything else, too few to say what a new policy that shows documentaries would get.
Delayed, sparse reward + the simulator gap. “Long-term satisfaction” arrives much later than the action that caused it and rarely (credit assignment, deciding which earlier action deserves the credit, is hard: if Ann subscribes on day 30 after 30 recommendations, splitting the credit equally gives each \(1/30\), which is only a guess), and RL often needs very many interactions, so teams build user simulators, which are themselves recommendation models and can bake in their own errors (a simulator that says Ann clicks comedy with probability \(0.7\) is only as right as that \(0.7\)).
Safety and non-stationarity (the data’s pattern changing over time). An exploring policy on a live platform can hurt real users and revenue, and user behavior drifts under the policy itself.

So a slate rules out plain Q-learning, and the other three obstacles are about data, reward and safety, which the choice of algorithm only partly fixes.

title: Appendix D — Reinforcement Learning for Recommendation
section: 3. The main approaches, in one line each
text:
3. The main approaches, in one line each
Once the obstacles are in view, the question is what to learn: how good each action is, or directly what to do. The third item below is a deep-network version of the first.

Value-based. Learn \(Q(s,a)\) (Q-learning) and act greedily; for slates, SlateQ makes it tractable by decomposition.
Policy-gradient. Directly optimize the policy \(\pi_\theta\) (the policy with parameters \(\theta\)) by gradient ascent on expected return. The basic method, REINFORCE (Williams, 1992), raises the probability of each action taken in proportion to the return that followed: with no baseline (a reference return, often the average, subtracted from each return) and positive returns, a title shown with return \(2.0\) is pushed up twice as hard as one with return \(1.0\). Chen et al. (2019) use an off-policy-corrected form (§2, item 2) at web scale, for action sets of millions of items.
Deep RL for news (DRN). Zheng et al. (2018) use deep Q-learning (Mnih et al., 2015: the \(Q\) values come from a neural network) for online news, explicitly modeling future reward and how soon the user comes back, a signal beyond the immediate click, a concrete case of optimizing for retention rather than the next tap.

The approaches differ in what they must learn: values (plus a choice model for slates) or the policy itself, with a neural network standing in for the values in the third.

title: Appendix D — Reinforcement Learning for Recommendation
section: 4. When the policy is a language model
text:
4. When the policy is a language model
Ask a chat model what Ann should watch tonight and it simply writes an answer; nothing yet says whether the answer was good. This section is about the scoring that turns such an answer into a learning signal.
A recommender built on a large language model (LLM) reuses §1’s words with one change of scale. The state \(s\) is the prompt (the user’s history, perhaps a query). The action \(a\) is the text the model writes: one item title, a ranked list or an explanation. The policy \(\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\) is the probability the model gives that text, piece by piece (each piece, a token, is a word or part of one). The reward scores the finished output. In the setups below the model writes its output in one go, so there is no next state and no discounting over time: this is nearer to the contextual bandit of §1 than to a long-horizon MDP.
Some methods below skip the reward in their final step and learn only from pairs of a preferred and a rejected output (for example, the title a user chose and one shown but not chosen). For the models themselves, see Large Language Models and Recommendation §2.2.
A learned reward. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF; Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022) trains a reward model (a model that scores outputs) on preferred and rejected outputs, then tunes the model against it while a penalty keeps it near its starting point; direct preference optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al., 2023, cited in Large Language Models and Recommendation §2.2) merges both steps into one loss on pairs. Softmax-DPO (S-DPO; Chen et al., 2024) widens the pair to one preferred item against several negatives (items the user did not choose), and its ablation (a test that removes one part to see what it was worth), which keeps one negative so that the loss reduces to plain DPO, reports gains from the extra negatives.
OneRec (Deng et al., 2025, a generative recommender from the video platform Kuaishou) starts from a problem: a platform shows one list per request, so it never sees a winner and a loser side by side. Its authors therefore train a reward model on whole sessions, with a binary cross-entropy loss (the yes/no log-loss of Loss Functions & Regularizers §2.2) against the logged outcomes of each session (watch time, views, follows and likes), and use it to rank the model’s own output: 128 lists per user from beam search (a search that keeps only the best few partial lists at each step), the highest-reward list paired with the lowest-reward one, so that the model builds for itself the winner-and-loser pair the logs never show. They apply this to a random 1% of the data, to limit the cost of the beam search.
A rule as the reward. Rec-R1 (Lin et al., 2025) scores text the model writes by the NDCG (a ranking-quality score) of a fixed recommender’s output (for example, the model rewrites Ann’s search query, the fixed recommender returns a ranked list for the rewrite, and that list’s NDCG is the reward), uses group relative policy optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024: score a group of outputs against their own mean, as in the example below) and trains no reward model, which its authors say limits reward hacking (the model learns to raise the score without improving the recommendations).
ReRe (Reinforced Preference Optimization for Recommendation; Tan et al., 2025) gives reward \(1\) when a generated title equals the target and \(0\) otherwise, and adds a ranking reward for the all-zero case (see the example). Rank-GRPO (Zhu et al., 2025), written for conversational recommenders that output ranked lists, adapts GRPO by treating each rank, rather than each token or the whole sequence, as the unit that is optimized and crediting each rank with the discounted relevance of itself and the ranks below it; its authors found that crediting only the rank’s own item (no look-ahead, so \(\gamma=0\) in §1’s terms) gave a simple, stable learning signal.

Worked example (GRPO). The model writes \(n=4\) titles for one prompt (the group size) and one matches the target, so the rewards are \((1,0,0,0)\). Their mean is \(0.25\) and their sample standard deviation \(0.5\), so the advantages \((r-\text{mean})/\text{std}\) are \((1.5,-0.5,-0.5,-0.5)\): the hit is made likelier, the misses less likely, and no value model (a second network that estimates \(V\)) is trained. If no title hits, every reward is \(0\) and the group gives no signal, the all-zero case for which ReRe adds a ranking reward.

What is open. ReRe reports that smoother rewards (text similarity, another recommender’s scores) kept rising while accuracy fell. In the parts read, none of these papers optimizes a multi-step return over time, such as retention, so §2’s delayed-reward problem is untouched. In the parts read, only OneRec reports an online test, for a whole system (Large Language Models and Recommendation §2.2); ReRe, OneRec and Rank-GRPO are cited here as preprints, and the papers’ datasets differ, so their gains are not comparable. All of this is reported there, not tested here. The takeaway is that with a language model as the policy, the new question is where the reward comes from (a reward model, pairs, or a rule), not the long-horizon return.

title: Appendix D — Reinforcement Learning for Recommendation
section: 5. Where it pays off — and an honest caveat
text:
5. Where it pays off — and an honest caveat
RL earns its complexity when the objective is genuinely long-horizon: total session length, multi-step journeys (a course syllabus, a show’s episode order), or retention (will the user come back next week?) — outcomes a one-step click model cannot express and a bandit can only credit to a single action. The caveat, in the spirit of the reproducibility caution of Datasets & Benchmarks §5: RL in recommendation is operationally heavy and often hard to reproduce, and a well-tuned bandit or supervised ranker is often competitive on the metrics that are actually measured. This is a view from practice, not tested here (the cited section shows the same caution for neural recommenders against tuned classical baselines, not for RL). Reach for RL when the objective itself is long-term and you can pay the engineering cost, not by default.
What the reading behind this appendix covers. The author’s reading of Chen et al. (2019), DRN and Afsar et al. rests on abstracts and scope. The reading of the §4 papers rests on abstracts and methods (for S-DPO also the ablation, for Rank-GRPO the reward definitions), and the reported results were not reproduced.
This is why RL lives here as a pointer appendix rather than a core chapter: the book’s through-line is collaborative filtering from classical to graph- and LLM-based models, and RL is an adjacent paradigm the through-line touches (via bandits) but does not need. For the one-step case, return to Bandits & Online Recommendation; for the full theory and a survey of the field (Afsar et al., 2022), the references below.

title: Appendix D — Reinforcement Learning for Recommendation
text:
6. Glossary







Term
Plain meaning




MDP
Markov Decision Process: states, actions, transition, reward and discount — the problem RL solves; the policy is its solution.


Reinforcement learning (RL)
Learning to choose actions to maximize long-term reward when actions can change the next state.


Reward \(r\) / action \(a\)
The immediate payoff (a click, a watch-minute, a return visit) / what the recommender does (show an item or slate).


State \(s\)
A summary of the current situation; what the agent conditions on.


Bandit
An MDP in which actions never change the next state (one state, or a fresh context each round); such actions are called one-shot.


Policy \(\pi(a\mid s)\)
The learned rule mapping a state to an action (\(\pi\) names the policy, not \(3.14159\)); what RL optimizes. A language model’s output rule in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is also called a policy (Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning, glossary); §4 applies the idea to LLM-based recommenders.


GRPO
Group relative policy optimization: sample a group of outputs for one prompt and score each against the group’s mean and spread, with no value model (§4).


Reward model
A model trained to score outputs: RLHF trains it on preferred and rejected outputs, OneRec on the logged watch-time, view, follow and like outcomes of whole sessions; Rec-R1 uses none (§4).


Return \(G\)
Cumulative discounted reward \(\sum_t \gamma^t r_t\) — the long-term objective.


Discount \(\gamma\)
How much a later reward is worth vs. now; \(\gamma\to0\) is myopic (cares only about the immediate reward, like a bandit’s objective), \(\gamma\to1\) far-sighted.


Value / \(Q\)-value
Expected return from a state (\(V\)) or a state–action pair (\(Q\)).


Q-learning
Learn \(Q(s,a)\) by moving it toward reward plus \(\gamma\times\) the best next \(Q\) (temporal-difference learning), then take the highest-\(Q\) (greedy) action; it must score every action, so slate methods avoid it. Deep Q-learning uses a neural network for \(Q\); DRN applies it to news.


Policy gradient
Optimize the policy directly by gradient ascent on expected return (REINFORCE is the basic algorithm; \(\theta\) are the policy’s parameters).


Retention
Whether the user comes back (next week); a long-horizon objective.


Credit assignment
Deciding which earlier action deserves credit for a reward that arrives later.


User simulator
A model of user behavior used to train RL without experimenting on real users.


Direct preference optimization (DPO) / S-DPO
A loss that learns from pairs of a preferred and a rejected output with no separate reward model; Softmax-DPO (S-DPO) widens the pair to one preferred item against several negatives (§4).


Advantage
How much better an output scored than the group’s mean reward, divided by the group’s standard deviation in GRPO (§4).


Ablation
A test that removes one part of a method to see what the part was worth (§4).


Beam search
A search that keeps only the best few partial lists at each step (§4).


Slate
A whole page/list of recommended items — the (combinatorial) action in slate RL.


Off-policy
Learning from data collected by a different (older) policy than the one being trained.


SlateQ
Decomposes a slate’s value into per-item \(Q\)-values, making value-based slate RL tractable.

title: Appendix E — Federated & Privacy-Preserving Recommendation
text:
1. The idea: move the model, not the data
Every model in this book assumed the training data sits in one place, a central log you can shuffle, split, and sweep. But what you watch, buy, read, and listen to is private: the paper that named federated learning (McMahan et al., 2017) starts from data that is often privacy sensitive, and regulation and user trust restrict collecting it into a central server (a claim from practice, not tested here). Federated learning asks the question that follows: can we train a single shared model without the raw data ever leaving the user’s device? The answer is yes, and recommendation adds a privacy twist: the items a client updates can reveal what it touched.
What this appendix assumes. It assumes gradient-descent training on a central dataset (Neural Networks & Back-propagation) and matrix factorization (Traditional Recommender Systems §5). It is a thin frontier appendix: a map, not a full course. It carries hand-checkable micro-examples (a federated-averaging step, and one user’s upload) and otherwise points to the standard references. The question it answers: how do you train a good recommender when the interaction data is too private to collect?
Federated learning inverts the usual flow. Instead of sending data to the model, you send the model to the data, and only model updates come back. One round of the standard protocol:
The raw data stays put; what travels is math. “Federated” is the apt word — many autonomous parties cooperate on a shared model under a coordinator, like a federation of states, without surrendering their local sovereignty (their data). The server merges the clients’ updates with Federated Averaging (FedAvg), the rule of §2. The takeaway: the server learns from updates, not from the data that produced them.

title: Appendix E — Federated & Privacy-Preserving Recommendation
Appendix E — Federated & Privacy-Preserving Recommendation
section: 2. FedAvg: aggregate by a data-weighted average
text:
2. FedAvg: aggregate by a data-weighted average
Ann’s phone trained on 1000 ratings and Bob’s on 5, and both send back an improved model: whose version should count more? The standard answer is Federated Averaging (FedAvg), McMahan et al. (2017): the new global model is the average of the clients’ local models, weighted by how much data each holds,
\[
w_{\text{global}} \;=\; \frac{\sum_k n_k\,w_k}{\sum_k n_k},
\]
where \(w_k\) is client \(k\)’s locally-updated model and \(n_k\) its number of local examples (the sums run over the round’s sampled clients). The weighting matters because clients hold unequal amounts of data.

Worked example — one FedAvg step. Take Ann’s and Bob’s phones again, now holding 30 and 10 examples. The server broadcasts a single parameter \(w=0.5\). Client 1 (Ann) has \(n_1=30\) local examples and ends at \(w_1=0.8\) (update \(\Delta_1=+0.3\)); client 2 (Bob) has \(n_2=10\) and ends at \(w_2=0.4\) (\(\Delta_2=-0.1\)). The data-weighted global is \[
w_{\text{global}} = \frac{30(0.8) + 10(0.4)}{30+10} = \frac{24+4}{40} = \mathbf{0.7}.
\] The same result from the updates: \(0.5+\frac{30(0.3)+10(-0.1)}{40}=0.5+0.2=0.7\). Note it lands at \(0.7\), pulled toward the data-rich client 1, not at the plain mean \(0.6\) you would get by ignoring the counts. And the server learned this without seeing a single raw interaction from either device: only the updates (or the models \(w_1,w_2\)) and the counts crossed the wire (§3 shows what updates can still reveal). With \(n_2=10\) fixed, a client 1 of \(n_1=10,30,90,1000\) examples gives \(0.6,\,0.7,\,0.76,\,0.796\): the global moves toward the data-rich client and never past \(0.8\), because a weighted average lies between its inputs and \(n_1/(n_1+10)\) stays below \(1\).
The takeaway: FedAvg is a count-weighted average, so data-rich clients count for more but never override the others entirely.







Figure E.2: FedAvg is a data-weighted average (the §2 worked example). The \(0.5\) tick is the broadcast \(w\) the clients started from. Two clients report \(w_1{=}0.8\) (from \(n_1{=}30\) examples — large dot) and \(w_2{=}0.4\) (from \(n_2{=}10\) — small dot). A plain mean would sit at \(0.6\); weighting by data size pulls the global model to \(\mathbf{0.7}\), toward the data-rich client 1 — and no raw interaction ever leaves a device.

title: Appendix E — Federated & Privacy-Preserving Recommendation
section: 3. Federated recommendation — and its rated-set leak
text:
3. Federated recommendation — and its rated-set leak
Cara’s phone holds her film ratings, and the service wants to learn from them without ever receiving them. Drop matrix factorization (Traditional Recommender Systems §5) into this loop and you get Federated Collaborative Filtering (FCF) (Ammad-ud-din et al., 2019, for implicit feedback): the item factors are the shared global model the server aggregates, while each user’s own factor vector stays on their device and is updated locally. A client computes from its private interactions how each item factor should change (a gradient) and sends only those gradients up.
One user’s upload, a toy with explicit ratings (scores the user gives, as against implicit feedback such as clicks or views; Traditional Recommender Systems §5.3–§5.4). Her user factor vector is \(\mathbf p_u=(1,0.5)\) and item \(i\)’s factor is \(\mathbf q_i\) (Traditional Recommender Systems §5.1). She has rated item 1 only, with \(r=1.35\), and item 1’s factor is \(\mathbf q_1=(0.9,0.7)\), so \(\mathbf p_u\!\cdot\!\mathbf q_1=0.9+0.35=1.25\) and the error on that rating is \(e=r-\mathbf p_u\!\cdot\!\mathbf q_1=0.1\).
For squared error, the gradient of \((r-\mathbf p_u\!\cdot\!\mathbf q_1)^2\) with respect to item 1’s factor \(\mathbf q_1\) is \(-2e\,\mathbf p_u=(-0.2,-0.1)\), and she uploads that, tagged with item 1’s id; other items, unrated, get none.
The server then sums the uploads for item 1 over all users and steps its factor against them, \(\mathbf q_1\leftarrow\mathbf q_1-\gamma\sum_u\mathbf g_{u1}\). This is a plain sum (FCF’s Eqs. 10-12), taking the regularizer weight \(\lambda=0\) so the server’s regularizer, the penalty on large factors of Traditional Recommender Systems §5.3, adds nothing. Here \(\gamma\) is the server’s step size, the \(\eta\) of §1 applied to the summed gradients, and \(\mathbf g_{u1}\) is user \(u\)’s upload.
For one user and \(\gamma=0.5\), \(\mathbf q_1\) moves by \((+0.1,+0.05)\), to \((1.0,0.75)\), so \(\mathbf p_u\!\cdot\!\mathbf q_1\) rises from \(1.25\) to \(1.375\), just past the target \(1.35\) (a step \(1.25\) times the gap). FCF applies the \(-2\) on the server; the toy uploads it.
Two things are visible to the server. If it can tell whose upload it is, an upload for item 1 says she rated item 1. And the uploaded gradient is a scaled copy of \(\mathbf p_u\), so \(\mathbf p_u\) itself is never sent, but every upload is a multiple of it and the server learns the line along which it points. The multiple \(-2e\) can be negative, so the server does not learn which way along the line. The upload is the squared-error part only; the regularizer is added on the server, as in FCF.
That is the rated-set leak, and it holds in this explicit-rating setting: sending an update for item \(i\) reveals that the user rated item \(i\) (when the server can tell whose update it is), because only rated items have a gradient. FCF as published uses implicit feedback and reports a gradient for every item, which hides the zero pattern. Whether the sign and size of its values still separate touched from untouched items is not tested here, and the values still carry \(\mathbf p_u\)’s line.
A note on step sizes: Traditional Recommender Systems §5.3 steps by \(\eta/2\) times the gradient (its \(\eta\) absorbs the 2), so the toy’s \(\gamma=0.5\) is \(\eta=0.5\) in §1’s sense and \(\eta=1\) in §5.3’s.
FedRec (federated recommendation with explicit feedback; Lin et al., 2021; see the glossary) addresses the rated-set leak by uploading gradients for extra randomly sampled unrated items (decoys, \(\rho\) of them per rated item) too, with virtual ratings filled in by a hybrid strategy (the user’s average rating or a predicted one), so the real interactions do not stand out among the decoys.
In the toy above, suppose she has rated only item 1, so her average rating is \(1.35\), and a decoy item 2 with \(\mathbf q_2=(0.6,0.5)\) gets that virtual rating: its error is \(1.35-0.85=0.5\) and its upload is \((-1.0,-0.5)\), a multiple of \(\mathbf p_u\) just like the real \((-0.2,-0.1)\), so the server sees two uploads and cannot tell from their direction alone which item she rated (the sizes differ, and here the decoy’s is five times the real one, so size would give it away in this toy; in general it cannot tell whether a large upload is a real rating with a big error or a decoy). With \(\rho=1\) here, the server is left a one-in-two guess by presence alone, and FedRec uses \(\rho\in\{1,2,3\}\). That value range is as FedRec++ (Liang et al., 2021), a later method that removes the decoy noise, describes it. The decoys add noise to the gradients, which costs accuracy, and they are an obfuscation; the stronger tools come next.
More generally, because raw gradients can still leak information, federated systems layer on two further tools.
Secure aggregation (Bonawitz et al., 2017): the server sees only the sum of the count-weighted updates, not any individual one. In §2 the sum \(30(0.3)+10(-0.1)=8\) gives \(0.5+8/40=0.7\), and the server never sees \(+0.3\) or \(-0.1\) alone.
Differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006, applied to model training by Abadi et al., 2016: noise added to updates, so the server cannot be sure of any single value, at some cost in accuracy).
Real differential privacy clips each update to a maximum size and adds random noise whose scale is set by the privacy budget \(\varepsilon\) (a smaller \(\varepsilon\) means more noise and more privacy); the numbers here are not calibrated to any \(\varepsilon\). As an illustration only, if client 2’s \(-0.1\) were perturbed to \(-0.05\), the global would be \(0.7125\) rather than \(0.7\), a shift of \(0.0125\). For a survey of horizontal federated recommendation, with users’ devices as the clients, see Wang et al. (2024). The takeaway: with explicit ratings an upload still tells the server which items a user rated, and decoys and differential privacy trade some of that leak for accuracy.

title: Appendix E — Federated & Privacy-Preserving Recommendation
section: 4. The catch, and where it pays off
text:
4. The catch, and where it pays off
Ann’s rating values never leave her phone; what does the service pay for that? Federation is not free, and its costs are these:

Communication cost. Many rounds of sending models to and from millions of devices is expensive; FedAvg’s several local steps per round exist to cut the number of rounds (its abstract reports \(10\) to \(100\) times fewer rounds than synchronized stochastic gradient descent, which averages after every step, Traditional Recommender Systems §5.3; the paper’s tables show speedups of up to \(95\) times, depending on the task and the baseline).
Statistical heterogeneity. The clients’ data are not independent and identically distributed (non-IID): each user’s data comes from a different distribution (one watches only horror, another only cartoons), so local updates pull the shared model in different directions. FedAvg’s own paper reports it robust on its benchmarks; that naive averaging converges slowly or poorly on harder splits is a claim from practice, not tested here. Separately, clients hold unequal amounts of data (30 against 10 in §2), which the \(n_k\) weights handle.
Residual privacy risk. Updates alone can leak; secure aggregation and differential privacy are needed for real guarantees, and differential privacy and decoys trade off against accuracy.
An accuracy gap, sometimes. Some federated schemes lose accuracy against a centralized model trained on the same pooled data, a price of privacy: FedRec’s accuracy worsens as its decoys grow, by the account of FedRec++ (Liang et al., 2021), which removes that noise, while FCF reports no loss of accuracy against a standard implementation on its datasets. Measure it on your own data.

It pays off where the data is too sensitive or too regulated to centralize (health, finance, on-device personalization: claims from practice, not tested here; McMahan et al. (2017) motivate the approach with text entry on phones), the setting where the alternative is not “a slightly better central model” but no model at all. Like Appendix D (Reinforcement Learning for Recommendation), this is a pointer: an adjacent paradigm the book’s collaborative-filtering through-line touches at the edge (it is matrix factorization and gradient descent, rearranged for privacy) rather than a core chapter. The takeaway: federation buys privacy at the price of communication, heterogeneity and sometimes accuracy, so use it where the data cannot be centralized.

title: Appendix E — Federated & Privacy-Preserving Recommendation
text:
5. Glossary







Term
Plain meaning




Federated learning
Train a shared model across devices that keep their raw data local; only updates are shared.


Client / server
Devices holding private data / the coordinator that aggregates their updates.


FedAvg
Aggregate by a data-size-weighted average of clients’ local models (McMahan et al., 2017).


FCF
Federated collaborative filtering: item factors are global; each user’s factor stays on-device (its uploads still carry the factor’s line, §3).


FedRec
Federated recommendation with explicit feedback (Lin et al., 2021): uploads gradients for decoy items as well as rated ones (§3); FedRec++ (Liang et al., 2021) removes the noise the decoys add.


Decoy items, hybrid filling
Randomly sampled unrated items whose gradients are uploaded with virtual ratings filled in (the user’s average rating or a predicted one), so the real ones do not stand out; \(\rho\) decoys per rated item (§3).


The rated-set leak
With explicit ratings, sending an update for item \(i\) reveals (to a server that knows whose it is) that the user rated \(i\), and the gradient is a scaled copy of the user’s vector; FedRec masks the rated set with decoy items (see §3).


Secure aggregation
The server sees only the sum of client updates, never any individual one (Bonawitz et al., 2017).


Differential privacy
Add calibrated noise to updates so that how much any single user’s data can be inferred is bounded — by a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\) (smaller means more noise and more privacy; not the exploration rate \(\varepsilon\) of the Bandits chapter), not reduced to zero; §3’s numbers are not calibrated to any \(\varepsilon\) (Dwork et al., 2006; Abadi et al., 2016).


Non-IID data (statistical heterogeneity)
Each client’s data comes from a different distribution (one user all horror, another all cartoons), so local updates pull the shared model in different directions — a core difficulty of federation.

title: Glossary
text:
A
A single alphabetical list of every term defined across the book. Each term is defined in full in its home chapter; this page gathers them for quick reference and search.

title: Glossary
text:
Term
Meaning




A/B test (online eval)
Serve two models to live user halves and compare a business metric — the real verdict.


Ablation
A test that removes one part of a method to see what the part was worth (§4).


Ablation study
An experiment that removes one component of a model at a time to see what each contributes (§8.6, Step 0).


Activation function
The fixed, simple nonlinear bend a layer applies to its weighted sums, e.g. the sigmoid or ReLU (§3).


Activation function \(\phi\)
Nonlinear function applied to \(z\) (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU); its output \(a\) is the neuron’s activation.


Activations
The numbers a layer outputs; each unit’s is computed from the previous layer’s (§5.2).


Adam
An optimizer that divides each parameter’s step by the recent size of its own gradient (§5; Kingma and Ba, 2015).


Adaptor
A small trained network that maps the LLM’s vector into the recommender’s space and shrinks it, as in KAR (§4).


Adjacency matrix \(A\)
The whole graph’s connections as a square grid of 0/1.


Advantage
How much better an output scored than the group’s mean reward, divided by the group’s standard deviation in GRPO (§4).


Agentic recommender
An LLM that plans, remembers, and calls tools over multi-turn conversation (§2.4).


Alignment
A positive pair is pulled together: two views of one node, or in DirectAU an interacting user and item (§3.3).


Alignment & uniformity
Pull positives together / spread embeddings on the sphere (DirectAU); its popularity-weighted uniformity is said to help reduce exposure bias (items the system showed more got more clicks; a claim of the DirectAU paper, not tested here).


Alignment loss (RLMRec)
Ties the vectors of LLM-written user/item profiles to the collaborative (CF) embeddings — contrastively (RLMRec-Con) or by rebuilding masked profiles (RLMRec-Gen).


ALS / iALS
Alternating least squares: fix \(Q\) and solve for \(P\) in closed form, then swap. iALS is the implicit-feedback version, weighting each cell by a confidence (§5).


Anchor
The node \(i\) whose first view a contrastive loss compares with all second views (§3.2).


Angle (of an arrow)
Its direction, measured from the romance axis and positive toward action (§8).


ANN
Approximate nearest-neighbor search — fast, slightly-inexact vector retrieval; the candidate-generation engine.


ANN (approximate nearest neighbor)
Fast similarity search that makes dot-product retrieval scale to millions of items.


ANN (approximate nearest-neighbor)
Fast vector search that returns almost the closest vectors to a query, trading a little accuracy for large speed-ups; how embedding retrieval is served (Training and Serving a Recommender §7).


ANN (Approximate Nearest-Neighbor) search
Search that finds almost-the-best items by consulting a precomputed index instead of scoring every item, trading exactness for a large speed-up.


AP / MAP
Average Precision (Precision@\(k\) summed over hit positions, divided by $


API (application programming interface) model
One you cannot download: your program sends each request to the maker’s servers over the internet and pays per use.


Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)
Finding items whose vectors are close to a query vector by skipping most of the catalogue, at the price of sometimes missing the very best one (§15).


Arm
One choosable option (an item); “pulling” it = showing it. From the slot-machine metaphor.


Arm (tower, stream)
One of the two parallel sub-networks whose outputs meet in one logistic head; the papers also say tower or stream. Not the retrieval chapters’ tower, an encoder of only the user or only the item.


Attention
\(\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\): each position takes a blend of the value vectors of the positions it may see, weighted by how well its query matches their keys (§4.1).


Attention mask
Which tokens each token may look at: all of them (bidirectional — BERT, BERT4Rec) or only itself and earlier ones (causal — GPT, SASRec; §5.1).


Attention weight
The softmax of the scaled query-key scores: how much one position attends to another; positive, summing to \(1\).


Attributed / featureless
Whether nodes carry input feature vectors; recsys nodes are featureless (IDs only).


AUC
Area under the ROC curve: the fraction of (positive, negative) pairs ordered correctly; BPR is its smooth stand-in (§9).


AUC / ROC
Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve = P(score of a random relevant > random irrelevant) = the fraction of correctly ordered (relevant, irrelevant) pairs.


Augmentation
A small change to the input that should not change what it is (a flipped photo is the same cat); the recipe comes from image learning (SimCLR) and gives GCL its views (§3.1).


Autoencoder
A network trained to reproduce its own input through a narrow middle layer (§6.2).


Autoregressive decoding
Generate one token, append it, run the model again, repeat — the GPT generation loop (SASRec’s next-item prediction is one step of it; §5.4).


Autoregressive generation
Writing an output one token at a time, each token chosen given the ones before it (§2.2).


Auxiliary task
The extra, label-free objective added alongside the main (BPR) loss.

title: Glossary
text:
B







Term
Meaning




Back-propagation
Computing all weight-gradients by the chain rule, backward through the net.


Back-propagation (backprop)
The chain rule run backward from the loss, to find how the loss changes with every weight (§3).


Backbone
The base model an extra loss is added to; here LightGCN (§1, §7).


Backbone, lift
The base model a method is added to, and the gain over it (§4, RLMRec).


Bag-of-words vector
A paper described by which vocabulary words occur in it: one entry per word; in the standard Cora files (\(1{,}433\) words) each entry is \(1\) if present and \(0\) if absent; counts in our toy (§6).


Bandit
An MDP in which actions never change the next state (one state, or a fresh context each round); such actions are called one-shot.


Bandit feedback
You observe the reward only for the action you took, never the alternatives.


Base-rate effect
A rare condition (low prior) makes even an accurate test’s positives mostly false.


Baseline
A simple model to compare others with, such as plain matrix factorization with BPR (§15).


Basis
A set of vectors from which every vector can be built in exactly one way as a weighted sum.


Batch / Layer Norm
Re-center/re-scale activations for training stability (LayerNorm is the normalization the Transformer uses, §7).


Batch normalization / layer normalization
Re-center and re-scale activations across a batch / within one example: \([2,4,6]\to[-1.22,0,1.22]\) (§5.2).


Bayes’ rule
posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior.


Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR)
A ranking loss for implicit data: train so that an item the user interacted with scores above a randomly sampled unobserved one (§1; Loss Functions & Regularizers §9).


Beam search
A search that keeps only the best few partial lists at each step (§4).


Beam search (decoding)
Keep the \(W\) best partial ID prefixes per step; the completed tuples, ranked, are the top-\(K\) recommendations (§2.2).


Beam width \(W\)
How many partial candidates beam search carries forward at each step; the surviving completed tuples, ranked by probability, are the top-\(K\) (§2.2).


Benchmark framework
RecBole / Cornac / Elliot / Microsoft Recommenders / LensKit — unified datasets + models + protocol.


Benchmaxxing
Training on (or near) benchmark data so a high score can reflect memorization, not ability — why one leaderboard number is untrustworthy.


Bernoulli
One yes/no with parameter \(p\); \(-\log\) → BCE.


Bernoulli trial
One try with two outcomes, such as click / no click, with unknown chance \(\mu\).


BERT
Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers: trained by masked language modeling (pick about 15% of the tokens, mostly replaced by [MASK], and predict them), originally with a next-sentence objective that was later often dropped; an encoder for understanding text → embeddings (Devlin 2019; §5.1).


BERT4Rec
A bidirectional Transformer trained with the cloze (masked-item) objective.


Beta
Distribution over a probability; conjugate prior for Bernoulli.


Beta posterior
\(\text{Beta}(1+s,1+f)\) for \(s\) clicks, \(f\) non-clicks; conjugate to the Bernoulli click.


Bias–variance trade-off
Error splits into systematic mis-fit (bias) and sensitivity to the sample (variance); model complexity trades one against the other (§4).


Biases \(\mu\), \(b_u\), \(b_i\)
The global mean rating, a user’s generosity or harshness, and an item’s broad appeal; added before the dot product in biased MF (§5).


BIGRec
Bi-step grounding: an instruction-tuned LLM writes the next item by name, and the written text is matched to the nearest catalog item by embedding (§5).


Binary entropy
The entropy of a two-outcome variable with probabilities \(\theta\) and \(1-\theta\): \(-\theta\log_2\theta-(1-\theta)\log_2(1-\theta)\), which peaks at \(1\) bit for \(\theta=\tfrac12\) (§7).


Bipartite graph
Nodes in two groups; edges only cross between groups (users ↔︎ films).


Bit
The information in one fair coin flip; an event of probability \(\tfrac12\) carries \(1\) bit, and \(-\log_2 p\) bits in general.


Bits / nats
Units of entropy: \(\log_2\) gives bits, \(\ln\) gives nats; \(1\) bit \(=\ln 2\approx0.693\) nats (§7).


Blockbuster
A film that very many people watch: a node of huge degree (§13).


BM25 / hybrid retrieval
“Best Matching 25”, the standard keyword-scoring refinement of TF-IDF / blending its (sparse) scores with embedding (dense) scores in one query.


BM3
A multimodal recommender that trains without negative samples by comparing an embedding with a dropout copy of itself (§5).


Bonferroni / Holm
Multiple-comparison fixes for \(m\) tests: Bonferroni compares each \(p\) to \(\alpha/m\); Holm is a stepwise version that is never more conservative: it keeps every result Bonferroni keeps, and sometimes more (for \(p=0.012,\,0.020,\,0.024\) Bonferroni keeps one, Holm all three; §8.6 Step 3).


Bootstrap
Estimating how much a score wobbles by re-drawing the test cases at random with replacement (a case may be drawn more than once) many times and recomputing the score each time; it needs no bell-shape assumption (Evaluation Metrics §11d; named in §8.7).


BPR
Bayesian Personalized Ranking: a loss that teaches a recommender to rank an item a user chose above one they did not; it applies a sigmoid to the score gap (§3).


BPR loss
Pairwise ranking loss: push observed pairs above sampled negatives; Ann’s triple (Titanic over Matrix) costs \(0.027\) (§15).

title: Glossary
text:
C







Term
Meaning




Calibration
A model is calibrated when the numbers mean what they say: of impressions scored \(0.3\), about \(30\%\) are clicked (Evaluation Metrics §11).


Calibration / ECE
A model is calibrated if items it scores \(0.8\) are clicked about \(80\%\) of the time; the Expected Calibration Error averages the per-bin absolute gap between predicted and observed rates, weighting each bin by its share of predictions.


Capacity
The range of functions a model can express; a weight matrix on already-trained vectors adds none (§14).


Categorical
One of \(K\) classes; \(-\log\) → cross-entropy; paired with softmax.


Causal mask
Lower-triangular mask: position \(t\) may attend only to positions \(\le t\) (no peeking at the future).


CDF \(F(x)\)
Cumulative distribution function \(F(x)=\Pr(X\le x)\) — the running total of probability; a different function describing the same distribution.


Cell state
The LSTM’s protected memory line, edited only by a forget multiply and a write add (§3.3).


Censored reward
A reward not yet known: no click so far, but one may still come (§7).


Central Limit Theorem
The average of many independent noisy pieces is approximately bell-shaped around the truth; with enough pairs it keeps the \(t\)-test a fair approximation when the differences are not exactly normal, but not with a handful (§8.3, Fact 2).


Chain rule
Derivative of \(f(g(x))\) = \(f'(g)\cdot g'\); the basis of back-propagation.


Characteristic equation / polynomial
\(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\); its left side is the characteristic polynomial, and its roots are the eigenvalues.


Chebyshev polynomials
The family \(T_0=1\), \(T_1=\lambda\), \(T_{j+1}=2\lambda T_j-T_{j-1}\): the same filters a plain polynomial can express, the basis ChebyCF interpolates in; interpolating at Chebyshev points spreads the error nearly evenly over \([-1,1]\).


CIN (compressed interaction network)
xDeepFM’s explicit-interaction arm: crosses between whole field vectors, mixed into a few new vectors by learned weights.


Citation network
A graph whose nodes are papers and whose edges are citations; the GCN paper treats them as undirected (§6).


Client / server
Devices holding private data / the coordinator that aggregates their updates.


Closed-form / training-free CF
Recommenders that apply a fixed filter with no gradient training (GF-CF, PSGE, by their authors’ account).


Cloze objective
Hide some of a user’s items and predict them from the rest (BERT4Rec; §10).


Codebook / codeword
A small fixed menu of prototype vectors (the codebook); each entry is a codeword. Quantizing a vector means replacing it by its nearest codeword’s symbol (§2.2).


Cold item
A film with almost no clicks yet (§4 box).


Cold start
No history yet for a new user/item; CF cannot act.


Cold start (serving)
Having no learned vector for a brand-new item to put in the index, or for a brand-new user to query it with (§8).


Cold-start
A new user or item with no history, so no learned row to look up (§3).


Collaborative filtering (CF)
Recommend using interaction patterns across users (no content).


Collaborative signal
What can be learned from who interacted with what (From Graphs to LightGCN, Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning, The Spectral / Graph-Filter View), independent of item content.


Column space / image
Every output a matrix can produce — all weighted sums of its columns.


Complement \(\neg B\)
“Not \(B\)”; \(\Pr(\neg B)=1-\Pr(B)\) (§1).


Component / entry
One number inside a vector.


Computational graph
One node per quantity, one arrow per “is computed from” — the picture back-propagation walks backward (§5).


Concat (early fusion)
Append the LLM feature vector to the ID embedding — the quick first try, at the cost of a fatter serving vector. A frozen vector adds a fixed content score; only an adaptor or an FM or MLP scorer lets the model re-weigh it (§4).


Concatenation
Gluing vectors side by side: three layers of \(2\) numbers give \(6\) numbers per node (§14).


Condition number
The largest singular value divided by the smallest, \(\sigma_1/\sigma_{\min}\) (§6); a huge value means a solve or inverse with that matrix is numerically unreliable.


Conditional probability \(\Pr(A\mid B)\)
Probability of \(A\) given \(B\) occurred \(=\Pr(A\cap B)/\Pr(B)\).


Confidence \(c_{ui}\)
How much to trust an implicit signal: \(c_{ui}=1+\alpha\,n_{ui}\), growing with the play count \(n_{ui}\) (§5).


Confidence interval (CI)
\(\bar d \pm t^{*}s_d/\sqrt n\); the effect size with its uncertainty. A \(95\%\) CI excludes \(0\) exactly when the two-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\) is significant (a \(99\%\) CI goes with \(\alpha=0.01\); §8.5, §8.6 Step 4).


Conjugate prior
A prior whose posterior is the same family (Beta↔︎Bernoulli).


Consistent policy
One whose regret grows more slowly than any power \(T^{c}\) on every bandit of the class; none can beat \(\ln T\) growth (Lai and Robbins, §2).


Constrained decoding
Restricting what the model may generate to a valid vocabulary (here, real item identifiers), so an invalid answer cannot be produced at all (§2.2).


Content-based filtering
Recommend items similar (in features) to what the user liked.


Context (context window)
The longest input a model reads at once, in tokens: “8K context” \(\approx\) 8,000 tokens (word pieces). Longer text is cut off.


Context vector
The weighted average of the values under the attention weights; the summary that scores the next item (§4).


Contextual bandit
The reward depends on a context (user/item features); LinUCB models it linearly.


Contour (level set)
A curve along which \(f\) keeps one constant value, like a height line on a map; the gradient is perpendicular to it (§4).


Contrastive (InfoNCE) term
Added to the recommender’s loss: it pulls a node’s collaborative and projected semantic vectors together (the numerator) and pushes its collaborative vector away from other nodes’ semantic vectors (the denominator).


Contrastive learning
SSL pretext: pull a node’s two views together, push other nodes apart; needs negatives (DirectAU: no, §3.3); discriminative mechanism (this chapter’s own reading, not a standard label; §6.3).


Contrastive learning / views
Learning embeddings by comparison: two views of the same thing are pulled together, other things pushed apart (§2.4).


Convex
Curves up everywhere: for a function with second derivatives, one variable \(f''\ge0\), many variables a Hessian that is PSD at every point. A bowl, a trough, or a slope with no bottom (like \(e^x\)) — no bad local minima; any minimum is global.


Cosine similarity
\(\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}\in[-1,1]\) for nonzero vectors; direction agreement, ignoring length.


Cost / objective / criterion
Near-synonyms for loss (cost = total; objective = neutral; criterion = the code object).


Coverage
The fraction of the catalog that ever appears in anyone’s top-\(K\) list (§6).


CPU / GPU / RAM / VRAM
The general-purpose processor / the chip that does thousands of multiplications at once / the computer’s fast working memory / the GPU’s own memory, which must hold the whole model.


Credit assignment
Deciding which earlier action deserves credit for a reward that arrives later.


Critical / stationary point
Where \(f'(x)=0\) (many variables: \(\nabla f=\mathbf 0\)): peak, valley, plateau or saddle.


Critical value
The cutoff that pure luck exceeds only \(\alpha\) of the time (\(2.776\) for df \(=4\), \(\alpha=0.05\), two-sided) (§8.3).


Croissant
MLCommons machine-readable dataset-metadata standard (2024); NeurIPS encouraged a record in 2024, worded it “should use” in 2025 and “must use” in 2026, with the Responsible Artificial Intelligence (RAI) fields only requested in the 2026 call (the organizers’ post of 4 May 2026 requires them, §6).


Cross network
Stacked layers that raise interaction degree by one each, explicitly and at linear cost (\(2d\) parameters per layer). DCN = a cross network beside a deep MLP.


Cross-encoder
A model that reads a (user, item) pair together in one forward pass, so its score cannot be precomputed. A specialist reranker is usually one, and it is not an LLM (§2.1).


Cross-entropy / BCE / log loss
Classification loss; average code length (nats with \(\ln\), bits with \(\log_2\)) to encode the truth \(p\) with a code built for the prediction \(q\); BCE = −log-likelihood of a Bernoulli (categorical cross-entropy: of a categorical).


Cross-entropy \(H(p,q)\)
\(-\sum p\log q\); surprise of \(p\)’s outcomes scored by model \(q\) — the standard classification loss.


Cross-view alignment
Pulling a node’s two embeddings (collaborative \(\mathbf{e}_i\) and semantic \(\mathbf{s}_i\)) together with InfoNCE (§3).


CTR (click-through rate)
\(P(\text{click}\mid \text{user, item, context})\); the score the ranking stage predicts.


CTR / impression
Click-through rate \(=\) clicks \(/\) impressions, where an impression is one showing of an item to a user.


Curvature
How a curve bends: \(f''\) in one variable; in many, the second derivative along a chosen direction (§6).


Cutoff \(K\)
The list length in Recall@\(K\) (not the layer count \(K\) of §3.4): only a user’s top \(K\) films count (§7).

title: Glossary
text:
D







Term
Meaning




\(D^{-1/2}\)
The degree matrix with each diagonal degree replaced by \(1/\sqrt{\deg}\) — an entry-by-entry shortcut that works only because \(D\) is diagonal (§7).


Data augmentation
Train on randomly perturbed copies of inputs; one history \([A,B,C,D]\) gives four views (§5.2).


Data leakage
Test-period information seeping into training; silently inflates every metric.


DCG / IDCG / NDCG
Discounted Cumulative Gain (gains \(2^{\text{rel}}-1\), each divided by \(\log_2(i+1)\) at rank \(i\)) / its ideal / the normalized ratio in \([0,1]\).


DCNv2
The cross network with a full weight matrix per layer instead of a vector; its authors report it better than DCN, a report §9 says to test (low-rank form and a mixture of experts keep it affordable).


Debiasing
Methods that correct for users rating mostly what they chose to see (§7).


Decision tree / information gain
A flowchart of yes/no questions that sorts examples into groups / how much a question reduces the entropy of the labels; the tree asks the question with the largest gain first (§7).


Decoder
A network that turns an embedding back into the input it came from; the generative end of a network (§6.3).


Decoy items, hybrid filling
Randomly sampled unrated items whose gradients are uploaded with virtual ratings filled in (the user’s average rating or a predicted one), so the real ones do not stand out; \(\rho\) decoys per rated item (§3).


DeepFM
Wide & Deep with the wide arm replaced by an FM, sharing one embedding layer; no hand-crossing.


Degree
How many neighbors a node has.


Degree matrix \(D\)
Diagonal matrix of degrees; used for normalization.


Degrees of freedom
The number of values still free to vary once their mean is fixed: \(n-1\) for \(n\) runs (\(4\) for \(5\) seeds).


Degrees of freedom (df)
\(n-1\) for the paired test; sets which Student-\(t\) curve gives the \(p\)-value.


Demographic parity
Equal selection / exposure rate across groups.


Density
Interactions \(\div\) (users \(\times\) items) — the share of the user–item grid that is filled. The graph-CF trio sits near \(0.1\%\) (§2), but MovieLens-1M is about \(4.5\%\) (\(1{,}000{,}209/(6{,}040\times3{,}706)\)) and Netflix about \(1.2\%\) (\(100{,}480{,}507/(480{,}189\times17{,}770)\)), so check.


Derivative \(f'(x)\)
Instantaneous rate of change = slope of the curve at a point.


Determinant \(\det A\)
Area/volume-scaling factor (\(ad-bc\) for \(2\times2\)); equals the product of the eigenvalues (shown here for \(2\times2\)); \(\det=0\) ⇒ collapses a dimension / non-invertible.


Diagonal matrix
A matrix whose only possibly-nonzero entries lie on its diagonal; it just scales each axis (its singular values are the absolute values of its diagonal entries, put in order of size).


Difference quotient
\(\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\) — rise over run before taking \(h\to0\).


Differential privacy
Add calibrated noise to updates so that how much any single user’s data can be inferred is bounded — by a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\) (smaller means more noise and more privacy; not the exploration rate \(\varepsilon\) of the Bandits chapter), not reduced to zero; §3’s numbers are not calibrated to any \(\varepsilon\) (Dwork et al., 2006; Abadi et al., 2016).


Differentiate
Compute a derivative (limit of differences).


Dimension
How many components a vector has (\(\mathbb{R}^d\) = all \(d\)-vectors).


Direct preference optimization (DPO) / S-DPO
A loss that learns from pairs of a preferred and a rejected output with no separate reward model; Softmax-DPO (S-DPO) widens the pair to one preferred item against several negatives (§4).


DirectAU
A negative-free loss (Wang et al., KDD 2022) that optimizes alignment and uniformity directly, instead of via a softmax; its positive pair is a user and an item she interacted with, not two views (§3.3).


Directed / undirected
Whether an edge has a direction (A→B \(\ne\) B→A) or not.


Directional derivative
Rate of change of \(f\) along a unit direction \(\hat{\mathbf d}\): \(\nabla f\cdot\hat{\mathbf d}\).


Discount \(\gamma\)
How much a later reward is worth vs. now; \(\gamma\to0\) is myopic (cares only about the immediate reward, like a bandit’s objective), \(\gamma\to1\) far-sighted.


Discriminative vs. generative
Axis 1 — whether a model learns \(p(y\mid x)\) (a boundary; can’t generate) or \(p(x)\)/\(p(x,y)\) (the data; can sample). BPR/LightGCN is discriminative; VAEs/LLMs are generative.


Distributional hypothesis
“You shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth 1957; Harris 1954) — words in similar contexts have similar meanings; word2vec turns this into similar vectors (§2.1).


Diversity
Average dissimilarity within a recommended list.


DNN (deep neural network)
DeepFM’s name for the MLP arm — the same object as Wide & Deep’s deep arm.


Dot / inner / scalar product \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\)
\(\sum_i u_iv_i\); one number measuring agreement.


Dot product
Multiply-and-sum two embeddings → a similarity / ranking score.


DPO (direct preference optimization)
Fine-tuning a model on pairs of preferred and rejected outputs so it favors the preferred kind; the “alignment” of OneRec’s training, not the embedding alignment of §3 (§2.2).


Dropout
Randomly zero units during training; an ensemble-like regularizer; “edge dropout” on graphs.


Dynamic negative sampling
Keeping hard negatives hard: draw a few un-clicked candidates and keep the one the current model scores highest (§3).

title: Glossary
text:
E







Term
Meaning




Early stopping
Stop when validation stops improving; implicit regularizer.


EasyRec
A language model tuned with contrastive learning so that vectors from text line up with collaborative behavior: the feature-encoding cell of the enhancer (§2.3).


Edge
A connection (user liked film, rated \(4\) or \(5\)).


Effect size
The magnitude of the difference (\(\bar d\)); report it alongside \(p\) (significance \(\ne\) size).


Eigenbasis
A basis made of eigenvectors; a real symmetric matrix always has one of mutually perpendicular unit eigenvectors (the spectral theorem, §5, stated without proof).


Eigenvalue
One of the two extreme curvatures of a symmetric \(2\times2\) Hessian; their product is \(D\) (§6 optional box; Linear-Algebra primer §5).


Eigenvalue \(\lambda\)
The stretch factor of an eigenvector.


Eigenvector
A direction a matrix only stretches, not rotates: \(A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\).


Eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}\)
A special direction a matrix only stretches (not rotates): \(\tilde{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}\). The graph’s eigenvectors are its “frequency patterns.”


Elastic net
L1 + L2 combined; “stretchable net” keeping correlated features.


ELBO
Evidence lower bound: a computable lower bound on the data’s log-likelihood that a VAE (variational autoencoder) maximizes; Mult-VAE minimizes reconstruction loss + β·KL, which is exactly −ELBO when β = 1 (§11).


Element-wise product \(\odot\)
Multiply two vectors number by number: \([2,-2]\odot[2,0]=[4,0]\); the dot product is the sum of the result (§14).


Elo
The chess rating system, reused for chatbot arenas: beating a strong opponent raises your rating more than beating a weak one.


Embedding
A learned vector representing a user/item as a point in space.


Embedding (layer)
The table that replaces each field’s active category by its learned dense vector \(\mathbf e_f\); one copy, read by every arm that needs it.


Embedding layer
A learnable lookup table; id → its row (= one-hot × matrix); the input side for discrete data.


Embedding matrix \(E\)
All embeddings stacked, one row per node: \(N\times d\); reading row \(k\) is the lookup of Neural Networks & Back-propagation §3 (§4).


Empirical mean
An arm’s clicks divided by its pulls so far, written \(\hat\mu_i\); \(2\) clicks in \(3\) pulls give \(0.667\) (§3).


Encoder
Whatever turns raw inputs into embeddings; here, LightGCN’s propagation over the ID table (§3.1).


Encoder / decoder
An encoder reads a sequence into context-aware vectors, every token seeing every other (BERT); a decoder writes text one token at a time, each token seeing only itself and earlier ones (GPT; §5.1).


Enhancer / reranker (LLM role)
Recsys LLM roles: generate item/user text features / re-order a candidate list — not chat.


Enhancer pipeline
Using an LLM offline to manufacture features for a fast collaborative backbone that serves.


Enhancer-style
An LLM enriches the inputs of an existing recommender instead of replacing it (§17).


Entropy bonus / exploring
In reinforcement learning (RL, learning by trial and reward), a reward proportional to the entropy of a model’s choices / what the bonus buys: trying actions other than the one that looks best so far (§7).


Entropy \(H(p)\)
\(-\sum p\log p\): average surprise / uncertainty (maximal at uniform). In bits with \(\log_2\) (the average yes/no questions, or bits to store one sample, as in §7’s examples), in nats with \(\ln\).


Epoch
One pass over all the training triples (§13; Neural Networks & Back-propagation §6).


Epoch / batch
One full pass over the training data / the small group of examples used for one update (§5.2).


Equal opportunity
Equal true-positive rate across groups (the truly-relevant are surfaced equally).


ERM
Empirical Risk Minimization — “fit the training data” (usually + a regularizer).


Euclidean distance \(\lVert\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\rVert\)
Straight-line gap between two arrow-tips; feels magnitude (unlike cosine).


Evidence \(p(D)\)
Normalizer; data probability averaged over \(\theta\), each \(\theta\) weighted by its prior (a.k.a. marginal likelihood).


Expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) / mean \(\mu\)
Probability-weighted average value.


Explicit / implicit feedback
Stated ratings (likes and dislikes) vs. behavioral positives (\(1\) = clicked / played / bought; blanks are unknown, not \(0\) — no true negatives).


Explicit vs implicit interaction
Explicit = built by a formula you can point at, with a known degree and a readable strength; implicit = mixed inside an MLP’s layers, where no single weight names a cross.


Explicit vs. implicit feedback
Star ratings vs. clicks/plays (positive-only, unlabeled negatives).


Explore vs. exploit
Try an uncertain option to learn (explore) vs. take the best-known one now (exploit).

title: Glossary
text:
F







Term
Meaning




F1@K
Harmonic mean of precision and recall.


Factor vector
A feature’s short learned vector \(\mathbf v_j\); the dot product of two is their interaction strength.


Factorization machine (FM)
MF generalized to any features: each feature gets a vector, each feature pair interacts via a dot product (Rendle, 2010). MF is the ids-only special case.


False negative
A “negative” the user would in fact have liked — pushed away by mistake (§3.4). Not the hypothesis-testing sense of the term.


FCF
Federated collaborative filtering: item factors are global; each user’s factor stays on-device (its uploads still carry the factor’s line, §3).


Feature
A given number about a node, measured outside the model (a paper’s word counts); training never changes it (§6).


Feature interaction / cross
A pair (or, higher-order, a larger group) of features whose combination matters (user \(\times\) genre); FM scores a pair as \(\langle\mathbf v_j,\mathbf v_{j'}\rangle\).


Feature matrix \(X\)
One row of features per node (\(N\times F\)); data, not learned (§6).


Feature store
The table of generated id → (profile, vector) the serving path reads; the LLM is never on the serving path.


FedAvg
Aggregate by a data-size-weighted average of clients’ local models (McMahan et al., 2017).


Federated learning
Train a shared model across devices that keep their raw data local; only updates are shared.


FedRec
Federated recommendation with explicit feedback (Lin et al., 2021): uploads gradients for decoy items as well as rated ones (§3); FedRec++ (Liang et al., 2021) removes the noise the decoys add.


Feed-forward (FFN)
Per-token MLP \(\max(0,\mathbf{x}W_1{+}\mathbf{b}_1)W_2{+}\mathbf{b}_2\) inside each block; transforms each token (about two thirds of each block’s weights when its hidden layer is 4× wider; §4.3).


Feedback loop
Recommend → click → log → retrain on skewed data → more skew; the “rich get richer” spiral that compounds bias.


Field
One attribute of the row (user, item, genre, device, daypart); each field contributes exactly one active category, and one embedding vector \(\mathbf e_f\).


Filter response \(h(\lambda)\)
The function deciding how much each frequency is kept; defines the filter.


FinalMLP, feature gate
A two-stream MLP model; its feature gate is a learned weight per input feature that decides how much of it a stream sees (§9).


Fine-tune / distil / gold & silver labels
Train a released model further on your data / train a small model to copy a big one’s outputs / hand-checked reference answers vs cheap machine-written ones.


Fine-tuning / instruction tuning
Continuing to train a pretrained model on task data. Instruction tuning uses prompt–answer pairs (“User liked A, B; will they like C? → Yes”), which is how TALLRec and BIGRec are trained (§2.1, §5).


Fine-tuning vs in-context prompting
Train the model’s weights on the task, or keep them fixed and put worked examples in the prompt (§5.2).


Focal loss
Cross-entropy times \((1-p_t)^\gamma\), with \(p_t\) the probability of the true class, to down-weight easy examples; for class imbalance.


Forward pass
Running an input through the net to a prediction + loss.


FPMC
Factorizing Personalized Markov Chains: MF term \(+\) a learned (factorized) transition term.


Frequency (on a graph)
An eigenvector pattern; on a path, the number of sign changes: low = smooth over neighbors, high = jagged.


Frobenius norm \(\lVert A\rVert_F\)
The square root of the sum of the squares of all a matrix’s entries — its L2 length, flattened.


Frozen split
A train/test partition released as files and reused unchanged by later papers of one lineage (the trio’s defining feature, §2), which makes their numbers mutually quotable; not every graph-CF paper reuses it (§4).


Frozen text encoder
Run text once through a fixed pretrained model and keep the output vector — the semantic \(\mathbf{s}_i\) RecSys aligns/consumes (§5.2).


Full ranking vs. sampled negatives
Score the held-out item against every item the user has not seen, or against a handful (99–100) drawn at random (negative sampling; a negative is an item the user did not interact with, treated as non-relevant). The two give different numbers for the same model (§4).


Full vs. sampled ranking
