Rank the true item against the whole catalog vs. a few sampled negatives; the latter is inconsistent across papers and optimistic (with one held-out item per user, as in leave-one-out, fewer competitors mean the item can only rank higher).


FuxiCTR, BARS-CTR
An open-source library for configuring and reproducing CTR models, and the benchmark built with it that re-ran the lineage under equal tuning (§9).

title: Glossary
text:
G







Term
Meaning




Gap \(\Delta_i\)
\(\mu^{*}-\mu_i\): how much less an arm pays per pull than the best arm; each pull of it adds this to the regret (§2).


Gate / GRU
A gate is a number between \(0\) and \(1\) the cell computes at each step to decide how much of the new candidate to write in (near \(0\) keeps the old summary, near \(1\) overwrites it); the gated recurrent unit (GRU) is the recurrent cell built on gates (§3).


Gaussian (Normal)
Bell curve \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\); \(-\log\) → squared error (MSE) when \(\sigma\) is the same fixed number for every point (§4).


GCL
Graph Contrastive Learning — contrastive SSL on a graph recommender.


GCN
The model built by stacking graph-convolution layers (plus a loss, a prediction step that turns two embeddings into a score, and — in vanilla GCN — \(W\) and \(\sigma\)). Operation vs. architecture.


Generative learning
SSL pretext: reconstruct the masked/corrupted input; no negatives (for a plain reconstruction error; RLMRec-Gen is the exception, §7); generative / reconstructive mechanism.


Generative recommendation
Recommend by generating an item’s Semantic ID token by token (§2.2).


Gini coefficient
Concentration of recommendations on few items: \(0\) = perfectly even; the maximum, all on one of \(n\) items, is \((n-1)/n\) — near \(1\) only for a large catalog.


Global temporal split
One cut-off date for everybody: train on everything before it, test on everything after (Evaluation Metrics).


GNN
Graph neural network: a network that updates each node’s vector from its neighbors’, as LightGCN does (§7).


GPT
Generative Pre-trained Transformer (next-token, causal); a decoder for generating text (the model of Radford 2018; the name came later; §5.1).


Gradient
The slope (or slopes) a model follows downhill when it trains (§3; Calculus primer).


Gradient \(\nabla f\)
Vector of all partials; points in the direction of steepest increase.


Gradient clipping
Capping the gradient’s length at a ceiling so it cannot explode; the direction is kept (§5).


Gradient descent
\(\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla f\): step against the gradient to minimize.


Gram matrix
A matrix’s transpose times itself, \(R^{\top}R\); entry \((i,j)\) counts the users who liked both films \(i\) and \(j\).


Graph
Nodes + edges.


Graph convolution
The operation (in LightGCN’s form): replace each node’s embedding with the degree-weighted sum of its neighbors’ (one matrix multiply by the normalized adjacency).


Graph Fourier Transform (GFT)
Projecting a graph signal onto the eigenvectors of the (normalized) adjacency.


Graph Laplacian
A matrix built from a graph, a close relative of its adjacency matrix; the standard forms are built like an \(A^{\top}A\) and so are PSD (taken as given in §6).


Graph signal
One value per node (e.g. a user’s interaction vector over films).


Graph Signal Processing (GSP)
Treating one-number-per-node data as a “signal” and processing it with graph frequencies.


Graph-CF trio
Gowalla / Yelp2018 / Amazon-Book — the frozen-split benchmark of graph-CF papers.


Graphics processing unit (GPU)
The chip that trains a model fast but holds little memory (§15).


GraphMAE
Graph masked autoencoder (Hou et al., KDD 2022): hides some nodes’ input features and rebuilds them with a scaled cosine error. A node- and graph-classification method; this chapter borrows its mask-and-rebuild idea as a recommender example (§6.2).


GraphSAGE
A model (Hamilton et al., 2017) that builds a node’s vector from a sample of its neighbors, so a new node gets a vector at once (§14).


ε-greedy
Exploit the best estimate with prob \(1-\varepsilon\); pull a uniform-random arm with prob \(\varepsilon\).


Greedy walk
HNSW’s search: from some item, step to the linked item that scores highest against the user vector, and stop when no link beats where you stand (§7).


GRPO
Group relative policy optimization: sample a group of outputs for one prompt and score each against the group’s mean and spread, with no value model (§4).


GRU
Gated Recurrent Unit: a lighter 2-gate cousin of the LSTM, with no separate cell state (Cho 2014; §3.4); GRU4Rec is its session-based recommender.


GRU4Rec
A gated RNN for session-based recommendation; session-parallel batches + a ranking loss.

title: Glossary
text:
H







Term
Meaning




Hadamard product (\(\odot\))
Entry-by-entry product of two vectors of the same length: \([1,2]\odot[3,4]=[3,8]\) (§7, §8).


Hallucination
An LLM confidently producing an item that is not in the catalog; reduced by constrained decoding, candidate-list forcing or post-hoc filtering (defined in §1, fixes in §2.2).


Hard negative
A negative that sits close to the anchor, so it dominates the loss; dangerous when it is closer than the positive (§3.3).


Harmonic mean
The reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals; for two numbers \(P,R\) it is \(2PR/(P+R)\), dragged down by the smaller one (\(0.6\) and \(0.75\) give \(0.667\)).


Harness / orchestration
The engineering around the LLM call — templates, validation, batching, retries, caching, cost control.


He / Kaiming init
Draw initial weights with variance \(2/\text{fan\_in}\) (fan_in = inputs per neuron) — the scale that keeps ReLU activations from shrinking or exploding layer by layer (§6).


Head
The few most popular items, at the left of the popularity curve (§6).


Heat kernel
The blur \(e^{-t(1-\lambda)}\): signal spreading over the graph like heat for a time \(t\) (the idea behind BSPM’s blur).


Hessian \(H\)
Matrix of second partial derivatives \(f_{xx},f_{xy},f_{yx},f_{yy}\) (multivariable curvature).


Hidden layer
A layer that is neither input nor output.


Hinge loss
The loss of the support vector machine (SVM), a classic classifier that separates two classes with the widest possible gap between them; flat once correct-with-margin (\(m=y\hat y\ge1\)), then a linear ramp — shaped like a hinge.


Hit Rate (HR@K)
Fraction of users with \(\ge 1\) relevant item in the top-\(K\).


Hit-Rate@K (HR@K) / NDCG@K
Was the held-out next item in the top \(K\)? / how high was it — normalized discounted cumulative gain (Evaluation Metrics).


HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)
An ANN index that links each item to its nearest neighbors in layered graphs and answers a query by a greedy walk of about \(\log_2 M\) steps, each scoring a few dozen linked items (a simple model of the walk, not a measurement; §7).


HNSW / IVF-PQ / DiskANN / CAGRA
ANN index types: graph (in-RAM default) / inverted-list + compression (memory-thrifty) / on-disk (billion-scale) / GPU graph (batched throughput).


Homogeneous / heterogeneous
One node type, vs. several (users and items).


Hop
One step along an edge (distance in the graph); fixed by the graph, not chosen. \(K\) layers mix the starting vectors of nodes a walk of \(K\) steps away (§5).


HR@\(K\), MRR, AUC
Hit rate: was the held-out item in the top \(K\); mean reciprocal rank: the average of \(1/\text{rank}\); area under the receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) curve: the chance a clicked impression outscores an unclicked one. Labels here; definitions in Evaluation Metrics (§4).


HSTU
Hierarchical Sequential Transduction Units: Meta’s generative recommender that reads a user’s sequence of actions and writes the next one (§2.2).


Hub
A node joined to many others (Vendetta in the film path).


Huber loss
Quadratic near 0, linear far out; robust compromise (after P. Huber).


Hybrid
Combine content-based + collaborative, e.g. a weighted blend of their predictions, or LLM features + a CF backbone (§7).


Hypergraph
A graph whose edges may join many nodes at once; HCCF contrasts one with the ordinary graph (§2, §4).


Hyperparameter
A setting fixed before training, such as the number of layers \(K\) (§5).

title: Glossary
text:
I







Term
Meaning




ID embedding
An embedding that exists only to tell one node from another, with nothing measured about the node; LightGCN’s \(E^{(0)}\) (§6).


ID table
The one freely trainable vector per user and per item, before any neighbor-averaging (§3.4).


Ideal low-pass
A hard cutoff: keep the top few patterns whole and zero the rest, as GF-CF’s ideal part and a truncated SVD do (§4, §6).


Idempotency
Re-running the pipeline on unchanged input does no new work (hash → cache hit), so a profile is regenerated only when its input or the prompt version changes.


Identity \(I\)
The “do-nothing” matrix; \(I\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}\).


Identity matrix \(I\)
A \(1\) on the diagonal, \(0\) elsewhere; as \(X=I\) it gives each node a one-hot ID, and \(XW\) then picks out the rows of \(W\) (§6).


Impression
One logged showing of one item to one user in one slot; the unit of a CTR row, labeled \(1\) (clicked) or \(0\) (not).


In-batch negative
A negative taken from the other nodes in the current mini-batch, rather than from the whole catalog (§3.4).


Indefinite
Curvature up in some directions and down in others (\(D<0\) for a \(2\times2\) Hessian; eigenvalues of both signs) — the Hessian at a saddle.


Independence
\(\Pr(A\cap B)=\Pr(A)\Pr(B)\); one event tells you nothing about the other.


Index
A lookup structure built once, offline, over the item vectors, that finds the best-scoring items without scoring them all (§7).


Index recall (recall@\(K\))
The share of the exact top-\(K\) items that the approximate index also returns: \(4\) of \(5\) is \(0.80\) (§7).


Inductive
A model that learns a rule building a vector from what is visible about any node (features, neighbors), so a new node needs no retraining (§14).


Inference / serving
Using the trained embeddings to return a user’s top-\(K\) list.


Inflection point
Where \(f''\) changes sign (the curve switches between bending up and down).


InfoNCE
A contrastive training loss: a softmax that must pick a matching pair out of mismatched ones (§3; §7 for its link to mutual information).


InfoNCE / NT-Xent
Contrastive loss: \(-\log\) of the positive’s softmax share, the denominator running over the positive and the negatives; Info = mutual-info bound, NCE = Noise-Contrastive Estimation; temperature \(\tau\).


Integral \(\int\)
Area under a curve; the reverse of differentiation; gives probabilities/expectations.


Interaction matrix \(R\)
Users-×-films table of 0/1 (who liked what).


Inverted file
A partition index: the catalog is split into buckets, each with a center point (the average of its vectors); a query scores the centers, then only the items in the best few buckets (§7).


Invertible / singular
Invertible = has an inverse \(A^{-1}\) that undoes it, \(A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I\) (\(\det\neq0\), full rank); singular = no inverse (\(\det=0\)).


IPS-weighted recall
Recall with each relevant item weighted by \(1/p\) and divided by the total weight: \(0.60\) against the raw \(0.75\) on the running list (§12.4).


Isotonic regression (PAV)
Calibrates with a fitted non-decreasing staircase; the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm averages neighbors that break the order, which can create ties.


Item-kNN
Recommend the items most similar, by who interacted with both, to those the user already liked; a strong simple baseline (§5).


item2vec
word2vec applied to users’ histories (“item = word, history = sentence”; item2vec itself ignores their order); a collaborative item embedding (§2.4).

title: Glossary
text:
J







Term
Meaning




Jaccard similarity
\(\lvert A\cap B\rvert/\lvert A\cup B\rvert\) on liked-sets; ignores rating values.


Jacobian
The matrix of all partial derivatives of a vector function; for \(\mathbf z=W\mathbf h\) it is \(W\), and back-prop multiplies by its transpose (§5).


Jacobian \(J\)
Matrix of partials of a vector-valued function (rows = outputs, columns = inputs).


Joint / marginal
Joint \(p(x,y)=\Pr(X{=}x\text{ and }Y{=}y)\), the chance of each pair of values; marginal \(p(x)=\sum_y p(x,y)\) (sum the joint over the other variable — the row totals in the margin of the grid).


JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)
A plain-text format for records, e.g. {"brand": "Acme", "fit": "slim"} — how an extractor returns structured fields.

title: Glossary
text:
K







Term
Meaning




@K
Evaluated over the top \(K\) recommended positions only.


k-core filter
Iteratively drop users/items with \(<k\) interactions until none remain; stabilizes the data. The guarantee holds before the split, not after it (§3).


\(k\)-fold
Cut the data into \(k\) parts; test on each in turn, train on the rest, average (§3). A random scheme.


\(k\)-NN / neighborhood
The \(k\) most-similar users/items used for a prediction.


KAR
Knowledge Augmented Recommendation: prompt an LLM for user reasoning and item facts offline, then feed them to any backbone through a mixture-of-experts adapter (§2.3).


KL divergence
Asymmetric “distance” between distributions (Kullback–Leibler); a divergence, not a metric.


KL divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)\)
\(H(p,q)-H(p)\ge0\); extra surprise from using \(q\) not \(p\); asymmetric (a divergence, not a distance).


Knob (hyperparameter)
A value set by hand before training (\(\delta\), \(\gamma\), \(\tau\), \(\eta\), \(\lambda\)), not learned from the data like the parameters \(\theta\) (§2.1).


Knowledge distillation
Training a small model to match a large model’s output probabilities; the KL divergence measures the mismatch (§7).


KV-cache
Key–value cache: store past tokens’ keys and values so each decode step pushes only the new token through the model — \(O(T)\) token-passes instead of \(O(T^2)\) (§5.4).

title: Glossary
text:
L







Term
Meaning




L1 / lasso
$


L2 / ridge / Tikhonov / weight decay
\(\sum\theta_k^2\) penalty; shrinks weights smoothly toward 0; = Gaussian prior centered at \(0\). Weight decay is the same thing under plain (stochastic) gradient descent, not under Adam (hence AdamW, §5.1).


L2 norm / L1 norm \(\lVert\boldsymbol\theta\rVert_2,\lVert\boldsymbol\theta\rVert_1\)
The length of the weight list as the root of the sum of squares / as the sum of absolute values; their penalties come from the Gaussian and Laplace priors (§6).


L2 penalty
The regularizer \(\lambda\lVert E^{(0)}\rVert^2\): \(\lambda\) times the sum of the squares of every entry of the starting vectors (\(0.01\times26.25=0.2625\) in the toy); LightGCN penalizes only the base embeddings (§15).


L2-normalize / ANN
Divide a vector by its length so a dot product becomes a cosine; approximate nearest-neighbor search finds the closest catalog vectors without scoring all (§4.4).


Lambda \(\lambda\) (regularization strength)
How much we weight the regularizer vs. the loss.


LambdaRank / LambdaMART
Listwise methods that write no loss, only a gradient weighted by each pair’s effect on NDCG (the per-pair gradients are Burges’s \(\lambda_{ij}\)).


Language model
A model that predicts a missing or next token from its context; an LLM is a very large Transformer one (§2.4, §5).


Laplace
Peaked/heavy-tailed \((\mu,b)\); \(-\log\) → absolute error (MAE) when \(b\) is the same fixed number for every point.


Laplacian \(L=I-\tilde A\)
The same patterns as \(\tilde A\) with labels \(\mu=1-\lambda\): smooth at \(0\), jagged at \(2\) (§1).


Large language model (LLM)
A model trained on large amounts of text, which can write and read descriptions of users and items (§13, §17).


Latency
How long the serving path takes, in milliseconds (ms); p50 is the median, the time half of the requests beat (§4.1).


Latency (and p99)
The time between a request arriving and the answer going back; a p99 budget is one that \(99\) of every \(100\) requests must meet (§8).


Latent dimension \(d\) (also called the rank)
Width of the factor vectors; the dial between under- and over-fitting (§5.2). Not the “rank” of ranking a list (§6).


Latent factor
A hidden, learned dimension of taste/content.


Latent vector
The short list of \(k\) numbers an FM learns for each category; its dot product with another category’s vector is the pair’s strength.


Law of Large Numbers
The sample average converges to the expectation as samples accumulate.


Law of total probability
\(\Pr(A)=\sum_j\Pr(A\mid B_j)\Pr(B_j)\) over cases \(B_j\) that do not overlap and together cover every outcome (e.g. \(B\) and \(\neg B\)); the engine of Bayes’ evidence term.


Layer
One application of the graph-convolution rule to all nodes (a computation step in the model); the number of layers \(K\) is a hyperparameter you choose.


Layer / width / depth
A bank of neurons / neurons-per-layer / number of layers.


Layer combination
Averaging the embeddings from all layers, \(\mathbf{e}_u=\sum_{k}\alpha_k\mathbf{e}_u^{(k)}\); for Ann’s pairs in this toy it slows over-smoothing rather than curing it, and Bob and Cara gain little from it (§12).


Layer superscript \((\ell)\)
A layer number, not a power: \(W^{(\ell)}\), \(\mathbf h^{(\ell)}\) belong to layer \(\ell\); subscripts pick entries.


Layer weights \(\alpha_k\)
The coefficients of that combination; usually all equal, \(\alpha_k = 1/(K+1)\) (§12).


Layer-combined embedding
A node’s final vector: the weighted sum of its vectors after 0, 1, …, \(K\) rounds of neighbor-averaging, as LightGCN produces it (§3.4).


LayerNorm / Pre-LN
Standardize a token’s vector to mean 0 and standard deviation 1; Pre-LN does it before each sub-layer, Post-LN after (§4.3).


Leaky-ReLU / GELU
ReLU variants that give negative inputs a small output and slope, so a unit at a negative \(z\) still passes some gradient (§2).


Learning rate
The size of each training step (§15).


Learning rate \(\eta\)
Step size in gradient descent.


Learning-rate schedule / warm-up / decay
The rate \(\eta_t\) chosen for each step \(t\) (§6) / a short rise from a small rate at the start / a fall as training ends, in jumps (step decay) or along half a cosine wave to \(0\) (cosine decay).


Leave-one-out (LOO)
Hold out one interaction per user — the chronologically last unless stated otherwise, often the second-last for validation. Leak-free within a user, not across users (§3). Some papers use the name for a random held-out interaction: check.


Leave-one-out (LOO) split
Hold out each user’s chronologically last interaction for test, the second-last for validation (a per-user cut).


License families / OSI
Permissive (Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD) / copyleft (GPL, AGPL) / non-commercial (CC-BY-NC) / custom (Llama, Gemma \(\le 3\)). Only the first two are open source as the Open Source Initiative (OSI) defines it. §1 rule 2.


LightGCN
(He et al., 2020) NGCF with \(W\), \(\sigma\), the product term and the self-loop removed, and the concatenation replaced by a weighted sum of layers; a commonly used graph-CF backbone (§14).


Likelihood / prior / posterior
\(p(\text{data}\mid\theta)\) / \(p(\theta)\) / \(p(\theta\mid\text{data})\).


Likelihood \(L(\theta)\)
\(p(\text{data}\mid\theta)\) read as a function of \(\theta\) (data fixed).


Limit
The value a quantity approaches (here as the run \(h\to0\)).


Linear (transformation)
A rule that respects adding and scaling: \(A(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})=A\mathbf{x}+A\mathbf{y}\), \(A(c\,\mathbf{x})=c\,A\mathbf{x}\); every matrix is one.


Linearly independent
A set of vectors none of which is a weighted sum of the others.


LinUCB
Ridge-regression reward estimate \(\theta^{\top}\mathbf x\) plus a feature-space confidence bonus \(\alpha\sqrt{\mathbf x^{\top}A^{-1}\mathbf x}\) (§6).


Lipschitz-smooth
The gradient changes at most in proportion to the step, \(\lVert\nabla f(\theta_1)-\nabla f(\theta_2)\rVert\le K\lVert\theta_1-\theta_2\rVert\); then one fixed learning rate, any \(\eta\) between \(0\) and \(2/K\), lowers \(f\) at every step where the gradient is not zero (§7).


LlamaRec
Two-stage recommendation: a small sequential model retrieves a shortlist, a fine-tuned LLM scores it in one pass from the probabilities of the candidates’ labels (§2.1).


LLM
Large language model: a Transformer language model with (today often) billions of weights, pretrained on a huge corpus; here, demystified as this chapter’s lineage at scale (§5).


LLM-as-enhancer
The LLM produces semantic features or profiles offline that feed or align with a classical model (§2.3).


LLM-as-recommender
The LLM directly ranks or selects items from a prompt of the user’s history (§2.1).


LLM-as-reranker
The recommender role in its common production form: the LLM re-scores a short top-\(K\) shortlist that a cheap retriever already fetched, instead of ranking the whole catalog. Reranking is the funnel’s ranking stage under a second name (§2.1).


Local / global minimum
Local = lowest within a neighborhood; global = lowest anywhere.


Log-likelihood
\(\log L(\theta)\); products become sums.


Log-odds (logit)
The raw score \(z=\ln\frac{\hat p}{1-\hat p}\) the sigmoid squashes; weights add up here, not in the probability.


log-\(Q\) correction
Subtract \(\log\) of an item’s sampling probability from its score, so negatives drawn in proportion to popularity (e.g. in-batch negatives) do not over-penalize popular items; under uniform sampling it removes no popularity skew and only rescales the negatives’ total (§10).


log-sum-exp / softplus
\(\log\sum_i e^{z_i}\), a smooth stand-in for the largest \(z_i\) that normalizes a softmax (\(1.313\) for logits \(1\) and \(0\), against a largest logit of \(1\)); \(\text{softplus}(z)=\log(e^0+e^{z})\) is its two-term case with one logit at \(0\) (§2.4).


Logistic loss
BCE written on the margin \(m=y\hat y\) with labels \(\pm1\): \(\ln(1+e^{-m})\) (§2.2).


Logistic regression
Linear score \(\to\) sigmoid \(\to\) probability; the CTR baseline and every model’s output head.


Logit
The raw score an output layer gives a label before the softmax turns the scores into probabilities (§2.1).


Logit (log-odds)
\(\ln\!\big(p/(1-p)\big)\); maps \((0,1)\to(-\infty,\infty)\).


LogLoss
Log loss, or binary cross-entropy: the average of \(-\ln\)(the probability given to what happened); \(0.9\) on a click and \(0.2\) on a non-click give \(0.164\).


Long tail
The many low-degree (niche) films, each with few watchers; each is named by few training triples (§13).


Long tail / popularity bias
A few blockbusters get most interactions; metrics can be gamed by pushing them.


Lorenz curve
The share of recommendations held by the least-recommended fraction of the catalog; Gini \(=A/(A+B)\), the gap below the diagonal over the whole triangle.


Loss
A single number scoring how badly a model’s predictions fit the data; training adjusts the model to make it small (§2).


Loss \(\mathcal{L}\)
A single number scoring how wrong a model’s predictions are; training makes it as small as possible (the chapter opener and §4; its letter \(\mathcal{L}\), §3; written \(f\) in §5 to §7).


Loss function
A single number measuring how wrong the model is; training minimizes it.


Low-pass filter
Keep low frequencies (smooth signal), suppress high (noise).


LSTM
Long short-term memory: an RNN with a cell state + forget/input/output gates; the cell line, edited only by a near-\(1\) multiply and an addition, keeps gradients from vanishing quickly (§3.3).

title: Glossary
text:
M







Term
Meaning




MAE / absolute loss
Mean of absolute errors; from Laplace noise; outlier-robust; targets the median.


MAE / MSE / RMSE
Mean Absolute / Mean Squared / Root-Mean-Squared rating error.


Main embedding / main view
The embeddings of the un-augmented graph, the ones BPR scores with; LightGCL uses them as one of its two views (§3.4, §5).


MAP
Maximum A Posteriori; the \(\theta\) at the peak of the posterior — it maximizes likelihood \(\times\) prior, i.e. minimizes loss \(+\) regularizer.


MAP (maximum a posteriori) estimate
Maximize posterior ∝ likelihood × prior; ⟹ minimize (−log-lik) + (−log-prior) = loss + regularizer.


Markov chain (first-order)
Next item depends only on the last one; transitions estimated by counting.


[mask] token
A placeholder that replaces a hidden item in BERT4Rec’s input, so the answer is not in what the model reads (§5).


Matrix
A rectangular grid of numbers; also a linear transformation of vectors.


Matrix Factorization (MF)
\(\hat r_{ui}=\mathbf{p}_u^\top \mathbf{q}_i\); trained with regularized MSE.


Matrix–vector product \(A\mathbf{x}\)
Dot each row of \(A\) with \(\mathbf{x}\); “\(n\) in, \(m\) out.”


Matryoshka (MRL)
Truncatable embeddings — a shorter prefix of the vector still works, so you index at a smaller dim to save memory/latency.


Maximum-entropy model
Among all distributions that match what you know, the most uncertain one: knowing nothing about a die, \(\tfrac16\) for each face (§7).


MDP
Markov Decision Process: states, actions, transition, reward and discount — the problem RL solves; the policy is its solution.


Mean pooling / [CLS]
Two ways to get one vector per text: average the token vectors, or read BERT’s summary token (§5.2).


Median
The middle value once the data are sorted; the single value that minimizes the total absolute error (§2).


Memory-based CF
Predict from similar rows/columns of \(R\) at query time (\(k\)-NN).


Message passing
Another name for one graph-convolution step (also called propagation): every node sends its vector along its edges, and replaces its own with the weighted sum it receives.


Mini-batch
A small group of training triples used for one update (§15; Neural Networks & Back-propagation §6).


Minibatch
A handful of training examples drawn at random; SGD estimates the gradient on it (§5).


MIPS (Maximum Inner-Product Search)
Finding the item vectors with the largest dot product against a query: what top-\(K\) scoring is. It coincides with nearest-neighbor search for every query when all the item vectors have the same length.


Mixture of experts
Several small sub-models whose outputs a learned gate weights input by input.


ML-20M
MovieLens 20M, a standard film-rating data set: 138,493 users, 27,278 films, 20,000,263 ratings, 0.53% of the cells filled (§1).


MLE
Maximum Likelihood Estimate; \(\theta\) that best explains the data.


MLP
Multi-layer perceptron — a feedforward stack of fully-connected layers.


MNAR data
Missing-Not-At-Random: whether an interaction is observed depends on what the system chose to show — recommender logs are the textbook case (the opposite, missing completely at random, is pure coin-flip missingness).


Mode
The most plausible value — where a distribution peaks (for a continuous variable the height of the curve at the mode is a density, not a probability: §1); for Beta\((\alpha,\beta)\) with \(\alpha,\beta>1\) it is \((\alpha-1)/(\alpha+\beta-2)\) (§2, §6).


Model card
The documentation page a publisher posts beside a released model: size, license, training data, scores. The primary source for every license claim in this appendix.


Model-agnostic
Added on top of an existing recommender, whichever one it is; RLMRec is described so by its authors (§17).


Model-based CF
Learn a compact model first (e.g. matrix factorization).


MoE (mixture of experts)
Several specialist sub-networks plus a trained gate that weights them and sums their outputs; KAR’s adapter for turning LLM knowledge into features (§2.3).


MoE (mixture-of-experts)
A model that holds many parameters but activates only a few per token — compute per token is below what the total size suggests, but every expert must still sit in memory.


Momentum
Gradient descent that steps on a running total of recent gradients, \(v\leftarrow0.9\,v+g\) (§5).


Momentum / Adam
SGD upgrades: a velocity term / a per-parameter adaptive step (§6).


Monotonic
Here, increasing (a bigger input always gives a bigger output), like \(\log\) and \(e^{x}\), so it keeps the ranking of any list (§3).


MRR
Mean Reciprocal Rank — each user’s reciprocal rank (RR), \(1/\)rank of the first relevant item (\(0\) if none in the top-\(K\)), averaged over users.


MSE / squared loss
Mean of squared errors; from Gaussian noise of the same spread for every point; outlier-sensitive.


MTEB / ann-benchmarks / LMArena / CoNLL
The standard benchmarks and leaderboards for embeddings / vector indexes / chat-LLMs / NER. Priors, not verdicts.


Mult-VAE
A variational autoencoder for recommendation with a multinomial likelihood; loss = reconstruction + \(\beta\cdot\)KL (§11).


Multi-head
Several attentions (“heads”) in parallel with different learned projections; their outputs are concatenated and mixed back to length \(d\) by \(W_O\) (§4.3).


Multi-head self-attention
Each field’s new vector is a weighted mix of all the fields’ vectors, the weights computed from dot-product scores and a softmax; several heads do it independently (AutoInt, §8; built in Representation Learning & the Transformer).


Multi-label
Several independent yes/no labels at once, such as a film that is both a comedy and a drama; each gets a sigmoid (§3).


Multiple comparisons
Running several tests at once: each carries its own \(\alpha\) chance of a false positive, so the chance that at least one fires by luck grows (\(1-0.95^{3}\approx0.14\) for three tests; §8.5, §8.6 Step 3).


Mutual information
How much knowing one variable tells you about another: the KL divergence between their joint distribution and the product of their separate ones; zero exactly when they are independent (§7).


Mutual information (MI)
How much knowing one of two quantities tells you about the other. For a batch of \(N\) nodes, \(\log N-\mathcal L_{\text{cl}}\), with the loss averaged over the batch, is a lower bound on the MI between the two views (§7; Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning §7). RLMRec frames its alignment as maximizing it.

title: Glossary
text:
N







Term
Meaning




Nabla / del (\(\nabla\))
The symbol for the gradient operator.


NCF / NeuMF
Neural collaborative filtering: feed user and item embeddings through a small network instead of a dot product; trained with BCE (§10).


NCL
Neighborhood-enriched Contrastive Learning — makes a node’s graph neighbors and cluster prototype its positives (§4).


NDCG
Normalized discounted cumulative gain: each relevant item earns \(1/\log_2(\text{rank}+1)\), divided by the best possible total; \(1\) = perfect list (§10; Evaluation Metrics §7).


NDCG@10
Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain at \(10\): a ranking score that rewards putting the items a user wanted near the top of a list of \(10\); bigger is better (§8.4).


NDCG@20
Normalized discounted cumulative gain: a score that also rewards ranking a user’s held-out films high in the top-20 list (§4).


Negative (sample)
An item the user did not choose next, used as a wrong answer that the true next item must outscore.


Negative sampling
Drawing un-interacted items to act as negatives — uniformly by default (mostly easy, obscure items; each candidate equally likely, so a popular item, being a positive for many users and never their negative, is drawn less often overall, §2.4), or in proportion to popularity / by hardness, which over-samples popular items (§2.4, §10).


NER (named-entity recognition)
Finding the names of things in text and labeling each span with a type (PERSON, BRAND, GENRE …). The list of types you want is your schema. §6.


Neuron / unit
A weighted sum of inputs + bias, passed through an activation.


Next-item prediction
The core task: given \((i_1,\dots,i_{t-1})\), score every item for being \(i_t\).


NGCF
Neural graph collaborative filtering (X. Wang et al., 2019): a GCN ported to recommendation, keeping \(W\) and \(\sigma\), adding a user–item product term (the element-wise product of the two vectors), and concatenating all layers (§14).


NLL
Negative log-likelihood \(=-\log L\); minimizing it = MLE; this is a loss.


Node
A thing (a user, a film).


Noise
A random error added on top of a true value (a bathroom scale’s reading is your true weight plus a small random wobble) (§2).


Non-IID data (statistical heterogeneity)
Each client’s data comes from a different distribution (one user all horror, another all cartoons), so local updates pull the shared model in different directions — a core difficulty of federation.


Non-stationarity
The arms’ true rates drift over time, so old evidence goes stale and a policy must keep exploring (§1).


Norm
The length of an arrow, \(\lVert\mathbf e\rVert=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) for two numbers (§8).


Norm / length \(\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\)
The arrow’s length; default L2 \(\sqrt{\sum_i u_i^2}\). L1 \(=\sum_i\lvert u_i\rvert\) (used in lasso).


Normalize (cosine)
Divide a vector by its length (\(\ell_2\)-normalize); the dot product of unit vectors is the cosine similarity, but it answers the cosine question, not the raw dot-product one (§7).


Normalized interaction matrix \(\tilde R\)
\(D_U^{-1/2}RD_I^{-1/2}\): each interaction divided by the square root of the user’s and the film’s degrees; the matrix GF-CF and LightGCL work on (§6).


Normalizing constant
The factor that makes a density’s area (or a list of probabilities) equal \(1\); Beta\((2,2)\) has \(6\) (§2).


Novelty
Non-obviousness, often \(-\log_2(\text{popularity})\).


Null hypothesis \(H_0\)
The skeptical default “no real difference”; a test asks whether the data are strong enough to reject it.


Null space
Every input a matrix sends to the zero vector \(\mathbf{0}\).

title: Glossary
text:
O







Term
Meaning




Odd cycle
A loop of an odd number of edges, such as a triangle; a connected graph with one has no \(-1\) mode.


Odds
\(p/(1-p)\).


Off-policy
Learning from data collected by a different (older) policy than the one being trained.


Off-policy, IPS, doubly-robust
Scoring a policy from another policy’s log; IPS reweights logged data by \(1/p(\text{action})\); doubly-robust adds a reward model that, when roughly right, cuts the variance, the run-to-run jitter of the estimate (§7).


Offline / online
Offline = computed in advance, in bulk, while nobody is waiting; online = computed live, while the user waits (§7).


Offline replay
Unbiased evaluation of a bandit policy on a log of actions served uniformly at random, independent of context (Li et al. 2011).


Omnibus / post-hoc test
An omnibus test (such as the Friedman test) asks one question across all the models and datasets at once; post-hoc pairwise tests, planned in advance, run only after it finds some difference (§8.5). This planned use is not the after-the-fact choice that §8.2 warns against.


One- vs two-sided test
Two-sided asks “A \(\ne\) B” (the default); one-sided asks “A \(>\) B”: it halves \(p\) when the result goes the pre-registered way and gives \(1-p/2\) (near \(1\) for a clear result) when it goes the other way; valid only if the direction was pre-registered (§8.6, Step 1).


One-hot
A list with a single \(1\) and \(0\)s elsewhere, like \([1,0,0]\) (§3).


One-hot vector
A length-\(V\) vector \(\mathbf{o}_k\), \(1\) in slot \(k\), \(0\) elsewhere; encodes identity but no similarity (all pairs orthogonal; §1.1).


One-hot vector \(\mathbf o_k\)
All zeros except a \(1\) in slot \(k\); \(\mathbf o_k^\top E\) picks row \(k\) of \(E\).


OneRec
Kuaishou’s end-to-end generative recommender, which replaces the retrieval-and-ranking cascade with one model tuned by iterative DPO (§2.2).


Open weights / open source / open data
Released weights only / released under an OSI-approved license (§1 vocabulary table) / training data published too. They are different and often confused.


Optimizer
The procedure that updates the parameters from the gradient; gradient descent is the basic one (§4, §5).


Order / degree
How many features an interaction multiplies together: second-order is a pair, third-order three at once.


Order of magnitude
A factor of 10; three orders of magnitude is a factor of 1,000 (§4.1).


Orthant
The region of space where the signs of all coordinates are fixed, the high-dimensional analogue of a quadrant; SimGCL keeps its noise in the orthant of the vector it nudges (§4).


Orthogonal
Perpendicular; dot product \(0\).


Orthonormal basis
A full set of axes that are mutually orthogonal and each unit length; a coordinate is then just a dot product (\(U,V\) in §6).


Outer product \(\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^{\top}\)
A column times a row = a whole rank-1 matrix, entry \((r,c)=u_rv_c\).


Over-smoothing
Too many layers make all embeddings point in (almost) the same direction, so users can no longer be told apart (§12). Their lengths still differ — it is a collapse of direction, not a collapse to a single point.


Overfitting
Memorizing training noise; great on train, poor on new data.

title: Glossary
text:
P







Term
Meaning




\(p\)-value
Probability, if \(H_0\) were true, of a result at least this extreme (for the \(t\)-test: a ratio \(\lvert t\rvert\) at least this large; either direction for a two-sided test); small = significant. NOT \(\Pr(H_0\text{ true})\).


P5
One text-to-text model for five families of recommendation task: “Pretrain, Personalized Prompt & Predict Paradigm”, five P’s (§2.1).


Paired \(t\)-test
Tests whether the true mean of the per-pair differences is \(0\), using their sample mean \(\bar d\): \(t=\bar d/(s_d/\sqrt n)\).


Parameter / free
A number the model stores and trains; a number is free when training may set it to any value, the opposite of a given number such as a feature (§6).


Parameters
A model’s adjustable numbers (e.g. weights, embeddings) — in a neural network mostly its weights, in a recommender also its embeddings (§5); training nudges them, step by step, until the loss is small.


Parameters, “7B”
The learned weights of a network, counted with M = million and B = billion; a 7B model has 7,000,000,000 of them. Sets memory and roughly sets speed.


Pareto frontier
The set of best-possible (recall, speed) points an index can reach by turning its accuracy/speed knob; off the frontier you can do better on both, on it you trade one for the other.


Partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\)
Derivative with respect to one variable, the others held fixed.


Pearson correlation
A similarity measure (centered cosine) for ratings — removes each user’s rating bias.


Percentile
The \(q\)th percentile is the value below which \(q\%\) of the values fall; the bootstrap reads its interval from the \(2.5\)th and \(97.5\)th.


PinSage
A GraphSAGE-like model (Ying et al., 2018) that picks neighbors by short random walks and ran at Pinterest on \(3\) billion nodes (§15).


Plain average
The matrix \(D^{-1}A\): each neighbor weighted \(1/\deg\) of the receiver; the weights in a row sum to \(1\) (§7).


Platt scaling
Calibrates a raw score \(s\) with a fitted S-curve \(\sigma(as+b)\); keeps the ranking exactly when the slope \(a>0\).


PMF / PDF
Probability mass (discrete) / density (continuous) function; sums/integrates to 1.


Pointwise
Scoring each candidate with its own separate model call, as against scoring a whole list at once (§4.1).


Pointwise / pairwise / listwise
Score each (user, item) pair alone / the order of two items / the whole list at once (softmax: does the positive top it; LambdaRank: pairs weighted by the metric).


Policy
The rule that picks the arm each round, using everything seen so far (§2).


Policy \(\pi(a\mid s)\)
The learned rule mapping a state to an action (\(\pi\) names the policy, not \(3.14159\)); what RL optimizes. A language model’s output rule in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is also called a policy (Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning, glossary); §4 applies the idea to LLM-based recommenders.


Policy gradient
Optimize the policy directly by gradient ascent on expected return (REINFORCE is the basic algorithm; \(\theta\) are the policy’s parameters).


Polynomial filter
A filter that is a polynomial in \(\tilde{A}\) (what LightGCN layers compute).


Popularity baseline
A simple recommender that shows everyone the same most-popular items.


Popularity bias
Tendency to over-recommend high-degree (blockbuster) items (§13).


Popularity bias (in eval)
Popular items dominate the test set, so pushing them inflates accuracy metrics.


Popularity bias / long tail
A recommender over-suggesting already-popular items at the expense of the long tail of rarely seen ones (§2.4).


Position bias
Higher-ranked slots draw more clicks regardless of true relevance.


Positional embedding
A learned per-position vector added to item embeddings so attention can see order.


Positional encoding
A per-position signal added to embeddings so order-blind attention can see order (sinusoidal or learned; many recent LLMs instead rotate queries and keys by a position-dependent angle — RoPE; §4.3).


Positive / negative pair
Positive = two views of the same node (in DirectAU, a user and an item she interacted with); negative = views of different nodes (§3.1, §3.3).


Positive definite
Curvature strictly \(>0\) in every direction (for a \(2\times2\) Hessian: \(f_{xx}>0\) and \(D>0\); all eigenvalues \(>0\)). Positive definite everywhere ⇒ at most one minimum (§6).


Positive semidefinite (PSD)
Curvature \(\ge0\) in every direction (for a \(2\times2\) Hessian: \(f_{xx}\ge0\), \(f_{yy}\ge0\), \(D\ge0\); equivalently all eigenvalues \(\ge0\)). A function whose Hessian is PSD at every point is convex.


Positive-semidefinite (PSD)
A symmetric matrix with all eigenvalues \(\ge0\) (equivalently, for a symmetric matrix, \(\mathbf{x}^{\top}A\mathbf{x}\ge0\) always); every \(A^{\top}A\) is PSD since \(\mathbf{x}^{\top}A^{\top}A\mathbf{x}=\lVert A\mathbf{x}\rVert^{2}\).


Post-activation \(a\) / layer output \(\mathbf h\)
\(a=\phi(z)\), one neuron’s output; \(\mathbf h^{(\ell)}=\phi(\mathbf z^{(\ell)})\) collects layer \(\ell\)’s outputs into one vector.


Posterior collapse
A VAE’s code pushed all the way to the prior, so it carries nothing about the user (§13).


Posterior \(p(\theta\mid D)\)
Updated belief after data.


Power
The probability that a test detects a real difference when there is one; having more pairs gives more power, and pairing the models on the same seeds helps when their scores rise and fall together (§8.1; §8.2, §8.3).


Pre-activation \(z\) (logit, for a classifier’s last layer)
The raw score \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b\) before the activation; for layer \(\ell\), the vector \(\mathbf z^{(\ell)}=W^{(\ell)}\mathbf h^{(\ell-1)}+\mathbf b^{(\ell)}\), starting from \(\mathbf h^{(0)}=\mathbf x\).


Pre-registered
Written down before running anything (a directional hypothesis, the tests to be run), so it cannot be chosen after seeing the data (§8.5).


Precision@K
Of the \(K\) shown, the fraction relevant.


Predicted score \(\hat y\)
The dot product of a user’s and an item’s embeddings (§4).


Predictive learning
SSL pretext: predict a property derived from the data (e.g. a masked item/attribute); one correct answer, no negatives; discriminative mechanism (this chapter’s own reading, not a standard label; §6.3).


Prefix
The beginning of a list, \((i_1,\dots,i_{t-1})\): the items seen so far, in order.


Pretext task
The self-supervised literature’s name for the auxiliary task; the two words mean the same thing (§6.2).


Pretraining
Train a big Transformer on a huge corpus with a self-supervised objective, then reuse it (§5).


Prior and posterior
Belief about a click chance before data (prior) and after data (posterior).


Prior \(p(\theta)\)
Belief about \(\theta\) before data.


Product rule
\((fg)' = f'g + fg'\) — the derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives (§2).


Production
The live system that answers real users’ requests, as opposed to an experiment on saved data.


Profile
A short LLM-written description of a user’s taste or an item’s character, used as input to an embedder.


Projection \(\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}\)
The shadow of \(\mathbf{u}\) on \(\mathbf{v}\)’s line, \(\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}}\mathbf{v}\); in an orthonormal basis a coordinate is just a dot product.


Projection \(g\)
The small network that maps the semantic vector into the collaborative space so the two can be compared (§4).


Projector \(\mathbf v\mathbf v^{\top}\)
The matrix that keeps the part of a signal along the unit vector \(\mathbf v\) and discards the rest.


Prompt
The text handed to an LLM: the question plus whatever it should know (§2).


Propensity
The probability \(p\) that the logging policy took the action it did; a film shown with \(p=0.1\) counts \(10\) times per click (§7).


Propensity / IPS
Propensity = probability an item was shown; inverse propensity scoring (IPS) re-weights each interaction by \(1/\)propensity to undo exposure bias.


Prototype / EM
NCL’s prototype is the center of a cluster of look-alike nodes; EM (expectation-maximization) alternates guessing the clusters and improving the embeddings against them (§4).


Provider vs. consumer fairness
Comparable exposure across item creators (provider) vs. comparable quality across user groups (consumer).


Pseudo-count
The heads and tails a Beta prior behaves as if already seen: \(\alpha-1\) and \(\beta-1\) (§2).

title: Glossary
text:
Q







Term
Meaning




Q-learning
Learn \(Q(s,a)\) by moving it toward reward plus \(\gamma\times\) the best next \(Q\) (temporal-difference learning), then take the highest-\(Q\) (greedy) action; it must score every action, so slate methods avoid it. Deep Q-learning uses a neural network for \(Q\); DRN applies it to news.


QPS (queries per second)
How many requests a system answers each second: its throughput, as distinct from any one request’s latency.


Quadratic form
The number \(\mathbf{x}^{\top}A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}\cdot(A\mathbf{x})\).


Quantization
Storing weights/vectors in fewer bits (4/8-bit, int8/binary) to shrink memory and speed inference, at a small quality cost.


Query / Key / Value
Soft database lookup: a query is matched (dot product) against keys to retrieve a blend of values (§4.1).


Query, key, value
In attention, each position’s query asks, each key says what that position is about, and each value is what it hands over when matched (§4).

title: Glossary
text:
R







Term
Meaning




RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
Retrieving relevant evidence and inserting it into the LLM’s prompt so it reasons over real data instead of pretrained memory (§5).


Random seed
The number that fixes a training run’s random choices; another seed gives a slightly different, equally valid result (§8).


Random split
Hold out a random fraction of interactions, per user or globally (say which) — leaks the future for time-ordered data.


Random variable
A quantity whose value is uncertain (coin, die, temperature).


Random walk
A path that steps along randomly chosen edges; one of SGL’s ways to damage the graph (§4).


Randomized SVD
A fast approximate way to find only the top-\(q\) singular vectors, using random projections (§5).


Rank
The matrix’s number of independent directions: independent rows/columns (§2) = nonzero singular values (§6). An \(n\times n\) matrix of rank \(n\) is full rank; below \(n\), rank-deficient.


Ranking
The expensive, high-precision second stage that reorders the shortlist with a feature-rich model; search and LLM writing call the same stage reranking.


Ranking scope
How many candidate items the held-out one is ranked against: all of them (full ranking) or a sample. Printed in Table B.5 as its own column (§4).


Recall vs QPS
The ANN trade-off: fraction of true neighbors found vs queries-per-second. Always compare at a fixed recall.


Recall@20
Of the films a user liked that were held back from training, the share found in the model’s top \(20\) (§12, §14; Evaluation Metrics).


Recall@K
Of all relevant items, the fraction in the top-\(K\).


Recall@K / Precision@K / NDCG@K
Top-\(K\) ranking quality: the share of the user’s relevant items found / the share of the list that is relevant / a score that rewards putting relevant items high (§6).


Reciprocal-rank fusion
How two ranked lists are merged: each item scores \(\sum 1/(60+\text{rank})\) over the lists it appears in, so steady agreement beats one top spot. §3.


Regime
A research community’s shared package of datasets + models + one evaluation protocol. Numbers are comparable only inside a regime, and only when split, preprocessing and ranking scope match as well (§4).


Regression
Predicting a real number, such as a price (§2).


Regret
\(\sum_t(\mu^{*}-\mu_{a_t})\): expected reward lost versus always pulling the best arm.


Regularization
Making an ill-posed solution “regular” (well-behaved); from Hadamard/Tikhonov.


Regularization strength \(\lambda\)
The weight on the penalty in “loss \(+\,\lambda\times\) penalty”; a narrower prior is a larger \(\lambda\) (\(1/(2s^2)\) for L2, \(1/b\) for L1, against a summed negative log-likelihood; rescaled for an average loss) (§6).


Regularizer
A penalty added to the loss that keeps the parameters well-behaved; under MAP it is \(-\log p(\boldsymbol\theta)\) — a Gaussian prior gives L2 (weight decay), a Laplace prior gives L1 (lasso) (§6).


Reinforcement learning (RL)
Learning to choose actions to maximize long-term reward when actions can change the next state.


Relevant item
A ground-truth item the user actually likes.


Reliability diagram
Predicted vs. observed rate, one point per bin; calibrated points lie on the diagonal.


ReLU
\(\max(0,z)\) — Rectified Linear Unit; in practice the most used hidden-layer activation (a claim from practice, not tested here).


ReLU (rectified linear unit)
\(\max(0,z)\); derivative \(1\) for \(z>0\) and \(0\) for \(z<0\) (§3).


Representation collapse
The failure where the encoder maps every node to the same vector; InfoNCE then sits at its collapse value \(\log N\) (§3.3).


Representation learning
The network learning useful features by itself.


Residual
\(r=\hat y-y\), the miss on one point (§2.1).


Residual (skip) connection
A shortcut that carries an earlier stage’s output past the later ones; in LightGCN the layer-\(0\) term of the layer combination (§12).


Residual connection
A sub-layer computes \(\mathbf{x}+f(\mathbf{x})\); the \(+1\) in its derivative is a gradient highway for deep stacks (kept clean in the Pre-LN form, §4.3).


Residual quantization
Quantize a vector, subtract the codeword, quantize what is left over against a second codebook, and so on. The chosen codewords add back up to the vector, and each level usually shrinks the error, though with an arbitrary codebook it can grow (§2.2).


Retention
Whether the user comes back (next week); a long-horizon objective.


Retrieval / candidate generation
The cheap, high-recall first stage that cuts millions of items to a few hundred.


Retrieval → ranking
The production funnel: a cheap, high-recall retrieval stage (candidate generation: MF/\(k\)-NN with ANN search) then a precise ranking stage, also called reranking (§7).


Return \(G\)
Cumulative discounted reward \(\sum_t \gamma^t r_t\) — the long-term objective.


Reward model
A model trained to score outputs: RLHF trains it on preferred and rejected outputs, OneRec on the logged watch-time, view, follow and like outcomes of whole sessions; Rec-R1 uses none (§4).


Reward \(r\) / action \(a\)
The immediate payoff (a click, a watch-minute, a return visit) / what the recommender does (show an item or slate).


Ridge / L2 penalty
A penalty on large coefficients added to least squares; in LinUCB it is the identity start \(A=I\).


Risk / empirical risk
Expected loss over the true distribution / its average on the training sample.


RLHF / policy
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: tuning a language model toward the answers people prefer / the rule a model uses to choose its outputs; a KL penalty keeps the tuned policy near the original (§7).


RLMRec
Representation Learning with Large Language Models for Recommendation (WWW 2024): aligns a graph backbone’s embeddings with LLM-written profile embeddings (§7).


RLMRec-Con / -Gen
RLMRec’s contrastive variant (pull a node’s embedding toward its mapped profile vector against other users, an InfoNCE-form loss) and generative variant (hide a node’s input, rebuild its profile vector; cosine inside the same ratio): the paper’s Eqs. 16 to 18 (§7).


RMSE / MAE
Root-mean-square error / mean absolute error: how far predicted ratings miss the true ones; RMSE squares the misses first, so big misses count more (§6).


RNN
Recurrent neural network: one shared cell that updates a hidden-state “memory” \(\mathbf{h}_t=\tanh(W\mathbf{h}_{t-1}+U\mathbf{x}_t+\mathbf{b})\) along a sequence (§3.1).


RNN / hidden state \(\mathbf h_t\)
A net that folds each item into a running fixed-length summary of the session.


Robustness
Resistance to a few wildly-off values: the Laplace / MAE / median are robust, the Gaussian / MSE / mean are not (§2).


RQ-VAE
The residual-quantized variational autoencoder that learns the Semantic-ID codebooks by reconstructing the content embedding (§2.2).

title: Glossary
text:
S







Term
Meaning




Saddle point
Critical point that is a min in some directions, a max in others (indefinite Hessian).


Sample space / event
The set of possible outcomes / a subset of them.


Sampled softmax
Training with a softmax over a sampled handful of items rather than the whole catalog; for in-batch negatives, over the batch (§7).


Sampled softmax (SSM)
Listwise cross-entropy over a positive + many sampled negatives; structurally = InfoNCE.


Sampling bias
In-batch sampling meets an item in proportion to how often it is a positive, so popular items are over-penalized as negatives; the log-\(Q\) correction repairs it (§3).


SASRec
Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation: a causal Transformer over the item sequence.


SASRec / BERT4Rec
Sequential recommenders: a causal (left-to-right) / bidirectional (masked) Transformer over the item history (§4.4).


Scalar
A single number (as opposed to a vector); multiplying by one scales a vector.


Scaled cosine error
GraphMAE’s loss: the mean over hidden nodes of \((1-\cos(\mathbf x,\mathbf z))^{\gamma}\) with \(\gamma\ge1\); at \(\gamma=1\) it is \(1-\cos\) (§6.2, §6.4).


Second derivative \(f''\)
Rate of change of the slope = curvature.


Second-derivative test
At a critical point of \(f(x,y)\), \(D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2\): \(D>0,\ f_{xx}>0\) bowl (min); \(D>0,\ f_{xx}<0\) cap (max); \(D<0\) saddle; \(D=0\) silent (§6).


Secure aggregation
The server sees only the sum of client updates, never any individual one (Bonawitz et al., 2017).


Selection / exposure bias
Only items the system showed can get feedback; un-shown items look “disliked” by silence.


Self-attention
Attention of a sequence to itself (Q, K, V all from the same tokens; §4.1).


Self-loop
An artificial edge from a node to itself, so that a node counts itself among its neighbors; present in GCN and NGCF, absent in LightGCN (§6, §14).


Semantic embedding
A fixed-length vector encoding the meaning of the profile text (from a frozen sentence encoder), distinct from the CF latent space.


Semantic ID
A short sequence of content-derived codewords identifying an item (a quantized text embedding) (§2.2).


Semi-supervised node classification
Predicting the label of unlabeled nodes when a few nodes are labeled; the task the GCN paper solves (§6).


Sensitivity / false-positive rate
\(\Pr(+\mid S)\), the chance a test flags a true case / \(\Pr(+\mid\neg S)\), the chance it wrongly flags a healthy one (§5).


Sequential recommendation
Predict the next item from a user’s ordered history.


Serendipity
Relevant and surprising: hits a popularity baseline would not have shown, divided by \(K\).


Serving path / serving
Serving is answering a live request; the serving path is everything that runs between the request and the list shown (§1).


Session
The ordered items one person goes through in one sitting, a visit or an evening; short, and sometimes anonymous.


Session-based recommendation
Same, but from a short, often anonymous current session (no user id).


SGD
Stochastic Gradient Descent — gradient steps on random mini-batches.


SGL / SimGCL / XSimGCL / LightGCL
Self-supervised Graph Learning / Simple Graph Contrastive Learning / eXtremely Simple GCL / Light Graph Contrastive Learning — GCL methods differing in how the two views are built (edge-drop / embedding noise / cross-layer noise / SVD). Note the final letter: LightGCL is a training method, LightGCN the backbone.


Shape \(m\times n\)
\(m\) rows by \(n\) columns.


Shrink factor
\(1-2\eta\lambda\), what one L2 step multiplies a weight by (§5.1).


Shrinkage
Multiplying a similarity by \(n/(n+\kappa)\), so one backed by few co-ratings \(n\) is pulled toward \(0\) (§4).


Side features
Information about a user or film beyond clicks, such as genre or text (§4 box).


\(\sigma\) (nonlinearity)
An activation function: the rectified linear unit (ReLU), \(\mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)\), in GCN, and LeakyReLU (a ReLU that lets a small slope through for negative inputs; NGCF’s paper uses it) in NGCF; removed in LightGCN. In this chapter \(\sigma\) means the sigmoid only inside the BPR loss of §15: \(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\), the S-shaped function that squeezes any number into \(0\) to \(1\).


Sigmoid / logit
\(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\) squashes a raw score \(z\) (the logit) into \((0,1)\) (§2.2).


Sigmoid \(\sigma(z)\)
\(\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\): an S-shaped curve squashing any \(z\) into the range between \(0\) and \(1\); \(\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)\le0.25\) (§3).


Significance (paired \(t\)-test)
Is a gain bigger than run-to-run seed noise? Report mean \(\pm\) standard deviation over seeds and a \(p\)-value.


Significance level \(\alpha\)
The pre-set bar (usually \(0.05\)); reject \(H_0\) if \(p<\alpha\).


SimCLR
A simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations (Chen et al., 2020b, ICML); the source of the two-augmented-views recipe (§3.1).


Singular value \(\sigma\)
The strength of an SVD pattern, \(A\mathbf{v}_i=\sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i\); \(\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i(A^{\top}A)}\ge0\), biggest first.


Singular value decomposition (SVD)
A standard way to split a table of numbers into its main patterns (§13).


Singular value decomposition (SVD) \(A=U\Sigma V^{\top}\)
Factor any matrix into orthonormal patterns (\(U,V\)) scaled by singular values (\(\Sigma\)).


Singular value decomposition, SVD (\(M=U\Sigma V^\top\))
Factorizes a (rectangular) matrix into patterns \(U,V\) and strengths \(\Sigma\); keeping the top-\(q\) is an ideal low-pass (LightGCL).


Singular vectors
The columns of \(U\) (left, \(\mathbf{u}_i\): output directions) and of \(V\) (right, \(\mathbf{v}_i\): input directions).


Slate
A whole page/list of recommended items — the (combinatorial) action in slate RL.


SlateQ
Decomposes a slate’s value into per-item \(Q\)-values, making value-based slate RL tractable.


SLM
Small language model (\(\approx 0.5\)–9B) — cheap, high-throughput; the recsys feature-generation workhorse.


Smooth / differentiable
Has a derivative everywhere — no kinks or jumps; looks straight up close.


Soft-thresholding
Move a weight a fixed amount toward zero and stop at \(0\) if it would cross: \(\lambda/2\) in §5.1’s one-weight solution.


Softmax
Multi-class sigmoid; scores → a probability distribution.


Softmax output
Multi-class output head: \(K\) scores → a probability distribution, paired with cross-entropy.


Sparse / one-hot feature
A category encoded as all-zeros with a single \(1\); CTR rows stack millions of these.


Sparse matrix
A table that is almost all zeros, stored as a list of its non-zero entries: \(10\) of the toy’s \(36\) (§15).


Sparse matrix-vector product
Multiplying a sparse matrix by a vector (or by each column of a matrix) while adding up only its stored non-zero entries (§15).


Sparsity
Most of \(R\) is unknown (MovieLens-20M: \({\sim}99.5\%\) empty); the core difficulty.


Spectrum
The list of a matrix’s singular values, biggest first (§6); a quickly falling spectrum means a few pieces capture most of the matrix.


SSL (self-supervised learning)
Training on an auxiliary task that needs no labels; supervision is manufactured from the data’s own structure.


Standard deviation \(\sigma\)
\(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[X]}\); the spread in the same units as \(X\) (§1).


Standard error (SE)
\(s_d/\sqrt n\) — how much an estimate wobbles across repeats; shrinks with more data.


State \(s\)
A summary of the current situation; what the agent conditions on.


Static vs contextual
word2vec gives one fixed vector per word; a Transformer gives a different vector per occurrence (context-dependent; §4.2).


Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
Gradient descent on a noisy gradient estimated from a random minibatch, not the full dataset.


Structured output
Forcing an LLM to emit schema-valid JSON via constrained decoding — valid shape, not guaranteed-correct values.


Structured output / JSON mode
Forcing the LLM to emit schema-valid JSON, so the result is very likely parseable (§5 still validates).


STT / ASR / TTS / WER
Speech-to-text (= automatic speech recognition) / text-to-speech / word error rate — (substituted + deleted + inserted words) / words in the correct transcript. §7.


Student-\(t\) distribution
The spread of \(t\)-values pure luck produces — a bell with fatter tails than the Gaussian when there are few pairs, shaped by the df (§8.3).


Subgradient
A stand-in slope at a kink where the true derivative is undefined (e.g. any value in \([0,1]\) for ReLU at \(0\)).


Subword tokenization (BPE)
Split text into reusable sub-word pieces by greedily merging the most frequent adjacent pair; fixed vocabulary, and no <UNK> when the base vocabulary is all 256 bytes (byte-level BPE); WordPiece and Unigram are relatives; SentencePiece is a library that runs BPE or Unigram (§5.3).


Supervised / self-supervised learning (SSL)
Learning from examples that come with their correct answers / from a task the data sets for itself, with no human labels (§1, §11).


Surprise
\(-\log p\) of what happened (§2.3).


Surprise / self-information
\(-\log p(x)\); how surprising an outcome is (\(0\) if certain, \(\to\infty\) if rare).


SVD / singular value
Singular value decomposition: a table of numbers written as a sum of simple patterns, each with a strength, its singular value (Linear Algebra for Machine Learning §6; used in §5).


Symmetric
\(A=A^{\top}\); for a real symmetric matrix, the eigenvectors can be chosen mutually orthogonal (§5).


Symmetrically normalized adjacency \(\tilde{A}\)
\(\tilde A = D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\): entry \((u,v)\) is \(A_{uv}/(\sqrt{\deg u}\sqrt{\deg v})\). One multiplication by it is one propagation layer (§7).

title: Glossary
text:
T







Term
Meaning




t-SNE / variational inference
Drawing high-dimensional data as a 2-D map by making a KL divergence small / replacing a hard-to-compute posterior (§5) by the closest member of a simpler family, closest measured by KL (§7).


TALLRec
An LLM fine-tuned on recommendation instructions: a Tuning framework to Align LLMs with Recommendation (§2.1).


Tangent
The line that just touches a curve at a point; its slope is the derivative there (§1).


Tanh
Hyperbolic tangent, \(\tanh(z)=\frac{e^{z}-e^{-z}}{e^{z}+e^{-z}}=2\sigma(2z)-1\) — a sigmoid stretched to \((-1,1)\).


Taylor / linear approximation
\(f(x+\delta)\approx f(x)+f'(x)\delta\); a curve looks straight up close.


Temperature \(\tau\)
Divides the scores before a softmax: a small \(\tau\) gives a nearly one-hot output, a large \(\tau\) a nearly uniform one (§3).


Test set / fold
Data held back to measure a trained model / one of the \(k\) slices of cross-validation, each taking a turn as the test set (§8).


TF-IDF
A way to turn text into a feature vector (term frequency × inverse document frequency).


The rated-set leak
With explicit ratings, sending an update for item \(i\) reveals (to a server that knows whose it is) that the user rated \(i\), and the gradient is a scaled copy of the user’s vector; FedRec masks the rated set with decoy items (see §3).


Thompson sampling
(Thompson, 1933) Keep a posterior per arm; sample one value from each and pull the largest sample.


TIGER
The system that introduced Semantic-ID generative recommendation: Transformer Index for Generative Recommenders (§2.2).


Token
One element of an input sequence — a word, a sub-word piece (§5.3) or, in a recommender, one item of a history; the unit attention works on (§4.1).


Top-\(K\)
The \(K\) highest-scoring unseen items returned to the user.


TPR / FPR
True- / false-positive rate: the share of the relevant / irrelevant items scoring at or above a threshold (a cut-off score); lowering the threshold step by step traces the ROC curve.


Trace
Sum of a square matrix’s diagonal entries; equals the sum of its eigenvalues (shown here for \(2\times2\)).


Train/test split
How held-out test data is chosen: a random split, leave-one-out (LOO: each user’s chronologically last interaction), or a global temporal split (one cut-off date for everyone).


Train–serve skew
One case of the wider train/serve difference: the mismatch between the logged, sampled data a model is trained on and the whole live catalog it is served over (§8).


Transductive
A model that keeps one stored vector per node seen in training and cannot embed a node it never saw; a brand-new user or film has no row in \(E^{(0)}\) (§14). The GCN paper uses the word in a different sense: test nodes are visible during training.


Transductive / inductive
A model that can represent only the ids seen in training / one that can give a new id a vector from its content (§3).


Transformer
A stack of (self-attention + add&norm + feed-forward + add&norm) blocks; no recurrence, so training processes all positions in parallel (Vaswani 2017; §4.3).


Transition probability
\(P(\text{next}=i\mid\text{last}=l)\) — count of \(l\!\to\!i\) over count of \(l\)-as-from.


Transpose \(A^{\top}\)
The matrix mirrored across its diagonal (rows ↔︎ columns).


Triple
A training example \((u,i,j)\): a user, a film she liked, and a film she has no edge to (§13, §15).


Triple \((u,i^+,i^-)\)
A training example for pairwise ranking: user \(u\) prefers positive \(i^+\) over sampled negative \(i^-\).


Truncated SVD
Keep the top-\(q\) singular components = best low-rank approximation (least-squares / Frobenius sense — the Eckart–Young theorem).


Two-stage funnel
Retrieval → ranking: fast-and-forgiving then slow-and-sharp, so a rich model can run on only a few hundred candidates; the final cut applies the already-seen filter and any business rules, then shows the top \(K\).


Two-tower LLM-embedding retrieval
Embed users and items with an LLM-grade encoder offline, then retrieve by ANN over those vectors at serve time: enhancer-class cost, LLM semantics on the retrieval path (§4).


Two-tower model
Embeds user and item with two separate networks and scores by dot product; trained with sampled softmax (§10).


Type I / II error
False positive (reject true \(H_0\)) / false negative (miss a real effect).

title: Glossary
text:
U







Term
Meaning




UCB
Pull \(\arg\max_i\,[\hat\mu_i + \sqrt{2\ln t / n_i}\,]\), with \(t\) the pulls so far and \(n_i\) the pulls of arm \(i\): highest upper bound, optimism under uncertainty.


Uniform / popularity-weighted / in-batch / hard negatives
Four sampling distributions for \(i^-\): equal-probability; \(\propto\text{pop}^{0.75}\); reuse the batch’s other positives; pick high-scoring (confusing) items.


Uniformity
Embeddings spread evenly over the sphere. It is the term that scores collapse as worst (§3.3); that it also helps the long tail is the papers’ claim, not tested here.


Unit circle / semi-axes
The unit circle is all vectors of length \(1\); a matrix sends it to an ellipse, whose longest and shortest radii (the semi-axes) have lengths \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\) (§6).


Unit vector
A vector of length \(1\); “normalizing” = dividing by your own length.


Unit vector / unit hypersphere
A vector of length 1; the set of all such vectors, a circle in 2-D (§3.3).


Universal approximation
A wide enough net can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region.


User profile
The average of the feature vectors of the items a user liked; content-based filtering scores items against it (§2).


User simulator
A model of user behavior used to train RL without experimenting on real users.


User–item matrix \(R\)
Rows = users, cols = items, entries = ratings/clicks (mostly unknown).

title: Glossary
text:
V







Term
Meaning




Validation loss
The loss on held-out examples the network never trains on — a stand-in for new data (§6).


Validation set
A slice of the data held out from training and used only to measure progress (§5.2).


Value / \(Q\)-value
Expected return from a state (\(V\)) or a state–action pair (\(Q\)).


Vanishing gradient
A chain-rule product of many small factors shrinks toward zero, so early layers stop learning (§3, §8; see also the §5 box on gradient pathologies).


Variance \(\sigma^2\)
Expected squared distance from the mean; spread.


Variational autoencoder (VAE) / ELBO
A network that learns to generate new data / its training objective, the evidence lower bound, which can never exceed the log of the evidence (§5); it contains a KL term that keeps each example’s code near a prior (§7).


Vector
An ordered list of numbers; equivalently, an arrow from the origin to a point.


Vector-wise vs bit-wise
A cross with one weight per pair of whole field vectors (xDeepFM’s CIN) versus one weight per coordinate (DCN, an MLP).


View
The embedding a node gets after an augmented input is encoded; contrastive learning needs two per node (§3.1).

title: Glossary
text:
W







Term
Meaning




\(W\) (weight matrix)
Learnable feature transform in GCN/NGCF; removed in LightGCN.


Walk
A path of \(K\) steps along edges that may turn back (Ann, Titanic, Ann); layer \(K\) mixes the starts of nodes a \(K\)-step walk reaches (§5).


Weight
One adjustable multiplier in a layer’s weighted sum; the main kind of parameter in a neural network (§3).


Weight / bias
Learned multiplier per input / learned constant offset.


Weight decay
The L2 penalty \(\lambda\lVert W\rVert^2\) on the weights; its gradient \(2\lambda W\) shrinks every weight a little at each step (§7).


Weighted / unweighted
Whether edges carry a number (rating/count) or are just 0/1.


Weighted sum
Scale several vectors by numbers and add the results, e.g. \(1\cdot[2,1]+2\cdot[0,3]=[2,7]\).


Weights
A model’s learned parameters, collected in one list \(\theta\) (§6), the numbers a regularizer keeps small.


Wide & Deep
Joint linear-with-hand-crosses over the raw features (memorize) \(+\) MLP-over-embeddings (generalize) model.


Wilcoxon signed-rank
Non-parametric paired test (ranks, not values); use when differences aren’t normal and there are at least \(6\) pairs (below that it cannot reach \(p<0.05\); §8.6).


word2vec
Predict-based word embeddings trained on word–context prediction: skip-gram predicts the context from a word, CBOW the word from its context (Mikolov 2013a, 2013b; §2.2).


WRMF / ALS
Weighted Regularized MF / Alternating Least Squares (implicit-feedback, squared error).

title: Glossary
text:
X







Term
Meaning




Xavier / Glorot init
The same idea for symmetric activations (tanh, sigmoid): variance \(2/(\text{fan\_in}+\text{fan\_out})\), with fan_out = neurons in the layer (§6).


xDeepFM / AutoInt / DIN
Vector-wise crosses (CIN) / attention-learned interactions / per-candidate behavior attention.

title: Glossary
text:
Z







Term
Meaning




Zero vector \(\mathbf{0}\)
The vector whose components are all \(0\); it has no direction, so it cannot be normalized and has no cosine.


Zero-shot / few-shot
Zero-shot: a frozen model is simply asked, with no examples and no extra training. Few-shot: still frozen, but a handful of solved examples are pasted into the prompt (§2.1).


Zero-shot NER
Extracting arbitrary entity types with no task-specific training (GLiNER, NuNER-Zero).

title: List of Symbols
text:
A quick reference for the symbols that recur across the book. Each is defined in full the first time it appears; this list is a reminder, grouped by where it is introduced. Where the same object is written two ways across the book, the change is flagged.
Linear algebra (Part I).







Symbol
Meaning




\(x,\ \alpha\)
a scalar (italic lower-case)


\(\mathbf{x},\ \mathbf{w}\)
a vector (bold lower-case; a Greek list such as all of a model’s weights is bold, \(\boldsymbol\theta\), where a chapter writes it out, though some formulas print the plain \(\theta\) for it, and the text says when \(\theta\) is the whole list)


\(M,\ A\)
a matrix (upper-case)


\(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\)
dot product (the universal “score two things” operation)


\(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\)
Euclidean (\(L_2\)) norm / length of a vector


\(\cos(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\)
cosine similarity, \(\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}\)


\(M^{\top}\)
transpose; \(I\) — identity matrix


\(\lambda,\ \mathbf{v}\)
eigenvalue and its eigenvector (\(M\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\))



Calculus and optimization (Part I).







Symbol
Meaning




\(f'(x),\ \frac{df}{dx}\)
derivative (slope / rate of change)


\(\partial,\ \nabla f\)
partial derivative; gradient (the vector of partials)


\(H\)
Hessian (matrix of second derivatives)


\(\eta\)
learning rate (gradient-descent step size)


\(\mathcal{L}\)
the loss (objective being minimized)


\(z,\ \mathbf{z}\)
pre-activation: \(z=\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b\) for one neuron, \(\mathbf{z}=W\mathbf{h}+\mathbf{b}\) for a layer (before the activation)


\(a,\ \mathbf{h}\)
post-activation: \(a=\phi(z)\) for one neuron; \(\mathbf{h}\) for a whole layer’s output


\(\mathbf{b}\)
a layer’s bias vector, added after the weight multiply


\(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\)
the network’s output / prediction — the last layer, \(\mathbf{h}^{(L)}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}\)



Probability (Part I).







Symbol
Meaning




\(\Pr(\cdot),\ \mathbb{E}[\cdot]\)
probability; expectation


\(X,\ x\)
a random variable (capital) and one value it can take (lower-case)


\(\mu,\ \sigma^2,\ \sigma\)
mean, variance (\(\operatorname{Var}[X]\)), standard deviation — this \(\sigma\) is not the sigmoid \(\sigma(z)\) below; context tells them apart


\(\theta\)
the parameters of a distribution or a model


\(\propto\)
“is proportional to”: equal up to a constant multiplier


\(x\sim p,\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}[\cdot]\)
\(x\) drawn from \(p\); the average over such draws


\(\neg B\)
“not \(B\)”, the complement of an event


\(x\in S\)
“\(x\) is a member of the set \(S\)”: \(x\in\{0,1\}\) reads “\(x\) is \(0\) or \(1\)”


\(H(p),\ H(p,q)\)
entropy; cross-entropy — this \(H\) is not the Hessian above


\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q),\ I(X;Y)\)
Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence; mutual information


\(H_0,\ \alpha\)
the null hypothesis; the significance level of a test (not the Beta’s \(\alpha\); \(\alpha_{\text{post}},\beta_{\text{post}}\) are a posterior Beta’s)


\(t^{*}\), df, SE, CI
a critical value; degrees of freedom; standard error (SE); confidence interval (CI)


\(\sigma(z)\)
the sigmoid (logistic) function, \(1/(1+e^{-z})\)


\(\tau\)
temperature (softmax / contrastive sharpness)


\(\mathcal{N},\ \text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\)
Gaussian; Beta distribution



Recommender systems (Parts III onward).







Symbol
Meaning




\(u,\ i,\ j\)
a user; an item; a second (often negative) item


\(r_{ui},\ \hat r_{ui}\)
observed rating; model-predicted score for \((u,i)\)


\(R\)
the user–item interaction / rating matrix


\(\mathbf{p}_u,\ \mathbf{q}_i\)
matrix-factorization user/item latent vectors (Part III), \(\hat r_{ui}=\mathbf{p}_u\cdot\mathbf{q}_i\)


\(\mathcal{R}\)
the set of relevant items (evaluation)


@\(K\)
“evaluated at the top \(K\) positions” of the ranked list



Sequence-based recommenders (Part IV).







Symbol
Meaning




\((i_1,\dots,i_{t-1})\)
a user’s ordered history / session prefix; the task is to predict the next item \(i_t\)


\(P(\text{next}=i\mid\text{last}=l)\)
a first-order Markov transition probability (estimated by counting)


\(\mathbf{h}_t\)
the hidden state of a recurrent neural network (RNN) — the running summary of the session up to step \(t\)


\(\alpha_{ij}\)
a self-attention weight: how much position \(i\) attends to position \(j\) (softmax of scaled dot products); the sequence chapter writes it \(\alpha_{tj}\), position \(t\) attending to \(j\)



Graphs and graph collaborative filtering (Part V).







Symbol
Meaning




\(A,\ \tilde A\)
adjacency matrix; its symmetric-normalized form \(D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\)


\(\deg(u)\)
degree (number of neighbors) of a node


\(\mathbf{e}_u,\ \mathbf{e}_i\)
the learned identifier (ID) embedding of a user/item (graph era) — the same kind of object as \(\mathbf{p}_u,\mathbf{q}_i\) above, now refined by graph propagation rather than plain factorization


\(\mathbf{e}_u^{(k)}\)
the embedding after \(k\) propagation layers; \(\alpha_k\) — layer-combination weight



Contrastive learning and large language models (Parts V–VI).







Symbol
Meaning




\(\mathbf{z},\ \mathbf{z}^{+},\ \mathbf{z}_k\)
an anchor; its positive (matching view); a negative — embeddings, so bold like every other vector


\(\operatorname{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)\)
a similarity (usually cosine)


\(\mathbf{s}_i\)
a semantic embedding (e.g. a frozen text-encoder applied to a profile that a large language model wrote), aligned with the collaborative \(\mathbf{e}_i\)




Two letters that carry a different job in different parts. Both are flagged here rather than forced into one symbol, because in each case the two uses are genuinely different objects and each chapter says so where it uses them.

\(d\) and \(\Delta\). In Loss Functions & Regularizers the pairwise score gap is \(d\) (as in \(-\ln\sigma(d)\)). Everywhere else \(d\) is the embedding dimension (it already is in the linear-algebra, Transformer and matrix-factorization chapters), and Training and Serving a Recommender writes the score gap \(\Delta\). Read \(d\) as “gap” only inside the losses chapter.
\(K\) and \(L\). \(L\) counts the layers of a neural network (so \(\mathbf{h}^{(L)}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}\)); the neural graph collaborative filtering (NGCF) sketch in From Graphs to LightGCN also writes \(L\) for the number of graph layers (the same \(K\) hops as in the other graph chapters), and in The Spectral / Graph-Filter View \(L=I-\tilde A\) is the graph Laplacian, a matrix. \(K\) counts propagation steps on a graph, and is chosen because it equals the number of hops a signal travels — \(K\) layers means reach \(K\) hops. Note also \(@K\) above, which is the cut-off of a ranked list and unrelated to both.

Other letters that are reused, each named where it changes meaning.

\(H\): entropy (Probability), the Hessian (Calculus), the number of attention heads (Representation Learning & the Transformer) and the graph filter (The Spectral / Graph-Filter View).
\(\mathcal R\): the set of relevant items in Evaluation Metrics, and the regularizer \(\mathcal R(\theta)\) in Loss Functions & Regularizers.
\(\sigma\) is the sigmoid, a standard deviation, a singular value (Linear Algebra, the spectral chapter), and, as \(\sigma_\downarrow,\sigma_\uparrow\), a projection in Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning; the chapters on large language models write that projection \(g\).
