\(\gamma\): the discount factor (Reinforcement Learning), a focal exponent (Loss Functions & Regularizers), the federated server’s step, an angle. \(\epsilon\): an exploration rate (Bandits), a perturbation radius (SimGCL, in Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning) and a privacy budget (Federated).
\(z\): the pre-activation of a neuron or layer (Neural Networks & Back-propagation) and, in bold, the anchor embedding of contrastive learning (Self-Supervised & Contrastive Learning).
\(I\): the identity matrix (Linear Algebra, and in the graph Laplacian \(L=I-\tilde A\)) and, in \(I(X;Y)\), mutual information.
The model’s score for \((u,i)\) is \(\hat r_{ui}\) in the losses, matrix-factorization and serving chapters; the graph chapters write the same score as \(\hat y_{ui}\), the sequence chapters write \(\hat s\), and the click-prediction chapter writes \(\hat p\) (a probability).
\(L\) also counts the propagation layers in Training and Serving (there \(K\) is the list length) and the cross layers in Click-Through Rate Prediction; the graph Laplacian is written \(L=I-\tilde A\) in plain type in the spectral chapter.

The cast. Ann, Bob and Cara are the three users of most chapters (the calculus and probability primers use none of them, and a few chapters use only one or two); Dave appears only in Appendix C. A few chapters add a one-off user for one worked example (Dan, Dana, Eve, Zed); each is a different person in each chapter and is introduced where used.
One notation change to keep in mind. Through the matrix-factorization chapter the user/item vectors are written \(\mathbf{p}_u,\mathbf{q}_i\); from From Graphs to LightGCN onward the learned user/item vector is written \(\mathbf{e}_u,\mathbf{e}_i\) (the ID embedding). They are the same kind of object — a vector whose location carries meaning — differing only in how it is learned.

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Linear Algebra for Machine Learning
E1. Dot product (§4): multiply entry-by-entry and sum, \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{s}=3\cdot2+4\cdot1=6+4=\boxed{10}\). It is positive, so the two arrows broadly point the same way (the dot product is positive when the angle between them is under \(90^\circ\), zero at a right angle, negative when they oppose).
E2. L2 norm (§1): \(\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=\sqrt{25+144}=\sqrt{169}=\boxed{13}\). Normalizing divides by that length: \(\mathbf{g}/\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert=\tfrac{1}{13}[5,12]=\boxed{[5/13,\,12/13]}\approx[0.385,\,0.923]\). Check it is a unit vector: its length is \(\sqrt{(5/13)^2+(12/13)^2}=\sqrt{(25+144)/169}=\sqrt{1}=1\). ✓
E3. Cosine similarity (§4). Dot product \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{t}=3\cdot0+4\cdot5=0+20=20\); lengths \(\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert=\sqrt{9+16}=5\) and \(\lVert\mathbf{t}\rVert=\sqrt{0+25}=5\). So \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{20}{5\cdot5}=\dfrac{20}{25}=\boxed{0.8}\) (an angle of about \(36.9^\circ\)). At \(0.8\) it sits between the two reference pairs but on the near-aligned side — closer to the chapter’s \(0.96\) than to its orthogonal \(0\).
E4. Matrix–vector product (§3): each output entry is a row of \(A\) dotted with \(\mathbf{y}=[2,1,3]\). \[
A\mathbf{y}=\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot2+0\cdot1+1\cdot3\\ 1\cdot2+3\cdot1+0\cdot3\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}4+0+3\\ 2+3+0\end{bmatrix}=\boxed{[7,\,5]}.
\] Column blend (picture (b), §3): \(2\,\mathrm{col}_1+1\,\mathrm{col}_2+3\,\mathrm{col}_3
=2[2,1]+1[0,3]+3[1,0]=[4,2]+[0,3]+[3,0]=[7,5]\) — the same vector. ✓ (A \(2\times3\) matrix took a 3-vector to a 2-vector: “3 in, 2 out.”)
E5. Characteristic equation (§5): \[
\begin{gathered}
\det(B-\lambda I)=\det\begin{bmatrix}5-\lambda&2\\2&2-\lambda\end{bmatrix}=(5-\lambda)(2-\lambda)-4\\[4pt]
=\lambda^2-7\lambda+6=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-6)=0\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\lambda=1,\ 6}.
\end{gathered}
\] Trace check: \(1+6=7=5+2\), the diagonal sum. ✓ For the larger eigenvalue \(\lambda=6\), solve \((B-6I)\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}-1&2\\2&-4\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\), i.e. writing \(\mathbf{v}=[x,y]\), \(-x+2y=0\Rightarrow x=2y\), so the eigenvector is \(\boxed{[2,1]}\). (Indeed \(B[2,1]=[12,6]=6[2,1]\); the other candidate \([1,-2]\) goes with \(\lambda=1\), since \(B[1,-2]=[1,-2]\), and the two are perpendicular, as for any symmetric matrix.)
E6. Eigenvalues (§5): \(R\) has trace \(0\) and determinant \(0\cdot0-1\cdot1=-1\), so \(\lambda^2-1=0\) and the eigenvalues are \(\boxed{1\ \text{and}\ -1}\) (the eigenvector \([1,1]\) is kept, \([1,-1]\) is sent to \([-1,1]\), its own negative). Singular values (§6): \(R^{\top}R=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=I\), whose eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(1\), so the singular values are \(\boxed{1\ \text{and}\ 1}\). The sets \(\{1,-1\}\) and \(\{1,1\}\) do not coincide, and the eigenvalue responsible is \(\boxed{-1}\). The reason: eigenvalues keep their sign, while singular values are lengths of stretches, \(\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i(A^{\top}A)}\ge0\), so a flip (here the mirror that swaps the coordinates) shows up in \(A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\) as a negative \(\lambda\) but in the SVD as the output direction \(\mathbf{u}\) being the input direction reversed.
Because \(R\) is symmetric, \(R^{\top}R=R^2\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda^2\), so \(\sigma_i=|\lambda_i|\) here; the two sets agree in absolute value, and fully only when no \(\lambda\) is negative, that is, when \(R\) is positive-semidefinite (§6), which \(R\) is not.
E7. (a) The dot products are \(c_1=\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}_1=3\cdot2+4\cdot0=6\) and \(c_2=\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}_2=3\cdot0+4\cdot3=12\). The sum is \(6[2,0]+12[0,3]=[12,0]+[0,36]=[12,36]\), which is not \(\mathbf{u}=[3,4]\). (b) The true coordinates solve \(a_1[2,0]+a_2[0,3]=[3,4]\), so \(2a_1=3\) and \(3a_2=4\): \(a_1=\boxed{3/2}\) and \(a_2=\boxed{4/3}\) (check: \(\tfrac32[2,0]+\tfrac43[0,3]=[3,0]+[0,4]=[3,4]\) ✓). The dot products overshoot by \(c_1/a_1=6/1.5=\boxed{4}\) and \(c_2/a_2=12/(4/3)=\boxed{9}\), which are \(\lVert\mathbf{f}_1\rVert^2=2^2\) and \(\lVert\mathbf{f}_2\rVert^2=3^2\). Perpendicularity already keeps each axis from feeling the others (that is why a coordinate exists on each axis alone), but a dot product counts the length of \(\mathbf{f}_i\) twice, once in \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}_i\) and once in the arrow it multiplies, and only a unit length makes that factor \(1\). Divide each \(\mathbf{f}_i\) by its length first (\(\mathbf{e}_1=[1,0]\), \(\mathbf{e}_2=[0,1]\)) and the plain formula \(\sum_i(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{e}_i)\mathbf{e}_i=[3,0]+[0,4]=\mathbf{u}\) works.
E8. Apply §6’s recipe to \(G=\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{bmatrix}\). Form \[
G^{\top}G=\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8&8\\8&8\end{bmatrix},
\] a symmetric matrix with trace \(16\) and determinant \(8\cdot8-8\cdot8=0\), so its eigenvalues are \(\boxed{16\ \text{and}\ 0}\). The singular values are their square roots: \(\sigma_1=\sqrt{16}=\boxed{4}\) and \(\sigma_2=\sqrt{0}=0\). One nonzero singular value means \(G\) has \(\boxed{\text{rank }1}\) — as expected, since its two rows lie on one line: they are multiples of each other (here even identical; for the chapter’s \(M\), row 2 is \(2\times\) row 1). Its single direction is \(\mathbf{u}_1=\mathbf{v}_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}[1,1]\), and rebuilding the one rank-1 piece — a column times a row, with no dot between them — gives \(\sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^{\top}=4\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}[1\ \ 1]=2\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}=G\). ✓
E9. The quadratic form (§6) is \(\mathbf{x}^{\top}E\mathbf{x}\) with \(E=\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\3&1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{x}=[2,-1]\). Compute \(E\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot2+3(-1)\\3\cdot2+1(-1)\end{bmatrix}=[-1,5]\), then \(\mathbf{x}^{\top}E\mathbf{x}=[2,-1]\cdot[-1,5]=-2-5=\boxed{-7}\). Because this is negative, \(E\) is not PSD — and that single \(\mathbf{x}=[2,-1]\) is the witness that proves it (PSD requires \(\mathbf{x}^{\top}E\mathbf{x}\ge0\) for every \(\mathbf{x}\); one negative value is enough to disqualify it; here it exposes \(E\)’s eigenvalue \(-2\), the other being \(4\)). Contrast the healthy \(S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) at the same vector: \(S[2,-1]=[3,0]\), so \(\mathbf{x}^{\top}S\mathbf{x}=[2,-1]\cdot[3,0]=6\ge0\) — consistent with \(S\) being PSD (its eigenvalues \(1,3\) are both \(\ge0\)).
E10. Scoring by dot product (§4), with \(\mathbf{p}=[2,1,3]\). (a) \(\hat r_1=\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}_1=2\cdot3+1\cdot3+3\cdot0=6+3+0=9\) and \(\hat r_2=\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}_2=2\cdot0+1\cdot1+3\cdot2=0+1+6=7\). Since \(9>7\), dot product ranks \(\mathbf{q}_1\) above \(\mathbf{q}_2\) (\(\boxed{\mathbf{q}_1\succ\mathbf{q}_2}\)). (b) Cosine needs the norms: \(\lVert\mathbf{p}\rVert=\sqrt{4+1+9}=\sqrt{14}\approx3.742\), \(\lVert\mathbf{q}_1\rVert=\sqrt{9+9+0}=\sqrt{18}\approx4.243\), \(\lVert\mathbf{q}_2\rVert=\sqrt{0+1+4}=\sqrt5\approx2.236\). Then \(\cos(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}_1)=\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{18}}\approx\boxed{0.567}\) and \(\cos(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}_2)=\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt5}\approx\boxed{0.837}\). The two rankings disagree: cosine puts \(\boxed{\mathbf{q}_2\succ\mathbf{q}_1}\), the reverse of (a). The reason is length. \(\mathbf{q}_1\) is the bigger vector (\(\sqrt{18}>\sqrt5\)) and wins on the dot product for that reason, not for pointing the user’s way — measured by direction alone it is the worse match (\(0.567\) against \(0.837\)). That is the popularity/length bias §4’s “serving trick” (L2-normalize first, which turns the dot product into cosine) is designed to remove.
E11. Rank-1 collapse (§2). (a) \(\det A=4\cdot3-2\cdot6=0\) — singular. (b) \(A[1,0]=[4,6]\), while \(A[1,-2]=[4\cdot1+2(-2),\,6\cdot1+3(-2)]=[0,0]\): the direction \([1,-2]\) is killed (mapped to the origin — the null space). (c) Both columns, \([4,6]\) and \([2,3]\), are multiples of \([2,3]\) (the first is \(2\times\) the second), so every output is too: the image is the line \(\{c\,[2,3]\}\), and \(\boxed{[2,3]}\) spans it — its multiples make up that whole line.
E12. Spot the singular matrix (§2). Determinants: \(\big[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{smallmatrix}\big]\to3\); \(\big[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\4&2\end{smallmatrix}\big]\to2\cdot2-1\cdot4=0\); \(\big[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\big]\to2-1=1\). Only the middle matrix has \(\det=0\), so it is the singular one (its rows \([2,1],[4,2]\) are dependent — one is twice the other).
E13. Eigenvalues from trace and determinant (§5). We need \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2=5\) and \(\lambda_1\lambda_2=6\), i.e. the roots of \(\lambda^2-5\lambda+6=(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)=0\). So \(\lambda=\boxed{2\text{ and }3}\) — recoverable from the trace and determinant alone, no matrix needed.
E14. \(B\) is symmetric with eigenvalues \(6\) and \(1\) (trace \(7\), determinant \(6\)), so its singular values are \(\sigma_1=6\), \(\sigma_2=1\), with unit eigenvectors \(\mathbf{u}_1=\mathbf{v}_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}[2,1]\) and \(\mathbf{u}_2=\mathbf{v}_2=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}[1,-2]\). (a) The larger piece is \(B_1=\sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^{\top}=6\cdot\tfrac15\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\2&1\end{bmatrix}=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}4.8&2.4\\2.4&1.2\end{bmatrix}}\). (b) The error is \(B-B_1=\begin{bmatrix}0.2&-0.4\\-0.4&0.8\end{bmatrix}\), whose Frobenius norm is \(\sqrt{0.04+0.16+0.16+0.64}=\sqrt{1}=\boxed{1}\) — exactly the dropped singular value \(\sigma_2=1\), as Eckart–Young promises. (With nothing kept the error would be \(\lVert B\rVert_F=\sqrt{25+4+4+4}=\sqrt{37}=\sqrt{6^2+1^2}\approx6.08\).)
E15. \(K^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}\). \(K^{\top}K=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot1+0\cdot0&1\cdot2+0\cdot1\\2\cdot1+1\cdot0&2\cdot2+1\cdot1\end{bmatrix}=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&5\end{bmatrix}}\) and \(KK^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot1+2\cdot2&1\cdot0+2\cdot1\\0\cdot1+1\cdot2&0\cdot0+1\cdot1\end{bmatrix}=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}5&2\\2&1\end{bmatrix}}\). They are not equal (order matters, §3), but each is symmetric, as every \(A^{\top}A\) is (§6); for \(KK^{\top}\) the same one-line transpose works, \((KK^{\top})^{\top}=(K^{\top})^{\top}K^{\top}=KK^{\top}\). For the singular values: \(K^{\top}K\) has trace \(6\) and determinant \(1\cdot5-2\cdot2=1\), so \(\lambda^2-6\lambda+1=0\) and \(\lambda=3\pm2\sqrt2\approx5.828,\ 0.172\); taking square roots, \(\sigma=\sqrt{3\pm2\sqrt2}=\boxed{1+\sqrt2\approx2.414\ \text{and}\ \sqrt2-1\approx0.414}\) (because \((1+\sqrt2)^2=3+2\sqrt2\) and \((\sqrt2-1)^2=3-2\sqrt2\)).
E16. \(N\) is not symmetric (its off-diagonal entries are \(1\) and \(0\)). It is triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, \(\boxed{1\ \text{and}\ 2}\). For \(\lambda=1\): \((N-I)\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\) forces \(v_2=0\), so \(\mathbf{v}=[1,0]\). For \(\lambda=2\): \((N-2I)\mathbf{w}=\begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}\) forces \(w_1=w_2\), so \(\mathbf{w}=[1,1]\). Their dot product is \([1,0]\cdot[1,1]=1\neq0\): not perpendicular. §5’s argument for symmetric matrices used \((A\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v}\cdot(A\mathbf{w})\), which is what symmetry buys; here \((N\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{w}=[1,0]\cdot[1,1]=1\) but \(\mathbf{v}\cdot(N\mathbf{w})=[1,0]\cdot[2,2]=2\), so that step fails and the eigenvectors need not be perpendicular.
E17. (a) \(\det P=4\cdot2-2\cdot3=8-6=2\neq0\), so \(P\) is invertible. (b) Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by \(\det P=2\): \(P^{-1}=\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}2&-2\\-3&4\end{bmatrix}=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1.5&2\end{bmatrix}}\). (c) Entry by entry, \(PP^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}4\cdot1+2(-1.5)&4(-1)+2\cdot2\\3\cdot1+2(-1.5)&3(-1)+2\cdot2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=I\) ✓. (d) \(\mathbf{x}=P^{-1}[10,8]=[1\cdot10+(-1)\cdot8,\ -1.5\cdot10+2\cdot8]=\boxed{[2,1]}\); check: \(P[2,1]=[4\cdot2+2\cdot1,\ 3\cdot2+2\cdot1]=[10,8]\) ✓.
E18. (a) \(AW\) is \((2\times3)(3\times2)\), so \(2\times2\); \(WA\) is \((3\times2)(2\times3)\), so \(3\times3\). (b) Column 1 of \(AW\) is \(A[1,2,0]=[2\cdot1+0\cdot2+1\cdot0,\ 1\cdot1+3\cdot2+0\cdot0]=[2,7]\); column 2 is \(A[0,1,3]=[2\cdot0+0\cdot1+1\cdot3,\ 1\cdot0+3\cdot1+0\cdot3]=[3,3]\). So \(AW=\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\7&3\end{bmatrix}}\). (c) No: the shapes differ (\(2\times2\) against \(3\times3\)), so they cannot be equal; order matters even more than in §3’s \(CB\neq BC\). (d) Entry \((3,2)\) of \(WA\) is row 3 of \(W\) times column 2 of \(A\): \([0,3]\cdot[0,3]=0+9=\boxed{9}\).

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Calculus for Machine Learning
E1. Derivative from the limit (§1). Expand and cancel the \(h\) in the denominator: \[
\frac{(2+h)^2-2^2}{h}=\frac{4+4h+h^2-4}{h}=\frac{4h+h^2}{h}=4+h\xrightarrow[h\to0]{}\boxed{4}.
\] So \(f'(2)=4\): near \(x=2\) the output of \(x^2\) grows about \(4\) units per unit of input. The power rule agrees — \(f'(x)=2x\) gives \(2\cdot2=4\). ✓
E2. Product rule (§2) on \(f=x^2(x+1)\), with \(f_1=x^2\) (\(f_1'=2x\)) and \(f_2=x+1\) (\(f_2'=1\)): \[
f'(x)=f_1'f_2+f_1f_2'=2x(x+1)+x^2\cdot1=2x^2+2x+x^2=3x^2+2x.
\] At \(x=2\): \(f'(2)=3(4)+2(2)=12+4=\boxed{16}\). Check by expanding first: \(f(x)=x^3+x^2\), so \(f'(x)=3x^2+2x\) and \(f'(2)=12+4=16\) ✓ — the two routes agree.
E3. Chain rule (§3) on \(k=(2x+1)^3=f(g(x))\): the outer \(f(u)=u^3\) has derivative \(f'(u)=3u^2\), evaluated at the inner value \(u=g(x)\), times the inner derivative \(g'(x)=2\): \[
k'(x)=\underbrace{3(2x+1)^2}_{f'(g(x))}\times\underbrace{2}_{g'(x)}=6(2x+1)^2.
\] At \(x=1\): \(k'(1)=6(2\cdot1+1)^2=6\cdot3^2=6\cdot9=\boxed{54}\). Check by expanding: \(k(x)=8x^3+12x^2+6x+1\), so \(k'(x)=24x^2+24x+6\) and \(k'(1)=24+24+6=54\) ✓.
E4. Sigmoid derivative (§3). At \(z=1\), \(\sigma(1)=\tfrac{1}{1+e^{-1}}\approx\boxed{0.7311}\), so \[
\sigma'(1)=\sigma(1)\big(1-\sigma(1)\big)\approx0.7311\cdot0.2689\approx\boxed{0.197}.
\] At \(z=3\), \(\sigma(3)=\tfrac{1}{1+e^{-3}}\approx\boxed{0.9526}\), so \(\sigma'(3)\approx0.9526\cdot0.0474\approx\boxed{0.045}\). The sigmoid passes back more gradient at \(z=1\) (\(0.197\)) than at \(z=3\) (\(0.045\)): the factor \(\sigma(1-\sigma)\) is largest where \(\sigma=\tfrac12\) (at \(z=0\), \(0.25\)) and shrinks as the sigmoid saturates, here by more than a factor of \(4\) (the weights multiply in separately, §3).
E5. Partial derivatives and the gradient (§4) of \(f(x,y)=x^2y+y\). Holding the other variable fixed each time: \[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2xy\quad(\text{treat }y\text{ constant}),\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=x^2+1\quad(\text{treat }x\text{ constant}).
\] At \((x,y)=(2,3)\): \(\nabla f=\big[\,2\cdot2\cdot3,\ 2^2+1\,\big]=\boxed{[12,\ 5]}\).
E6. The second-derivative test (§6).
For \(f=x^2+3y^2\): \(\nabla f=[2x,\ 6y]\) is \(\mathbf 0\) only at \((0,0)\), and \(f_{xx}=2\), \(f_{yy}=6\), \(f_{xy}=0\), so \[
H_f=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&6\end{bmatrix},\qquad D=2\cdot6-0^2=\boxed{12}>0\ \text{ and }\ f_{xx}=2>0
\ \Rightarrow\ \textbf{bowl}\text{ (a minimum)}.
\] \(H_f\) is the same at every point, with \(f_{xx}>0\) and \(D>0\): positive definite everywhere, so \(f\) is a convex bowl with one bottom.
For \(g=xy\): \(\nabla g=[y,\ x]\) is \(\mathbf 0\) only at \((0,0)\), and \(g_{xx}=0\), \(g_{yy}=0\), \(g_{xy}=1\), so \[
H_g=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad D=0\cdot0-1^2=\boxed{-1}<0
\ \Rightarrow\ \textbf{saddle}.
\] Check directly: along the line \(y=x\), \(g=x^2\) curves up; along \(y=-x\), \(g=-x^2\) curves down. Up one way, down another — the Hessian is indefinite, so \(g\) is not convex (the horse-saddle shape).
(Optional eigenvalues, from \(\lambda^2-(a+d)\lambda+(ad-b^2)=0\): for \(H_f\), \(\lambda^2-8\lambda+12=0\) gives \(\lambda=2,\ 6\), with product \(12=D\); for \(H_g\), \(\lambda^2-1=0\) gives \(\lambda=\pm1\), with product \(-1=D\) ✓.)
E7. Stacked sigmoids (§3). Multiplying the per-layer activation ceilings of \(0.25\) over \(6\) sigmoid layers gives at most \[
0.25^{6}=\Big(\tfrac14\Big)^{6}=\frac{1}{4^6}=\frac{1}{64\cdot64}=\frac{1}{4096}\approx0.00024,\qquad\text{so }\boxed{1/4096}
\] — the most the activation factors alone let through. By hand, \(4^3=64\), so \(4^6=4^3\cdot4^3=64\cdot64=4096\). With a weight of \(3\) at every layer, each layer’s full factor is at most \(3\cdot0.25=0.75\), and \[
0.75^{6}\approx\boxed{0.178}.
\] The chain passes back at most about \(18\%\) of the gradient: it still shrinks, though far more slowly than with the activation factors alone, because \(0.75\) is only a little below \(1\) (a weight above \(4\) could lift the factor above \(1\)).
E8. Gradient descent on \(f(x)=x^2\) (so \(f'(x)=2x\)), \(x_0=2\), \(\eta=0.1\), via \(x\leftarrow x-\eta f'(x)\) (§5): \[
x_1=2-0.1(2\cdot2)=2-0.4=\boxed{1.6},\qquad
x_2=1.6-0.1(2\cdot1.6)=1.6-0.32=\boxed{1.28},
\] and \(f(x_2)=1.28^2=\boxed{1.6384}\) — the value marched downhill \(4\to2.56\to1.6384\) toward the minimum at \(0\). Taylor check of the first step (§7): the step is \(\delta=-\eta f'(x_0)=-0.4\), and the first-order predicted change is \[
f'(x_0)\cdot\delta=4\times(-0.4)=-1.6<0,
\] negative, so to first order the step lowers \(f\) (predicted \(f\approx4-1.6=2.4\) vs the actual \(f(1.6)=2.56\) — close, and both below the starting \(4\)). This is the §7 argument \(f(\theta-\eta\nabla f)\approx f(\theta)-\eta\lVert\nabla f\rVert^2\le f(\theta)\) in one number; exactly, one step multiplies \(f=x^2\) by \((1-2\eta)^2=0.8^2=0.64\), and \(4\times0.64=2.56\) ✓.
E9. Jacobian (§8) of \(F(x,y)=[\,xy,\ x+y^2\,]\). With \(F_1=xy\) and \(F_2=x+y^2\), fill \(J_{ij}=\partial F_i/\partial x_j\) (row = output, column = input): \[
J=\begin{bmatrix}\partial_x(xy)&\partial_y(xy)\\[2pt]\partial_x(x+y^2)&\partial_y(x+y^2)\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}y&x\\1&2y\end{bmatrix}
\;\xrightarrow{(2,3)}\;\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\1&6\end{bmatrix}}.
\] Row \(1\) is \([\,y,\ x\,]=[\,3,\ 2\,]\) at \((2,3)\), which is exactly \(\nabla(xy)=[\partial_x(xy),\partial_y(xy)]=[y,x]\) — the gradient of the first output, just as §8 says “row \(i\) is the gradient of output \(i\).” ✓
E10. One gradient-descent step on a squared-error loss (§3 chain rule + §5 step). With \(\mathcal{L}(w)=(2w-1)^2\), differentiate by the chain rule (outer: squaring, \(u^2\to2u\); inner \(\tfrac{d}{dw}(2w-1)=2\)): \[
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw}=2(2w-1)\cdot2=4(2w-1)=8w-4.
\] At \(w_0=0\): \(\dfrac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw}=8(0)-4=\boxed{-4}\). The step (\(\eta=0.1\)) is \[
w\leftarrow w_0-\eta\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw}=0-0.1(-4)=\boxed{0.4}.
\] Loss before: \(\mathcal{L}(0)=(2\cdot0-1)^2=(-1)^2=\boxed{1}\); loss after: \(\mathcal{L}(0.4)=(2\cdot0.4-1)^2=(-0.2)^2=\boxed{0.04}\). The loss dropped \(1\to0.04\) in a single step — one literal turn of the training loop \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla f\) behind most learned models in the series (here on one weight; in practice on a whole parameter vector at once).
E11. Linear-approximation error (§7). With the tangent line \(T(x)=4x-4\): at \(x=2.5\), \(T=6\) and \(f=6.25\), error \(0.25\); at \(x=3\), \(T=8\) and \(f=9\), error \(1.0\). Expanding, \(f(x)-T(x)=x^2-4x+4=(x-2)^2\), and both errors match it (\(0.5^2=0.25\), \(1^2=1\)): the error is the dropped curvature term, growing with the square of the step away from \(x_0=2\).
E12. Convexity (§6). (a) \(f''=12x^2\ge0\) everywhere → convex. (b) \(f''=20x^3\) is negative for \(x<0\) and positive for \(x>0\) → not convex (it changes bending at \(x=0\)). (c) \(f''=4e^{2x}>0\) everywhere → convex. (d) \(f''=-2<0\) everywhere → a cap (concave: an upside-down bowl), not convex.
E13. Convergent learning rate (§5). (a) \(|1-8\eta|<1\) means \(-1<1-8\eta<1\), i.e. \(0<\eta<\tfrac14\): any step in that range shrinks \(x\) toward \(0\). (b) \(\eta=0.25\) gives multiplier \(1-2=-1\), so \(x\) oscillates \(x\to-x\to x\) forever and never settles; \(\eta=0.3\) gives \(1-2.4=-1.4\), so \(|x|\) is multiplied by \(1.4\) every step and diverges. (c) Here \(f''=8\), so \(2/K=2/8=\tfrac14\), the same bound as in (a).
E14. \(\lVert\hat{\mathbf d}\rVert=\tfrac15\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\tfrac55=1\) ✓. The directional derivative is \(\nabla f\cdot\hat{\mathbf d}=[4,1]\cdot\tfrac15[3,4]=\tfrac15(12+4)=\boxed{3.2}\): positive, so \(f\) is rising that way, but more slowly than along \(x\) (slope \(4\)) — the gradient direction is the steepest.
E15. \(f_{xx}v_1^2+2f_{xy}v_1v_2+f_{yy}v_2^2=2\cdot\tfrac{9}{25}+2\cdot1\cdot\tfrac{12}{25}+0=\tfrac{18+24}{25}=\boxed{1.68}\): positive, and it lies between the two eigenvalues \(1-\sqrt2\approx-0.41\) and \(1+\sqrt2\approx2.41\), as every unit-direction curvature must.
E16. \(\nabla f=[2x,6y]=[6,6]\) at \((3,1)\), so \((x,y)\leftarrow(3-0.1\cdot6,\ 1-0.1\cdot6)=\boxed{(2.4,\ 0.4)}\). \(f(3,1)=9+3=12\) before and \(f(2.4,0.4)=5.76+0.48=\boxed{6.24}\) after. \(x\) moved by \(0.6\) of \(3\) (\(20\%\)) and \(y\) by \(0.6\) of \(1\) (\(60\%\)). For the range of \(\eta\): the slopes are \(2x\) and \(6y\), so each step multiplies \(x\) by \(1-2\eta\) and \(y\) by \(1-6\eta\), and a coordinate shrinks only when its factor lies between \(-1\) and \(1\): \(0<\eta<1\) for \(x\) and \(0<\eta<\tfrac13\) for \(y\). Both shrink exactly when \(\boxed{0<\eta<\tfrac13}\), so the more sharply curved direction sets the limit (the \(2/K\) of §7 with \(K=6\); at \(\eta=\tfrac13\) the \(y\) factor is \(-1\) and \(y\) bounces forever).

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Probability & Statistics for Machine Learning
E1. Expectation and variance (§1) of the fair four-sided die, \(p(x)=\tfrac14\) for \(x\in\{1,2,3,4\}\). Mean: \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\tfrac14(1+2+3+4)=\tfrac{10}{4}=\boxed{2.5}\) — the balance point of the four bars (a value you never roll). For the variance use the shortcut \(\operatorname{Var}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2\): \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=\tfrac14(1+4+9+16)=\tfrac{30}{4}=7.5\), so \(\operatorname{Var}[X]=7.5-2.5^2=7.5-6.25=\boxed{1.25}\) (exactly \(5/4\)). (Smaller than the six-sided die’s \(35/12\approx2.92\), as it should be — four faces spread less than six.)
E2. Naming the distributions (§2). (a) One yes/no outcome is a Bernoulli, parameter \(p\). (b) One pick out of \(5\) unordered labels is a Categorical, parameters \(p_1,\dots,p_5\) (summing to \(1\)). (c) A real value with a few wildly-off entries is a Laplace, parameters \(\mu,b\). (d) A belief about a probability is a Beta; the pseudo-count reading “\(\alpha-1\) heads, \(\beta-1\) tails already seen” with \(6\) heads and \(2\) tails gives \(\alpha-1=6,\ \beta-1=2\), i.e. \(\boxed{\text{Beta}(7,3)}\), whose mean is \(\mathbb{E}[\theta]=\dfrac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=\dfrac{7}{10}=\boxed{0.7}\) (leans toward heads, as “6 heads vs 2 tails” should; not \(6/8=0.75\): that is the peak, the mode \((7-1)/(7+3-2)=0.75\), and the mean sits a little nearer the middle, as §2’s Beta\((2,5)\) showed). Finally, the Bernoulli of (a) with \(p=0.8\): \(\mathbb{E}[X]=p=\boxed{0.8}\) and \(\operatorname{Var}[X]=p(1-p)=0.8\cdot0.2=\boxed{0.16}\).
E3. Odds → logit → sigmoid (§3) for the \(p=0.7\) coin. (a) Odds \(=\dfrac{p}{1-p}=\dfrac{0.7}{0.3}=\dfrac73\approx\boxed{2.333}\) (\(2.33\times\) as likely to land heads as not). (b) Logit \(=\ln\!\big(\tfrac{p}{1-p}\big)=\ln\tfrac73\approx\boxed{0.847}\). (c) Feed that score \(z=\ln\tfrac73\) back through the sigmoid: \(e^{-z}=\tfrac37=0.4286\), so \(\sigma(z)=\dfrac{1}{1+0.4286}=\dfrac{1}{1.4286}=\boxed{0.7}\) ✓ — exactly the \(p\) we started from, because the sigmoid is the logit’s inverse (and the odds are exactly \(e^{z}=\tfrac73\)). (d) \(\sigma(3)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-3}}=\dfrac{1}{1+0.0498}=\boxed{0.953}\): a score of \(3\) is odds of \(e^{3}\approx20\) to \(1\), so a probability a little above \(0.95\).
E4. Softmax (§3) of \(\mathbf z=[1,0,0]\). Exponentiate: \(e^{1},e^{0},e^{0}=2.718,\,1,\,1\), summing to \(4.718\). Divide each by the total: \[
\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf z)=\Big[\tfrac{2.718}{4.718},\,\tfrac{1}{4.718},\,\tfrac{1}{4.718}\Big]
=\boxed{[0.576,\,0.212,\,0.212]},
\] and \(0.576+0.212+0.212=1.000\) ✓. Class \(A\) wins (it had the largest score), and \(B\) and \(C\) are equal because each class gets \(e^{z_c}\) over the same total \(4.718\), and \(z_B=z_C=0\) gives both \(e^{0}=1\), so both get \(1/4.718=0.212\). The top score takes the lion’s share but the others keep nonzero probability (a soft max, not a hard one).
E5. MLE for the coin (§4): 6 heads, 2 tails, \(L(\theta)=\theta^{6}(1-\theta)^{2}\), \(\log L(\theta)=6\ln\theta+2\ln(1-\theta)\). Set the derivative to zero, using the toolkit’s slopes \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\ln\theta=\frac1\theta\) and \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\ln(1-\theta)=-\frac{1}{1-\theta}\): \[
\frac{d\log L}{d\theta}=\frac{6}{\theta}-\frac{2}{1-\theta}=0\;\Rightarrow\;6(1-\theta)=2\theta\;\Rightarrow\;6=8\theta
\;\Rightarrow\;\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=\frac{6}{8}=\boxed{0.75}.
\] So the MLE is just the observed frequency \(6/8\). Hand-check at \(\theta=0.75\): \(\tfrac{6}{0.75}=8\) and \(\tfrac{2}{0.25}=8\) — the two terms cancel ✓.
E6. Bayes’ rule, a bot detector (§5’s test with new numbers: prior \(0.02\), sensitivity \(0.95\), false-positive rate \(0.10\)). (a) Evidence by the law of total probability: \[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(+)&=\Pr(+\mid S)\Pr(S)+\Pr(+\mid\neg S)\Pr(\neg S)\\[4pt]
&=0.95(0.02)+0.10(0.98)=0.019+0.098=\boxed{0.117}.
\end{aligned}
\] Then the posterior: \[
\Pr(S\mid+)=\frac{\Pr(+\mid S)\Pr(S)}{\Pr(+)}=\frac{0.019}{0.117}\approx\boxed{0.162}.
\] (b) Counting over \(10{,}000\) accounts: the \(2\%\) prior makes 200 bots, of whom the detector catches \(0.95\times200=\) 190 (true positives); of the 9,800 humans, \(10\%=\) 980 are flagged anyway (false positives). Total flagged \(=190+980=1170\), of which only \(190\) are bots: \(190/1170\approx\boxed{0.162}\) — the same \(\sim16\%\) ✓. It is far below the detector’s \(95\%\) sensitivity because bots are rare (low prior), so the \(980\) false positives from the large human majority swamp the \(190\) true ones — the base-rate effect. (Its accuracy, the share of all accounts it labels correctly, is \(0.019+0.882=90.1\%\), a different number again.)
E7. MLE vs MAP — the prior as a regularizer (§6). Same coin as E5 (6 heads, 2 tails) with a Beta\((4,4)\) prior. (a) Beta is conjugate to Bernoulli, so the posterior just adds the data counts to the prior exponents: \(\theta^{6}(1-\theta)^{2}\cdot\theta^{3}(1-\theta)^{3}=\theta^{9}(1-\theta)^{5}\), i.e. \(\boxed{\text{Beta}(10,6)}\) (\(\alpha_{\text{post}}=4+6=10,\ \beta_{\text{post}}=4+2=6\)). (b) The MAP estimate is the mode of Beta\((10,6)\): \(\dfrac{\alpha_{\text{post}}-1}{\alpha_{\text{post}}+\beta_{\text{post}}-2}=\dfrac{9}{14}\approx\boxed{0.643}\). (c) The three numbers — MLE \(=0.75\), prior mean \(=0.5\), MAP \(\approx0.643\) — show the prior pulled the estimate down from \(0.75\) toward \(0.5\), landing at \(0.643\).
That is the same kind of pull toward a center as an L2 regularizer, which pulls a weight from its data-driven value toward \(0\) (here the “toward \(0.5\)” prior plays the role of “toward \(0\)”). With far more data the likelihood would dominate and MAP would slide back toward the MLE — a prior is a finite nudge, washed out by enough evidence.

With the Beta\((10,10)\) prior, \(k\) heads and \(8-k\) tails give the posterior Beta\((10+k,\,18-k)\), whose mode is \(\dfrac{9+k}{26}\). It exceeds \(0.6\) once \(9+k>15.6\), so the MAP needs \(\boxed{7}\) heads: \(16/26=0.615\), while \(6\) heads give \(15/26=0.577\). A firm prior takes more evidence to move.

E8. Entropy, cross-entropy, KL (§7) for truth \(p=[0.5,0.5]\), model \(q=[0.7,0.3]\). (a) Entropy in bits: \(H(p)=-0.5\log_2 0.5-0.5\log_2 0.5=-\log_2 0.5=\boxed{1}\) bit — the maximal uncertainty of a fair coin. (b) Cross-entropy in nats: \[
\begin{aligned}
H(p,q)&=-\big(0.5\ln 0.7+0.5\ln 0.3\big)=-\big(0.5(-0.357)+0.5(-1.204)\big)\\[4pt]
&=0.178+0.602=\boxed{0.780}\ \text{nats}.
\end{aligned}
\] (c) KL divergence in nats: \[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)=0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.7}+0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.3}
=0.5(-0.336)+0.5(0.511)=-0.168+0.255=\boxed{0.087}\ \text{nats}.
\] (d) Identity check: \(H(p,q)-H(p)=0.780-0.693=0.087=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)\) ✓ (using \(H(p)=0.693\) nats, which is the same as the \(1\) bit from (a)). KL is the extra surprise from coding with the wrong \(q\) instead of the truth \(p\); this \(q\) is closer to the truth than §7’s \([0.8,0.2]\) (\(0.223\) nats), so it pays less.
E9. Paired \(t\)-test (§8) on \(d=[3,5,4,6,2]\), \(n=5\). (a) \(\bar d=\dfrac{3+5+4+6+2}{5}=\dfrac{20}{5}=\boxed{4}\) milli-NDCG@10. (b) Deviations from the mean: \([-1,1,0,2,-2]\); sum of squares \(=1+1+0+4+4=10\), so \(s_d^2=\dfrac{10}{5-1}=2.5\) and \(s_d=\sqrt{2.5}\approx\boxed{1.581}\). (c) Standard error \(=\dfrac{s_d}{\sqrt n}=\dfrac{1.581}{\sqrt5}\approx0.707\), so \(t=\dfrac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt n}=\dfrac{4}{0.707}\approx\boxed{5.657}\) with \(df=n-1=4\). Since \(5.657>2.776\) (the critical value for df \(=4\)), we reject \(H_0\) — the gain is statistically significant (two-sided \(p\approx0.0048\)). (d) 95% CI: \(\bar d\pm 2.776\,(s_d/\sqrt n)=4\pm 2.776(0.707)=4\pm1.963=\boxed{[2.04,\,5.96]}\) milli-NDCG@10, which excludes \(0\) ✓ — the same significant verdict as (c), now with the effect size and its uncertainty in one object.
E10. The standard error and how it shrinks (§8.3). (a) The standard error is \(s_d/\sqrt n\), so going from \(n=5\) to \(n=10\) (twice the pairs, \(s_d\) and \(\bar d\) unchanged) shrinks it by \(\sqrt{10/5}=\sqrt2\approx\boxed{1.41}\) (from \(\approx0.707\) to \(0.500\)). Because \(t=\bar d/(s_d/\sqrt n)\) has that shrinking quantity in the denominator, \(t\) grows by the same factor (here \(5.66\to8.00\); the critical value also falls as df rises from \(4\) to \(9\), from \(2.776\) to \(2.262\), which is what scipy.stats.t.ppf(0.975, 9) returns, as in §8.3), so a real gain sits more standard errors above \(0\) and is easier to detect — i.e. more seeds give the test more power.

The variances of independent differences add, so ten of them, each with variance \(4\), sum to variance \(10\times4=40\); dividing the sum by \(10\) to get the average divides that variance by \(10^2=100\), leaving \(\boxed{0.4}\), which is \(4/10\): the variance shrinks by the factor \(n=10\). The standard deviation is the square root, \(\sqrt{0.4}\approx\boxed{0.632}=2/\sqrt{10}\): it shrinks only by \(\sqrt n=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16\), from \(2\) to \(0.632\). That \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) is the standard error \(s_d/\sqrt n\), with the unknown \(\sigma\) estimated by \(s_d\). (The Central Limit Theorem, §8.3’s Fact 2, is a separate fact: it says the average is approximately bell-shaped, and it does not supply the \(\sqrt n\).)

E11. Wilcoxon by hand (§8.7). (a) \(|d|=\{3,1,5,2,4,6\}\) sorted is \(1,2,3,4,5,6\), so matched back to the data, \(d=+3\) gets rank \(3\), \(+1\) rank \(1\), \(+5\) rank \(5\), \(-2\) rank \(2\), \(+4\) rank \(4\), \(+6\) rank \(6\). (b) The only negative is \(-2\) (rank \(2\)), so \(W^{-}=2\) (and \(W^{+}=1+3+4+5+6=19\)).

\(W=\min(19,2)=2\). Because one sign disagrees, \(W\neq0\), so we are above the \(n=6\) floor — and already \(W=1\) has \(p=4/64=0.0625>0.05\), so \(W=2\) cannot be significant. Exactly: of the \(64\) equally likely sign patterns, \(6\) are at least as extreme as \(W=2\) (two each with \(W=0\), \(1\) and \(2\), counting both directions), so the two-sided \(p\) is \(6/64\approx0.094\) — not significant at \(\alpha=0.05\). (Only an all-same-sign set, \(W=0\), reaches \(p=0.031\).) Five wins were promising, but six seeds with one loss cannot clear the bar — collect more seeds.

E12. Ship-or-not with multiplicity (§8.7). (a) Yes, barely — the \(95\%\) CI \([+0.0003,+0.0077]\) excludes \(0\), so judged as a single test the \(+0.004\) gain clears the bar, consistent with its raw \(p=0.04<0.05\); but its lower end allows a gain of only \(0.0003\) (\(0.3\) milli-NDCG@10), §8.6 Step 4’s warning about width. (b) With \(m=4\) tests, Bonferroni compares each \(p\) to \(\alpha/m=0.05/4=0.0125\); since \(0.04>0.0125\), it does not survive.

Do not ship — and this is the case where the single-test reading (a) and the multiplicity-corrected reading (b) disagree. Taken alone, that interval says the gain is positive at \(\alpha=0.05\); but that interval and that \(p\) were the best of four tries: if none of the four models were better, at least one of the four tests would still give \(p<0.05\) about \(19\%\) of the time (\(1-0.95^{4}\), independent tests, §8.5), so luck is a live explanation — the gain may be real, but these data cannot tell it apart from luck. Re-run the single most promising model on fresh seeds before believing it.

(A check beyond this chapter: a CI excludes \(0\) exactly when the test at the same level rejects (§8.6, Step 4), so Bonferroni’s level \(0.05/4=0.0125\) goes with a \(98.75\%\) interval, whose critical value on \(4\) df is \(t^{*}=4.315\), scipy.stats.t.ppf(1-0.0125/2, 4). With the standard error \(0.0037/2.776=0.001333\), where \(0.0037\) is the half-width of \([0.0003,\,0.0077]\), it becomes \(0.004\pm4.315\times0.001333=[-0.00175,+0.00975]\), straddling \(0\).)

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Loss Functions & Regularizers
E1. MAE/MSE/Huber on the residual set \(r=\{0.5,-2,1\}\) (§2.1), with \(N=3\) and \(\delta=1\). The MAE is the mean of \(|r|\): \(\tfrac13(0.5+2+1)=\tfrac{3.5}{3}=\boxed{1.167}\). The MSE is the mean of \(r^2\): \(\tfrac13(0.25+4+1)=\tfrac{5.25}{3}=\boxed{1.75}\). For Huber (\(\delta=1\)), the two small residuals \(|r|\le1\) use the quadratic \(\tfrac12 r^2\) (\(0.5\mapsto0.125\), \(1\mapsto0.5\)), while the outlier \(r=-2\) has \(|r|>1\) so it uses the linear arm \(\delta|r|-\tfrac12\delta^2=1\cdot2-0.5=1.5\); the mean is \(\tfrac13(0.125+1.5+0.5)=\tfrac{2.125}{3}=\boxed{0.708}\). The single point \(r=-2\) is what blows MSE up — squaring turns its miss into \(4\) (more than the other two combined) — and it is exactly the point Huber treats as linear, limiting its influence (which is why mean-Huber \(0.708\) is below half the MSE, \(0.875\): the quadratic arm of Huber is \(\tfrac12r^2\), and on the linear arm the outlier’s cost grows only linearly, \(1.5\) against \(\tfrac12 r^2=2\)).
E2. Binary cross-entropy (§2.2), \(\hat p=0.65\). For a positive (\(y=1\)) only the first term lives: \(-[1\cdot\ln 0.65+0]=-\ln 0.65=\boxed{0.431}\). For a negative (\(y=0\)) only the second term lives: \(-[0+1\cdot\ln(1-0.65)]=-\ln 0.35=\boxed{1.050}\). The negative costs more (\(1.050>0.431\), about \(2.4\times\)): predicting \(\hat p=0.65\) is a fair guess when the truth is class 1 (small surprise \(-\ln 0.65\)) but a poor guess when the truth is class 0 (larger surprise \(-\ln 0.35\)). BCE is precisely \(-\log\) of the probability the model assigned to the right answer — \(\hat p\) for a positive, \(1-\hat p\) for a negative — so the worse-matched label is punished more.
E3. BCE rewards correct confidence (§2.2; natural logs). (a) At \(z=1\), \(\hat p=\sigma(1)=0.7311\): \(y{=}1\to-\ln0.7311=0.313\) (confident and right — small loss); \(y{=}0\to-\ln(1-0.7311)=-\ln0.2689=1.313\) (confident and wrong — large loss). (b) At \(z=-1\), \(\hat p=\sigma(-1)=0.2689\): \(y{=}1\to-\ln0.2689=1.313\) (the model leaned the wrong way); \(y{=}0\to-\ln(1-0.2689)=-\ln0.7311=0.313\) (it leaned the right way). (c) At \(z=2.5\), \(\hat p=0.9241\): \(y{=}1\to-\ln0.9241=0.0789\), which is \(0.313-0.0789=0.234\) nats lower than at \(z=1\); \(y{=}0\to-\ln(1-0.9241)=-\ln0.0759=2.579\), which is \(2.579-1.313=1.266\) nats higher. The wrong-way loss changed by far more (\(1.266\) against \(0.234\)): more confidence earns a small gain when right and costs a large amount when wrong.
E4. One gradient step (§3) on the point \((x{=}1,\,y{=}4)\), then with L2. Unregularized: \(\hat y=wx=1\cdot1=1\); loss \((\hat y-y)^2=(1-4)^2=9\); gradient \(\tfrac{\partial\ell}{\partial w}=2(\hat y-y)x=2(-3)(1)=-6\); update \(w\leftarrow 1-0.1(-6)=\boxed{1.6}\). Now add \(\lambda w^2\) with \(\lambda=0.25\) (§5.1): the penalty contributes gradient \(2\lambda w=2(0.25)(1)=0.5\), so the total gradient is \(-6+0.5=-5.5\) and \(w\leftarrow 1-0.1(-5.5)=\boxed{1.55}\). The regularized step lands \(0.05\) short of the unregularized \(1.6\) — the penalty pulled \(w\) back toward \(0\) by exactly \(\eta\cdot2\lambda w=0.05\) on this single step. That nudge-toward-zero, repeated every step, is weight decay.
E5. Weight decay step by step (§5.1). (a) Factor \(=1-2(0.05)(2)=0.8\). (b) Multiplying by \(0.8\) each step: \(w: 2\to1.6\to1.28\to1.024\). (c) \(w_k=2\times0.8^k\). After \(34\) steps \(w=2\times0.8^{34}=0.00101\), still above \(0.001\); after \(35\) steps \(w=2\times0.8^{35}=0.00081\), the first value below it, so \(\boxed{35}\) steps.
E6. BPR loss and gradient (§9), positive \(\hat r_{ui}=1.0\), negative \(\hat r_{uj}=0.2\). Gap \(d=1.0-0.2=0.8\); sigmoid \(\sigma(0.8)=\tfrac{1}{1+e^{-0.8}}=\tfrac{1}{1.4493}=\boxed{0.6900}\); per-triple loss \(-\ln\sigma(0.8)=-\ln 0.6900=\boxed{0.3711}\); gradient \(-(1-\sigma(d))=-(1-0.6900)=\boxed{-0.3100}\). Swapping the scores (a wrong triple, \(\hat r_{ui}=0.2,\hat r_{uj}=1.0\)) gives \(d=-0.8\), \(\sigma(-0.8)=0.3100\), loss \(-\ln 0.3100=\boxed{1.1711}\), gradient \(-(1-0.3100)=\boxed{-0.6900}\). The loss grows by \(\tfrac{1.1711}{0.3711}\approx3.2\times\), but the gradient grows by only \(\tfrac{0.6900}{0.3100}\approx2.2\times\). The two factors differ because the loss scales with \(-\ln\sigma(d)\) while the gradient scales with \(1-\sigma(d)\) — two different functions of \(d\): the gradient factor is exactly \(e^{d}\) (\(e^{0.8}=2.23\), \(e^{2.5}=12.18\)), while the loss factor grows roughly like \(d\,e^{d}\) once the gap is large (\(30.5\) against the exact \(32.7\) at \(d=2.5\)), so it pulls away. (Either way, the more-wrong triple gets both the bigger penalty and the bigger corrective push.)

For scores \(1.5\) and \(-1.0\) (\(d=2.5\)): correct, \(\sigma(2.5)=0.9241\), loss \(0.0789\), gradient \(-0.0759\); wrong (\(d=-2.5\)), loss \(2.5789\), gradient \(-0.9241\). The loss grows \(\tfrac{2.5789}{0.0789}\approx32.7\times\) and the gradient \(\tfrac{0.9241}{0.0759}\approx12.2\times\). Both factors grow, but the loss factor grows faster: \(32.7\) against \(12.2\) here, \(3.2\) against \(2.2\) at \(d=0.8\). A confidently correct triple has both a tiny loss and a tiny gradient, while a confidently wrong one has a loss that keeps growing with the gap but a gradient whose size levels off toward \(1\).

E7. InfoNCE (§2.4), similarities \(0.6\) (positive), \(0.3,-0.1\) (negatives), \(\tau=0.5\). Divide by \(\tau\): \(\tfrac{0.6}{0.5}=1.2\), \(\tfrac{0.3}{0.5}=0.6\), \(\tfrac{-0.1}{0.5}=-0.2\). Exponentiate: \(e^{1.2}=3.320\), \(e^{0.6}=1.822\), \(e^{-0.2}=0.819\). The positive’s softmax share is \(\tfrac{3.320}{3.320+1.822+0.819}=\tfrac{3.320}{5.961}=0.5570\), so \(\ell_{\text{InfoNCE}}=-\ln 0.5570=\boxed{0.585}\). If the positive’s similarity collapses to \(-0.1\), its scaled score is \(-0.2\), its exponential is \(0.819\), and its share falls to \(\tfrac{0.819}{0.819+1.822+0.819}=\tfrac{0.819}{3.460}=0.2367\), so the loss jumps to \(-\ln 0.2367=\boxed{1.441}\). The loss grows by \(\tfrac{1.441}{0.585}\approx\boxed{2.5\times}\): the positive is no longer the most-similar item — it now ties the weakest negative, owns only a small fraction of the softmax mass, and the gradient pulls the anchor back toward its positive.
E8. L1 (lasso) is the one that drives weights to exactly zero; L2 (ridge) only shrinks them smoothly toward zero but never to zero (§5.1). The reason is geometric (§5.1’s figure Why L1 is sparse and L2 is not): the penalized solution is where the growing loss contour (an ellipse around the unregularized optimum) first touches the penalty’s constraint region. L1’s region is a diamond \(|w_1|+|w_2|\le t\), whose corners sit on the axes — and an ellipse expanding outward often meets a corner first, as in the figure, and at a corner one coordinate is exactly \(0\) (e.g. \(w_1=0\)). How often depends on the shape of the contours and on where the unpenalized optimum lies; when the contour instead first touches a face (a flat side) of the diamond, both weights survive.
L2’s region is a smooth circle \(w_1^2+w_2^2\le t\) with no corners, so the contour touches it at a generic off-axis point where both coordinates are nonzero. So the sharp corners of the absolute-value penalty are what manufacture exact zeros (sparsity); the roundness of the squared penalty cannot, giving only shrinkage.
With \(\lambda=0.6\) the one-weight formulas give: L1 subtracts \(\lambda/2=0.3\) from each pull and stops at zero, so \(0.2\mapsto\boxed{0}\), \(-0.5\mapsto\boxed{-0.2}\), \(2\mapsto\boxed{1.7}\); L2 divides by \(1+\lambda=1.6\), so \(0.2\mapsto\boxed{0.125}\), \(-0.5\mapsto\boxed{-0.3125}\), \(2\mapsto\boxed{1.25}\). L1 makes one exact zero (the weak pull below \(0.3\)), L2 none: it shrinks the small weight to \(62.5\%\) of its pull, exactly as it shrinks the large one.
E9. L1 vs L2 (§5.1), with \(\eta=0.1\) and \(\lambda=0.1\). (a) \(\frac{d}{dw}\lambda|w| = \lambda\,\text{sign}(w)\) — a constant pull: each step subtracts \(\eta\lambda=0.1\times0.1=\boxed{0.01}\) from both the weight of \(10\) and the weight of \(0.01\); \(\frac{d}{dw}\lambda w^2 = 2\lambda w\) — proportional to the weight: each step subtracts \(\eta\cdot2\lambda w\), which is \(0.1\times0.2\times10=\boxed{0.2}\) from the large weight and \(0.1\times0.2\times0.01=\boxed{0.0002}\) from the small one. So L1 pulls a weight of \(10\) and a weight of \(0.01\) by exactly the same amount, which is why, at the optimum, small weights sit exactly at \(0\) (§5.1’s one-weight formula), while L2 shrinks everything by a constant fraction and never quite arrives.
(A plain gradient step with that constant pull would overshoot and jitter around \(0\) — from \(w=0.015\) with the pull of \(0.01\) per step: \(0.015\to0.005\to-0.005\to0.005\to\cdots\) — so practical L1 solvers clip a weight to \(0\) when a step would carry it past zero, soft-thresholding: \(0.015\to0.005\to0\), and there it stays while the penalty acts alone (a data gradient can move it again).)

L1 — the “selection” in lasso — zeroes the irrelevant features and keeps a sparse handful. For the pull \(a=0.04\) with \(\lambda=0.1\): L1 has \(\lambda/2=0.05>0.04\), so \(w^\star=\boxed{0}\) exactly; L2 gives \(a/(1+\lambda)=0.04/1.1=\boxed{0.0364}\), small but not zero.
L1 with soft-thresholding subtracts \(0.01\) a step and stops at zero: \(0.03\to0.02\to0.01\to\boxed{0}\), exactly zero after three steps. L2 multiplies by \(1-2\eta\lambda=0.98\) a step: \(0.03\to0.0294\to0.02881\to\boxed{0.0282}\), still \(94\%\) of where it started, and it will never reach \(0\) (this per-step shrink is what §5.1 calls weight decay). The constant pull finishes a small weight off; the proportional pull barely touches it.

E10. From §6’s MAP table: Gaussian noise on \(y\), with the same spread \(s_y\) for every label, gives the MSE loss (its \(-\log\) is \((\hat y-y)^2/2s_y^2\) plus a constant), and a Gaussian prior centered at \(0\), of spread \(s_\theta\), on \(\theta\) gives the L2 regularizer (its \(-\log\) is \(\|\theta\|_2^2/2s_\theta^2\) plus a constant). The MAP objective maximizes the posterior \(p(\theta\mid\text{data})\propto
p(\text{data}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\) — a product of likelihood and prior. Taking \(-\log\) does two things at once: because \(\log\) of a product is the sum of the logs, the product splits into \(-\log p(\text{data}\mid\theta)-\log p(\theta)\); and because \(-\log\) is monotone decreasing, the \(\theta\) that maximizes the posterior is the same \(\theta\) that minimizes this sum. The first piece is the loss (negative log-likelihood) and the second is the regularizer (negative log-prior) — so “loss \(+\) regularizer” is just the \(-\log\) of “likelihood \(\times\) prior.”
With \(s_y=1\), §6’s formula \(-\ln p=\tfrac12(\hat y-y)^2+\ln\sqrt{2\pi}\) gives \(0.5+0.919=\boxed{1.419}\) for the miss of \(1\) and \(4.5+0.919=\boxed{5.419}\) for the miss of \(3\); the difference is \(\boxed{4}\), which is exactly the difference of the halved squared errors (\(4.5-0.5\)). The squared-error part depends on the prediction; the constant \(0.919\) is the same for every prediction, so it can never change which one is best, which is why it is dropped.
E11. Regularized-MSE for matrix factorization (§8), \(\mathbf{p}=[2,1]\), \(\mathbf{q}=[1,2]\), \(r=5\), \(\lambda=0.1\). Score \(\hat r=\mathbf{p}^{\top}\mathbf{q}=2\cdot1+1\cdot2=\boxed{4}\). Squared-error term \((r-\hat r)^2=(5-4)^2=\boxed{1}\). L2 term: \(\|\mathbf{p}\|^2=2^2+1^2=5\) and \(\|\mathbf{q}\|^2=1^2+2^2=5\), so \(\lambda(\|\mathbf{p}\|^2+\|\mathbf{q}\|^2)=0.1\cdot(5+5)=\boxed{1.0}\). Total objective \(\mathcal{L}=1+1.0=\boxed{2.0}\). Now the implicit-feedback reading: the skipped item has score \(\mathbf p^\top\mathbf q'=2\cdot1.5+1\cdot0.5=3.5\), so the gap is \(d=4-3.5=\boxed{0.5}\) and the BPR loss is \(-\ln\sigma(0.5)=-\ln0.6225=\boxed{0.474}\) — a correct order but a thin margin, so much is left to learn from this triple (§9).
E12. Numerically stable forms (§2.4 “in practice”). (a) \(\sigma(-800)=1/(1+e^{800})\), and \(e^{800}\) is past the largest storable number, so the denominator is \(\infty\) and \(\sigma(-800)\) comes out as \(0\) — then log(0) \(=-\infty\). The exact value is \(-\ln\sigma(-800)=\ln(1+e^{800})\), which cannot be formed directly either; pull out the big exponent: \(\ln(1+e^{a})=a+\ln(1+e^{-a})\) for \(a>0\), here \(800+\ln(1+e^{-800})\). The last term is about \(e^{-800}\), below the range, so it underflows to \(0\); that is harmless, because it lies far below the third decimal (log1p handles it the same way): \(\boxed{800.000}\) (this is the softplus identity, \(-\ln\sigma(x)=\operatorname{softplus}(-x)\); in PyTorch, -F.logsigmoid(x)).

Subtract the largest logit, \(m=802\): \(\ln(e^{800}+e^{802})=m+\ln(e^{800-m}+e^{802-m})=802+\ln(e^{-2}+1)=802+0.1269=\boxed{802.127}\) — log-sum-exp with the max subtracted, so every exponent is at most \(0\) and nothing overflows (in PyTorch, F.cross_entropy / F.log_softmax). Both identities are exact; the routes avoid every overflow, and the one underflow drops only a term far below the third decimal.

E13. Sampled-softmax log-\(Q\) correction (§10), raw score \(\hat r_{uj}=1\) for both negatives. The corrected contribution to the denominator is \(e^{\hat r_{uj}}/Q=e^{\,\hat r_{uj}-\ln Q}\). Popular item, \(Q=0.4\): \(e^{1}/0.4=\tfrac{2.718}{0.4}=\boxed{6.80}\) (equivalently \(e^{\,1-\ln 0.4}=e^{1.916}=6.80\)). Rare item, \(Q=0.05\): \(e^{1}/0.05=\tfrac{2.718}{0.05}=\boxed{54.4}\) (i.e. \(e^{\,1-\ln 0.05}=e^{3.996}=54.4\)). The rare item is up-weighted by \(\tfrac{54.4}{6.80}=\boxed{8\times}\), exactly the inverse ratio of the two sampling probabilities (\(0.4/0.05=8\)).
The positive’s share. The positive (raw score \(3\), left uncorrected) contributes \(e^{3}=20.09\); the third negative contributes \(e^{1.5}/0.5=8.96\); the two negatives above contribute \(6.80\) and \(54.37\). The corrected denominator is \(20.09+6.80+54.37+8.96\approx90.21\) (the unrounded terms add to \(90.210\); the rounded ones to \(90.22\)), so the positive’s share is \(20.09/90.21=\boxed{0.223}\). The rare negative alone takes more than half of the denominator (\(54.37\) of \(90.21\)), because each sampled copy of it stands in for about \(1/Q=20\) items like it (§10).

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Neural Networks & Back-propagation
E1. Single neuron (§1–§2). The pre-activation is the dot product plus bias: \(z=\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b=2\cdot1+(-1)\cdot4+0.5=2-4+0.5=\boxed{-1.5}\). ReLU then clips it: \(a=\max(0,-1.5)=\boxed{0}\). ReLU clipped the negative score \(-1.5\) down to \(0\) — that flat “off for \(z<0\)” behavior is exactly the bend §2 calls the nonlinearity. (Had we used sigmoid instead, \(\sigma(-1.5)=0.1824\): positive, never exactly \(0\).)
E2. Activations at three points (§2). At \(z=1\): \(\sigma(1)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-1}}=\boxed{0.7311}\), \(\tanh(1)=\dfrac{e^{1}-e^{-1}}{e^{1}+e^{-1}}=\dfrac{2.7183-0.3679}{2.7183+0.3679}=\dfrac{2.3504}{3.0862}=\boxed{0.7616}\), \(\mathrm{ReLU}(1)=\boxed{1}\). At \(z=-2\): \(\sigma(-2)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{2}}=\boxed{0.1192}\), \(\tanh(-2)=\dfrac{e^{-2}-e^{2}}{e^{-2}+e^{2}}=\dfrac{0.1353-7.3891}{0.1353+7.3891}=\dfrac{-7.2538}{7.5244}=\boxed{-0.9640}\), \(\mathrm{ReLU}(-2)=\boxed{0}\). At \(z=2\): \(\sigma(2)=\boxed{0.8808}\), \(\tanh(2)=\boxed{0.9640}\), \(\mathrm{ReLU}(2)=\boxed{2}\). (Check with §2’s identity \(\tanh(z)=2\sigma(2z)-1\): \(2\sigma(2)-1=2(0.8808)-1=0.7616\) and \(2\sigma(-4)-1=2(0.0180)-1=-0.9640\).) Tanh is the one with \(f(-2)=-f(2)\): \(-0.9640=-(0.9640)\). For the sigmoid, \(f(-2)+f(2)=0.1192+0.8808=\boxed{1}\), so it is symmetric about \(0.5\) rather than about \(0\) (\(\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)\)); for ReLU, \(f(-2)+f(2)=0+2=\boxed{2}\), since it ignores the negative side altogether.
E3. Layers against one matrix (§2). (a) Layer by layer: \(W^{(1)}\mathbf{x}=[2\cdot1+0\cdot(-2),\ 1\cdot1+1\cdot(-2)]=[2,-1]\), then \(W^{(2)}[2,-1]=[1\cdot2+(-1)(-1),\ 0\cdot2+2(-1)]=[3,-2]\). The single matrix is \(W^{(2)}W^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot2+(-1)\cdot1&1\cdot0+(-1)\cdot1\\0\cdot2+2\cdot1&0\cdot0+2\cdot1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\2&2\end{bmatrix}\), and \(\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\2&2\end{bmatrix}[1,-2]=[1+2,\ 2-4]=[3,-2]\): the two agree, as regrouping a matrix product (Linear-Algebra primer §3) guarantees. (b) With the ReLU between the layers, \(\mathbf h=\mathrm{ReLU}([2,-1])=[2,0]\) and \(W^{(2)}\mathbf h=[1\cdot2+(-1)\cdot0,\ 0\cdot2+2\cdot0]=[2,0]\), which is not \([3,-2]\). The ReLU changed the second entry of the first layer’s output, \(-1\to0\); the clipped entry no longer contributes, so the net is no longer the one matrix \(W^{(2)}W^{(1)}\) — the bend is what separates the two cases.
E4. Tiny \(2\!\to\!2\!\to\!1\) forward pass (§3), input \(\mathbf{x}=[2,1]\). Hidden pre-activations (each row of \(W^{(1)}\) dotted with \(\mathbf{x}\), plus the bias): \[
\mathbf z^{(1)}=W^{(1)}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot2+1\cdot1\\ -1\cdot2+(-1)\cdot1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}3\\-3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-2\end{bmatrix}.
\] Apply ReLU elementwise: \(\mathbf{h}^{(1)}=\mathrm{ReLU}([2,-2])=\boxed{[2,\,0]}\) — the second entry, the negative \(-2\), is the one ReLU clipped to \(0\). Output layer: \(\hat y=\mathbf{w}^{(2)}\cdot\mathbf{h}^{(1)}+b^{(2)}=2\cdot2+1\cdot0+1=\boxed{5}\). Each layer is a matrix–vector product plus an elementwise activation, exactly as §3 states; the clipped \(-2\) is the nonlinearity at work (without it the net would be one linear map, E3).
E5. One neuron, forward and backward (§5), with \(x=2\), \(w=1\), \(b=0\), \(y=0\). (a) Forward: \(z=wx+b=1\cdot2+0=\boxed{2}\), \(a=\sigma(2)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-2}}=\dfrac{1}{1+0.1353}=\boxed{0.8808}\), \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12(0.8808-0)^2=\boxed{0.3879}\). (b) Backward — the three local derivatives are \[
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial a}=a-y=0.8808,\qquad
\frac{\partial a}{\partial z}=a(1-a)=0.8808\times0.1192=0.1050,\qquad
\frac{\partial z}{\partial w}=x=2,
\] so \[
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z}=0.8808\times0.1050=0.0925,\\[4pt]
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial w}=0.0925\times2=\boxed{0.1850},\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial b}=0.0925\times1=\boxed{0.0925}.
\end{gathered}
\] \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial w\) is the larger, by the factor \(2\): \(\partial z/\partial w=x=2\) while \(\partial z/\partial b=1\), so \(0.1850/0.0925=2\). (Notice also \(\sigma'(2)=0.1050\), less than half of §5’s \(\sigma'(0.5)=0.2350\): the sigmoid is flatter at \(z=2\) — it is starting to saturate — so less gradient gets through.) (c) One gradient-descent step with \(\eta=0.5\): \(w\leftarrow w-\eta\dfrac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial w}=1-0.5(0.1850)=1-0.0925=\boxed{0.9075}\). The weight moved toward \(0\) (down from \(1\)): lowering \(w\) lowers the score \(z\), pushes \(a\) toward the target \(y=0\), and shrinks the loss.
E6. Softmax + cross-entropy (§4), logits \(\mathbf z=[2,0,0]\), true class \(0\). (a) The exponentials are \(e^{2},e^{0},e^{0}=7.389,1,1\) (sum \(9.389\)), so the true-class probability is \(\hat p_0=\dfrac{7.389}{9.389}=\boxed{0.787}\) (the other two get \(\dfrac{1}{9.389}=0.107\) each), and the cross-entropy loss is \(\mathcal L=-\ln\hat p_0=-\ln 0.787=\boxed{0.240}\). It is smaller than §4’s \(0.41\) because the true class now leads both rivals by \(2\) (in §4 one rival was only \(1\) behind), so the model puts more of its mass on the right answer: \(0.787\) instead of \(0.665\). (b) If the model were maximally unsure, \(\hat p_0=\tfrac13\), the loss would be \(-\ln\tfrac13=\boxed{1.0986}\approx1.10\). The uncertain case has the larger loss (\(1.10>0.240\)), which is the right direction: cross-entropy rewards putting probability mass on the correct class (\(\hat p_0\to1\Rightarrow\mathcal L\to0\)) and penalizes spreading it thin — exactly the pressure that trains a classifier (§4).
E7. One Adam step from rest (§6), with \(g_1=-0.3\), \(m_0=v_0=0\), \(\beta_1=0.9\), \(\beta_2=0.999\), \(\eta=0.1\). \[
\begin{gathered}
m_1=(1-0.9)\,g_1=0.1\times(-0.3)=\boxed{-0.03},\\[4pt]
v_1=(1-0.999)\,g_1^2=0.001\times0.09=\boxed{9\times10^{-5}}.
\end{gathered}
\] Bias-correct (divide by \(1-\beta^{\,1}\), i.e. by \(0.1\) and \(0.001\)): \(\hat m_1=\dfrac{-0.03}{0.1}=\boxed{-0.3}=g_1\) and \(\hat v_1=\dfrac{9\times10^{-5}}{0.001}=\boxed{0.09}=g_1^2\). The step is \[
\eta\,\frac{\hat m_1}{\sqrt{\hat v_1}}=0.1\times\frac{-0.3}{\sqrt{0.09}}=0.1\times\frac{-0.3}{0.3}=\boxed{-0.1},
\] so the update \(w\leftarrow w-(-0.1)=w+0.1\) moves the weight up by \(0.1\): the gradient is negative, so downhill is the \(+\) direction. For \(g_1=-3\) the same steps give \(\hat m_1=-3\), \(\hat v_1=9\) and the step \(0.1\times(-3)/3=\boxed{-0.1}\) again. Plain SGD’s steps are \(\eta g_1=0.1\times(-0.3)=-0.03\) and \(0.1\times(-3)=-0.3\), ten times apart, while Adam’s two steps are equal: at the first step the ratio is \(g_1/|g_1|=\operatorname{sign}(g_1)=-1\), so the gradient’s magnitude cancels and the size of the move is set by \(\eta\).
E8. All weights equal (§3, §5, §6). (a) \(\mathbf z^{(1)}=W^{(1)}\mathbf x=[0.5\cdot1+0.5\cdot2,\ 0.5\cdot1+0.5\cdot2]=[1.5,1.5]\), so \(\mathbf h^{(1)}=\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf z^{(1)})=[1.5,1.5]\) and \(\hat y=0.5\cdot1.5+0.5\cdot1.5=\boxed{1.5}\), with \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12(0.5)^2=0.125\). (b) \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y=\hat y-y=0.5\); rule 3 gives \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf h^{(1)}=0.5\,[0.5,0.5]=[0.25,0.25]\); both ReLU slopes are \(1\) (both scores are positive), so \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf z^{(1)}=[0.25,0.25]\), and rule 2 gives \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial W^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}0.25\cdot1&0.25\cdot2\\0.25\cdot1&0.25\cdot2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0.25&0.5\\0.25&0.5\end{bmatrix}\): the two rows are identical. (c) \(W^{(1)}\leftarrow0.5-0.1\,[0.25,\,0.5]=\begin{bmatrix}0.475&0.45\\0.475&0.45\end{bmatrix}\): the rows are still identical. The two hidden units started as copies and received the same gradient, so they stay copies however long training runs; that is the silent failure of a constant start, which random initial weights avoid.
E9. Dropout and early stopping (§7). (a) The survivors are scaled by \(1/(1-p)=1/0.75=\tfrac43\), so \([4,8,12]\) with the second unit zeroed becomes \(\boxed{[\tfrac{16}{3},\,0,\,16]}\approx[5.33,0,16]\). The first output survives with probability \(0.75\) (as \(4/0.75=5.33\)) and is zeroed with probability \(0.25\), so its average over many steps is \(0.75\times5.33+0.25\times0=\boxed{4}\): the scaling keeps the layer’s output unchanged on average. (b) The held-out loss falls to \(0.27\) at epoch \(60\) and then rises to \(0.29\) at epoch \(80\), so early stopping keeps the model from epoch \(\boxed{60}\).
E10. Neuron as the recommender’s dot-product score (§1), \(\mathbf{p}=[2,1,3]\), \(\mathbf{q}=[1,2,1]\). (a) The affinity \(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}\) is a single linear neuron \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b\) with the item vector as the weights (\(\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{q}\)), the user vector as the input (\(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{p}\)), and no bias (\(b=0\)). Its value: \(\hat r=\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}+0=2\cdot1+1\cdot2+3\cdot1=2+2+3=\boxed{7}\). (b) The second item \(\mathbf{q}_2=[3,0,1]\) scores \(\hat r_2=\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}_2=2\cdot3+1\cdot0+3\cdot1=6+0+3=\boxed{9}\), and \(9>7\), so it indeed ranks above the first — verified. This bare dot-product head is exactly matrix factorization / LightGCN’s scoring rule, and the embeddings \(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}\) are the learned lookup rows of §3’s embedding layer — trained by the same back-prop (§5) as any other weight.
E11. Embedding lookup and the sparse gradient (§3, §7). (a) Id \(2\) returns the last row, \(E_2=[2,1,0]\) — a row read, no arithmetic. (b) Only rows \(\boxed{0\text{ and }2}\) can receive a nonzero gradient: the other row, row \(1\), enters the output multiplied by \(0\), so \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial E_1=\mathbf 0\) under plain SGD with no penalty. (c) Weight decay multiplies every row, present in the batch or not, by \(1-\eta\cdot2\lambda=1-0.1\cdot2\cdot0.05=\boxed{0.99}\), so the absent row becomes \(0.99\,[0,3,1]=[0,\,2.97,\,0.99]\) (momentum and Adam also move absent rows, §6).
E12. The same neuron, flipped target (§5), now with \(x=2\), \(w=0.25\). (a) With \(y=1\): \(\partial \mathcal L/\partial a=a-y=0.6225-1=-0.3775\), so \(\partial \mathcal L/\partial w=-0.3775\times0.2350\times2=-0.1774\). (b) Step: \(w\leftarrow0.25-0.1(-0.1774)=0.2677\) — \(w\) moves up. That makes sense: the target rose from \(0\) to \(1\), so we now want a larger output \(a\), hence a larger score \(z=wx\), hence a larger \(w\). (The error flipped sign, so the gradient — and the step — flipped with it: with \(y=0\), §5’s weight had moved down.)
E13. A content vector for an unseen id (§3). (a) \(\mathbf c\,G=[1,1]\begin{bmatrix}0.3&0.2&0.0\\0.1&0.0&0.6\end{bmatrix}=[0.3+0.1,\ 0.2+0.0,\ 0.0+0.6]=\boxed{[0.4,\,0.2,\,0.6]}\). (b) \(\mathbf p\cdot(\mathbf c\,G)=1\cdot0.4+2\cdot0.2+0\cdot0.6=\boxed{0.8}\). The film had no row in the table, yet it gets a usable vector and a score, because the vector is computed from its content instead of looked up by id.
E14. (a) \(z_1=w_1x=(-0.3)(2)=\boxed{-0.6}\); \(h=\sigma(-0.6)\approx\boxed{0.3543}\); \(\hat y=w_2h=1.5(0.3543)=\boxed{0.5315}\); \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12(0.5315-1)^2=\tfrac12(-0.4685)^2\approx\boxed{0.1097}\). (b) \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y=\hat y-y=-0.4685\); \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2=-0.4685\cdot h=-0.4685\cdot0.3543\approx\boxed{-0.1660}\); \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial h=-0.4685\cdot w_2=-0.7027\); \(\partial h/\partial z_1=h(1-h)=0.3543\cdot0.6457\approx0.2288\); so \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial z_1=-0.7027\cdot0.2288\approx-0.1608\) and, since \(\partial z_1/\partial w_1=x=2\), \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1=-0.1608\cdot2=\boxed{-0.3216}\). (c) \(w_1\leftarrow-0.3-0.1(-0.3216)=\boxed{-0.2678}\) and \(w_2\leftarrow1.5-0.1(-0.1660)=\boxed{1.5166}\); both gradients are negative, so both weights rise, and the loss falls to about \(0.0968\).
E15. \(u_1=g_1=0.2\) and \(w=1-0.1(0.2)=\boxed{0.98}\); \(u_2=0.9(0.2)+0.2=\boxed{0.38}\) and \(w=0.98-0.1(0.38)=\boxed{0.942}\); \(u_3=0.9(0.38)-0.2=\boxed{0.142}\) and \(w=0.942-0.0142=\boxed{0.9278}\). The gradient flipped, but the velocity is still positive (\(0.142\)), so the weight keeps moving down — momentum carries it through the sign change before it turns.
E16. The steps are \(0.1+0.2+0.3+0.4+0.2+0.1=1.3\), so \(w=1-1.3=\boxed{-0.3}\) (with \(g=1\) each step subtracts its learning rate). A constant \(\eta=0.4\) for six steps subtracts \(6(0.4)=2.4\) and gives \(w=\boxed{-1.4}\): the schedule starts gently, peaks, and then decays, moving the weight less overall.
E17. The columns are \([1,5,9]\) and \([3,7,11]\), with means \(5\) and \(7\) and standard deviations \(\sqrt{32/3}\approx3.266\) each, so (a) BatchNorm gives \(\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}-1.22&-1.22\\0&0\\1.22&1.22\end{bmatrix}}\). (b) Each row \([1,3]\), \([5,7]\), \([9,11]\) has mean \(2,6,10\) and standard deviation \(1\), so LayerNorm gives \(\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\-1&1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}}\). (c) For the single row \([5,7]\), LayerNorm uses only that row’s own mean \(6\) and standard deviation \(1\) and returns \(\boxed{[-1,1]}\). BatchNorm’s column means are now the row’s own values, \(5\) and \(7\), so each entry minus its mean is \(0\) and with a tiny \(\varepsilon\) the output is \(\boxed{[0,0]}\) whatever the input was (\(0/\sqrt{0+\varepsilon}=0\); with \(\varepsilon\) ignored it would be \(0/0\)): a batch of one gives BatchNorm nothing to standardize (at test time it uses statistics saved from training instead).
E18. (a) He: variance \(2/50=\boxed{0.04}\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.04}=\boxed{0.2}\). Xavier: variance \(2/(50+50)=\boxed{0.02}\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.02}\approx\boxed{0.141}\) (half of He’s variance, as §6 says for \(\text{fan\_in}=\text{fan\_out}\)). (b) With variance \(3/\text{fan\_in}\) the per-layer factor is \(\text{fan\_in}\times\tfrac{3}{\text{fan\_in}}/2=1.5\), so after \(10\) layers it is \(1.5^{10}\approx\boxed{57.7}\): the signal grows more than fifty-fold, a milder case of §6’s blow-up.
E19. \(t(0.125)=2(0.125)-4\cdot0=\boxed{0.25}\); \(t(0.25)=2(0.25)-4(0)=\boxed{0.5}\), so \(t(t(0.125))=0.5\). Five stacked tents make \(2^5=\boxed{32}\) pieces from \(10\) units; a single hidden ReLU layer of \(m\) units makes at most \(m+1\) pieces, so it needs at least \(\boxed{31}\) units for \(32\) pieces.

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Representation Learning & the Transformer
E1. One-hot bags (§1.1). The bag is \(\mathbf p=\mathbf o_1+\mathbf o_3=[1,0,1,0,0]\). (a) \(\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf o_3=\boxed{1}\), since the \(1\) in slot \(3\) meets the \(1\) of \(\mathbf o_3\), and \(\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf o_2=\boxed{0}\), since slot \(2\) of \(\mathbf p\) is \(0\). (b) \(\lVert\mathbf p\rVert=\sqrt2\), so \(\cos(\mathbf p,\mathbf o_3)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\cdot1}=\boxed{0.707}\) and \(\cos(\mathbf p,\mathbf o_2)=\boxed{0}\). (c) Neither number shows it: movie \(2\) gets exactly \(0\), the same as a movie unrelated to everything the user watched. The one-hots of movies \(1\) and \(2\) are orthogonal, so a score built from them can only say “this exact movie was watched”, never “a movie like one that was watched”, which is the flaw §1.2’s dense embedding fixes.
E2. Cosine of two small word vectors (§1.1 / Linear Algebra for Machine Learning §4). Dot product \(\mathbf{v}_{\text{coffee}}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\text{tea}}=4\cdot3+3\cdot4=12+12=24\); lengths \(\lVert\mathbf{v}_{\text{coffee}}\rVert=\sqrt{16+9}=5\) and \(\lVert\mathbf{v}_{\text{tea}}\rVert=\sqrt{9+16}=5\). So \(\cos=\dfrac{24}{5\cdot5}=\dfrac{24}{25}=\boxed{0.96}\) (an angle of about \(16.3^\circ\)) — very near \(+1\), i.e. the two arrows point almost the same way. The distributional hypothesis (§2.1) reads this geometrically: coffee and tea keep similar company (drink, cup, morning), so a predict-based model pushes their vectors close together, and a near-\(1\) cosine is exactly the “these two words mean similar things” signal.
E3. What negative sampling saves (§2.2). (a) The full softmax sums over every word of the vocabulary, so its cost depends on \(V\) and not on \(k\): the denominator of \(P(c\mid w)\) is the expensive sum over \(V\), and negative sampling replaces it by contrasting the positive against a few negatives (the same move as BPR and InfoNCE). (b) The full softmax needs \(V=\boxed{50{,}000}\) dot products, one per word; negative sampling scores the one true context and the \(k=10\) negatives, \(k+1=\boxed{11}\) dot products, which is \(50000/11\approx\boxed{4{,}545}\) times fewer. (c) The cost of negative sampling stays at \(11\) while the full softmax grows to \(500{,}000\), so the saving grows with \(V\) to \(500000/11\approx\boxed{45{,}455}\) times: the trick pays most exactly where the vocabulary is large.
E4. Skip-gram probabilities (§2.2). (a) Dot products with \(\mathbf v_w=[1,1]\): \(\mathbf u_A\cdot\mathbf v_w=2+1=3\), \(\mathbf u_B\cdot\mathbf v_w=0+1=1\), \(\mathbf u_C\cdot\mathbf v_w=-1+1=0\). (b) Softmax of \([3,1,0]\): \(e^3,e^1,e^0=20.086,\,2.718,\,1.000\), which sum to \(23.804\), so \(P(A)=20.086/23.804=\boxed{0.844}\), \(P(B)=0.114\), \(P(C)=0.042\). (c) Most sure of A (\(0.844\)) — and \(\mathbf u_A=[2,1]\) is the best aligned with \(\mathbf v_w=[1,1]\): largest dot product, and also the largest cosine (\(0.949\), against \(0.707\) and \(0\)), so direction alone already picks A. “Predict your neighbors” rewards alignment.
E5. LSTM cell, one step (§3.3). With \(c_{t-1}=0.50\) and gates \(f_t=0.40\), \(i_t=0.90\), \(\tilde c_t=0.80\), \(o_t=0.50\): (a) the new cell state is \(c_t=f_t c_{t-1}+i_t\tilde c_t=0.40(0.50)+0.90(0.80)=0.20+0.72=\boxed{0.92}\). (b) the readout is \(h_t=o_t\tanh(c_t)=0.50\tanh(0.92)=0.50(0.726)=\boxed{0.363}\).

This step is the LSTM overwriting: a low forget gate (\(0.40\)) with a high input gate (\(0.90\)) discards most of the old memory (\(0.50\)) and lets the new candidate dominate (\(c_t=0.92\)). §3.3’s worked step was the opposite — \(f_t=0.95\), \(i_t=0.10\) held the memory essentially fixed (\(0.80\to0.80\)), the LSTM remembering. Two knobs, set independently: the forget gate decides how much old memory survives, the input gate how much of the candidate is written. Keep \(f_t=0.40\) but lower \(i_t\) to \(0.10\) and \(c_t=0.20+0.08=0.28\): the memory is forgotten, not overwritten.

E6. Scaled dot-product (§4.1). (a) With \(d_k=16\), \(\sqrt{d_k}=4\), so \([6,2,0]\to\boxed{[1.5,\,0.5,\,0]}\). (b) Softmax of the raw scores: \(e^6,e^2,e^0=403.4,\,7.39,\,1.00\), summing to \(411.8\), so \(\boxed{[0.980,\,0.018,\,0.002]}\). Softmax of the scaled scores: the exponentials are \(4.48,\,1.65,\,1.00\) and sum to \(7.13\), so the weights are \(\boxed{[0.629,\,0.231,\,0.140]}\). (c) With the top raw score at \(7\), the raw weights are \([0.992,\,0.007,\,0.001]\): the top weight moves from \(0.9796\) to \(0.9924\), only \(\boxed{0.013}\). Scaled by \(4\), the scores \([1.75,\,0.5,\,0]\) give \([0.685,\,0.196,\,0.119]\): the top weight moves from \(0.629\) to \(0.685\), \(\boxed{0.056}\), about \(4.4\) times more. The raw version has almost nowhere left to move and gives the second and third keys almost no weight, so the gradient through those weights is tiny; the scaled version keeps all three in play and leaves the token more to learn from.
E7. Self-attention, first row of a new history (§4.2’s method). The value rows are \(V=X\) and \(\sqrt{d_k}=\sqrt2\approx1.414\). (a) The query is \(\mathbf{x}_1=[2,0]\); the scaled scores \(\mathbf{x}_1\cdot\mathbf{x}_j/\sqrt2\) are \[
\frac{4}{\sqrt2}=2.828,\qquad \frac{2}{\sqrt2}=1.414,\qquad \frac{0}{\sqrt2}=0.000 .
\] (b) Softmax: \(\exp([2.828,1.414,0])=[16.92,\,4.11,\,1.00]\), summing to \(22.03\), so the weights are \(\boxed{[0.768,\,0.187,\,0.045]}\). (c) The output is \[
0.768[2,0]+0.187[1,1]+0.045[0,1]=[\,1.536+0.187,\ 0.187+0.045\,]=\boxed{[1.723,\,0.232]}.
\] (d) The first film gets the most weight (\(0.768\)), because its own score is the largest (\([2,0]\cdot[2,0]=4\)), and the third the least (\(0.045\)), because it is at right angles to the query. The output stays close to the first film’s own \([2,0]\), pulled a little toward the second.
E8. \(Q,K,V\) as learned views (§4.2). (a) Entry \(a\) of a row-times-matrix product is the row dotted with column \(a\). The columns of \(W_Q\) are \([1,0]\) and \([0,0]\), so \(\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{x}W_Q=[\,2\cdot1+1\cdot0,\ 2\cdot0+1\cdot0\,]=[2,0]\); the columns of \(W_K\) are \([0,1]\) and \([0,0]\), so \(\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{x}W_K=[\,2\cdot0+1\cdot1,\ 0\,]=[1,0]\); and \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{x}W_V=[2,1]\). (b) Yes — \([2,0]\), \([1,0]\), \([2,1]\) are three different vectors built from the one token \(\mathbf{x}=[2,1]\): the query keeps only its romance, the key only its musical/drama side, the value all of it.

\(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}=2\cdot1+0\cdot0=\boxed{2}\). For \(\mathbf{x}'=[0,2]\) the key is \(\mathbf{k}'=\mathbf{x}'W_K=[2,0]\) (its entry is \(\mathbf x'\) dotted with the column \([0,1]\) of \(W_K\)) and \(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}'=2\cdot2+0\cdot0=\boxed{4}\). So \(\mathbf q\) matches the second token’s key more strongly: the query asks for a high musical/drama side (\(m=2\) against \(1\)). The raw similarity ranks them the other way: \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x}=2\cdot2+1\cdot1=5\) against \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x}'=0\cdot2+1\cdot2=2\), because it only measures how alike two vectors are. The learned pair of matrices pairs one feature of the asker (romance, through \(W_Q\)) with a different feature of the candidate (musical/drama, through \(W_K\)).

E9. Multi-head attention (§4.3). (a) Concatenated, the outputs are \([0.5,\,1.0,\,1.0,\,0.5]\); the \(W_O\) that adds the heads coordinate by coordinate gives \([0.5+1.0,\ 1.0+0.5]=\boxed{[1.5,\,1.5]}\), a vector of the original length \(d=2\). The heads disagreed (one leans to the second coordinate, one to the first) and the mix keeps both.

With the third head the concatenation is \([0.5,\,1.0,\,1.0,\,0.5,\,0.0,\,0.5]\), and the \(W_O\) with six rows that adds the heads coordinate by coordinate gives \([0.5+1.0+0.0,\ 1.0+0.5+0.5]=\boxed{[1.5,\,2.0]}\). It has length \(2=d\) again, however many heads run. Each head contributed its own relation, and the mix keeps all three. (c) The block adds a sub-layer’s input back to its output (add & norm, §4.3), and a sum needs two vectors of the same length, so \(W_O\) must map back to \(d\); the next block also expects length-\(d\) vectors, which is what lets blocks be stacked. A length-\(6\) output would break both.

E10. Positional encoding (§4.3) with \(d=4\), \(\text{pos}=2\). Using \(10000^{0}=1\) and \(10000^{1/2}=100\), with every angle in radians (a calculator in degree mode would give \(\sin 2^\circ=0.035\) instead): \[
\begin{aligned}
PE(2,0)&=\sin 2=0.909\ \text{(given)}, & PE(2,1)&=\cos 2=-0.416\ \text{(given)},\\
PE(2,2)&=\sin(2/100)=\sin 0.02=\boxed{0.020}, & PE(2,3)&=\cos(2/100)=\cos 0.02=\boxed{1.000},
\end{aligned}
\] so \(PE(\text{pos}=2,\,d=4)\approx[\,0.909,\,-0.416,\,0.020,\,1.000\,]\) — a different fingerprint from \(\text{pos}=1\)’s \([0.841,0.540,0.010,1.000]\), with the slow pair, \(PE(\cdot,2)\) and \(PE(\cdot,3)\), barely moving (\([0.010,1.000]\to[0.020,1.000]\)) while the fast pair, \(PE(\cdot,0)\) and \(PE(\cdot,1)\), changes a lot (\([0.841,0.540]\to[0.909,-0.416]\)). The slow pair barely moves because its angle, \(\text{pos}/100\), grows by only \(0.01\) radian per position, where the fast pair’s grows by a whole radian.
At \(d=6\) the third pair has \(i=2\), so \(2i/d=4/6\) and \(10000^{2/3}=464.16\): at \(\text{pos}=1\) the angle is \(1/464.16=0.00215\) radian, so \(PE(1,4)=\sin 0.00215=\boxed{0.002}\) and \(PE(1,5)=\cos 0.00215=\boxed{1.000}\). The later the pair, the slower its wave and the closer its coordinates stay to \((0,1)\) at small positions.
E11. SASRec / item2vec scoring (§4.4 / §2.4). The intent vector is \(\mathbf{h}=[1,3]\) (leaning toward axis 2), and the score of item \(j\) is the dot product \(\mathbf{h}\cdot\mathbf{e}_j\). (a) Raw dot products: \[
\mathbf{h}\cdot[1,0]=1,\qquad \mathbf{h}\cdot[1,1]=1+3=4,\qquad \mathbf{h}\cdot[0,1]=3,
\] so the dot-product ranking is Notebook \((4)\) \(\succ\) La La Land \((3)\) \(\succ\) Titanic \((1)\). (b) Cosine needs the norms: \(\lVert\mathbf{h}\rVert=\sqrt{1+9}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.162\), and the items have norms \(\lVert[1,0]\rVert=1\), \(\lVert[1,1]\rVert=\sqrt2\approx1.414\), \(\lVert[0,1]\rVert=1\). Then \[
\begin{gathered}
\cos(\mathbf{h},[1,0])=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\approx\boxed{0.316},\\[4pt]
\cos(\mathbf{h},[1,1])=\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}\sqrt2}\approx\boxed{0.894},\\[4pt]
\cos(\mathbf{h},[0,1])=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\approx\boxed{0.949}.
\end{gathered}
\] The cosine ranking is La La Land \((0.949)\) \(\succ\) Notebook \((0.894)\) \(\succ\) Titanic \((0.316)\) — the rankings disagree at the top. The raw dot product puts Notebook first (\(4\) vs \(3\)) partly because Notebook is the larger-norm vector (\(\sqrt2>1\)), not because its direction matches the intent better: under cosine, which divides the length out, La La Land leads. That length sensitivity is exactly the popularity/length bias §4.4’s serving aside (L2-normalize first, turning the dot product into cosine; Linear Algebra for Machine Learning §4) is designed to remove.
E12. BPE on an unseen word (§5.3). (a) Replay the two learned rules in order on s l o w _: \[
\texttt{s l o w \_}\ \xrightarrow{\ \texttt{o+w}\ }\ \texttt{s l ow \_}\ \xrightarrow{\ \texttt{l+ow}\ }\ \texttt{s low \_}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{tokens } \boxed{[\,\texttt{s},\ \texttt{low},\ \texttt{\_}\,]}.
\] The stem low is the same piece slow shares with low and lowest, so the model reuses what it already learned about that stem — and there is no <UNK>, exactly §5.3’s payoff. (b) In the corpus low ×5, lowest ×2, the pair e,s appears only inside lowest, so its count is \(\boxed{2}\). BPE merges greedily by frequency, and the pair o,w occurs in both word-types (\(5+2=7\)), so o+w (count \(7\)) is merged before e,s (count \(2\)).
E13. KV-cache cost (§5.4). (a) Without the cache each step re-encodes the whole prefix, so the total for \(T=5\) is \(1+2+3+4+5=\boxed{15}\) token-passes (\(=\tfrac{T(T+1)}{2}=\tfrac{5\cdot6}{2}=15\), the \(O(T^2)\) row). (b) With the cache each step pushes only the one new token, so the total is \(1+1+1+1+1=\boxed{5}\) passes (\(=T\), the \(O(T)\) row). (c) The ratio is \(15/5=\boxed{3\times}\) at \(T=5\), larger than the \(10/4=2.5\times\) the chapter shows at \(T=4\). (d) In general the ratio is \(\dfrac{T(T+1)/2}{T}=\boxed{\dfrac{T+1}{2}}\). It reaches \(10\) when \(T+1=20\), that is at \(T=\boxed{19}\) (\(190\) passes against \(19\)). At \(T=1{,}000\) it is \(500.5\times\), the chapter’s “about \(500\times\)”.
E14. What the KV-cache stores (§5.4). (a) The cache holds a key and a value (\(2\) vectors), each \(d=5{,}120\) numbers of \(2\) bytes, in each of \(40\) layers: \(2\times40\times5{,}120\times2=\boxed{819{,}200}\) bytes, \(800\) KiB, per token. (b) For \(2{,}048\) tokens that is \(819{,}200\times2{,}048=1{,}677{,}721{,}600\) bytes, \(1.5625\) GiB (\(\boxed{\approx1.56}\) GiB) per sequence. (c) The weights take \(13\times10^9\times2=26\times10^9\) bytes, \(\approx24.2\) GiB, and \(24.2/1.5625\approx15.5\): about \(\boxed{15}\) sequences fit before the cache outweighs the weights (the sixteenth tips it). At large batches and long contexts, cache memory rather than the weights then limits how many requests a server can hold (a claim from practice this book does not test).

In layer \(1\) a key is \(\mathbf{x}_iW_K\) of the token’s own embedding, which no mask can change: all \(\boxed{6}\) cached keys stay valid. But the layer-1 output of token \(6\) now looks at token \(7\), so it changes, while the outputs of tokens \(1\) to \(5\) do not (token \(5\) sees token \(6\)’s embedding, which is the same). Layer-\(2\) keys are computed from the layer-1 outputs, so token \(6\)’s is stale and tokens \(1\) to \(5\) are valid: \(\boxed{5}\). Each further layer loses one more (token \(5\)’s layer-2 output has seen token \(6\)’s changed layer-1 output, so \(4\) remain in layer \(3\)). With the causal mask nothing is ever stale, and in a fully bidirectional encoder (§5.1) every layer-2 key goes stale, so almost nothing can be reused.

E15. Mean pooling (§5.2). (a) The sum is \([2+0+1+3,\ 0+4+1+3]=[6,8]\), so the mean is \(\boxed{[1.5,\,2.0]}\). (b) \(\lVert[1.5,2]\rVert=2.5\), so \(\cos\) with \([1,0]\) is \(1.5/2.5=\boxed{0.6}\) and with \([0,1]\) is \(2/2.5=\boxed{0.8}\). The review leans toward La La Land, the film on the axis where the pooled vector is larger.
E16. Attention masks (§5.1). (a) Item \(3\) may see items \(1\) to \(3\), so the cell for item \(4\) is blocked (score \(-\infty\), weight \(0\)). Softmax of \([0,1,1]\): \(e^0,e^1,e^1=1,\,2.72,\,2.72\), summing to \(6.44\), so the weights are \(\boxed{[0.155,\,0.422,\,0.422,\,0]}\). (b) Without the mask, \(e^9=8{,}103\) joins the sum (\(8{,}109.5\)), so the weights are \(\boxed{[0.0001,\,0.0003,\,0.0003,\,0.9992]}\). (c) The weights of (b) put \(99.9\%\) (\(0.9992\)) on item \(4\), the answer it is asked to predict, so the model gains by copying it and learns nothing about the history; at serving time item \(4\) does not exist yet, so there is nothing to copy. (d) \(0.15\times200=\boxed{30}\) tokens are picked; of those \(0.8\times30=\boxed{24}\) get [MASK], \(\boxed{3}\) a random token and \(\boxed{3}\) no change (the recipe is Devlin et al.’s, §5.1).
E17. Pre-LN and Post-LN (§4.3). (a) The mean of \([1,2,6]\) is \(3\), the deviations are \(-2,-1,3\), the variance is \((4+1+9)/3=4.667\) and the standard deviation \(2.160\), so \(\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf x)=\boxed{[-0.926,\,-0.463,\,1.389]}\). (b) \(\mathbf x+f(\mathbf x)=3\mathbf x=[3,6,18]\), and normalizing it gives the same \(\boxed{[-0.926,\,-0.463,\,1.389]}\): the factor \(3\) cancels. (c) \(f(\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf x))=[-1.852,\,-0.926,\,2.777]\), so the Pre-LN output is \(\boxed{[-0.852,\,1.074,\,8.777]}\). (d) For \(10\mathbf x=[10,20,60]\), \(\mathrm{LN}\) gives the same \([-0.926,\,-0.463,\,1.389]\) (the standard deviation is now \(21.60\) and the deviations \(10\) times larger), so the Post-LN output, \(\mathrm{LN}\) of \(30\,[1,2,6]\), is unchanged. The Pre-LN output is \(10\mathbf x+2\,\mathrm{LN}(10\mathbf x)=[10,20,60]+[-1.852,-0.926,2.777]=\boxed{[8.148,\,19.074,\,62.777]}\), so the Pre-LN output changed and its last entry is \(62.777\): \(\mathbf x\) itself is added back, whereas Post-LN normalizes every trace of its size away.
E18. Sampling (§5.4). (a) Argmax picks \(\boxed{a}\) every time. (b) Two independent runs both pick \(a\) with probability \(0.5\times0.5=\boxed{0.25}\).
