The first per-query model is the expensive jump (400 of the 2,025); swapping a cheap reranker for a general LLM is a further factor of about 5.

E4. Residual quantization, §2.2’s recipe (snap, subtract, snap the residual):

Distances of \((0.7,0.4)\) to the level-1 codebook:

\[d_{\textsf{A}}=\sqrt{(-0.3)^2+0.4^2}=\sqrt{0.25}=0.5,\quad d_{\textsf{B}}=\sqrt{0.7^2+0.6^2}\approx0.922,\] \(d_{\textsf{C}}\approx1.746\) and \(d_{\textsf{D}}\approx1.565\). The nearest is \(\boxed{\textsf{A}=(1,0)}\), and the residual is \((0.7,0.4)-(1,0)=\boxed{(-0.3,\,0.4)}\).

Distances of the residual \((-0.3,0.4)\) to the level-2 codebook: \(d_{\textsf{p}}=0\) (exact hit), \(d_{\textsf{q}}=0.6\), \(d_{\textsf{r}}=0.8\), \(d_{\textsf{s}}=1.0\). So the second code is \(\textsf{p}\) and the Semantic ID is \(\boxed{(\textsf{A},\,\textsf{p})}\). Reconstruction: \(\textsf{A}+\textsf{p}=(0.7,0.4)\), zero residual here.
The second item \((0.6,0.5)\): \(d_{\textsf{A}}=\sqrt{0.41}\approx0.640\) against \(d_{\textsf{B}}=\sqrt{0.61}\approx0.781\) (and \(\textsf{C},\textsf{D}\) farther), so it also snaps to \(\textsf{A}\), the same level-1 prefix. Its residual is \((0.6,0.5)-(1,0){=}(-0.4,0.5)\), whose distances to the level-2 codebook are \(d_{\textsf{p}}=\sqrt{0.02}\approx0.141\), \(d_{\textsf{q}}\approx0.707\), \(d_{\textsf{r}}\approx0.906\), \(d_{\textsf{s}}\approx1.140\). The nearest is \(\textsf{p}\) again, so its full tuple is also \(\boxed{(\textsf{A},\textsf{p})}\).

The two items collide: with identical IDs the sequence model cannot tell them apart at all. That is the collision case of §2.2, and TIGER’s cure is to append one extra disambiguating token, e.g. \((\textsf{A},\textsf{p},0)\) against \((\textsf{A},\textsf{p},1)\). Prefix sharing is what lets what is learned about one item carry onto another; whole-tuple sharing is the bug.
E5. The cosines are the dot products \(0.6\) (own view), \(0.8\) (near negative) and \(-0.8\) (far negative).

At \(\tau=0.5\) the weights are \(e^{1.2}=3.320\), \(e^{1.6}=4.953\) and \(e^{-1.6}=0.202\), which add to \(8.475\). The own share is \(3.320/8.475=\boxed{0.39}\) and the loss is \(-\ln0.392=\boxed{0.94}\).
At \(\tau=0.1\) the weights are \(e^{6}=403.4\), \(e^{8}=2981.0\) and \(e^{-8}\approx0.0003\), which add to \(3384.4\). The own share is \(0.119\) and the loss is \(\boxed{2.13}\). The near negative sits \(0.2\) above the own view in cosine; at \(\tau=0.5\) that is \(0.4\) in the exponent, so its weight exceeds the own view’s by a factor \(e^{0.4}=1.5\), and at \(\tau=0.1\) it is \(2\) in the exponent, a factor \(e^{2}=7.4\) (\(2981/403\)).
A turn of \(20^\circ\) takes \(\mathbf{e}_i\) to \((0.940,\,0.342)\), with cosines \(\boxed{0.84}\) (own), \(0.96\) (near negative) and \(-0.55\) (far negative). The weights are \(e^{1.675}=5.34\), \(e^{1.914}=6.78\) and \(e^{-1.093}=0.34\), the own share is \(0.43\), and the loss is \(\boxed{0.85}\): it fell, by \(0.09\). In §3’s toy case the loss rose, because the near negative’s cosine gained more than the own view’s. Here the own view gains \(0.24\) (\(0.60\to0.84\)) and the near negative only \(0.16\) (\(0.80\to0.96\)), so the own view closes the gap on it and its share grows.

Which case you are in depends on whether the own view’s gain beats the average gain of the negatives, each weighted by its share of the negatives’ total weight, as the two toys of §3 show. Here the near negative carries about 96% of the negatives’ weight (95% after the turn) and gains \(0.16\), the far negative gains \(0.25\), so the weighted average is about \(0.16\), below the own view’s \(0.24\): the loss falls.
E6. (a) A plain epoch takes \(20\) s, so a night is \(50\times20=1{,}000\) s; with the alignment term an epoch is \(20\times1.9=38\) s and a night is \(1{,}900\) s. The extra is \(900\) s, \(\boxed{15\text{ min}}\) per night, and over a year \(365\times15=5{,}475\) min \(=\boxed{91.25\text{ h}}\) (about 91 hours), not counting profile writing.

One profile call per new film: \(\boxed{1{,}000}\) per day and \(365\times1{,}000=\boxed{365{,}000}\) per year. Per request: \(\boxed{0}\), so all 2 million daily requests are served by the dot product. The three scales of cost are different: once per film (the profile), once per retrain (the alignment adds 15 minutes a night), and per request (nothing).
The films added since the 02:00 retrain were not in it. From 02:00 to 18:00 is \(16\) h, so \(16\times1{,}000/24=\boxed{667}\) films (about 667) have no trained vector, and the next retrain’s vectors go live at 02:00, \(\boxed{8\text{ h}}\) later. A trained model with one vector per item has none for a new item (§2.3), so a 2.3a enhancer built on one, as RLMRec on LightGCN is, cannot place them meanwhile; the feature-encoding cell, 2.3b (two-tower retrieval), could, because it embeds a film from its text when it is added (by construction; not tested here).

E7. (a) The whole-catalog design reads \(5{,}000\times500=2.5\) million tokens per request, so \(2.5\times10^{6}\times1{,}000/10^{6}=2{,}500\) million tokens per 1k requests, and at $1 per million tokens it costs \(\boxed{\$2{,}500}\) per 1k requests. The 50-film reranker reads \(50\times500=25{,}000\) tokens and costs $25 per 1k, so the whole-catalog design is \(2{,}500/25=\boxed{100\times}\) dearer. Setting aside that 2.5 million tokens may not fit in the model’s input window, the 2 s budget is not what rules the design out: cost does. The cheaper design that wins is a cheap retriever or CF model that fetches a shortlist of about 50 films, with the LLM at most reranking those (§2.1’s production sub-pattern), or the LLM kept offline as an enhancer.

No. The number is an average over every test user and item, and it says nothing about which items the gain came from; the claim is about a subset (thin-data items). To support it you would ask for Recall@20 per popularity bucket, say the least-clicked third of items against the most-clicked third, with a paired significance test in each bucket. §3 adds that RLMRec’s own paper reports no such breakdown, so the claim cannot be borrowed from it either. (The figure in the stem is the paper’s LightGCN and Amazon-book Recall@20 for RLMRec-Con, a \(+5.1\%\) rise.)

E8. (a) \(2{,}000{,}000\times768\times4=6.144\times10^{9}\) bytes, \(\boxed{6.1\text{ GB}}\); at 2 bytes per number, \(3.1\) GB.

Each new film’s text is embedded once by the encoder (offline) and its vector appended to the index. That is one encoder call per new film, \(10{,}000/2{,}000{,}000=\boxed{0.5\%}\) of the catalog, and \(10{,}000\times768\times4\approx\boxed{30.7\text{ MB}}\) of new vectors. Re-embedding all 2 million would be \(200\times\) more work and is unnecessary, since a film’s vector depends on its text alone. No retrain of any ranking model is involved.
From 02:00 to 14:05 is \(12\text{ h }5\text{ min}=12.08\) h, and \(12.08/24=\boxed{50\%}\) of a day (0.503). The vector reflects the logs as they stood at 02:00, so the 14:05 click, and everything since 02:00, is missing from it. The oldest a batch vector can be is just under \(\boxed{24\text{ h}}\) (a click at 01:59). To reflect a click made minutes ago, the user side must run at request time: one small network (or one embedding call) over the user’s recent history, then an ANN lookup against the stored film vectors. That is one small call per request and no LLM ranking call, so it stays enhancer-class on cost (the 2.3b cell, §4).
The day’s \(10{,}000/200=\boxed{50\text{ s}}\) on one GPU; a full re-embedding is \(2{,}000{,}000/200=10{,}000\) s, about \(\boxed{2.8\text{ h}}\), which is \(200\times\) the daily job, the ratio found in part b. A new film needs only its text: embed it with the same encoder and insert the vector, with no clicks and no retraining, so it is findable by semantic proximity (by construction; no paper read here tests it).

E9. (a) A time-based split uses as targets only interactions after the model’s knowledge cutoff, 31 March 2025: C (20 April), D, E and F. A (12 January) and B (3 March) precede it and may have been in training. That is \(\boxed{4}\) of the 6, \(67\%\) of the log.

The second model’s cutoff, 30 September 2025, is after every date in the log, so \(\boxed{0}\) of the 6 qualify. The evaluator should test on a log that post-dates the cutoff, or use held-out or obfuscated item IDs so that a memorized title cannot be recognized, and state which was done (§5).
It would measure, at least in part, whether the model remembers films and interactions it was trained on, not how well it predicts behavior it has not seen. That is a measurement problem and not a modeling one: the model need not be any better at the task, but the number is contaminated. A random hold-out does nothing about this, since every held-out interaction lies inside the model’s training period.

E10. (a) Against the \(1.5\) s budget, using §4.1’s latency column:

Enhancer (2.3): single-digit to tens of ms, so it is open.
Recommender as a reranker (2.1): the vendor’s p50 is about \(0.7\) to \(2\) s; the low end fits and the high end does not, and a p50 is a median, so half the requests are slower. It is marginal, and open only with a shortlist and a margin. The specialist cross-encoder, at \(0.1\) to \(0.2\) s, fits.
Agent (2.4): four steps at \(0.7\) s each is \(4\times0.7=2.8\) s, already over \(1.5\) s (three steps would be \(2.1\) s), and at \(2\) s per step it is \(8\) s. It is ruled out.
Generator (2.2): the column gives no figure, so the budget cannot be decided from it.


Per day, \(200{,}000\) requests are \(200\) thousand-query units. The pure-CF serve costs \(200\times\$0.004=\boxed{\$0.80}\) and the 50-film reranker \(200\times\$25=\boxed{\$5{,}000}\), a ratio of \(5{,}000/0.80=6{,}250\). (At the cross-encoder anchor of $2 the bill is $400.)
Split: offline, the LLM writes a profile for each new title when it is added and embeds it for the ANN index; LightGCN is retrained with the alignment term on a regular schedule, so the per-epoch overhead (about 1.9 times on a light backbone like LightGCN) recurs at every retrain. Until a new title’s first retrain it has no trained \(\mathbf{e}_i\), so, of the parts of this split, only the two-tower retriever can surface it (a pure content-reading part such as the decision table’s Recommender 2.1 could, but it is not in this split). Serve: LightGCN dot product, or ANN over the offline vectors, with no LLM call.

What to still measure per bucket instead of trusting top-line NDCG: Recall or NDCG restricted to titles added since the last retrain, and separately to items with few clicks, since a top-line metric is an average over all test interactions and can rise while the cold-start problem you care about does not (§5).

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Training and Serving a Recommender
E1. Ann \(=[2,0.5]\), positive The Notebook \(\mathbf q^{+}=[2,0.2]\), negative La La Land \(\mathbf q^{-}=[1.5,0.5]\). \(\hat r^{+}=(2)(2)+(0.5)(0.2)=4.1\); \(\hat r^{-}=(2)(1.5)+(0.5)(0.5)=3.25\); gap \(\Delta=4.1-3.25=0.85\). Since \(\Delta=0.85>0\), the order is already correct, but only narrowly: both films are romance-leaning.
E2. With \(\Delta=0.85\) and \(\sigma(0.85)=0.7006\): loss \(=-\ln(0.7006)=0.356\), and the gradient factor is \(1-\sigma(0.85)=0.2994\). Both are larger than §4’s triple (loss \(0.2014\), factor \(0.1824\) at \(\Delta=1.5\)). That is correct and desirable: this triple is ranked correctly by a narrower margin (\(0.85\) against \(1.5\)), so the model is less sure of it and the update pushes harder.
E3. The gradient is
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf p}&=-(1-\sigma(\Delta))(\mathbf q^{+}-\mathbf q^{-})\\
&=-0.2994\,([2,0.2]-[1.5,0.5])=-0.2994\,[0.5,-0.3]=[-0.1497,\,0.0898].
\end{aligned}\]
Update with \(\eta=0.1\): \(\mathbf p\leftarrow[2,0.5]-0.1\,[-0.1497,0.0898]=[2.0150,\,0.4910]\). Ann’s romance factor moved up (\(2\to2.0150\)) and her action factor down (\(0.5\to0.4910\)), because the positive is more romantic than the negative in the first entry (\(2>1.5\)) and less action-leaning in the second (\(0.2<0.5\)).
E4. \(1-\sigma(5)=1-0.9933=0.0067\) for \(X\) and \(1-\sigma(-2)=\sigma(2)=0.8808\) for \(Y\). The ratio is \(0.8808/0.0067\approx131\) on the printed four-decimal values (\(131.6\) at full precision), so \(Y\)’s update is about 130 times as large as \(X\)’s. With \(\mathbf q^{+}-\mathbf q^{-}=[2,-2]\) and \(\eta=0.1\), the first entry of its user’s vector moves by \(0.1\times0.0067\times2=0.0013\) for \(X\) and by \(0.1\times0.8808\times2=0.1762\) for \(Y\): \(X\)’s step is almost nothing, \(Y\)’s is visible.
E5. (a) Plain-popularity shares: \(80/100=0.80\), \(15/100=0.15\), \(5/100=0.05\); uniform: each \(\tfrac13=0.333\). (b) The \(\text{pop}^{0.75}\) weights \(26.75, 7.62, 3.34\) sum to \(37.71\), so the probabilities are (La La Land), \(7.62/37.71=0.202\) (The Notebook), \(3.34/37.71=0.089\) (Die Hard). (c) La La Land’s probability fell (\(0.80\to0.709\)); The Notebook’s (\(0.15\to0.202\)) and Die Hard’s (\(0.05\to0.089\)) rose. The power \(0.75\) pulls the skew back toward uniform: it softens the skew without removing it.
E6. (a) Each user gets the other \(128-1=127\) positives in the batch as free negatives. (b) \(X\) turns up four times as often as \(Y\), so with no correction it is used as a negative, and pushed down, about four times as often, although it is no worse a film: it is over-penalized for being frequent. (c) The correction takes off \(\ln(0.04/0.01)=\ln 4=1.386\) from \(X\)’s score relative to \(Y\)’s, the handicap that cancels being drawn four times as often.
E7. (a) Exact scan \(\approx Md=4\times10^{6}\times128=5.12\times10^{8}\) multiply-adds, per user, per request. (b) \(\log_2(4\times10^{6})\approx21.9\), so about \(22\) steps. Each step scores about \(24\) linked items: \(22\times24=528\). At the bottom layer the working list of \(60\) candidates scores \(60\times24=1{,}440\) more. Altogether about \(528+1{,}440=1{,}968\), roughly \(2{,}000\) item scores, against \(4\times10^{6}\) for the full scan: a speed-up of about \(4\times10^{6}/1{,}968\approx2{,}000\).
E8. (a) \(X\): dot product \((1)(0.8)+(2)(1.6)=4.0\), distance \(\sqrt{0.2^2+0.4^2}=0.447\). \(Y\): dot product \((1)(3)+(2)(3)=9.0\), distance \(\sqrt{2^2+1^2}=2.236\). The dot product prefers \(Y\); the distance prefers \(X\). (b) The lengths are \(\sqrt5=2.236\), \(0.8\sqrt5=1.789\) and \(3\sqrt2=4.243\), so the unit vectors are \([0.447,0.894]\) for the query and for \(X\) (they point the same way), and \([0.707,0.707]\) for \(Y\). The dot products are now \(1.000\) for \(X\) and \(0.949\) for \(Y\): it prefers \(X\), in agreement with the distance. For unit vectors the dot product is the cosine similarity.
E9. (a) Retrieval scores with \([1,2]\): La La Land \((1)(1.5)+(2)(0.5)=2.5\); Die Hard \((1)(0.5)+(2)(1.8)=4.1\); Matrix \((1)(0)+(2)(2)=4.0\). Interactions with \([1.5,-1]\): La La Land \((1.5)(1.5)+(0.5)(-1)=+1.75\); Die Hard \((0.5)(1.5)+(1.8)(-1)=-1.05\); Matrix \((0)(1.5)+(2)(-1)=-2.0\). The ranker scores are La La Land \(4.25\), Die Hard \(3.05\), Matrix \(2.0\). (b) Final ranking: La La Land \(>\) Die Hard \(>\) Matrix, against retrieval’s order Die Hard, Matrix, La La Land. La La Land rose from rank 3 to 1, Die Hard fell from 1 to 2 and Matrix from 2 to 3. (c) With only Die Hard and Matrix passed on, the final list is Die Hard \((3.05)>\) Matrix \((2.0)\): it loses La La Land, the film the ranker would put first, which never reaches it. Once retrieval drops a film the ranker cannot recover it.
E10. (a) \(10\ \text{ms}\times(2\times10^{6}/300)\approx66{,}667\) ms, about \(67\) seconds, which is \(66{,}667/30\approx2{,}200\) times the budget. (b) At \(20\) ms per \(300\) candidates, a \(10\) ms slice fits \(150\) candidates. (c) A shorter shortlist has fewer slots for good films, so retrieval has to pack the films the user would like into fewer places: it must keep its recall high at a smaller list size, because the ranker can only reorder what retrieval kept.

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Click-Through Rate Prediction & Feature Interactions
E1. A clicked impression keeps the term \(-\ln\hat p\). At \(\hat p=0.25\): \(-\ln 0.25=1.3863\). At \(\hat p=0.75\): \(-\ln 0.75=\mathbf{0.2877}\). A non-clicked impression keeps \(-\ln(1-\hat p)\), so at \(\hat p=0.75\) it costs \(-\ln 0.25=\mathbf{1.3863}\): exactly the cost of a click called \(0.25\). In words: calling a non-click “\(0.75\) likely” is as wrong as calling a click “\(0.25\) likely”, and the clicked impression at \(0.75\) is the one the model got more right, with the smaller cost.
E2. Replace Bob/Matrix’s term \(\ln 0.4\) with \(\ln 0.7\). The four label-selected logs are now \(\ln 0.8\), \(\ln 0.5\), \(\ln 0.7\), \(\ln 0.7\), i.e. \(-0.22314\), \(-0.69315\), \(-0.35667\), \(-0.35667\), summing to \(-1.62964\). LogLoss \(=-\tfrac14(-1.62964)\) \(=\mathbf{0.4074}\) — down from \(0.5473\). In words: the model got more confident on a true click, so the score improved.
E3. New terms: \(\ln 0.8\), \(\ln 0.5\), \(\ln 0.45\), \(\ln 0.7\), i.e. \(-0.22314\), \(-0.69315\), \(-0.79851\), \(-0.35667\), summing to \(-2.07147\), so LogLoss \(=\mathbf{0.5179}\), down from \(0.5473\). For AUC the clicks score \(\{0.8,\,0.45\}\) and the non-clicks \(\{0.5,\,0.3\}\): \(0.8>0.5\) ✓, \(0.8>0.3\) ✓, \(0.45>0.5\) ✗, \(0.45>0.3\) ✓, so AUC stays \(\tfrac34=\mathbf{0.75}\). In words: LogLoss noticed the better probability; AUC did not, because \(0.45\) is still below Ann’s un-clicked \(0.5\) and the order of the pairs has not changed.
E4. The clicks are Ann–Titanic (\(0.6\)) and Bob–Matrix (\(0.3\)); the non-clicks are Ann–Matrix (\(0.6\)) and Cara–Titanic (\(0.2\)). The four pairs: \(0.6\) vs \(0.6\) is a tie, worth \(0.5\); \(0.6\) vs \(0.2\) is correct, \(1\); \(0.3\) vs \(0.6\) is wrong, \(0\); \(0.3\) vs \(0.2\) is correct, \(1\). Total \(2.5\) of \(4\), so AUC \(=\mathbf{0.625}\). In words: of every \(8\) random (click, non-click) pairs this model orders \(5\) correctly, counting each tie as half right.
E5. Layer \(0\): \(\mathbf x_0^{\top}\mathbf w_0=(2)(0.25)+(1)(0.5)=1.0\), so \(\mathbf x_1=1.0\,[2,1]+[2,1]=\mathbf{[4,\,2]}\). Layer \(1\): \(\mathbf x_1^{\top}\mathbf w_1=(4)(1)+(2)(0.5)=5\), so \(\mathbf x_2=5\,[2,1]+[4,2]=\mathbf{[14,\,7]}\), which is \(7\,\mathbf x_0\): a multiple of \(\mathbf x_0\). With \(\mathbf b_1=[1,\,0]\): \(\mathbf x_2=[10,5]+[1,0]+[4,2]=\mathbf{[15,\,7]}\). The entries are \(15/2=7.5\) and \(7/1=7\) times those of \(\mathbf x_0\): two different factors, so it is no longer a multiple of \(\mathbf x_0\). In words: with zero biases the layers only stretch the direction of \(\mathbf x_0\) (xDeepFM’s Theorem 2.1 proves this for every cross layer without biases); a bias is what lets the output turn away from it.
E6. On the log-odds scale the four rates are \(z=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}\): \(0.40\to-0.4055\), \(0.10\to-2.1972\), \(0.08\to-2.4423\), \(0.04\to-3.1781\). The last row gives \(b=\mathbf{-3.1781}\); the second row gives \(w_{\text{rom}}=-2.1972-(-3.1781)=\mathbf{0.9808}\) and the third \(w_{\text{tab}}=-2.4423-(-3.1781)=\mathbf{0.7357}\). The romance-on-tablet row is then predicted \(z=-3.1781+0.9808+0.7357=-1.4615\) (summing the unrounded logits), so \(\sigma(-1.4615)=\mathbf{0.1882}\), less than half of the true \(0.40\). To fit it the cross weight must be \(-0.4055-(-1.4615)\approx\mathbf{1.0561}\) (the rounded figures give \(1.0560\)). In words: the argument of §2 survives the change of scale and the change of table: the additive model still has no room for the interaction, and one cross weight, now on the log-odds scale, makes room.
E7. The pair strength is \(\langle\mathbf e_{\text{romance}},\mathbf e_{\text{desktop}}\rangle=(-0.5)(0.6)+(1)(0.2)=\mathbf{-0.1}\). First order: \(-2.0+0.2+0.1=-1.7\), so \(y_{\text{FM}}=-1.7+(-0.1)=-1.8\) and \(\sigma(-1.8)=\mathbf{0.1419}\). The wide arm has cross weight \(0\) for this never-trained pair: \(-1.7\), and \(\sigma(-1.7)=\mathbf{0.1545}\). In words: the FM arm shades the score a little downward, using vectors learned from other impressions of romance and of desktop; the wide arm cannot say anything about the pair, so it stays at the sum of the single-feature weights.
E8. With the residual, \(\mathbf x_0^{\top}\mathbf w=0.5(3)+0.5(1)=2\): \(\mathbf x_1=2\,\mathbf x_0+\mathbf x_0=[9,3]\); then \(\mathbf x_1^{\top}\mathbf w=6\) and \(\mathbf x_2=6\,\mathbf x_0+\mathbf x_1=[27,9]\). Without it: \(\mathbf x_1=2\,\mathbf x_0=[6,2]\); \(\mathbf x_1^{\top}\mathbf w=4\) and \(\mathbf x_2=4\,\mathbf x_0=[12,4]\). Tripling the input to \([9,3]\) (so \(\mathbf x_0^{\top}\mathbf w=6\)): with the residual \(\mathbf x_1=6[9,3]+[9,3]=[63,21]\), then \(\mathbf x_1^{\top}\mathbf w=42\) and \(\mathbf x_2=42[9,3]+[63,21]=[441,147]\); growth factors \(63/9=\mathbf{7}\) and \(441/27\approx\mathbf{16.33}\). Without it \(\mathbf x_1=6[9,3]=[54,18]\), then \(\mathbf x_1^{\top}\mathbf w=36\) and \(\mathbf x_2=36[9,3]=[324,108]\); factors \(54/6=\mathbf{9=3^2}\) and \(324/12=\mathbf{27=3^3}\). In words: only the version without the residual grows by a clean power of \(3\), \(3^{L+1}\), because its output is made of one degree, \(L+1\). With the residual the factors are not powers of \(3\) because degrees mix: the first entry of \(\mathbf x_1=[9,3]\) is a degree-\(1\) part \(3\) plus a degree-\(2\) part \(6\), and tripling the input gives \(3\cdot3+6\cdot9=63\). So the residual keeps the degrees \(1\) to \(L+1\) all present.
E9. The free weight \(w_{\text{romance},\text{tablet}}\) multiplies the feature \(x_{\text{romance}}x_{\text{tablet}}\), which is \(1\) only when both are active, so only the \(\mathbf{7}\) impressions that show both can move it. FM’s \(\mathbf v_{\text{romance}}\) is moved by every impression in which romance is active together with some other active feature, \(\mathbf{500}\) of them, and \(\mathbf v_{\text{tablet}}\) by \(\mathbf{300}\). The vectors therefore stand on \(500/7\approx\mathbf{71}\) and \(300/7\approx\mathbf{43}\) times more impressions than the free weight. In words: the free weight rests on \(7\) examples while each vector rests on hundreds, so for this rare pair the dot product of the two vectors is the steadier estimate (the authors’ argument of §6, with its count made concrete here).
E10. \(\sigma(0.8)=\mathbf{0.6900}\), \(\sigma(-0.3)=\mathbf{0.4256}\), \(\sigma(-1.5)=\mathbf{0.1824}\): the ranking is film 1, film 2, film 3. Cara clicks only film 1, so the pairs are (film 1, film 2) and (film 1, film 3), both ordered correctly: AUC \(=\mathbf{1}\). LogLoss keeps \(-\ln 0.6900=0.3711\), \(-\ln(1-0.4256)=0.5544\) and \(-\ln(1-0.1824)=0.2014\): sum \(1.1269\), LogLoss \(=\mathbf{0.3756}\). After the retraining \(\sigma(0.2)=\mathbf{0.5498}\), \(\sigma(0.5)=\mathbf{0.6225}\) and film 3 is unchanged at \(0.1824\): the ranking is now film 2, film 1, film 3. Film 1 is scored below the non-clicked film 2 but still above film 3, so one pair of two is right and AUC \(=\mathbf{0.5}\). The terms are \(0.5981\), \(0.9741\) and \(0.2014\), sum \(1.7736\), LogLoss \(=\mathbf{0.5912}\): worse.
In words: the change moved film 1 down and film 2 up, which flipped one pair, so both metrics got worse; AUC counts flipped pairs, LogLoss also prices how far the probabilities moved. The fields to feed: user (Cara), item (each candidate), the item’s genre, device=mobile, daypart=evening, each one-hot and embedded; log AUC (the ordering) and LogLoss (the probabilities) against held-out clicks.
E11. \(W_0\mathbf x_0+\mathbf b_0=[(1)(2)+(0.5)(1)+0.5,\ (0)(2)+(1)(1)+0]=[3,\,1]\), so \(\mathbf x_1=[2,1]\odot[3,1]+[2,1]=\mathbf{[8,\,2]}\). The old DCN layer: the scalar is \(\mathbf x_0^{\top}\mathbf w_0=2.5\), so \(\mathbf x_1=2.5\,[2,1]+[0.5,0]+[2,1]=\mathbf{[7.5,\,3.5]}\). The ratios to \(\mathbf x_0=[2,1]\) are \(4\) and \(2\) for DCNv2 and \(3.75\) and \(3.5\) for DCN: neither output is a multiple of \(\mathbf x_0\), and DCNv2 has moved further (its ratios differ by \(2\), the old layer’s by \(0.25\)). In words: in the old layer only the bias turns the output away from \(\mathbf x_0\), and slightly; in DCNv2 the second row gives that entry its own mix, so the direction is free, as in §7.

title: Appendix F — Solutions to Exercises
text:
Bandits & Online Recommendation
E1. Each pull of the sub-optimal arm adds its gap to the regret, so \(8 \times 0.25 =
\mathbf{2.0}\) expected clicks given up. In words: eight small mistakes of a quarter click each cost two clicks.
E2. \(K=4\), \(\varepsilon=0.2\). The best arm is pulled on exploit (prob \(0.8\)) or when explore lands on it (prob \(0.2/4=0.05\)): \(P(\text{best}) = 1-\varepsilon+\varepsilon/K = 0.8+0.05 =
\mathbf{0.85}\). Each specific other arm is pulled only via explore: \(\varepsilon/K =
\mathbf{0.05}\). (Check: \(0.85 + 3\times0.05 = 1.00\).) In words: the best arm gets \(85\%\) of rounds and each of the other three gets \(5\%\).
E3. With \(t\) as the pulls so far, \(t=3+2=5\) and \(\ln 5 = 1.609\): \(\text{UCB}_M = 0.667 + \sqrt{2(1.609)/3} = 0.667 + 1.036 =
\mathbf{1.703}\); \(\hat\mu_T=1/2=0.5\) and \(\text{UCB}_T = 0.5 + \sqrt{2(1.609)/2} = 0.5 + 1.268 = \mathbf{1.768}\). UCB pulls T again, by \(0.066\) (computed before rounding the scores). In words: T has been tried only twice, so its bonus (\(1.268\)) still outweighs M’s higher mean (by \(0.167\)).
E4. Means: \(\hat\mu_M=22/40=0.55\) and \(\hat\mu_T=4/10=0.40\). With \(\ln 50=3.912\): \(\text{UCB}_M = 0.55 + \sqrt{2(3.912)/40} = 0.55 + 0.442 =
\mathbf{0.992}\); \(\text{UCB}_T = 0.40 + \sqrt{2(3.912)/10} = 0.40 + 0.885 = \mathbf{1.285}\). UCB pulls T, the arm with the lower mean (by \(0.15\)), because its bonus is larger (by \(0.442\)). In words: UCB pulls the highest upper bound, not the highest mean, so a lightly tried arm gets a turn.
E5. Starting from \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) and adding \(s=4\) clicks, \(f=6\) non-clicks: \(\text{Beta}(1+4,\,1+6) = \mathbf{\text{Beta}(5,7)}\), posterior mean \(\dfrac{5}{5+7} =
\dfrac{5}{12} = \mathbf{0.417}\). In words: the best guess for this arm’s click chance is about \(42\%\).
E6. (a) The explore slice is spread over all \(20\) films, so the \(19\) poor films get \(\varepsilon\cdot\frac{K-1}{K}=0.05\times\frac{19}{20}=\mathbf{0.0475}\) of all impressions, \(4.75\%\), forever; one specific poor film gets \(\varepsilon/K=\mathbf{0.0025}\). (b) The bonus is \(\sqrt{2\ln(10^{6})/10^{4}}=\sqrt{0.002763}=0.0526\), so its score is \(0.1+0.0526=\mathbf{0.153}\), far below the best film’s \(0.5\) or more: it is not pulled. (c) A bonus of \(0.4\) needs \(2\ln t/10^{4}=0.16\), so \(\ln t=800\), a \(t\) with more than \(300\) digits: in practice never. In words: ε-greedy keeps paying \(0.25\%\) of the traffic to a film it already knows is poor, while UCB’s bonus for a film with \(10{,}000\) pulls is too small to matter.
E7. (a) \(12.4\%\), \(3.2\%\) and \(0.5\%\) (\(124/1{,}000\), \(323/10{,}000\), \(503/100{,}000\)). (b) The counts rise by \(323-124=199\) and then by \(503-323=180\), so a tenfold step adds about \(190\) and the count at \(T=1{,}000{,}000\) is about \(503+190\approx\mathbf{690}\). (A \(100\)-run simulation, seed 16, to \(T=1{,}000{,}000\) gives \(662\pm12\), within about \(5\%\) of the estimate \(690\); the \(20\)-run counts are noisier.) (c) The gap is halved, so \(1/\Delta^{2}\) quadruples: expect about \(\mathbf{4}\) times as many worse-arm pulls at a given \(T\). (The \(0.6\) and \(0.5\) game, simulated the same way as the problem’s \(20\) runs, seed 16, gives \(253\), \(854\) and \(1{,}673\) at the three horizons, \(2.0\), \(2.6\) and \(3.3\) times the counts above; the factor \(4\) is the large-\(T\) limit and the early rounds fall short of it.) In words: a small gap costs many more pulls to rule out.
E8. (a) \(\text{Beta}(2,2)\): \(P(X>0.55)=1-(3\cdot0.55^{2}-2\cdot0.55^{3})=1-(0.9075-0.3328)=\mathbf{0.425}\). \(\text{Beta}(40,40)\): mean \(0.5\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.25/81}=0.0556\), so \(0.55\) is \(z=0.9\) above the mean and the normal tail is \(\mathbf{0.184}\) (the exact Beta value is \(0.186\)). (b) The \(\text{Beta}(2,2)\) film is drawn above \(0.55\) about \(0.425/0.184\approx\mathbf{2.3}\) times as often (\(0.425/0.186\) with the exact value gives the same \(2.3\)). (c) The posterior is \(\text{Beta}(2+160,\,2+240)=\text{Beta}(162,242)\) with mean \(0.40\); the chance of a draw above \(0.55\) is about \(10^{-9}\), so it is no longer drawn above the known film. In words: the same arm that was explored at about \(43\%\) falls to almost never once data has narrowed it.
E9. ε-greedy: with the plain rule of section 3 the established film is the best, and the new film’s average, \(0\) after its one miss, ranks below the established \(0.6\), so it can only be reached by the explore slice, and then only by the coin landing on it: \(\varepsilon/K=0.1/2=\mathbf{0.05}\).
UCB: with \(t=101\), \(\ln 101=4.615\). The established film (mean \(0.6\), \(n=100\)) scores \(0.6+\sqrt{2(4.615)/100}=0.6+0.304=\mathbf{0.904}\); the new film (mean \(0\), \(n=1\)) scores \(0+\sqrt{2(4.615)/1}=\mathbf{3.038}\). The new film has the higher score, so it is shown: chance \(\mathbf{1}\).
Thompson: after its one non-click the new film’s posterior is \(\text{Beta}(1,2)\), whose chance of exceeding a value \(x\) is \((1-x)^2\); with \(X\sim\text{Beta}(61,41)\) the established film’s draw, \(1-X\sim\text{Beta}(41,61)\) and the average is \(41\cdot42/(102\cdot103)=\mathbf{0.164}\) (a \(200{,}000\)-round simulation, seed 16, gives \(16.4\%\)). Ranking: UCB (\(1\)) \(>\) Thompson (\(0.164\)) \(>\) ε-greedy (\(0.05\)). In words: UCB gives the barely-tried film a pull while its bonus dwarfs the established film’s, Thompson gives it about one chance in six, and ε-greedy a slice of \(5\%\) that does not depend on how little we know.
E10. The viewer’s context for Matrix is \((0,1)\). Four pulls, \(2\) clicks: \(A=I+4\,(0,1)^{\top}(0,1)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix}\), \(\mathbf b=2\,(0,1)^{\top}=(0,2)^{\top}\), \(\hat\theta=A^{-1}\mathbf b=(0,\,0.4)^{\top}\), with \(A^{-1}=\mathrm{diag}(1,\,0.2)\).
For Ann, Titanic \(\mathbf x=(1,0)\): \(0+1.2\sqrt{1}=\mathbf{1.200}\). Matrix \(\mathbf x=(0,0.5)\): \(0.2+1.2\sqrt{0.25\times0.2}=0.2+0.268=\mathbf{0.468}\). She is shown Titanic.
For Cara, Titanic \(\mathbf x=(0.5,0)\): \(0+1.2\sqrt{0.25}=\mathbf{0.600}\). Matrix \(\mathbf x=(0,1)\): \(0.4+1.2\sqrt{0.2}=0.4+0.537=\mathbf{0.937}\). She is shown Matrix.
If Ann clicks Titanic (\(r=1\), \(\mathbf x=(1,0)\)): \(A\to\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix}\), \(\mathbf b\to(1,\,2)^{\top}\). Ann’s Titanic bonus was \(1.2\sqrt{1}=1.200\); with \(A^{-1}=\mathrm{diag}(0.5,\,0.2)\) it is \(1.2\sqrt{0.5}=\mathbf{0.849}\), smaller by \(0.351\), because her click put data in the romance direction. In words: one shared model gives two viewers two different films, because their contexts differ; Titanic wins for Ann as no one has been shown it, and Matrix wins for Cara since its direction is the one with a positive estimate.

title: Acknowledgements
text:
This handbook grew, over many iterations, out of a simple conviction: that the path from first principles to the frontier of recommendation can be walked one hand-checkable step at a time.
My deepest gratitude goes first to my wife, who has stood quietly behind me through all of it — carrying our family so that I could give my full attention to this work. Whatever time and focus the book asked for, she made room for it. It exists because she did.
To my young son: you are my strongest motivation, and my surest one. Your laughter has a way of turning the longest day light, and you have kept me smiling and happy all the way through. This book is for you, too.
To my father and my mother, who gave me everything long before I could give anything back — a home, an education bought with their own sacrifice, and the love of learning that set me on this path together with the discipline to stay on it. Whatever is good in this work began with what they taught me, and I hope it makes them proud.
I am deeply indebted to my teachers and supervisors, Dr. Dang Quang Hieu and Assoc. Prof. Dr. Nguyen Duc Minh of the School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, HUST, who guided me from my engineer’s thesis through my master’s and on to the doctorate. The years of patient mentorship they gave me are the foundation everything in these pages rests upon.
I owe a special debt to Dr. Dinh Anh Tuan — Co-founder and Chief Data Science Officer at Cogitativo (USA) — who has believed in me without fail, taught me, pushed me forward, and waited patiently for me to keep going when the road was slow. His generous, clear-sighted counsel has shaped how I think about research and about bringing artificial intelligence to bear in both academia and industry; this book is the better for it in more places than I can name.
Finally, to my students and colleagues at Minastik — many of them students of mine first, and colleagues since — who have stayed with me through the very first, hardest days of the company. You are dear to me, and you have mattered far beyond our research: in the real industry projects we have built together, with real clients and real data, your hands are in all of it. Thank you for keeping going alongside me through the hard days and the good ones. I am proud of you.
— Duong Tan Nghia
Tran Manh Hoang writes:
For my part, I want to thank the people who made my share of this book possible — and who made the long road toward it worth walking.
To my family, for the evenings and weekends this work quietly borrowed, and for the patient, unconditional love that asks for nothing while giving everything; nothing I do, these pages included, would be possible without you. To the teachers and mentors who shaped how I think — who taught me that a hard idea is not a wall but a door whose handle you simply have not found yet, and that the best thing a teacher can offer is not the answer but the patience to let a student reach it for themselves. And to the colleagues and collaborators whose questions, over many years, sharpened these ideas more than they know; the best of them never let a vague explanation pass, and the book is clearer for it.
A particular word about the friend whose name shares this cover. I have known Nghia for more than fifteen years, and I have had the rare privilege of watching a curious young engineer grow into a careful researcher and a builder who turns ideas into systems that work. Whatever encouragement I offered along the way, what he made of it was entirely his own — the courage to begin again from zero whenever the field demanded it, and the generosity to take his own hard-won understanding and shape it into something a complete beginner can actually use. That generosity is the spirit of this whole book, and helping it into the world has been one of the quiet joys of my career. To have walked a road this long beside a friend this good is a gift I do not take for granted.
And to you, the reader: we wrote this so that the path we once walked alone might be a little less lonely for you. Read it with a pen, check every number, and I hope that somewhere in these pages an idea clicks quietly into place — that small, bright oh, I see that kept both of us going.
— Tran Manh Hoang
A note on method: every worked example in this book was checked numerically before it was written down, and each figure plots the numbers of its own section. Any errors that remain are our own — corrections and suggestions from readers are warmly welcomed.
A note on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools: in preparing this book the authors used AI assistants (large language models) as a drafting, editing, and cross-checking aid — to help structure explanations, refine prose, and stress-test derivations. The authors directed all content and editorial decisions, independently verified every worked example numerically (as above), produced every figure from original source, and are solely responsible for the final text, including any errors. No AI system is an author of this work.

title: About the Authors
text:
Duong Tan Nghia received his Engineer’s degree (2011), his M.Sc. in ultra-wideband systems (2013), and his Ph.D. in recommender systems (2023), all from Hanoi University of Science and Technology (HUST), Vietnam. In 2016, he carried out research on computer vision and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) design and implementation at the Kyushu Institute of Technology, Japan. He is a lecturer in the School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering at HUST and the Chief AI Officer of Minastik Technology JSC. His research interests span recommender systems, computer vision, natural language processing, fingerprint recognition, and ultra-wideband systems.
Tran Manh Hoang received his M.Sc. from the Technical University of Kaiserslautern, Germany (2003), and his Ph.D. in ultra-wideband systems from Hanoi University of Science and Technology (HUST), Vietnam (2016). He is a lecturer in the School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering at HUST, where his current research focuses on computer vision, recommender systems, and natural language processing.
